Acknowledgments

致谢

I t was out of the Seva Foundation that the initial impetus for this book arose. The foundation, which was created as a vehicle for compassionate service, saw as one of its functions that of helping others find ways to serve, ways which would also be beneficial to the servers themselves. A book for a general audience, addressing the issues all of us face when called upon to care for one another, seemed a useful way to share the values that Seva represents.

本书的最初灵感源于塞瓦基金会。该基金会旨在践行慈悲服务，其职能之一是帮助他人找到服务他人的方式，同时也要让服务者自身受益。对于普通读者而言，撰写一本探讨我们在彼此关怀时所面临的各种问题的书籍，似乎是分享塞瓦基金会所代表价值观的有效途径。

As we began work on the book and we sought to identify issues to treat and individuals to talk to, it often seemed as if we were being sent on a treasure hunt, not knowing what wonderful person we would meet or story we would hear next. Many, many people—too many to enumerate—helped speed us along this journey. In the files of Voluntary Action Centers in several cities—agencies which place volunteers in service positions—we were able to locate a number of unsung heroes and heroines; we are indebted to these remarkable clearing houses of good works. From the greater chorus of these voices we have been able to include only the words of a few. With their agreement, we have presented their accounts without attribution in the text. Here, we all felt, was a way to evoke the universality of experience and power of common wisdom which is so central a theme in the book. A number of people even requested anonymity. But there are those, who talked to us at length and whose accounts we have included in some detail, whom we can thank publicly: William Hirscher, Marie Rapello, Mischa Avramoff, Bill Donaldson, Wavy Gravy, Patricia Lowery, Robert Louden, Charles Piera, Larry and Girija Brilliant, Raphael Flores, Peggy Dillon, and Harriet Krasnoff. The inspiration of their example has remained with us long after the time we spent together.

当我们开始着手撰写这本书，努力寻找需要探讨的问题和需要采访的人时，我们常常感觉像是在进行一场寻宝之旅，永远不知道接下来会遇到怎样的奇妙之人，听到怎样的故事。许多人——多到无法一一列举——帮助我们加快了这段旅程。在几个城市的志愿行动中心（这些机构负责安排志愿者从事服务工作）的档案中，我们找到了许多默默奉献的无名英雄；我们对这些卓越的善行汇聚中心深表感激。在众多声音中，我们最终只选取了其中几位的讲述。经他们同意，我们在正文中隐去了他们的姓名。我们都认为，这样做能够更好地展现经验的普遍性和共同智慧的力量，而这正是本书的核心主题。甚至有些人要求匿名。但有一些人，他们与我们进行了深入的交谈，他们的讲述我们也已详细记录在案，在此我们要公开感谢他们：威廉·赫舍尔、玛丽·拉佩洛、米沙·阿夫拉莫夫、比尔·唐纳森、韦维·格雷维、帕特里夏·洛厄里、罗伯特·劳登、查尔斯·皮埃拉、拉里和吉里娅·布里兰特、拉斐尔·弗洛雷斯、佩吉·狄龙以及哈丽特·克拉斯诺夫。他们的榜样激励着我们，即使在我们相聚的时光结束后，这份激励依然长久地伴随着我们。

Much shorter excerpts have come from conferences and broadcasts in which participants did not identify themselves by name but understood they were collaborators in our work and expressed willingness to have their remarks included. We thank them, and are especially grateful to Omega Institute in Rhinebeck, New York, and WBAI-FM in New York City, for hosting a number of particularly valuable meetings and conversations.

还有一些篇幅较短的摘录来自会议和广播节目，与会者虽然没有透露姓名，但他们都明白自己是我们工作的合作者，并表示愿意将他们的发言收录其中。我们感谢他们，尤其感谢位于纽约州莱茵贝克的欧米茄研究所和纽约市的WBAI-FM电台，感谢他们为我们举办了多次极具价值的会议和对话。

Lillian North assisted us by transcribing interviews and conferences. Enid Gorman was a steady source of perspective and good judgment. And to Toinette Lippe, our friend and editor, our deepest thanks for her faith in this project from the outset, her patience and emotional support, and her own very special understanding of the issues we have treated. To N. K. B., thank you.

莉莲·诺斯协助我们转录了访谈和会议记录。伊妮德·戈尔曼始终为我们提供了独到的见解和明智的判断。我们还要衷心感谢我们的朋友兼编辑托伊内特·利佩，感谢她从一开始就对这个项目的信任，感谢她的耐心和情感支持，以及她对我们所探讨议题的深刻理解。感谢N. K. B.。

Preface

前言

T his book began, in a sense, with people asking, “How can I help?” Sometimes the question was raised in specific circumstances: a woman concerned about her best friend’s depression, a nurse wondering what she might offer patients in addition to medical care, someone with time on his hands, eager to be more useful. On other occasions broader political issues were the catalyst. Often the inquiry grew out of very personal introspection into what constitutes a good and happy life. It was asked of us individually, regarding projects in which we ourselves were directly involved. However, more often than not, we heard it as “something in the air,” an open-ended question about people’s relationship to one another and to human suffering in general.

从某种意义上说，这本书的缘起是人们的提问：“我能做些什么？”有时，这个问题是在具体情境中提出的：一位女士担心她最好的朋友患有抑郁症；一位护士思考除了医疗护理之外，她还能为病人提供什么；一位闲暇时间充裕、渴望发挥更大作用的人。有时，更广泛的政治议题才是催化剂。很多时候，这种询问源于对美好幸福生活本质的深刻反思。我们每个人都曾被问及这个问题，尤其是在我们直接参与的项目中。然而，更多时候，我们听到的是一种“弥漫在空气中的氛围”，一个关于人与人之间关系以及人与人类苦难之间关系的开放式问题。

“How can I help?” is a timeless inquiry of the heart. Yet we often heard it asked in the context of our own culture and moment. As commitment to service has ebbed and flowed, many of us have spent a great deal of time considering the deeper values of our helping work. What exactly is the nature of conscious service? What are the challenges posed by present conditions? Our book grows out of this collective reflection.

“我能帮上什么忙？”这是一个永恒的、发自内心的疑问。然而，我们常常在特定的文化和时代背景下听到这个问题。随着服务精神的起伏变化，我们中的许多人花费了大量时间思考助人工作的深层价值。有意识的服务究竟是什么？当下的境况又带来了哪些挑战？本书正是源于这种集体思考。

As if to underscore the degree of shared concern, the book evolved into a wider collaboration than we had initially intended. “How can I help?” led us to investigate “How are we helping?” We met with many people active in the mainstream and tributaries of service and social action in America. What were the important issues they were encountering?

仿佛为了强调我们共同关注的程度，这本书的创作最终演变成一场比我们最初设想的更为广泛的合作。“我能做些什么？”这个问题促使我们去探究“我们正在如何提供帮助？”我们与许多活跃于美国主流及周边服务和社会行动领域的人士进行了交流。他们面临的重要问题是什么？

At a national conference of such organizations, one response came from an officer of Volunteer, the nation’s largest umbrella organization for voluntary action centers and groups. “Recruitment, administration, publicity, funding, lobbying … we know something about all these. But what really helps? Deep down, whatever we’re doing, what really helps?” His words resonated strongly with all assembled, and continue to do so in this book.

在一次全国性组织大会上，来自全国最大的志愿行动中心和团体伞式组织“志愿者”（Volunteer）的一位官员发表了讲话：“招募、行政、宣传、筹款、游说……我们对这些都略知一二。但真正有效的是什么？归根结底，无论我们做什么，真正有帮助的是什么？”他的话语引起了所有与会者的强烈共鸣，并且在本书中也继续引起共鸣。

Our journey took us to workplaces, as well. We spent many hours listening to stories from those who face suffering and serve others, day in and night out. We discovered an extraordinarily deep pool of wisdom and compassion in so many different people: a doctor in an intensive care unit, an organizer of a church food drive for the homeless, a Rotary Club volunteer, a drug counselor, a peace activist, a stroke patient, a group of senior citizens in a community center basement.…

我们的旅程也带我们走进了各个工作场所。我们花了许多时间聆听那些日夜面对苦难、服务他人的人们的故事。我们发现，在许多不同的人身上，都蕴藏着无比深厚的智慧和慈悲：重症监护室的医生、为无家可归者组织教会食物募捐活动的志愿者、扶轮社的志愿者、戒毒辅导员、和平活动家、中风患者、社区中心地下室里的一群老年人……

We found many of their accounts so moving that we resolved to include them as central elements of the book. What better way to remind ourselves of how much we all have to offer one another? Here, in effect, was one part of our answer to the question posed by the book’s title. Look to one another. Look to what we already know or have learned.

我们发现他们的许多叙述都非常感人，因此决定将它们作为本书的核心内容。还有什么比这更好的方式来提醒我们，我们每个人都能为彼此带来多少呢？实际上，这正是我们对本书标题所提出的问题的一种回答：彼此扶持，关注我们已知的或已学到的知识。

To these stories we have added our own reflections. Sometimes our impulse was simply to appreciate and ponder essential truths revealed by these tales; these were living parables. On other occasions, the testimonies helped us identify and examine specific challenges all of us face, caring for one another. Such movement from story to reflection may mirror the way we all live and work—now immersed in action, now stepping back to make sense of it all. Counterpoint, then, is the rhythm of this book, conversation its tone—a dialogue in which we now invite our readers to join.

在这些故事中，我们融入了自己的思考。有时，我们只是想欣赏和思考这些故事所揭示的本质真理；它们本身就是鲜活的寓言。有时，这些故事帮助我们识别和审视我们每个人在彼此关爱中面临的具体挑战。这种从故事到反思的转换，或许反映了我们生活和工作的方式——时而全身心投入，时而退后一步，思考这一切的意义。因此，本书的节奏是对比，其基调是对话——我们诚邀读者加入这场对话。

Authors usually come to such an inquiry with a bias. We seem to have had several. One of us was trained in psychology, the other in philosophy. One has had experience as a therapist, the other in politics. Both of us have been deeply influenced by spiritual practice and the teachings of the world’s religions, all of which emphasize service. We honor and draw from these traditions, although what we have to share should be accessible to those who follow none.

作者在进行此类探究时通常带有某种倾向。我们似乎就带有好几种倾向。我们两人中，一人受过心理学训练，另一人受过哲学训练。一人有过心理咨询师的经历，另一人则从事政治工作。我们都深受灵修实践和世界各大宗教教义的影响，而这些宗教都强调服务。我们尊重并借鉴这些传统，但我们所分享的内容也应该能够被那些不信奉任何宗教的人所理解。

Many perspectives as well as many voices, then, sound through these pages. Perhaps this is appropriate, for it is our hope that this book might be useful to everyone. How much time, after all, does each and every one of us spend helping and being helped? The forms may vary: the helping professions, self-help groups, service as religious practice, movements for social change, voluntary service. A 1983 Gallup poll found that 55 percent of all Americans spend at least a few hours volunteering to assist neighbors and communities. But how could any poll measure common courtesies, thoughtful gestures, the simplest moments of human affirmation?

因此，本书汇集了众多观点和声音。或许这恰如其分，因为我们希望这本书能对每个人都有所帮助。毕竟，我们每个人究竟有多少时间用于帮助他人和接受帮助呢？帮助的形式多种多样：助人行业、自助团体、宗教服务、社会变革运动、志愿服务等等。1983 年盖洛普民意调查发现，55% 的美国人至少会抽出几个小时的时间来做志愿者，帮助邻居和社区。但是，任何民意调查又如何能衡量那些日常的礼貌、体贴的举动以及人与人之间最简单的肯定呢？

We have resolved to consider what is common to all these forms. Seeking to care for others, each of us inevitably faces certain fundamental challenges. These are what draw us to explore the very heart of helping. We offer this book, then, with great respect for the work each reader is already embarked upon.

我们决心探究所有这些形式的共通之处。在关爱他人的过程中，我们每个人都不可避免地会面临一些根本性的挑战。正是这些挑战促使我们去探索助人行为的本质。因此，我们怀着对每位读者已投入的工作的崇敬之情，奉上本书。

Natural Compassion
自然同情心

I was in about forty feet of water, alone. I knew I should not have gone alone, but I was very competent and just took a chance. There was not much current, and the water was so warm and clear and enticing. But when I got a cramp, I realized at once how foolish I was. I was not very alarmed, but was completely doubled up with stomach cramp. I tried to remove my weight belt, but I was so doubled up I could not get to the catch. I was sinking and began to feel more frightened, unable to move. I could see my watch and knew that there was only a little more time on the tank before I would be finished with breathing! I tried to massage my abdomen. I wasn’t wearing a wet suit, but couldn’t straighten out and couldn’t get to the cramped muscles with my hands .

我当时独自一人在大约四十英尺深的水里。我知道自己不该独自前往，但我自认为经验丰富，所以就冒险一试。水流很缓，水温温暖清澈，令人心旷神怡。然而，当我突然抽筋时，我立刻意识到自己有多愚蠢。我当时并没有很惊慌，只是因为胃痉挛而蜷缩成一团。我试图解开配重带，但由于身体蜷缩得太厉害，根本够不到扣环。我开始下沉，动弹不得，恐惧感也与日俱增。我看了看手表，知道氧气瓶里的氧气只剩下一点点了，我很快就要耗尽了！我试图按摩腹部。我没有穿潜水服，但身体无法直起，双手也够不到痉挛的肌肉。

I thought, “I can’t go like this! I have things to do!” I just couldn’t die anonymously this way, with no one to even know what happened to me. I called out in my mind, “Somebody, something, help me!”

我心想：“我不能就这样死去！我还有事要做！”我不能就这样默默无闻地死去，甚至没有人知道我发生了什么事。我在心里呼喊：“有人吗？有什么东西吗？救救我！”

I was not prepared for what happened. Suddenly I felt a prodding from behind me under the armpit. I thought, “Oh no, sharks!” I felt real terror and despair. But my arm was being lifted forcibly. Around into my field of vision came an eye—the most marvelous eye I could ever imagine. I swear it was smiling. It was the eye of a big dolphin. Looking into that eye, I knew I was safe .

我完全没有预料到接下来会发生什么。突然，我感觉腋下被人从后面顶了一下。我心想：“糟了，鲨鱼！”我感到一阵恐惧和绝望。但我的胳膊却被人用力抬起来。一只眼睛出现在我的视野里——那是我见过的最奇妙的眼睛。我发誓它在微笑。那是一只巨大的海豚的眼睛。看着那只眼睛，我知道自己安全了。

It moved farther forward, nudging under, and hooked its dorsal fin under my armpit with my arm over its back. I relaxed, hugging it, flooded with relief. I felt that the animal was conveying security to me, that it was healing me as well as lifting me toward the surface. My stomach cramp went away as we ascended, and I relaxed with security, but I felt very strongly that it healed me too .

它继续向前游去，轻轻地钻入水中，用背鳍勾住我的腋下，我的手臂搭在它的背上。我放松下来，紧紧地抱着它，如释重负。我感觉这只动物在给我带来安全感，它不仅在治愈我，也在把我托向水面。随着我们上升，我的胃痉挛消失了，我感到无比安心，但我强烈地感觉到，它也治愈了我。

At the surface, it drew me all the way in to shore. It took me into water so shallow that I began to be concerned for it, that it would be beached, and I pushed it back a little deeper, where it waited, watching me, I guess to see if I was all right .

在水面上，它一路把我拉到岸边。它把我带到水很浅的地方，我开始担心它会搁浅，于是我把它推回更深的地方，它在那里等着，看着我，我想是在看看我是否安好。

It felt like another lifetime. When I took off the weight belt and oxygen, I just took everything off and went naked back into the ocean to the dolphin. I felt so light and free and alive, and just wanted to play in the sun and the water, in all that freedom. The dolphin took me back out and played around in the water with me. I noticed that there were a lot of dolphins there, farther out .

感觉就像过了一个世纪。当我解开配重带和氧气瓶后，我脱光了所有东西，赤身裸体地回到海里，回到海豚身边。我感到无比轻松、自由和充满活力，只想在阳光和海水中尽情玩耍，享受这份自由。海豚带着我回到海里，和我一起在水中嬉戏。我注意到更远的地方还有很多海豚。

After a while it brought me back to shore. I was very tired then, almost collapsing, and he made sure I was safe in the shallowest water. Then he turned sideways with one eye looking into mine. We stayed that way for what seemed like a very long time, timeless I guess, in a trance almost, with personal thoughts of the past going through my mind .

过了一会儿，他把我送回了岸边。那时我筋疲力尽，几乎要晕倒了，他确保我安全地待在最浅的水里。然后他侧过身，一只眼睛直视着我。我们保持着这个姿势，仿佛过了很久很久，时间仿佛静止了，我几乎进入了一种恍惚的状态，脑海中浮现出许多往事。

Then he made just one sound and went out to join the others, and all of them left .

然后他只发出了一声声音，就出去和其他人会合了，他们都离开了。

~

At times, helping happens simply in the way of things. It’s not something we really think about, merely the instinctive response of an open heart. Caring is a reflex. Someone slips, your arm goes out. A car is in a ditch, you join the others and push. A colleague at work has the blues, you let her know you care. It all seems natural and appropriate. You live, you help.

有时候，助人就发生在日常生活中。我们并非刻意去想，而只是发自内心的本能反应。关心他人是一种本能。有人滑倒，你会伸出援手；一辆车掉进沟里，你会加入其他人的行列帮忙推车；同事心情不好，你会让她知道你很关心她。这一切都显得自然而然，合情合理。人活着，就应该帮助别人。

When we join together in this spirit, action comes more effortlessly, and everybody ends up nourished. Girding against the flood … setting up a community meeting … preparing a funeral … people seem to know their part. We sense what’s called for, or if we don’t, and feel momentarily awkward, someone comes quickly with an idea, and it’s just right, and we’re grateful. We baby-sit the kids while their parents move possessions to homes farther from the rising river … we bring a comfortable chair for an older person who might attend the meeting … we call the rabbi with a favorite psalm of the one who has just died. Needs are anticipated, and glances of appreciation among us are enough to confirm that it’s all going well.

当我们本着这种精神团结起来时，行动就变得更加轻松，每个人都能从中受益。抵御洪水……组织社区会议……筹备葬礼……人们似乎都清楚自己的职责。我们能感受到需要做什么，即便我们一时不知所措，感到有些尴尬，也会有人迅速提出一个恰到好处的建议，我们对此感激不尽。我们帮忙照看孩子，让他们的父母把东西搬到远离上涨河水的家中……我们为可能参加会议的老人准备了一把舒适的椅子……我们打电话给拉比，请他朗诵一位刚刚去世的人生前最喜欢的诗篇。需求被提前考虑到，我们彼此间流露出的感激之情足以证明一切都在顺利进行。

We take pleasure not only in what we did but in the way we did it. On the one hand, the effort was so natural it might seem pointless or self-conscious to make something of it. It was what it was. Yet if we stop to consider why it all felt so good, we sense that some deeper process was at work. Expressing our innate generosity, we experienced our “kin”-ship, our “kind”-ness. It was “Us.” In service, we taste unity.

我们不仅为所做的事情感到愉悦，也为做事情的方式感到愉悦。一方面，这种努力如此自然，以至于刻意去做似乎毫无意义，甚至显得有些矫揉造作。事情就是这样。然而，如果我们停下来思考这一切为何如此美好，就会感受到某种更深层次的因素在起作用。当我们表达与生俱来的慷慨时，我们体验到了彼此间的“亲情”，感受到了彼此间的“善意”。这就是“我们”。在服务中，我们体会到了团结的真谛。

~

The state had just released many people from its mental institutions with very little preparation. Our halfway house was about to be flooded with applicants. We had only so much room. Who to shelter? Who to clothe? Who to feed? Deep questions to be faced very suddenly .

州政府几乎没有任何准备就释放了一大批精神病院的病人。我们的中途之家即将迎来大量申请者。我们的床位有限。该安置谁？该给谁提供衣物？该给谁提供食物？这些沉重的问题我们必须突然面对。

An hour before we opened, we agreed to sit together in silence. Meditation, prayer, just plain calming down … everyone went for their ammo. Then we opened the doors, somehow trusting .

开业前一小时，我们约定一起静坐。冥想、祈祷，或者只是单纯地让自己平静下来……每个人都拿出了各自的“武器”。然后，我们打开了大门，心中充满了信任。

Everything we did, we agreed to do with love. Those people we accepted, we accepted with love. Those we turned away or helped find alternatives … love. Everyone seemed to understand. The differences between us all, staff and applicants alike, seemed less solid. The whole idea that it all had to do with mental illness even seemed a little artificial. Nobody was really thinking that much, or had time to, or needed to, or something. So much of it was just coming from the heart. So many people, with so many problems. But it went so smoothly. How?

我们所做的一切，都是出于爱。我们接纳的人，也是出于爱。我们拒绝的人，或是帮助我们寻找其他出路的人……同样是出于爱。每个人似乎都理解了。我们彼此之间的差异，无论是员工还是申请者，似乎都变得不那么明显了。甚至连“这一切都与精神疾病有关”这种说法都显得有些牵强。其实，没有人真的想得那么多，或者有时间想，或者需要想，或者别的什么原因。很多事情都源于内心。那么多人，那么多问题。但一切却进行得如此顺利。这是怎么做到的？

The day after we were done, we sat down to discuss what had happened—your classic evaluation procedure. “Can we come to order?” Which met with some laughter. “So …?” someone said. Then this one person stood up and said, “These past three days … that was about who we all really are. The way we were … that was the truth about us, deep down.”

第二天，我们坐下来讨论发生的事情——典型的评估流程。“我们能开始了吗？” 这引来一阵笑声。“所以……？” 有人问道。然后，一个人站起来说：“过去三天……让我们看到了我们真正的自己。我们当时的样子……那才是我们内心深处的真相。”

There was a moment’s silence. Someone said, “Right.” And that was the meeting. We waited a little longer; you’re not used to things becoming clear like that. But after a minute or two, people gradually got up and went back to work .

一阵沉默。有人说了声“好的”。会议就此结束。我们又等了一会儿；事情不常这么快就明朗起来。但过了一两分钟，人们陆续起身，继续工作。

~

Caring for one another, we sometimes glimpse an essential quality of our being. We may be sitting alone, lost in self-doubt or self-pity, when the phone rings with a call from a friend who’s really depressed. Instinctively, we come out of ourselves, just to be there with her and say a few reassuring words. When we’re done, and a little comfort’s been shared, we put down the phone and feel a little more at home with ourselves. We’re reminded of who we really are and what we have to offer one another.

彼此关爱，有时能让我们瞥见自身存在的本质。或许我们独自一人，沉浸在自我怀疑或自怜之中，这时电话铃声响起，是位情绪低落的朋友打来的。出于本能，我们走出自己的世界，陪伴在她身边，说几句安慰的话。当一切结束，彼此给予了一些慰藉之后，我们放下电话，感到内心也平静下来。我们重新认识到自己是谁，以及我们能为彼此带来什么。

When the experience of helping seems so natural, it’s not surprising we find ourselves wishing or wondering if things could be like that more or even most of the time.

当助人为乐的体验如此自然时，我们自然会希望或想知道，事情是否可以更多地、甚至大部分时间都如此，这也就不足为奇了。

~

I went as a representative of the hippie community of San Francisco to meet the Hopi Indian elders to arrange a Hopi-Hippie Be-In in Grand Canyon. We wanted to honor their tradition and affirm our common respect for the land. As you can guess, this was during the sixties .

我当时作为旧金山嬉皮士社群的代表，去拜访霍皮族印第安长老，商讨在大峡谷举办一场霍皮嬉皮士聚会。我们希望尊重他们的传统，并表达我们对这片土地共同的敬意。正如你所料，那是在六十年代。

Four elders sat at a kitchen table in an adobe building on four chairs. There were no more chairs when I got there. So I sat on the floor kneeling opposite them, so I could see over the table, but under it as well .

四位长者坐在土坯房的厨房餐桌旁，桌边只有四把椅子。我到的时候，椅子已经没了。于是我跪在地上，对面坐着，这样我既能看到桌子对面，也能看到桌子底下。

The youngest was sixty-five, the eldest one hundred and ten. I could see their hands on their knees under the table. They looked like roots in the earth. There was something so absolutely connected about the whole quality of their presence .

最年轻的六十五岁，最年长的一百一十岁。我能看到他们双手放在桌子底下的膝盖上，像扎根于大地的根须。他们整个人散发出的气息，是如此浑然一体。

We discussed what it might mean to bring together these different groups and generations of Americans. They told me about difficulties they had been having with white people. One of their braves had recently become involved in an auto accident with a truck from the Bureau of Indian Affairs. The BIA truck had been at fault. But the next day, the BIA found a liquor bottle nearby and claimed the brave had been drinking .

我们讨论了将这些不同群体和世代的美国人聚集在一起的意义。他们告诉我他们与白人之间遇到的困难。他们的一位勇士最近与一辆印第安事务局的卡车发生了车祸。事故责任在于印第安事务局的卡车。但第二天，印第安事务局在附近发现了一个酒瓶，并声称这位勇士喝了酒。

“We called the young man in and we asked him if he had been drinking,” one of them told me. He said, “No.” And then this elder looked at me very directly and very simply and said, “And he speaks truth.”

“我们把那个年轻人叫进来，问他有没有喝酒，”其中一人告诉我。他说：“没有。”然后这位长者直视着我，语气非常平静地说：“他说的是实话。”

A chill went through me at that moment. It wasn’t just that I believed him or that any doubt or suspicion I might have had was immediately silenced. I experienced a kind of primordial memory of a time when you just spoke truth, a time when relationships were built on trust. That’s the way it was done, because that’s just how people were .

那一刻，我感到一阵寒意袭来。不仅仅是因为我相信了他，也不仅仅是因为我心中任何的疑虑或猜忌瞬间烟消云散。我仿佛回到了远古时代，那时人们坦诚相待，彼此信任。那时人们就是这样相处的，因为那时的人们就是这样。

~

Somewhere deep within many of us is a vision of how helping would flow from trust in ourselves and in others. Or perhaps we might recall images of life in a town in which doors didn’t have to be locked, responsibilities were more commonly shared, and going out of your way was hardly out of the ordinary. Or maybe we find ourselves yearning for a future society where the care of others wouldn’t have to be mandated. Service wouldn’t be a duty, it would be a habit—the way of natural compassion.

在我们许多人的内心深处，都憧憬着一种互助的景象：信任自己和他人，便会自然而然地流露出来。或许我们会想起某个小镇的景象：门不必锁，责任更常被分担，乐于助人也并非什么稀奇事。又或许，我们渴望着一个未来的社会，在那里，关爱他人无需强制。服务他人不再是义务，而是一种习惯——一种自然而然流露的慈悲之心。

And yet …

然而……

Although at times helping may happen simply in the way of things, all too often helping isn’t happening at all. Even if it is, it can be anything but natural: self-conscious, half-hearted, begrudging. How much are we willing to give, and what are we holding on to? How do we really feel about the place of helping in our lives? We needn’t go deep beneath the surface before we encounter our ambivalence. We note the interplay of generosity and resistance, self-sacrifice and self-protectiveness.

虽然有时助人为乐可能只是顺理成章的事，但更多时候，助人根本不会发生。即便发生了，也可能很不自然：拘谨、敷衍、勉强。我们愿意付出多少？我们又在执着于什么？我们究竟如何看待助人在我们生活中的地位？我们无需深入探究，就能感受到内心的矛盾。我们会注意到慷慨与抗拒、自我牺牲与自我保护之间的相互作用。

What do we hear as we imagine the mind wrestling with the impulses of the heart?

当我们想象大脑与心脏的冲动进行斗争时，我们听到了什么？

~

Sometimes I help, and sometimes I don’t .

有时我会帮忙，有时我不会。

I hold the door open for one behind me, or I rush through preoccupied in thought. I vote, but not always. When solicitations come through the mail, some catch my eye or heart and I send at least something. Others I basket as junk mail. A friend is having a hard time. I think I should phone to see how she is, but I just don’t feel like doing it tonight .

我会为身后的人开门，或者心不在焉地匆匆穿过。我会投票，但并非每次都去。当收到推销邮件时，有些会吸引我的目光或触动我的心弦，我会至少寄点东西回去。其他的则会被我直接扔进垃圾桶，当作垃圾邮件。一位朋友最近过得不太好。我想我应该打电话问候一下，但我今晚实在提不起劲。

I’d do anything to help the family. But how much is enough? When to stretch a little further? Whose needs come first?

我愿意尽一切努力帮助这个家庭。但是，多少才算足够？什么时候应该再多帮一点？谁的需求应该优先考虑？

Those close to me get an immediate hearing. The suffering of people more remote gets sporadic attention. I’m only vaguely aware of it. It’s out there somewhere .

亲近之人的遭遇总能立刻得到关注，而那些与我关系疏远之人的苦难则只能偶尔得到一些关注。我对他们的苦难只有模糊的感知，它们确实存在于某个地方。

Whom should I help anyway? Senior citizens, battered children, human-rights victims, whales? Well, if we don’t defuse the nuclear threat, there’ll be no tomorrow. But if we don’t support education and the arts, what kind of tomorrow will it be?

我到底应该帮助谁？老人、受虐儿童、人权受害者、鲸鱼？如果我们不消除核威胁，就没有明天。但如果我们不支持教育和艺术，明天又会是什么样的呢？

If I stop to think about it, I help out for all kinds of reasons. Maybe it’s because I should; it’s a matter of responsibility . But there’s usually a maze of other motives: a need for self-esteem, approval, status, power; the desire to feel useful, find intimacy, pay back some debt .

仔细想想，我帮忙的理由五花八门。也许是因为我应该这么做，这是责任所在。但通常还隐藏着其他种种动机：对自尊、认可、地位和权力的渴望；想要觉得自己有用、寻求亲密关系、偿还债务的愿望。

Sometimes I’ll help through organizations. But the purpose of helping and the people who really need it often seem to fall through the cracks. Maybe I’d rather do it one-to-one, keep my options open, help out here and there .

有时候我会通过一些机构提供帮助。但帮助的目的和真正需要帮助的人往往被忽略了。也许我更愿意一对一地提供帮助，保持选择的灵活性，随时随地伸出援手。

I expect my government to relieve suffering. Sometimes it does. But it also pays farmers not to produce wheat while somewhere, every forty-five seconds, a small child starves to death. And a public official, no better or worse a person than I, finds reason to justify this policy—but would probably do everything he could, faced with one starving child .

我期望政府能够减轻民众的苦难。有时，政府的确做到了。但与此同时，政府却补贴农民不种小麦，而与此同时，每隔45秒，就有一个幼童在某个地方饿死。一位公职人员，即便他的人品并不比我好，也能找到理由为这项政策辩护——但如果他面对的是一个挨饿的孩子，他或许会竭尽全力去救人。

There are times when service is effortless. Other days, burnout. With one person, I’m totally open and present. With the next, I might as well be on Mars. Sometimes the chance to care for another human being feels like such grace. But later on, I’ll hear myself thinking, “Hey, what about me?”

有时候，服务他人毫不费力；有时候，却会精疲力竭。面对一个人，我能全心全意、全神贯注；而面对另一个人，我却仿佛置身火星。有时，能够照顾他人，感觉就像是一种恩赐。但事后，我总会听到自己问：“嘿，那我呢？”

Over Gandhi’s tomb are inscribed words that say: Think of the poorest person you have ever seen and ask if your next act will be of any use to him. That’ll flash through my mind as I prepare to throw a Frisbee. And when I spend fifteen bucks dining out and going to a movie to ward off boredom, I might recall that a fifteen-dollar operation could restore someone’s sight in a third-world country. I’m moved by the power of Gandhi’s invitation, “Live simply that others might simply live.” But I’m not at all clear about how to heed that, day in and day out, here in the affluent West. Sometimes I feel a little guilty .

甘地的陵墓上镌刻着这样一句话：想想你见过的最贫穷的人，问问自己，你接下来的举动对他是否有用。每当我准备扔飞盘时，这句话都会在我脑海中闪现。当我花十五美元外出吃饭看电影打发时间时，我或许会想起，在第三世界国家，十五美元的手术就能让一个人重见光明。甘地那句“生活简朴，他人才能生活简朴”的教诲深深打动了我。然而，在富裕的西方世界，我却不知该如何日复一日地践行这句话。有时，我甚至感到有些愧疚。

I’m fortunate, for the moment, to have good health and loving friends, to be housed and fed, with work to do and some time to play. When I myself need help, there’s usually someone to call. I’m able to spend some time away from places where suffering is really visible and just can’t be screened out .

目前，我很幸运，身体健康，朋友亲切，有房有饭吃，有工作可做，也有时间玩乐。当我需要帮助时，通常都能找到人帮忙。我还能暂时远离那些苦难触目惊心、无法视而不见的地方。

Yet there are few days when I’m not feeling human pain, my own or another’s. If it’s not there in front of me, I see a steady stream of images of misery on the evening news of a suffering planet: homeless one huddled by a doorway or tree; old one looking vacant in a nursing home; slain revolutionary or national guardsman, both teenagers; drunk driver just realizing he’s killed his whole family; starving child’s bloated belly and haunted eyes; victims of natural disasters; helpless leaders, helpless helpers .

然而，几乎每天我都能感受到人类的痛苦，无论是自己的还是他人的。即便痛苦并非直接呈现在我眼前，我也会在晚间新闻中看到一连串令人痛心的画面：无家可归的人蜷缩在门口或树旁；老人在养老院里神情呆滞；被杀害的革命者或国民警卫队员，他们都是十几岁的少年；酒驾司机刚刚意识到自己撞死了全家；饥饿的孩子腹部肿胀，眼神空洞；自然灾害的受害者；无助的领导者，无力的援助者。

Some images I ponder; what’s that one saying? Others make me uneasy; I tune them out. Some make me angry; I want to get up and do something. Others make me sigh; horror and compassion. And finally I might have to turn away, close off, and escape into some philosophical sanctuary. It’s all just too much .

有些画面我会反复琢磨；那幅画到底在说什么？有些画面让我不安；我选择视而不见。有些画面让我愤怒；我想起身做点什么。有些画面让我叹息；既有恐惧，也有怜悯。最后，我或许不得不转身离开，封闭自己，逃进某个哲学的避难所。这一切都太沉重了。

How can I keep my heart open and not go under? I’ve got my own life to live, after all. Still, I’d like to do more for others. What do I have to offer, and what would help most? Complicated business, all this .

我该如何保持一颗开放的心，不至于被它吞噬？毕竟，我还有自己的生活要过。但我仍然想为他人做更多的事情。我能提供什么？什么才能最有帮助？这一切真是复杂。

Look, you do the best you can.…

你看，你已经尽力了……

~

So we face an interesting situation. Our impulses to care for one another often seem instinctive. The more we’re able to act on them freely, the more opportunity we have to feel whole and be helpful. But there are clearly many ways in which we hesitate to reach out or we get confused when we try. The reasons for this don’t appear to be simple at all. Perhaps it’s due to conditioning or custom.

我们面临着一个有趣的局面。我们彼此关怀的冲动往往似乎是本能的。我们越能自由地付诸行动，就越有机会感到身心完整，也越能帮助他人。但显然，我们常常因为各种原因而犹豫不决，不敢伸出援手，或者在尝试时感到困惑。造成这种情况的原因似乎并不简单。或许是受制于某种习惯或习俗。

When people lost sight of the way to live

当人们迷失了生活的真谛

Came codes of love and honesty ,

随之而来的是爱与诚实的准则，

Learning came, charity came ,

学习来了，慈善来了，

Hypocrisy took charge;

虚伪占据了主导地位；

When differences weakened family ties

当分歧削弱了家庭纽带时

Came benevolent fathers and dutiful sons;

仁慈的父亲和孝顺的儿子来了；

Came ministers commended as loyal .

部长们因忠诚而受到称赞。

In The Way of Life , written twenty-five hundred years ago, Lao Tsu evokes circumstances that affect us today. We can see them at work even in a very simple request for help. Up comes a stranger and asks, “Can you spare a quarter?” Almost immediately, certain biases rise to the surface and make us hesitate.

在两千五百年前写成的《生活之道》中，老子描绘的种种境况，至今仍影响着我们。即使是最简单的求助，也能体现出这些境况的影响。比如，一个陌生人走过来问：“你能借我两毛五吗？”几乎就在那一刻，某些偏见浮现出来，让我们犹豫不决。

Perhaps we hold back because works of compassion have become formalized. We’ve already put money in the collection plate. We gave at the office. Those funds should have been put to work for this guy already, or they’re waiting for him, in one form or another, at the local shelter or soup kitchen. So we’re about to say no to his request, but we pause a second longer; we can’t quite let it go at that, any more than we can comfortably leave it all to Uncle Sam.

或许我们之所以犹豫，是因为行善已经变得程式化了。我们已经把钱放进奉献箱了。我们在办公室捐过款了。这些钱本该已经用在这个人身上了，或者以某种形式，在当地的收容所或救济食堂等着他。所以我们正要拒绝他的请求，却又犹豫了一秒；我们无法就此罢休，就像我们无法心安理得地把一切都交给政府一样。

Perhaps we’ve been taught “family first.” Beyond a certain perimeter, our standards change. This fellow asking for money—he’s not really “Us.” We might feel tentative or hesitant because we haven’t had a strong experience of family. As a result of “weakened ties,” whether in marriages, between generations, or among distant relatives, our habits of giving have become less than spontaneous. We’re not quite sure of what we owe one another even in our immediate circle.

或许我们从小就被教导“家庭至上”。但一旦超出某个界限，我们的标准就会改变。这个人向我们要钱——他并不真正属于“我们”这一类。我们可能会感到犹豫不决，因为我们缺乏与家人亲密相处的经验。由于“关系疏远”，无论是在婚姻关系中、代际之间，还是在远房亲戚之间，我们的付出习惯都变得不那么自然。即使在最亲近的人当中，我们也不确定彼此之间究竟应该付出什么。

Has our education helped? We’ve had canned-food drives in school. But have we been brought face to face with those who are hungry? Human need, helplessness, the experience of suffering … do we study and discuss these as we grow up?

我们的教育有帮助吗？学校里组织过罐头食品募捐活动。但是，我们是否真正接触过那些饥饿的人？人类的需求、无助、苦难的经历……我们在成长过程中是否学习和讨论过这些？

We probably won’t get any sense of who this man asking for money really is, because we find it hard to look him in the eye; we find it hard to look most people in the eye on the street. We stand next to each other in elevators and suddenly get interested in our shoes. In many of our dwellings and communities, we’ve invested a good deal in our privacy. If we speak infrequently to neighbors, are we any more likely to respond to this stranger? With nothing to go on, we guess who he is. Newly released mental patient? We might go to our pocket. Alcoholic? We’d only be making things worse. Who knows? So we give … or we don’t … and we walk on.

我们可能根本无法判断这个乞讨者究竟是谁，因为我们很难直视他的眼睛；事实上，我们很难直视街上大多数人的眼睛。我们并肩站在电梯里，却突然开始关注彼此的鞋子。在许多人的住所和社区里，我们都投入了大量精力来保护自己的隐私。如果我们很少与邻居交谈，我们是否更有可能对这个陌生人有所回应呢？在没有任何线索的情况下，我们只能猜测他是谁。刚出院的精神病患者？我们可能会掏钱。酗酒者？我们只会让情况变得更糟。谁知道呢？所以，我们给……或者不给……然后继续前行。

If all these questions and doubts can arise in so ordinary a situation, they’ll surely be felt when the demand on us is greater. Do we agree to tithe a portion of our income for famine relief? Do we welcome the establishment of a shelter for the homeless right around the corner? Do we take in our aging father or send him to a nursing home?

如果这些问题和疑虑在如此平常的情况下都会出现，那么当我们面临更大的挑战时，它们肯定会更加强烈。我们是否同意捐出部分收入用于救济饥荒？我们是否欢迎在自家附近设立无家可归者收容所？我们是会把年迈的父亲接回家照顾，还是把他送到养老院？

The effect of conditioning, of course, doesn’t disappear once we’ve agreed to help out. Whether it’s for a few hours a week or as a full-time job, we’ll still find ourselves asking where to draw the line, how much we’re prepared to give, and what we need to hold on to.

当然，即便我们同意帮忙，条件反射的影响也不会消失。无论是每周几个小时，还是全职工作，我们仍然会问自己：界限在哪里？我们愿意付出多少？以及我们需要坚守什么？

But it’s difficult to attribute our uncertainties to the influence of custom and circumstances alone. The roots of these external forces are apparent within each of us, if we’re the least bit honest with ourselves.

但很难将我们的不确定性仅仅归因于习俗和环境的影响。如果我们对自己稍有诚实，就会发现这些外部因素的根源其实就在我们每个人的内心深处。

We may cling to familiar circles of association because we’re afraid of being rejected. We’ll help a friend who understands our sensitivities, but volunteering to cross class lines and work with young unwed mothers might be a little threatening. Are we ready for that? Are they “Us”?

我们或许会固守熟悉的社交圈，因为害怕被拒绝。我们会帮助那些理解我们敏感点的朋友，但主动跨越阶级界限，去帮助年轻的未婚妈妈们，可能会让我们感到有些不安。我们准备好了吗？她们是“我们”吗？

We may have a difficult time facing the suffering of others because we don’t know how to deal with our own pain and fear. We’ve waited for weeks to visit a terminally ill colleague with whom we’ve worked for years. It’s clear that it’s our own death, not his, we’re afraid of, and if we realize that, our guilt may only block us further.

我们或许难以面对他人的痛苦，因为我们不知道如何应对自身的痛苦和恐惧。我们等了几个星期才得以探望一位身患绝症、共事多年的同事。很显然，我们害怕的并非他的死亡，而是自己的死亡。如果我们意识到这一点，内疚感或许只会让我们更加难以释怀。

Our choice of how to help may turn on personal motives and needs. We’re genuinely eager to aid the physically or mentally ill. But, frankly, we like the status, even the power, of being a “health professional.” Some part of us takes pride at being the apparent source of another’s well-being.

我们选择如何提供帮助可能取决于个人动机和需求。我们真心渴望帮助身心疾病患者。但坦白说，我们喜欢“医疗专业人士”的身份，甚至是权力。我们内心深处会为自己成为他人健康的守护者而感到自豪。

And when we wonder what we have to offer anyone under any circumstances, aren’t we really questioning our self-worth? Whatever outside influences are at work, aren’t we still asking the most basic inner question of all: Who am I?

当我们思考在任何情况下我们能为别人提供什么时，我们难道不是在质疑自身的价值吗？无论外界因素如何作用，我们最终不还是在问自己那个最基本的内心问题：我是谁？

Often we reach out to help one another and succeed. The expression of our natural compassion comes easily and we’re equal to the challenge. But clearly these deep internal questions of identity and relationship are going to arise much of the time we are caring for one another. The more wrenching the situation, the more likely such issues will be central. Who are we to ourselves and to one another?—it will all come down to that.

我们常常互相帮助，并最终取得成功。我们天生富有同情心，也能够轻松应对挑战。但显然，在我们彼此关怀的过程中，关于身份认同和人际关系的深刻内心问题也常常会浮现。情况越是令人揪心，这些问题就越有可能成为核心。我们对自己和他人究竟意味着什么？——最终一切都将归结于此。

Will we look within? Can we see that to be of most service to others we must face our own doubts, needs, and resistances? We’ve never grown without having done so. This wouldn’t be the first time we’ve fought the inertia of conditioning.

我们是否愿意审视内心？我们能否意识到，要想更好地服务他人，我们必须直面自身的疑虑、需求和阻力？没有经历过这些，我们就无法成长。这也不是我们第一次与根深蒂固的惯性作斗争。

Here, then, is a path we can follow in this book, in the company and with the testimony of others like us who are facing these essential questions in their own daily work. We can seek to identify certain basic inner obstacles to the expression of our caring instincts. As these rise to the surface in familiar concrete situations, we can bring them into the clear light of awareness: we see how this resistance is affecting our ability to hear people’s needs; how this habit is shaping our attitude to social action; how this expectation is contributing to burnout. By carefully observing these hindrances we can strip away some of their hidden power and reduce their influence over us. With a certain amount of perspective, in fact, we can come to see them not only as problems to overcome but as information leading to a deeper understanding of service. We can make use of them, helping ourselves help others.

因此，本书、公司以及其他与我们一样在日常工作中面临这些关键问题的人们的经验，为我们指明了一条前进的道路。我们可以努力识别阻碍我们表达关怀本能的某些基本内在障碍。当这些障碍在熟悉的具体情境中浮现时，我们可以将其置于清晰的意识层面：我们看到这种阻力如何影响我们倾听他人需求的能力；这种习惯如何塑造我们对社会行动的态度；这种期望如何导致职业倦怠。通过仔细观察这些障碍，我们可以削弱它们潜藏的力量，减少它们对我们的影响。事实上，只要我们拥有一定的视角，就能将它们视为信息，而不仅仅是需要克服的问题，从而更深入地理解服务的真谛。我们可以利用它们，从而更好地帮助自己，更好地帮助他人。

As the hold of these obstructions lessens, then, our generosity will flow more spontaneously and effortlessly. Compassion will come forth as needed, as appropriate, simply because it is its nature to do so. Able to help in ways we might not have imagined, we will find this inner work making itself felt in everything we do. Our notion of helping itself will expand. We will grow … and be of greater service as a result.

随着这些阻碍的减弱，我们的慷慨之心将更加自然流畅地流露。慈悲之心会在需要时、在恰当时自然流露，因为这是它的本性。我们将能够以我们可能从未想象过的方式去帮助他人，并会发现这种内在的转变在我们所做的每一件事中都发挥着作用。我们对助人的理解也将随之扩展。我们将不断成长……并因此能够更好地服务他人。

On this path we will stumble, fall, and often look and feel a little foolish. We are confronting long-standing patterns of thought and action. Compassion for ourselves, perspective, humor … these are our allies. With their help, we can come to see, in the words of the Bhagavad Gita, that “no step is lost on this path … and even a little progress is freedom from fear.” The reward, the real grace, of conscious service, then, is the opportunity not only to help relieve suffering but to grow in wisdom, experience greater unity, and have a good time while we’re doing it.

在这条道路上，我们会跌倒、会踉跄，常常会显得有些愚蠢。我们正在挑战根深蒂固的思维和行为模式。对自己的慈悲、开阔的视野、幽默感……这些都是我们的盟友。有了它们的帮助，我们就能像《薄伽梵歌》中所说的那样，领悟到“这条路上的每一步都不会白费……哪怕只是一点点的进步，也能让我们摆脱恐惧”。因此，有意识地服务他人的回报，真正的恩典，不仅在于有机会帮助减轻他人的痛苦，更在于让我们在智慧中成长，体验更深层次的合一，并在过程中享受快乐。

~

I’m ninety-two years old, all right. I get up every morning at seven a.m. Each day I remind myself, “Wake up. Get up.” I talk to my legs, “Legs, get moving. Legs, you’re an antelope.” It’s a matter of mind over matter. You have to have the right spirit. And I’m out on the streets, seven-thirty a.m. sharp .

我今年九十二岁了，没错。我每天早上七点起床。每天我都提醒自己：“醒醒。起床。” 我跟我的腿说话：“腿，动起来。腿，你就像羚羊一样。” 这完全是意志力战胜一切。你必须要有正确的精神。而我，每天早上七点半准时出门。

I’m wearing my Honorable Sanitation Commissioner badge they gave me from City Hall. I’m alert, I’m ready, I’m out there. And I got my whistle. My job is I help get parked cars off the street so they can bring in the sanitation trucks and the Wayne Broom, the big one—thirty grand for a broom! So when they show up, I go around blowing my whistle to get people to move their cars. I have a great time .

我戴着市政厅发给我的“荣誉环卫专员”徽章。我精神抖擞，准备就绪，随时待命。我还带了哨子。我的工作是帮忙把停在街上的车挪走，这样环卫车和“韦恩扫帚”（Wayne Broom，就是那台巨型扫帚——一把扫帚就要三万美元！）才能开进来。所以，当它们出现的时候，我就吹哨子，提醒人们挪车。我乐在其中。

People are asleep. They’re busy with businesses. They’re busy taking time off from the businesses. They’re busy having a good time. They’re busy not having a good time. Whatever. I don’t care. I blow my whistle. I’m all over the place .

人们都在睡觉。他们忙着生意。他们忙着从生意中抽身出来。他们忙着享受生活。他们忙着过得不好。随便吧。我不在乎。我吹响哨子。我到处乱窜。

I don’t discriminate, either. I go after the sanitation men too. The union got them a coffee break. Some coffee. They’re having eggs, they’re having bacon, they’re having toast … they’re having French toast. I kid them about it. And I go right into the restaurant and blow my whistle. They love it, they understand. Everybody loves it, everybody understands. It’s the whistle that gets them. Sometimes I’m having such a laugh, I can’t blow it. Then I get back to work. “Schleppers, get moving, let’s go!”

我也不歧视任何人。清洁工我也照样捉弄。工会给他们争取到了咖啡休息时间。一些咖啡。他们吃鸡蛋，吃培根，吃吐司……吃法式吐司。我拿这事儿跟他们开玩笑。然后我就直接走进餐厅，吹响我的哨子。他们喜欢，他们明白。每个人都喜欢，每个人都明白。就是这哨声让他们笑个不停。有时候我笑得太厉害，都吹不响哨子了。然后我就回去工作。“清洁工们，快点儿，走吧！”

This used to be a beautiful city. People cared. If you didn’t pay your rent, the sheriff would come and put your furniture out on the street. But the poorest of the poor would come automatically and drop their pennies and nickels at your house and put you back into your apartment. That’s neighborhood .

这里曾经是个美丽的城市。人们彼此关爱。如果你不交房租，治安官就会来把你的家具搬到街上。但最贫困的人也会自发地来你家，把他们的零钱扔到你家门口，让你重新住进公寓。这才是邻里情谊。

Now it’s different. Things have gotten out of kilter—hard to say why. People seem to be lost in their own lives. I see them on the street, lost in their own thoughts. Not that I’m all that different. I’m a schlepp myself. I have as many bad habits as anyone. You should see my apartment. It’s a mess. Me, Mr. Clean! But I’m trying. Let’s try. It’s all possible .

现在不一样了。一切都乱了套——很难说为什么。人们似乎都沉浸在自己的世界里。我看到他们在街上，各想各的。其实我也好不到哪儿去。我自己也是个邋遢鬼。我的坏习惯跟其他人一样多。你应该看看我的公寓。简直一团糟。我，可是个爱干净的人！但我正在努力。让我们一起努力吧。一切皆有可能。

What can I tell you? I’m not a saint or a wise man. I’m not the Two-Thousand-Year-Old-Man, I’m only the ninety-two-year-old man. Just a senior citizen. But what do I know that everybody doesn’t know? We know. I just go out there in the morning and blow my whistle. That’s what I do. You do what you do. Me, I’m having a great time. Wonderful fun. And when people see how much fun I’m having, they have to laugh. What else can they do? Then I hit them with it: “Move your car!”

我还能说什么呢？我既不是圣人，也不是智者。我不是两千岁的老人，我只是个九十二岁的老人。一个普通的老年人。但我知道什么别人不知道的事呢？我们都知道。我每天早上出去吹口哨。这就是我的日常。你们也做你们该做的。我呢，玩得可开心了。真是太有趣了。人们看到我这么开心，都忍不住笑了。他们还能怎么办呢？然后我就冲他们喊：“把车挪开！”

Who’s Helping?
谁在帮忙？

I n the early stages of my father’s cancer, I found it very difficult to know how best to help. I lived a thousand miles away and would come for visits. It was hard seeing him going downhill, harder still feeling so clumsy, not sure what to do, not sure what to say .

父亲患癌初期，我感到非常不知所措，不知道该如何才能更好地帮助他。我远在千里之外，只能偶尔来看望他。眼睁睁看着他的病情每况愈下，我心如刀绞；而自己却笨手笨脚，不知所措，不知道该做什么，该说什么，这更让我难受。

Toward the end, I was called to come suddenly. He’d been slipping. I went straight from the airport to the hospital, then directly to the room he was listed in .

临近结束时，我突然接到电话，被叫过去。他的病情已经恶化。我直接从机场赶到医院，然后直奔他登记的病房。

When I entered, I saw that I’d made a mistake. There was a very, very old man there, pale and hairless, thin, and breathing with great gasps, fast asleep, seemingly near death. So I turned to find my dad’s room. Then I froze. I suddenly realized, “My God, that’s him!” I hadn’t recognized my own father! It was the single most shocking moment of my life .

我进去后才发现自己搞错了。那里躺着一位非常非常老的老人，脸色苍白，头发稀疏，瘦骨嶙峋，呼吸急促，睡得很沉，似乎奄奄一息。于是我转身去找我父亲的房间。然后我愣住了。我突然意识到：“我的天哪，那就是他！”我竟然没认出自己的父亲！那是我一生中最震惊的时刻。

Thank God he was asleep. All I could do was sit next to him and try to get past this image before he woke up and saw my shock. I had to look through him and find something beside this astonishing appearance of a father I could barely recognize physically .

谢天谢地他睡着了。我只能坐在他身边，努力让自己不去想这件事，免得他醒来看到我震惊的表情。我必须透过他的外表，找到除了眼前这个我几乎认不出的父亲之外的其他东西。

By the time he awoke, I’d gotten part of the way. But we were still quite uncomfortable with one another. There was still this sense of distance. We both could feel it. It was very painful. We both were self-conscious … infrequent eye contact .

等他醒来的时候，我已经走了一段路。但我们彼此之间仍然很不自在，隔着一层距离感。我们俩都能感觉到，这很痛苦。我们都有些不自在，很少眼神交流。

Several days later, I came into his room and found him asleep again. Again such a hard sight. So I sat and looked some more. Suddenly this thought came to me, words of Mother Teresa, describing lepers she cared for as “Christ in all his distressing disguises.”

几天后，我走进他的房间，发现他又睡着了。这景象依然令人心痛。于是我坐着，继续看着他。突然，我想起了特蕾莎修女的话，她把她照顾的麻风病人比作“基督所有令人痛苦的伪装”。

I never had any real relation to Christ at all, and I can’t say that I did at that moment. But what came through to me was a feeling for my father’s identity as … like a child of God. That was who he really was, behind the “distressing disguise.” And it was my real identity too, I felt. I felt a great bond with him which wasn’t anything like I’d felt as father and daughter .

我以前从未真正与基督有过任何联系，当时我也无法说自己与他有任何联系。但我感受到的是一种父亲作为……上帝之子的身份。那才是他真正的身份，在“令人不安的伪装”之下。我也觉得，那也是我真正的身份。我与他之间建立了一种强烈的联系，这种联系与我作为父女之间的感觉截然不同。

At that point he woke up and looked at me and said, “Hi.” And I looked at him and said, “Hi.”

这时他醒了过来，看着我说：“嗨。” 我也看着他说：“嗨。”

For the remaining months of his life we were totally at peace and comfortable together. No more self-consciousness. No unfinished business. I usually seemed to know just what was needed. I could feed him, shave him, bathe him, hold him up to fix the pillows—all these very intimate things that had been so hard for me earlier .

在他生命的最后几个月里，我们相处得非常平静舒适。不再有任何拘束，也没有任何未了之事。我似乎总能准确地知道他需要什么。我可以喂他吃饭，给他刮胡子，给他洗澡，扶着他整理枕头——所有这些之前对我来说都无比艰难的、极其私密的事情。

In a way, this was my father’s final gift to me: the chance to see him as something more than my father; the chance to see the common identity of spirit we both shared; the chance to see just how much that makes possible in the way of love and comfort. And I feel I can call on it now with anyone else .

从某种意义上说，这是我父亲留给我的最后一份礼物：让我有机会看到他不仅仅是我的父亲；让我有机会看到我们共同拥有的精神纽带；让我有机会看到这种纽带能带来多么巨大的爱与慰藉。我觉得现在我可以把这份爱和慰藉传递给任何人。

~

The most familiar models of who we are—father and daughter, doctor and patient, “helper” and “helped”—often turn out to be major obstacles to the expression of our caring instincts; they limit the full measure of what we have to offer one another. But when we break through and meet in spirit behind our separateness, we experience profound moments of companionship. These, in turn, give us access to deeper and deeper levels of generosity and loving kindness. True compassion arises out of unity.

我们最熟悉的那些角色模式——父女、医生与病人、“帮助者”与“被帮助者”——往往会成为我们表达关爱本能的重大障碍；它们限制了我们彼此能够给予的全部。但当我们突破这些隔阂，在精神层面超越彼此的差异而相遇时，我们便能体验到深刻的陪伴时刻。而这些时刻反过来又让我们得以触及更深层次的慷慨和慈爱。真正的慈悲源于合一。

All the more painful, then, are the moments in which we feel cut off from one another, when we reach out to help or be helped and don’t quite meet. Despite the yearning of the heart, so often when we seek to care for one another we feel far apart. Albert Einstein speaks to this question and the challenge it poses to service:

因此，当我们伸出援手或寻求帮助却未能真正相通时，那种彼此疏离、倍感痛苦的时刻就更加令人难受了。尽管内心充满渴望，但我们常常在寻求关爱时却感到彼此相距甚远。阿尔伯特·爱因斯坦曾就此问题及其对服务提出的挑战发表过看法：

~

A human being is a part of the whole called by us universe, a part limited in time and space. He experiences himself, his thoughts and feelings as something separated from the rest, a kind of optical delusion of his consciousness. This delusion is a kind of prison for us, restricting us to our personal desires and to affection for a few persons nearest to us. Our task must be to free ourselves from this prison by widening our circle of compassion to embrace all living creatures and the whole of nature in its beauty .

人是宇宙整体的一部分，一个受时间和空间限制的部分。他体验到自身、自己的思想和情感与万物分离，这是一种意识上的错觉。这种错觉如同牢笼，将我们禁锢于个人的欲望和对少数至亲之人的情感之中。我们的任务是挣脱这牢笼，将我们的慈悲之心扩展到所有生灵和整个自然界的美丽之中。

~

It is to ourselves, then, that we must first look in our effort to see what limits the spontaneous expression of helping instincts. How does who we think we are affect what we have to give? How does this “delusion of consciousness” which “separates us from the rest,” narrow the range of our compassion? What different understanding of our being might nourish and deepen what we have to offer one another?

因此，我们首先必须审视自身，探究是什么限制了我们自发表达助人本能。我们对自身的认知如何影响我们能够给予什么？这种“意识错觉”如何“将我们与他人隔离开来”，从而缩小了我们同情的范围？对自身存在的不同理解，又能滋养和深化我们彼此之间的关爱吗？

All of us seem to be born into the experience of separateness. In infancy, we come to distinguish between “self” and “other.” As we develop, we arrive at or devise a complex group of ideas about who we are, our ego. This includes our identity on a variety of planes in which we function simultaneously—as bodies, personalities, citizens, and souls. And we have many roles to play in the course of a single day, each of which is functional and tends to call attention to itself.

我们似乎生来就体验着分离。在婴儿时期，我们开始区分“自我”和“他人”。随着成长，我们逐渐形成或构建出一套关于“我是谁”——即自我意识——的复杂观念。这包括我们在多个层面上的身份认同，我们同时在这些层面上发挥作用——作为身体、人格、公民和灵魂。在一天之中，我们扮演着许多角色，每个角色都具有功能性，并且往往会引起人们的注意。

Working a busy afternoon at the mental health clinic, we are more conscious of our professional identity. When we get home and see the children, we’re most aware of ourselves as parents. Then the evening news comes on, and for a little while we are responding to life, say, as a liberal or as a conservative. The phone rings, and it’s our mother; now we’re someone’s child. But that model falls away quickly enough as we prepare for bed, notice that we’re aging, wonder about our sex life, and drift off to sleep perhaps anticipating tomorrow’s tasks at the clinic. Hundreds of times a day, we shift costumes to fit appropriate roles. This is the life of the separate self, moving through the world of “other.”

在精神健康诊所忙碌的下午，我们更加关注自己的职业身份。回到家，看到孩子，我们最先意识到的是自己作为父母的角色。然后晚间新闻开始播放，我们会短暂地以自由派或保守派的身份回应生活。电话铃响了，是母亲打来的；这时，我们又成了别人的孩子。但这种模式很快就会消失，当我们准备睡觉，意识到自己正在变老，开始思考自己的性生活，或许还在想着明天诊所的工作，渐渐进入梦乡。一天数百次，我们变换着不同的角色。这就是独立自我的生活，在“他者”的世界中穿梭。

For the most part, this model “self” or “ego,” with its individual attributes and roles, serves us in good stead. It preserves our physical and, to a degree, our psychological integrity. It gives us a sense of continuity through time, directing and documenting personal growth. It catalogues past experiences, makes available our skills, helps keep track of capacities and limitations.

在大多数情况下，这种“自我”或“本我”的模式，及其个体属性和角色，对我们大有裨益。它维护了我们的生理完整性，并在一定程度上维护了我们的心理完整性。它赋予我们一种时间上的延续感，引导并记录个人成长。它梳理过往经验，让我们能够运用自身技能，并帮助我们了解自身的能力和局限。

Frequently we relish or simply enjoy our individuality and sense of uniqueness. The freedom to define who we are is a challenge. As we acquire a certain degree of equanimity in self-image, we are that much more likely to feel empathy for those around us. We know what it’s like to be a “self” moving through the world of “others.” When someone feels particularly isolated or in pain, we don’t need a great deal of information in order to come to his or her aid. Our own experience of separateness guides us to appropriate understanding and support. Perhaps there are more specific parallels of experience. We too have gone through a divorce, lost a loved one, struggled with alcoholism, or experienced a debilitating illness. From this body of common experience, much caring is born. As separate selves, we spend much time reaching out to one another.

我们常常珍视或享受自己的个性和独特性。自由地定义自我是一种挑战。当我们对自我认知达到一定程度的平和时，就更容易对周围的人产生同理心。我们深知作为一个“自我”穿梭于“他人”世界是怎样的体验。当有人感到特别孤独或痛苦时，我们无需了解太多信息就能伸出援手。我们自身的分离经历引导我们给予恰当的理解和支持。或许我们还有更多类似的经历。我们也经历过离婚、失去挚爱、与酗酒作斗争，或饱受疾病折磨。正是从这些共同的经历中，我们萌生了关爱。作为独立的个体，我们花费大量时间彼此关怀。

Yet it is only fair to say that the quality of our helping sometimes suffers from the hold our sense of separateness might have on us. As happily and healthily as we may function within it, the degree to which we believe ourselves to be individual, isolated entities has consequences for how we care for one another.

然而，公平地说，我们助人的质量有时会受到我们自身独立感的影响。即便我们能在这种独立感中保持快乐和健康，我们认为自己是独立个体的程度也会影响我们彼此关怀的方式。

~

I canvass from door to door looking for voter registration volunteers, asking for just a few hours a week. Not a big job for someone, no great risk, and it can make a difference. That’s what we believe, anyway .

我挨家挨户地招募选民登记志愿者，每周只需要几个小时。这对任何人来说都不是什么繁重的工作，也没有什么风险，但却能产生影响。至少我们是这么认为的。

What I usually get is a list of reasons Why Not: “I’m busy elsewhere.” “I’d be embarrassed to ring someone’s doorbell.” “What’ll I do with the kids?” Things like that .

我通常得到的是一长串“为什么不行”的理由：“我还有其他事要忙。”“我不好意思按别人的门铃。”“我怎么照顾孩子？”诸如此类。

I’ll try to loosen it up a little. “Wouldn’t you like to meet some new friends?” “Wouldn’t it be nice to not be a mother for three hours a week?”

我试着缓和一下气氛。“你不想认识一些新朋友吗？”“每周有三个小时不用当妈妈，难道不好吗？”

It generally doesn’t break through. And the reasons Why Not usually sound a little hollow as well. Something else is at work .

它通常无法突破瓶颈。而那些“为什么不行”的理由听起来也往往有些空洞。肯定还有其他因素在起作用。

~

Operating from the model of the separate self, fear and caution may be the first responses we notice that block the spontaneous expression of our innate generosity. In infancy, when the foundation stones of ego are developed and the world seems very big, our survival mechanisms are called into play very quickly. We feel powerless and vulnerable, and because these ideas are learned emotionally, before reason and perspective are fully operating, they may be surprisingly resistant to change as we grow older. So perhaps we are a little wary of the world around us. However much we might wish to reach out, a habit of self-protectiveness buried within may still hold us back. “Keep the doors locked and we’ll be secure,” says the ego. Our heart responds, “But I’m not happy like that.” To which the ego replies, “Better safe than sorry.”

从“分离自我”的模式出发，恐惧和谨慎可能是我们最先察觉到的阻碍我们自发表达内在慷慨本性的反应。在婴儿时期，当自我意识的基石逐渐形成，世界显得无比广阔时，我们的生存机制便会迅速启动。我们感到无力且脆弱，而这些观念是在理性和视角尚未完全发挥作用之前，通过情感习得的，因此随着年龄的增长，它们可能出人意料地难以改变。所以，我们或许会对周围的世界保持些许警惕。无论我们多么渴望与他人建立联系，内心深处根深蒂固的自我保护习惯仍然会阻碍我们。“把门锁好，我们就安全了，”自我说道。我们的内心回应道：“但我并不快乐。”对此，自我则回答：“小心驶得万年船。”

We may feel a little nervous and tentative, even defensive, about responding to the needs of others—particularly of those in considerable pain, who may make demands on us, whose reactions may be unpredictable, who may indeed remind us of our own vulnerability. One response of the separate self to the impulse to help out, then, may simply be a reluctance or inability to get involved.

我们或许会对回应他人的需求感到些许紧张、犹豫，甚至有些防备——尤其是那些正承受巨大痛苦、可能对我们提出要求、反应难以预料、甚至可能让我们意识到自身脆弱的人。因此，我们作为独立个体，面对想要伸出援手的冲动，可能会产生一种不愿或无力参与的抵触情绪。

We may also have to contend with inertia. An anxious, self-protective ego is most comfortable in a familiar role in which it knows exactly what’s expected of it. This attachment, in the face of changing conditions or new demands, leads the ego to hold on to one model of identity unless it has another equally comfortable one to slip into. It’s reluctant to grow, which means opening to the ambiguity of the unknown and learning new roles. This clinging can hold us back from even the simplest actions.

我们或许还要与惯性作斗争。焦虑、自我保护的自我最喜欢待在熟悉的角色中，因为它清楚地知道别人对它的期望是什么。面对变化的环境或新的需求，这种执着会让自我固守一种身份模式，除非它能找到另一种同样舒适的模式来转换。它不愿成长，而成长意味着敞开心扉去面对未知的模糊性，并学习新的角色。这种执着甚至会阻碍我们去做最简单的事情。

I’m just not the kind of person who signs petitions .

我不是那种会签署请愿书的人。

Inasmuch as we are caught up in any sense of personal inadequacy, we may wonder what we really can do for others, even in those moments when we’re not fearful or tentative. Because we often identify ourselves, consciously or not, with our shortcomings, we may feel that we don’t have enough, that we just aren’t enough, to help meet the needs of others. We give very little because we feel very small.

当我们深陷于自我不足的感受中时，即使在那些我们并不恐惧或犹豫的时刻，我们也会怀疑自己究竟能为他人做些什么。因为我们常常会不自觉地将自己与自身的缺点联系起来，所以我们会觉得自己拥有的不够多，觉得自己不够优秀，无法满足他人的需求。我们付出甚少，是因为我们觉得自己很渺小。

It’s not that I don’t care—I’m just sure you could find somebody better than me to do it .

并非我不在乎——我只是确信你能找到比我更适合做这件事的人。

Our caution and sense of inadequacy may also lead us to cling to a private agenda that limits the full freedom and generosity of those helpful acts we can initiate. Insofar as we feel lonely, angry, or powerless, for example, our caring efforts may be largely motivated by the need to gain intimacy, vent rage, or win power. Catering to our own needs and expectations, we may be less likely to hear what others feel they really need. We may be willing to give, but our self-image has its terms.

我们的谨慎和无力感也可能使我们固守私心，限制了我们主动施予的自由和慷慨。例如，当我们感到孤独、愤怒或无力时，我们的关怀行为可能很大程度上是出于获得亲密感、发泄怒火或赢得权力的需要。迎合自身的需求和期望，我们可能不太愿意倾听他人真正的需求。我们或许愿意付出，但我们的自我认知却有其限制条件。

~

Even now, after years of experience, I’m very reluctant to challenge a colleague on a tricky diagnosis. It’s a kind of dirty little secret in the medical profession. Everyone has a lot at stake. We all cling to our authority and persona. It becomes a sort of unwritten code among physicians, the license to do that. Very delicate stuff. And who pays, by the way?

即使现在，拥有多年经验，我仍然很不愿意质疑同事在疑难诊断上的判断。这在医疗界算是一个不为人知的秘密。每个人都牵涉其中，都紧紧抓住自己的权威和声誉不放。这在医生之间形成了一种不成文的潜规则，一种“特权”。非常微妙的事情。顺便问一句，谁来承担后果呢？

~

Frequently, in our efforts to remain secure and protect the integrity of the separate self, we give greater weight to one aspect of our identity over another. Though we may acknowledge, in the abstract, that we are simultaneously physical, emotional, moral, political, and spiritual beings, we seem to cling to one dimension of our identity at the expense of the others. We specialize. As a consequence, however, we often end up shortchanging what we have to offer one another.

为了维护自身安全感和独立人格的完整性，我们常常会过分强调自身身份的某一方面而忽略其他方面。尽管我们可能在抽象层面上承认自己同时拥有生理、情感、道德、政治和精神层面，但我们似乎更倾向于执着于身份的某一维度，而忽略了其他维度。我们专注于某一方面。然而，结果往往是，我们最终无法给予彼此更多。

“I’m just a surgeon. You really ought to discuss your reactions to this experience with someone else.” Why? What of the wellspring of compassion from having seen so many people go through similar experiences as patients? Thinking of ourself simply as a surgeon may cut off access to our empathy, potentially a source of great comfort and counsel.

“我只是个外科医生。你真的应该找别人聊聊你对这次经历的感受。” 为什么？难道我们作为患者，目睹过那么多人经历类似的遭遇，心中不就涌现出无数的同情心吗？仅仅把自己看作一名外科医生，可能会让我们与同理心隔绝，而同理心恰恰是给予我们莫大安慰和建议的源泉。

Or perhaps we think of ourself primarily as a “seeker.” “Oh well, I’m basically a religious person. I don’t have much to do with politics.” Yet by simply opening to acknowledge a fuller sense of identity, we might see that the very inner tranquillity we may have cultivated in spiritual practice is precisely what is needed in social action.

或许我们首先把自己看作一个“求道者”。“哦，我基本上是个宗教人士，对政治不太感兴趣。”然而，只要我们敞开心扉，承认更完整的自我认知，我们或许就会发现，我们在灵修中培养的内心平静，恰恰是社会行动所需要的。

So often we deny ourselves and others the full resources of our being simply because we’re in the habit of defining ourselves narrowly and defensively to begin with. Less flexible, less versatile, we inevitably end up being less helpful.

我们常常因为习惯于狭隘和防御性地定义自己，而错失了自己和他人的全部潜能。缺乏灵活性和适应性，我们最终必然变得无能为力。

While some self-images are more likely to facilitate the expression of our compassion than others, it is also true that any model of the self, positive or negative, will limit our capacity to help. Each form we identify with, each role we attach to, is ultimately incomplete and transient. It can dissolve in a moment. A social worker gets fired—budget cuts, nothing open in the field: “Now I can’t even read the want ads.” A therapist starts losing patients, and fewer new ones come in: “What’s happening? Is it me?” A model mother can’t let go as her youngest child turns adolescent: “I’m so depressed. My kids don’t need me anymore.”

虽然有些自我认知比其他认知更容易促进我们表达同情心，但任何自我模式，无论积极还是消极，都会限制我们助人的能力。我们认同的每一种自我，我们依附的每一个角色，最终都是不完整且短暂的，它们可能瞬间消散。一位社工被解雇了——预算削减，这个领域没有空缺职位：“现在我连招聘广告都看不懂了。”一位心理咨询师开始流失病人，新病人也越来越少：“到底发生了什么？是我的问题吗？”一位模范母亲无法放手，因为她最小的孩子即将进入青春期：“我好沮丧。我的孩子们不再需要我了。”

If any of these roles are who we think we are—social worker, therapist, mother—what’s left when they fall away? “Where’s the rest of me?”

如果我们认为自己就是社会工作者、治疗师、母亲——那么当这些角色消失时，我们还剩下什么？“我的其他部分在哪里？”

Even if we may momentarily be secure in our chosen roles, they can still impede the quality of our service at the deepest level.

即使我们暂时在自己选择的角色中感到安全，这些角色仍然可能在最深层次上阻碍我们的服务质量。

~

I’ve been chronically ill for twelve years. Stroke. Paralysis. That’s what I’m dealing with now. I’ve gone to rehab program after rehab program. I may be one of the most rehabilitated people on the face of the earth. I should be President .

我患慢性病已经十二年了。中风。瘫痪。这就是我现在面临的困境。我参加过一个又一个康复项目。我可能是地球上康复程度最高的人之一。我应该去当总统。

I’ve worked with a lot of people, and I’ve seen many types and attitudes. People try very hard to help me do my best on my own. They understand the importance of that self-sufficiency, and so do I. They’re positive and optimistic. I admire them for their perseverance. My body is broken, but they still work very hard with it. They’re very dedicated. I have nothing but respect for them .

我曾与很多人共事，见识过各种各样的人和态度。大家都很努力地帮助我发挥出自己的最佳水平。他们明白这种自力更生的重要性，我也一样。他们积极乐观，我敬佩他们的毅力。我的身体状况不佳，但他们仍然努力工作。他们非常敬业，我对他们只有敬意。

But I must say this: I have never, ever, met someone who sees me as whole.…

但我必须说：我从未遇到过一个真正把我视为完整的人……

Can you understand this? Can you? No one sees me and helps me see myself as being complete, as is. No one really sees how that’s true, at the deepest level. Everything else is Band-Aids, you know .

你能理解吗？你能吗？没有人真正了解我，也没有人帮助我认识到我自己的完整。没有人真正理解这背后的真相，在最深层次上。你知道，其他的一切都只是创可贴而已。

Now I understand that this is what I’ve got to see for myself, my own wholeness. But when you’re talking about what really hurts, and about what I’m really not getting from those who’re trying to help me … that’s it: that feeling of not being seen as whole .

现在我明白，我必须亲眼见证自己的完整性。但当你谈到真正让我痛苦的事情，以及那些试图帮助我的人并没有真正给予我什么时……那就是：那种不被视为完整的感觉。

~

Implicit in any model of who we think we are is a message to everyone about who they are . It’s not as if there are any real secrets. If we’re only seeing one part of the picture about ourselves, positive or negative, that’s all we’ll be able to make real to anybody else. Caught in the models of the separate self, then, we end up diminishing one another. The more you think of yourself as a “therapist,” the more pressure there is on someone to be a “patient.” The more you identify as a “philanthropist,” the more compelled someone feels to be a “supplicant.” The more you see yourself as a “helper,” the more need for people to play the passive “helped.” You’re buying into, even juicing up, precisely what people who are suffering want to be rid of: limitation, dependency, helplessness, separateness. And that’s happening largely as a result of self-image.

任何关于“我们是谁”的认知模式都隐含着对他人身份的解读。这并非什么真正的秘密。如果我们只看到自身形象的某一部分，无论是积极的还是消极的，那么我们所能传递给他人的也就只有这一部分。因此，当我们陷入分离自我的模式中时，最终只会贬低彼此。你越把自己视为“治疗师”，就越会给别人施加压力，让他们觉得自己是“病人”。你越把自己视为“慈善家”，就越会迫使别人成为“求助者”。你越把自己视为“帮助者”，就越会让人们扮演被动的“被帮助者”。你正在迎合，甚至强化那些正在遭受痛苦的人想要摆脱的东西：局限、依赖、无助和分离感。而这一切，很大程度上都源于自我认知。

To identify with the separate self, however functional it may often be, is to make this model of reality more real for everyone else. How much is this helping, and how much is it hindering?

认同于独立于其他事物的自我，无论这种认同在很多情况下多么实用，都会让这种现实模式对其他人而言更加真实。这究竟有多大帮助，又有多大阻碍呢？

Perhaps we recognize the predicament; we see the problem of always having to be “somebody.” So we decide to let it all go, become the model of humility, and aspire to the ideal of selflessness.

或许我们意识到了这种困境；我们看到了总是要成为“某个重要人物”的问题。所以我们决定放下一切，成为谦逊的典范，并追求无私的理想。

~

One day a rabbi, in a frenzy of religious passion, rushed in before the ark, fell to his knees, and started beating his breast, crying, “I’m nobody! I’m nobody!”

有一天，一位拉比在宗教狂热的驱使下，冲进约柜前，跪倒在地，捶打着自己的胸膛，哭喊道：“我算什么！我算什么！”

The cantor of the synagogue, impressed by this example of spiritual humility, joined the rabbi on his knees. “I’m nobody! I’m nobody!”

犹太教堂的领唱被这种谦卑的精神所感动，也和拉比一起跪了下来。“我算什么！我算什么！”

The “shamus” (custodian), watching from the corner, couldn’t restrain himself, either. He joined the other two on his knees, calling out, “I’m nobody! I’m nobody!”

角落里的看守也按捺不住，跪倒在地，和另外两人一起喊道：“我什么都不是！我什么都不是！”

At which point the rabbi, nudging the cantor with his elbow, pointed at the custodian and said, “Look who thinks he’s nobody!”

这时，拉比用胳膊肘碰了碰领唱，指着管理员说：“瞧瞧，是谁以为自己是谁啊！”

~

What’s to be done? When there’s too much “somebody,” it’s trouble. But we can’t make believe we’re nobody, either. It’s enough to make you throw up your hands and quit!

怎么办？人太多就会惹麻烦。但我们也不能假装自己是无名小卒。那样真让人想放弃！

Time for humor and perspective. The least we can do is acknowledge or remind ourselves that this is part of the predicament of being human. We all must deal with conditioning. The sense of ourselves as separate is what we are contending with virtually all of the time. It’s our curriculum, and everybody’s enrolled.

是时候展现幽默和视角了。我们至少可以承认或提醒自己，这是身为人类的困境之一。我们都必须面对各种制约因素。我们几乎时时刻刻都在与自身与外界的割裂感作斗争。这是我们每个人都必须学习的课程。

So how do we get on with our course of study?

那么，我们的学习计划该如何进行呢？

~

As an intern, part of my work was to travel around in teams, examining patients. I would notice their look as we entered. Intimidated, apprehensive, feeling like case studies of various illnesses. I hated that. But I was an intern .

实习期间，我的工作之一是跟团队一起巡诊，给病人做检查。我注意到我们进门时，他们脸上的表情：紧张、焦虑，感觉自己就像各种疾病的案例研究对象。我讨厌这种感觉。但我当时只是个实习生。

I remember one guy distinctly, however, who was altogether different. I think this guy changed my life. He was a black man in his sixties—very cute, very mischievous, and very sick .

然而，我清楚地记得一个与众不同的人。我想这个人改变了我的一生。他是一位六十多岁的黑人——非常可爱，非常调皮，而且身患重病。

What brought us repeatedly to him was the utter complexity of his illness, condition on top of condition, and the mystery of why he was still alive. It was so strange. We were visiting not to fìnd out what was wrong with him, but why he was still here at all .

我们一次又一次地去看望他，是因为他病情的复杂性，各种病症层层叠加，以及他为何还活着的谜团。这太奇怪了。我们来探望他，不是为了弄清楚他到底得了什么病，而是为了弄明白他为何还活着。

I had the feeling he could see right through us. He’d say, “Hey, boys!” when we’d come in—the way you might when a gang of ten-year-olds come barging into a house for a snack in the middle of an intense game outside. He was so pleased, and so amused. It made some people nervous. I was intrigued. But for some weeks, I never had a chance to be alone with him .

我感觉他好像能看穿我们。每次我们进门，他都会喊一声“嘿，孩子们！”——就像一群十岁左右的孩子在外面玩得正酣的时候突然闯进屋里要吃零食一样。他看起来既高兴又觉得好笑。这让一些人感到不安。我却很感兴趣。但接下来的几个星期，我始终没有机会和他单独相处。

Now and then he’d get into very serious trouble, and he’d be moved into intensive care. Then he’d rally, to everyone’s amazement, and we’d move him back. And we’d visit him again, and he’d say, “You boys here again?”—pretending to be surprised that we were still around .

他时不时会遇到非常严重的麻烦，然后就会被送进重症监护室。但过一会儿，他又会奇迹般地好转，让所有人都感到惊讶，然后我们就把他转回普通病房。之后我们再去看他，他会说：“你们几个又来了？”——假装很惊讶我们还在。

One night there was an emergency, and I took the initiative and went to see him alone. He looked pretty bad. But he came alert a few seconds after I entered. He gave me a grin and said, “Well …,” sort of like he’d expected me. Like he’d known how much I’d come to love him. That happens in hospitals .

一天晚上出了点急事，我主动独自去看他。他看起来情况很糟糕。但我进去几秒钟后，他就清醒过来了。他冲我咧嘴一笑，说了句“嗯……”，好像早就料到我会来似的。好像他知道我有多喜欢他。这种事在医院里经常发生。

I imagine I looked a little surprised at the “Well …,” but we just laughed a minute, and I stood there just so taken by who he was. And then he hit me with a single remark, half a question and half a … something else .

我猜我当时听到他那句“嗯……”的时候，看起来有点惊讶，但我们只是笑了一会儿，我站在那里，完全被他这个人吸引住了。然后他突然抛给我一句话，一半像个问题，一半又像……别的什么。

“Who you?” he said, sort of smiling. Just that. “Who you?”

“你是谁？”他带着一丝微笑问道。仅此而已。“你是谁？”

I started to say, “Well, I’m Doctor.…” And then I just stopped cold. It’s hard to describe. I just sort of went out. What happened was that all kinds of answers to his question started to go through my head. They all seemed true, but they all seemed less than true. “Yeah, I’m this or I’m that … and also … but not just … and that’s not the whole picture, the whole picture is.…” The thought process went something like that. Nothing remotely like that had ever happened to me. But I remember feeling very elated .

我刚开口说：“嗯，我是医生……”然后就突然停住了。很难形容那种感觉。我感觉自己好像一下子就消失了。当时，各种各样的答案开始在我脑海里翻腾。它们听起来都对，但又都感觉不够真实。“是啊，我是这个，我是那个……而且……但不仅仅是……而且这并非全部，全部是……”我的思绪大概就是这样。我以前从未经历过这种事。但我记得当时我感到非常兴奋。

It must have shown, because he gave me this big grin and said, “Nice to meet you.” His timing killed me .

他肯定表现出来了，因为他咧嘴一笑，对我说：“很高兴认识你。”他这番话的时机真是绝了。

We talked for five minutes about this and that—nothing in particular; children, I think. At the end, I ventured to say, “Is there anything I can do for you?” He said, “No, I’m just fine. Thanks very much … Doctor …?” And he paused for the name, and I gave it to him this time, and he grinned at me again, really he did. And that was it .

我们闲聊了五分钟，谈天说地，也没什么特别的，大概是聊孩子吧。最后，我试探性地问他：“我能帮您做点什么吗？” 他说：“不用了，我很好。非常感谢……医生……？” 他停顿了一下，等着我报上名字，这次我告诉了他，他又对我笑了笑，真的，他笑了。就这样，我们结束了对话。

He died a few days later. And I carry him around today. I think of him now and again in the midst of my rounds. A particular moment or particular patient brings him back. “Who you?” For years, I’d trained to be a physician, and I almost got lost in it. This man took away my degree, and then gave it back to me with “And also?… and also … and also?” scribbled across. I’ll never forget that .

几天后他就去世了。直到今天，我依然带着他。查房的时候，我时不时会想起他。某个特定的时刻，或者某个特定的病人，都会让他浮现在我的脑海里。“你是谁？”多年来，我一直接受医学训练，几乎迷失了方向。这个人夺走了我的学位，然后又把它还给我，上面潦草地写着“还有……还有……还有？”。我永远不会忘记这件事。

~

How good it can feel to regain perspective. Our feeling of confinement as narrow, limited, isolated entities begins to dissolve as we take a few steps back and recognize that who we are is “this … and also … and also … and also.” Moving in and out of these various identities, each is “real” only at the moment we are invested in it. A moment later it may not be relevant at all. We see, in other words, the relative reality of these various identities, “real” only in relation to the situation which calls them forth.

重拾视角的感觉真好。当我们后退几步，意识到我们是谁是“这个……也是……也是……也是”时，那种被狭隘、局限、孤立的自我束缚感便开始消融。我们不断切换于各种身份之间，每一种身份都只在我们投入其中的那一刻才是“真实的”。片刻之后，它可能就完全无关紧要了。换句话说，我们看到的是这些不同身份的相对真实性，它们只有在与唤起它们的具体情境相关时才是“真实的”。

But if all of our identities are only relatively real, coming and going as circumstance warrants, is there any part of us that remains steady and stable behind all our roles? If we observe our own minds at work, we see that behind all these identities is a state of awareness that incorporates them all and yet is still able to rest behind them. As we loosen the hold of each identity so that we don’t get completely lost in it, we are able to remain light and loose—able to play among these various aspects of being without identifying exclusively with any. We don’t have to be anybody in particular. We don’t have to be “this” or “that.” We are free simply to be .

但如果所有的身份都只是相对真实的，会随着环境的变化而来去无常，那么在我们所有角色背后，是否存在一个始终稳定不变的自我呢？如果我们观察自己的思维运作，就会发现，在所有这些身份背后，存在着一种觉知状态，它包容一切，却又能够安然地存在于其后。当我们逐渐放松对每个身份的执着，不至于完全迷失其中时，我们就能保持轻盈自在——能够在不同的存在面向之间游刃有余，而不执着于任何单一的身份。我们不必成为任何特定的人。我们不必是“这个”或“那个”。我们拥有自由，只需存在。

To taste this freedom increases our flexibility immensely, and enables us to be fuller instruments of service to others. For example, as a skillful nurse, we’ll sense those moments with certain patients in which all the nurturing we’ve learned as a mother is needed. Or perhaps a situation arises, say with an imperious physician, when who we are is simply a strong woman—one who’s gained that resolve through the consciousness raising and insights of feminism. Or in the presence of one who is dying, we feel that part of ourself which is merely God’s child; humility, prayer, and faith are what we have to share now.

体验这种自由会极大地增强我们的灵活性，使我们能够更好地服务他人。例如，作为一名技艺精湛的护士，我们会感受到在某些病人身上，我们需要运用作为母亲所学到的所有关爱和呵护。又或许，面对一位专横跋扈的医生，我们会意识到，我们内心深处其实是一位坚强的女性——这种决心源于女性主义的觉醒和洞见。再比如，在一位临终之人面前，我们会感受到自己作为上帝之子的那一部分；此时此刻，我们所能分享的，唯有谦卑、祈祷和信仰。

We often move among these various identities with much fluidity and skill. When we discover how exhilarating this is, what we’re getting is just a taste of real freedom, the liberation that comes from loosening our identification with self-image altogether. We experience the versatility of our being and the independence of our awareness. We’re opening up the windows of our little homes and letting in a little cross-ventilation.

我们常常能游刃有余地在不同的身份之间切换。当我们发现这种体验有多么令人兴奋时，我们所感受到的仅仅是真正自由的滋味，是摆脱对自我形象的执着所带来的解脱。我们体验到自身存在的多变性和意识的独立性。我们打开了小家的窗户，让空气流通进来。

Humor also serves to support this awakening perspective. What else, in the end, do we laugh at but our own vanity and puffy attachment to who we think we are? The Marx Brothers have no respect—no respect, that is, for anyone who’s busy taking himself seriously as “somebody.” Everybody’s fair game. Groucho’s cracks and Harpo’s horn shake us all up. We sit there watching, laughing, loving it, grateful. How often we recognize ourselves in portrayals of human foolishness. How much freer we feel when a friend kids us about some quality of self-importance, and we’re able to gulp, take it, and finally join in the general laughter. We come off self-image. We’re even able to direct this same irreverence toward our own behavior and attachments.

幽默也有助于这种觉醒的视角。归根结底，我们嘲笑的除了我们自身的虚荣和对自我身份的盲目执着之外，还能是什么呢？马克思兄弟毫无尊重可言——也就是说，他们不尊重任何自以为是、把自己当成“重要人物”的人。每个人都是他们的笑料。格劳乔的妙语连珠和哈波的滑稽表演让我们都感到震撼。我们坐在那里观看，开怀大笑，享受其中，心怀感激。我们常常能在对人类愚蠢行为的刻画中看到自己的影子。当朋友拿我们某种自负的特质开玩笑时，我们感到多么轻松自在，能够坦然接受，最终加入到大家的笑声中。我们摆脱了自我形象的束缚。我们甚至可以将这种不敬的态度运用到我们自身的行为和执着之中。

~

I catch myself in self-importance ten times a day—check that, five—well, maybe once. It’s appalling anyway. A little flashbulb goes off and I’m exposed … like Jimmy Olsen caught Superman changing clothes in the phone booth .

我一天要自以为是十次——不对，五次——好吧，也许只有一次。反正这很糟糕。就像闪光灯一闪，我就暴露了……就像吉米·奥尔森撞见超人在电话亭里换衣服一样。

Of course, whoever I’m with has probably been seeing all this self-importance in me for hours before I ever notice. And my colleagues … they’ve been shrugging or giving up for years. So there’s no sanctuary. And I’ve stopped trying to hide it. No, that’s a lie! Don’t trust this man! Don’t print this interview!

当然，跟我在一起的人可能在我察觉之前几个小时就已经看出我这副自以为是的样子了。至于我的同事们……他们早就耸耸肩或者放弃了。所以，根本无处可逃。我也不再试图掩饰了。不，那是谎话！别相信这个人！别刊登这篇采访！

What I’ve done really is I’ve begun. I’ve just started to watch myself as I go through these little prances. I actually have this exercise I sometimes perform. What I do when I catch myself being Mr. Administrator of Social Services is I get up out of my chair, walk away a few steps, stand for a moment, and then turn around and walk back and sit down again. The one who is now seated is usually not the same one who was there before. I’m no longer that guy, Mr. Administrator. For a while, anyway .

我真正做的，其实就是开始了。我开始观察自己，观察自己如何不自觉地做出这些小动作。我有时会做这样一个练习。当我发现自己又像个“社会服务机构的行政主管”时，我会从椅子上站起来，走几步，站一会儿，然后再转身走回来坐下。这时坐在我面前的，通常已经不是之前那个人了。我不再是那个“行政主管”了。至少暂时是这样。

I should add that this exercise frequently appears quite mad to other people in the room, particularly if they’re people who have come to me for some kind of assistance. (“This is the guy I’ve come to for help?”) Funny. So I perform these exercises at considerable cost to my aura of authority, you understand. But it’s definitely worth it. Freedom is priceless … worth whatever the cost .

我得补充一句，这种做法在房间里的其他人看来常常显得相当疯狂，尤其是那些来找我寻求帮助的人。（“我找的就是这个人？”）真可笑。所以，你明白，我做这些练习会严重损害我的权威感。但这绝对值得。自由是无价的……值得付出任何代价。

~

With increasing perspective, we see that all of our ego identities, models, and self-images can be useful, but need not be entrapping. We may gain this perspective very slowly, but the direction is clear. As we lighten our attachment to self-image, we find a different vantage point from which to observe who we are.

随着视野的拓展，我们会发现，我们所有的自我认同、模型和自我形象都有其价值，但并非一定会束缚我们。这种认知或许需要时间才能形成，但方向却很清晰。当我们逐渐放下对自我形象的执着时，便能找到一个全新的视角来审视自己。

It’s as if you lived in a little town, and you go up to a mountaintop and, looking down, you see how you move about in the course of an ordinary day. You see your route to work, how you go shopping, the main thoroughfares, your shortcuts, your daily routines—you’re seeing all that from up there. Then you return to the village. But now, when you’re moving around town thereafter, there’s a part of you that always recalls the perspective from above. As you go through a day, you’re still watching it all from up there.

这就像你住在一个小镇，然后爬到山顶，俯瞰下方，看到自己平凡的一天是如何度过的。你看到上班的路线，购物的路线，主要干道，捷径，以及日常的作息——所有这一切，你都从高处尽收眼底。然后你回到村子里。但之后，当你再次在镇上活动时，你总会想起从高处俯瞰的视角。每一天，你都仿佛仍在从高处观察着这一切。

Sometimes, however, the process of breaking through attachment to our separateness happens simply because we’ve reached the boundaries of all our roles and self-images: “I gave it everything I had.” “I tried everything I knew.” Nothing worked, couldn’t help. Perhaps we give up in resignation; the separate self, by definition, has its limits, after all. But maybe we find another way. We surrender into the unknown. With nothing left to do , we let our heart and intuitive wisdom reveal another way to be .

然而，有时，我们之所以能够突破对自我分离的执着，仅仅是因为我们已触及所有角色和自我认知的极限：“我已经竭尽全力。”“我尝试了我所知道的一切。”一切都无济于事，我们无能为力。或许我们会无奈地放弃；毕竟，分离的自我，从定义上来说，就是有其局限性的。但也许我们会找到另一条路。我们臣服于未知。在无计可施的情况下，我们让内心和直觉的智慧揭示另一种存在方式。

~

You might say I’m the gatekeeper here, the first person people meet when they come in for help. My friends at work, they’ll call up and say, “St. Peter?” I say, “He’s not here right now, can I take a message?”

你可以说我是这里的守门人，是人们来寻求帮助时遇到的第一个人。我的同事们会打电话来问：“圣彼得？”我会说：“他现在不在，我可以帮你们留言吗？”

Anyhow, Family Services is the name of our department. People come in, I direct them to the appropriate office: food, shelter, child protection, welfare, legal services, your basics. My job is to get a sense of who someone is and then find the right place for them. Not simple .

总之，我们部门叫家庭服务部。人们进来后，我会引导他们去相应的办公室：食物、住所、儿童保护、福利、法律服务，都是些基本服务。我的工作是了解来访者的情况，然后为他们找到最合适的帮助。这可不是件容易的事。

For a long time I found this an uncomfortable assignment. I don’t like sizing up someone according to their problem. It may help them get to the right office, but it also reduces them somehow. Reduces me too. I’ll find myself resisting this way of going about things. But I had an experience which changed my way of thinking about it .

很长一段时间以来，我都觉得这项工作让我很不舒服。我不喜欢根据一个人的问题来评判他。这样做或许能帮他找到合适的部门，但某种程度上也会贬低他。也贬低我自己。我常常会抗拒这种处理方式。但我的一次经历改变了我的看法。

There was this woman who was living on the street, one I used to pass on my way to the bus. She was homeless, alcoholic; later it developed she had had a cancer diagnosis. For some reason I decided to take up with her. I liked her smile. Enough of sending everyone elsewhere. I knew the whole maze of social services; I’d take her around myself—clinics, shelters, Medicare, whatever. I guess I wanted to know you could help one person yourself. She was very uncomplaining. Viola. She was willing, even funny about it. “Well, Marie,” she’d say, “what are you going to do for me today?”

有个女人流落街头，我以前每次去公交车站都会路过她。她无家可归，酗酒；后来才知道她得了癌症。不知怎么的，我决定帮帮她。我喜欢她的笑容。我不想再把所有人都推来推去。我对各种社会服务机构都了如指掌；我会亲自带她去——诊所、收容所、医疗保险，等等。我想，我大概是想知道，一个人也能帮到别人。她从不抱怨。瞧，她很乐意帮忙，甚至还挺幽默的。“玛丽，”她会说，“你今天打算帮我什么呢？”

Oh, the scenes we went through! They called me once from the Women’s Shelter. Somehow she’d brought in three pints of Seagram’s Seven that night, and a group had gotten drunk. That was against the rules, and I had to take her out. “You told me you’d be good,” I said. “You were warm there.” She said, “Well, we got warmer.”

哦，我们经历过的那些事！有一次，妇女庇护所的人给我打了个电话。那天晚上，她不知怎么带了三品脱西格拉姆七号威士忌进去，一群人都喝醉了。这违反了规定，我不得不把她带出去。“你跟我说过你会表现好的，”我说。“你在那里很热情。”她说：“嗯，我们变得更热情了。”

Or I set her up once with a counselor. After a while he called. “Look, she shows up irregularly, and she always wants to argue with me when she does. What’s she here for?” And I’d tell Viola, and she’d say, “Sure, I love to argue with these people. He wants to talk about my childhood all the time. But he doesn’t even remember what childhood was like himself. Trust me, Marie.”

或者，我曾经给她介绍过一位咨询师。过了一段时间，咨询师打电话来说：“你看，她来得断断续续，而且每次来都想跟我争论。她来这儿干嘛？” 我跟维奥拉说了，她会说：“是啊，我就是喜欢跟这些人争论。他总是想聊我的童年。但他自己都记不清童年是什么样的了。相信我，玛丽。”

And I did. I’d have to laugh. She was so insightful and honest. Oh, I really did love her, that one—I really did. But the problems went on for months. Nothing seemed to work out. She kept going back on the street, drinking, getting sicker, all the rest. The more helpless I felt, the more I just loved her; what else could I do? And I’d try again. “Look, Viola,” I’d say. “Look where, Marie?” she’d reply. It became a kind of joke between us: “Look.” “Look where?”

我确实这么做了。我忍不住笑了。她那么有洞察力，那么坦诚。哦，我真的爱她，真的爱她。但问题持续了好几个月。似乎什么办法都行不通。她不断地回到街头，酗酒，病情加重，等等等等。我越感到无助，就越爱她；我还能做什么呢？于是我又试了一次。“你看，维奥拉，”我会说。“看哪儿，玛丽？”她会回答。这成了我们之间的一个玩笑：“看。”“看哪儿？”

She moved to a park near my house, and there she started to really go downhill. One evening I went to see her and she was sitting under a tree. She looked awful. I had this powerful feeling that she was getting very close to death. So I went through everything with her one more time: her drinking, her health, her eating, her shelter. She could come live with me. I’d reached that point of willingness .

她搬到了我家附近的一个公园，在那里她的状况开始急转直下。一天晚上我去看她，她正坐在树下。她看起来很糟糕。我强烈地感觉到她快要死了。于是我又和她详细地谈了一遍：她的饮酒情况、健康状况、饮食习惯、住所等等。她可以来和我一起住。我已经下定决心了。

She just listened, and finally she said, “You know, dear, there’s nothing you can do for me anymore.” And I saw she was right, I just saw that. And I heaved this big sigh, just let go. About then, it started raining lightly. I finally said, “Well, it’s getting late and wet. Shall we go get some coffee?”

她只是静静地听着，最后说道：“亲爱的，你知道，你再也帮不了我了。” 我明白她说的没错，我当时就明白了。我长叹一声，彻底放手了。就在这时，开始下起了小雨。我终于开口说道：“天色已晚，雨也下得很大了，我们去喝杯咖啡吧？”
