She said, “You go, Marie. I’ll be all right here.”

她说：“你去吧，玛丽。我在这里没事的。”

I said, “Yeah … well … I’ll see you later then.” But somehow it felt to both of us like I wouldn’t .

我说：“嗯……好吧……那我待会儿再见。”但不知为何，我们俩都觉得我不会再见了。

I went to the bus, and I was crying on the bus. I felt just brokenhearted. I felt there was something else, I didn’t know what. Then this thought came to me that she was out there alone in the rain. Just that. So I got off and took the other bus back and went into the park with a newspaper on my head. I must have looked pretty funny .

我上了公交车，在车上哭了起来。我感觉心都碎了。我感觉还有别的原因，但我不知道是什么。然后我突然想到，她独自一人在雨中。就是这样。于是我下了车，坐另一辆公交车回去，头上顶着份报纸，走进了公园。我当时的样子肯定很滑稽。

She was under the tree. She looked up at me. I sat down. She said, “What are you doing here?” I said, “Nothing, really. I just felt like being with you a little more.” She said, “Okay.”

她坐在树下，抬头看着我。我坐了下来。她问：“你在这儿干什么？”我说：“没什么，只是想多陪陪你。”她说：“好吧。”

So we sat in the rain. There we were. It was relatively dry, because this was a big sycamore tree. I told her about how my father taught me to identify trees by their bark and how I loved trees and nature and felt happiest there. She told me about the desert. She used to live in Arizona. Her favorite place was the desert; it was so peaceful there .

于是我们就坐在雨里。我们就那样坐着。因为这是一棵高大的梧桐树，所以雨水相对来说比较干燥。我告诉她，我父亲教我通过树皮来辨认树木，我多么热爱树木和大自然，在那里我感到最快乐。她跟我讲了沙漠的故事。她以前住在亚利桑那州。她最喜欢的地方是沙漠；那里非常宁静。

We watched the rain. We watched how the squirrels ran around and the last few people scurrying out. We watched how the park looked with no one in it: some birds, a stray dog.… some mist beginning to appear. And I felt finally at peace, and we were both at peace, and we stayed silent a long time. I felt such love .

我们看着雨，看着松鼠四处奔跑，看着最后几个人匆匆离开。我们看着空荡荡的公园：几只鸟，一只流浪狗……雾气开始弥漫。我终于感到平静，我们也都平静下来，我们沉默了很久。我感受到了如此深沉的爱。

She walked me to the bus. She said, “Thanks.” I said, “For what?” She said, “For nothing.” We laughed. “You’ve been very good to me,” she added. We were teary. We hugged. Then I got on the bus, and we waved good-bye. I never saw her again. I’ll always love her .

她送我到公交车站。她说：“谢谢。”我问：“谢什么？”她说：“没什么。”我们都笑了。“你对我很好，”她补充道。我们都热泪盈眶。我们拥抱了一下。然后我上了公交车，我们挥手告别。我再也没见过她。我会永远爱她。

~

When our models of who we are fall away, we are free simply to meet and be together. And when this sense of being encompasses all—one another, the park, the rain, everything—separateness dissolves and we are united in compassion.

当我们不再执着于自我认知时，我们便能自由地相遇、相伴。当这种存在感包容一切——彼此、公园、雨水、万物——分离便消融，我们在慈悲中合而为一。

Helpful Being, then, is the goal. What we have to offer others will come from our sense of unity. So we look for and cherish those experiences in which we feel ourselves connected to all things in the universe.

因此，乐于助人是我们的目标。我们能给予他人的，都源于我们对万物一体的感知。所以，我们要寻找并珍惜那些让我们感到与宇宙万物相连的体验。

Out under the stars, stretching to encompass notions of distance and galaxies, “light years,” until the mind just boggles and goes “tilt”—and suddenly your sense of specialness or separateness is replaced by a feeling of identity with the all-inclusive immensity of the universe.

在星空下，延伸到距离和星系的概念，“光年”，直到你的思维变得混乱，发出“倾斜”的声音——突然间，你特殊或分离的感觉被与包罗万象的宇宙的同一感所取代。

Listening to a Bach chorale and feeling transported into a sense of order and harmony far beyond the music itself.

聆听巴赫的合唱曲，感觉自己被带入了一种超越音乐本身的秩序与和谐之中。

Harvesting the garden, smiling as you remember the spring planting, and appreciating the lawfulness of fruition in nature, the same life energy in you.

收获花园的果实，想起春天播种的情景，脸上不禁露出微笑，欣赏大自然中万物生长的规律，以及你自身所蕴含的生命能量。

Making love, when you suddenly merge with someone very dear; two become one, and you somehow feel more truly yourself than you ever had before.

做爱时，你突然与你非常爱的人融为一体；两个人合二为一，你会感觉比以往任何时候都更真实地认识自己。

Or in service itself—comforting a crying child, reassuring a frightened patient, bringing a glass of water to a bedridden elder—when you feel yourself to be a vehicle of kindness, an instrument of love. There’s more to the deed than the doer and what’s been done. You yourself feel transformed and connected to a deeper sense of identity.

或者在服务本身中——安慰哭泣的孩子，安抚受惊的病人，给卧床不起的老人端上一杯水——当你感受到自己是善意的传递者，爱的使者时，这种感受就更加强烈。此时，行动的意义远不止于行动者和行动本身。你自身也会感到蜕变，并与更深层次的自我认同感相连。

~

When I was working in New York with elderly, poor orthodox Jews, I’d come upon a number of old synagogues—dirty, filthy, vandalized. I’d always had ambivalent feelings about synagogues—a kind of no-man’s-land for me. If anything, they made me less sure of what it meant to be a Jew .

我在纽约为年迈贫困的正统犹太教徒服务时，曾多次路过一些破旧的犹太教堂——肮脏不堪，破败不堪。我对犹太教堂一直抱有矛盾的感情——对我来说，它们就像一片无人区。如果说有什么影响的话，那就是它们让我更加不确定身为犹太人的意义。

But one day I came upon one that somehow caught me. That night I went to the service—very few people there, all down and out. And suddenly the thought came to me that I would clean the synagogue. Just that. And I did it .

但有一天，我偶然遇到一个让我印象深刻的人。那天晚上我去参加礼拜——那里人很少，都是些落魄潦倒的人。突然，我萌生了一个念头：我要去打扫犹太教堂。就这么简单。然后我就真的这么做了。

That’s how it began. We’d bring in young people to clean these synagogues and in so doing get a sense of what they really meant—not a social club but a place where the entire life cycle of a people and their continuing relationship with God was to be celebrated .

事情就是这样开始的。我们会带年轻人来打扫这些犹太教堂，通过这种方式，我们就能真正体会到它们的意义——它们不是一个社交俱乐部，而是一个庆祝一个民族整个生命周期以及他们与上帝之间持续关系的地方。

Myself, I found it hard to pray there. That was the stage I was at. But I helped bring a sense of order and beauty. You see, I had had an immense respect for that generation of Jews which had come to Palestine in the twenties and thirties, who went back to the land not simply to rebuild the land but to be rebuilt by the land, by the work itself .

我自己当时在那里很难祈祷。那是我当时的处境。但我帮助那里恢复了秩序和美感。你知道，我对二三十年代来到巴勒斯坦的那一代犹太人怀有无比的敬意，他们回到这片土地，不仅仅是为了重建家园，更是为了被这片土地、被重建本身所滋养。

That’s what this became for me. This was a mitzvah, an act of service, but it was also an act by which I myself was being rebuilt—rebuilt into a deeper relationship with my tradition and my people and that living faith .

对我而言，这就是这件事的意义所在。这既是一项善举，一次服务他人的行为，也是一次自我重塑的过程——让我与我的传统、我的人民以及那鲜活的信仰建立起更深层次的联系。

~

Finally, profound moments of spiritual and religious experience take us beyond identification with our isolated egos. The sense of separateness falls away as we come into some deeper understanding of “It All.” While these experiences do not always easily lend themselves to words, the message of all the teachings that support them have much in common. Don’t get lost in what’s apparent. Go beyond the evidence of the senses and the rational mind. Acknowledge that there are more things in heaven and earth than are dreamt of in our philosophies. Whatever else we may seem to be, we’re also reflections or expressions of … and then we get names for the nameless: “Awareness,” “Being,” “God,” “Life,” “the Formless,” “the Way.” Whatever it is, whatever it’s called, there’s only One of it . It’s present in all creation. We ourselves are rooted in it. It is our essence.

最终，深刻的灵性与宗教体验会将我们带离孤立的自我。当我们对“万物”有更深刻的理解时，分离感便会消散。虽然这些体验并非总能轻易用语言表达，但所有支持它们的教义都蕴含着许多共通之处。不要迷失于表象。超越感官和理性思维的局限。要认识到，天地间存在着远超我们哲学所能想象的事物。无论我们看似如何，我们也是……的反映或表达，而我们为这无名之物赋予了各种名称：“觉知”、“存在”、“神”、“生命”、“无形”、“道”。无论它是什么，无论它被称为什么，它都只有一个。它存在于万物之中。我们自身也根植于它。它是我们的本质。

Who we are, from this perspective, begins with the One . Unity, not separateness, is our starting point. And while our ego doesn’t disappear, its importance is certainly put in perspective as a result of having experienced a higher Self.

从这个角度来看，我们是谁始于“一”。合一，而非分离，才是我们的出发点。虽然我们的自我不会消失，但体验到更高的自我之后，它的重要性无疑会得到更清晰的认识。

Whether these experiences—through nature, art, love, service, spirit—are frequent or rare, we see that when we are not caught up in self-conscious separateness, not defined by self-image, we still survive. Indeed, we thrive and function happily, freely, and efficiently. We feel exalted. Despite all our ego’s concerns and warnings of the dire consequences of not being “somebody special,” we are capable of simply resting in our being. We simply are .

无论这些体验——通过自然、艺术、爱、服务、精神——是频繁还是罕见，我们都能看到，当我们不被自我意识的分离所束缚，不被自我形象所定义时，我们依然能够生存。事实上，我们能够蓬勃发展，快乐、自由、高效地生活。我们感到无比的升华。尽管我们的自我充满担忧，不断警告我们，如果我们不是“特别的人”，将会带来可怕的后果，但我们依然能够安住于自身的存在之中。我们只是存在着。

The geese have no intention to cast their reflections .

这些大雁无意在空中倒影。

The lake has no mind to receive their image .

湖泊并不想接收他们的影像。

Fortune Cookie

幸运饼干

From this perspective, the whole question of identity can look very different. We can enter into the world of the separate self with a certain amount of freedom, even irony and whimsy. As long as we’re here, we might as well play.

从这个角度来看，身份认同的问题就完全不同了。我们可以带着一定的自由，甚至是讽刺和奇思妙想，进入一个独立自我的世界。既然我们身处其中，何不尽情玩乐呢？

~

In a Seattle newspaper there was a picture of a man behind bars. The caption explained that he had been caught with a dispatch case full of papers and cards claiming various and different identities. The police had thus far ascertained that he was none of these. The problem was that they couldn’t find out who he really was .

西雅图一家报纸上刊登了一张男子身陷囹圄的照片。照片说明解释说，他被捕时携带一个装满文件和卡片的公文包，上面列有各种不同的身份信息。警方目前已查明，他并非其中任何一个身份。问题是，他们无法查明他的真实身份。

The man said, “They’re the ones who arrested me. It’s their problem to find out who I am. I know who I am.” The police sergeant said, “This man has boggled our system.”

那人说：“是他们逮捕我的。查明我是谁是他们的事。我知道我是谁。” 警官说：“这个人把我们的系统搞得一团糟。”

~

Tastes of self-transcendence draw us to further exploration. We recognize that these insights need to be cultivated. We may easily fall back into old habits and patterns of thought. But having come into contact with the higher Self, we’re motivated to find ways to strengthen our acquaintance. There are many paths, and each in its own way can help us to move beyond identification with the separate isolated ego.

体验到自我超越的滋味，会引领我们进一步探索。我们意识到，这些洞见需要培养。我们很容易重蹈覆辙，陷入旧有的习惯和思维模式。但既然已经与更高的自我接触，我们便会更有动力去寻找方法来加深彼此的了解。道路有很多条，每条道路都能以其独特的方式帮助我们超越对孤立的自我的认同。

To study the Way is to study the Self .

研究道就是研究自我。

To study the Self is to forget the Self

研究自我即是遗忘自我

To forget the Self is to he enlightened by all things .

忘却自我，方能领悟万物之美。

To be enlightened by all things is to remove the barrier between Self and Other .

从万物中汲取智慧，就是消除自我与他人之间的隔阂。

DOGEN ZENJI

道元禅师

We may choose to explore those forms of therapy that encourage us to understand just how our models of self have arisen through past experience. Earlier forms of psychotherapy seemed to deify the ego and, by focusing on its genesis, invest it with more and more solid reality. Recent approaches of transpersonal, humanistic, and Gestalt therapies, and those derived from Jung, encourage the liberation of the self and the exploration of a more expansive sense of identity.

我们可以选择探索那些鼓励我们理解自我模型如何通过过往经验形成的疗法。早期的心理疗法似乎将自我神化，并通过关注其起源，赋予其越来越坚实的现实性。而近年来兴起的超个人疗法、人本主义疗法、格式塔疗法以及源自荣格的疗法，则鼓励自我解放，并探索更为广阔的身份认同。

As we shall see in a subsequent chapter, the practice of meditation can help us to develop our ability to penetrate the process whereby the mind is constantly creating and reinforcing attributes of the separate self, ideas of “me.” We can systematically observe these ideas as they pass by, seeking to draw us into identification: “I’m this, I’m that.” But we can learn to remain mindful behind these thoughts, lessening our attachment to them as we watch them rise and pass away.

正如我们将在后续章节中看到的，冥想练习可以帮助我们培养洞察力，从而更好地理解心智不断创造和强化“我”的属性和观念的过程。我们可以系统地观察这些观念的来来往往，它们试图引导我们认同这些观念：“我是这个，我是那个。” 但我们可以学会觉察这些念头背后的本质，在观察它们生起和消逝的过程中，逐渐减少对它们的执着。

Other traditions, in effect, use the mind to beat the mind. In Rinzai Zen Buddhism, a teacher gives a student a particular koan to solve—for example, “What was your original face before you were born?” Of course, no rational answer is possible. But the student makes regular appearances to offer a response. Usually he comes armed with some artifice designed to make him appear wise and insightful. But these answers are quickly discerned as creations of ego and brusquely dismissed, and the student is rejected. This continues until the moment the student gives up the effort to look impressive and a spontaneous answer just comes out. The teacher honors it. The student has “forgotten the self.”

其他一些传统实际上是利用思维来战胜思维。在临济宗禅宗中，老师会给学生一个特定的公案——例如，“你出生前的本来面目是什么？” 当然，这不可能有理性的答案。但学生会定期前来作答。通常，他会精心准备一些技巧，让自己显得睿智而有见地。但这些答案很快就会被识破，被老师断然拒绝，学生也会被拒之门外。这种情况会一直持续下去，直到学生放弃装腔作势，自然而然地脱口而出一个答案。老师会给予肯定。学生已经“忘我”了。

Some of us may experience the call to congregation and find ourselves drawn deeply to collective devotion and ritual. Whether in worship, formal ceremony, song, dance, or services, we experience the coming together of our many hearts. As joy and exaltation grow, our sense of separateness falls away. This becomes our path for strengthening our sense of unity.

我们当中有些人或许会感受到归属感的召唤，并深深地被集体的虔诚和仪式所吸引。无论是在敬拜、正式的仪式、歌唱、舞蹈还是其他礼拜中，我们都能体验到彼此心灵的交融。随着喜乐和振奋的增长，我们的分离感逐渐消散。这便成为我们增强团结意识的途径。

Or perhaps the experience comes through solitary, interior prayer and contemplation. We lift up our hearts, minds, and souls. We reach out to God. Through our surrender, love, and faith, we feel a sense of profound communion in which our individuality merges into His Being. In these moments we are One. And though they may not last or retain their intensity, we’re not likely to forget these moments when they happen. We seek them more often.

或许，这种体验源于独自的内心祈祷和冥想。我们敞开心扉，敞开思想，敞开灵魂。我们与神亲近。通过我们的臣服、爱和信仰，我们感受到一种深刻的联结，在这种联结中，我们的个体融入祂的存在。在这些时刻，我们合而为一。虽然这些时刻可能不会持续太久，也不会始终保持其强烈，但我们不太可能忘记它们发生时的情景。我们会更加频繁地寻求这样的时刻。

All these methods, and many others, strengthen our ability to recognize and dwell in our higher Self, beyond separateness. In pursuing these practices, however, it’s important to remember that the object is not to destroy the ego. We’re not declaring war on our separate self. It helps assure our survival and effectiveness. It has a role to play at an appropriate level of our lives. What we’re doing instead is working to establish a new balance between the ego and the higher Self and allowing our higher Self to expand, explore, and root itself more fully in a consciousness of unity.

所有这些方法，以及其他许多方法，都能增强我们认识并安住于更高自我的能力，超越分离的界限。然而，在实践这些方法时，重要的是要记住，其目的并非摧毁自我。我们并非向分离的自我宣战。它有助于确保我们的生存和效能，并在我们生活的适当层面上发挥着作用。我们所做的，是努力在自我和更高自我之间建立新的平衡，并允许更高自我扩展、探索，并在合一的意识中更加充分地扎根。

Ramakrishna, the great Indian saint, likened the situation to a coach in which the driver (the ego) sits atop in command of the horses. The owner (the higher Self) sits quietly within. Because the coachman has never seen the owner, he begins to think himself totally in charge. But when the owner makes himself known, quietly but firmly, the coachman, perhaps begrudgingly but ultimately in his best interests, relinquishes his fantasy and becomes content in the role of … of what? Of servant , it turns out. For then it responds more and more to the call “Not my but Thy Will, O Lord.” The ego finds joy and relief in attuning to the greater Way of All Things, to the larger harmonies of the universe in which it can find its proper place and need no longer be driven by the insatiable need to control. In surrender to its proper station, the ego finds peace. The higher Self is now freer to guide the work of loving kindness and compassion. The character of service also begins to change.

印度伟大的圣人罗摩克里希那将这种情况比作一辆马车，车夫（自我）坐在车顶，指挥着马匹。车主（更高的自我）则静静地坐在车内。由于车夫从未见过车主，他便开始自以为是，认为自己拥有绝对的掌控权。但当车主平静而坚定地现身时，车夫或许心怀不满，但最终为了自身利益，他放弃了幻想，并开始满足于扮演……什么角色呢？原来是仆人。因为那时，他越来越能回应“主啊，并非出于我的意愿，而是出于你的旨意”的呼唤。自我与万物之道、与宇宙更宏大的和谐相契合，从而找到了喜悦和解脱，找到了自己应有的位置，不再受那永无止境的控制欲驱使。在臣服于自身应有的位置时，自我找到了平静。更高的自我现在可以更自由地引导慈悲与仁爱的实践。服务的本质也开始发生改变。

~

Now there are two theories about crime and how to deal with it. Anticrime guys say, “You have to think like a criminal.” And some police learn that so well they get a kind of criminal mentality themselves .

现在关于犯罪及其应对方法有两种理论。反犯罪人士认为，“你必须像罪犯一样思考。”有些警察对此深信不疑，以至于他们自己也形成了某种犯罪心态。

How I’m working with it is really pretty different. I see that man is essentially pure and innocent and of one good nature. That’s who he is by birthright. And that’s what I’m affirming in the course of a day on the job. In fact, that is my job. The “cop” part of it … well, they call us “cops”; to me, my job is I’m a peace officer .

我处理这件事的方式确实很不一样。我认为人本质上是纯洁无辜的，本性善良。这是他与生俱来的权利。而这正是我在日常工作中要肯定的。事实上，这就是我的工作。“警察”这个身份……嗯，他们叫我们“警察”；对我来说，我的工作是维护治安。

Now it’s interesting how this works. For example, when you are holding in thought a vision of our unity in good, you frequently spot a criminal motive arising or evident in someone. It’s a kind of spiritual radar. Crimes can be prevented that way—I’ve seen that. And not only that. At the same time, I’m holding to the view that such a person is complete already, and doesn’t need to steal, and will be provided for from universal abundance. So I work not only to prevent the crime but to eliminate its causes—its causes in fear and greed, not just the social causes everyone talks about .

现在，这其中的原理很有意思。例如，当你心中默想我们因善而合一的景象时，你常常会察觉到某人身上正在萌生或显露出的犯罪动机。这就像一种精神雷达。犯罪可以通过这种方式预防——我亲眼见过。不仅如此，与此同时，我坚信这样的人本身已经圆满，无需偷窃，宇宙的丰盛会满足他的一切所需。因此，我的工作不仅是预防犯罪，更是消除犯罪的根源——恐惧和贪婪，而不仅仅是人们常说的社会因素。

Even when it gets to conflict. I had arrested a very angry black man who singled me out for real animosity. When I had to take him to a paddy wagon, he spit in my face—that was something—and he went after me with a chair. We handcuffed him and put him in the truck. Well, on the way, I just had to get past this picture of things, and again I affirmed to myself, “This guy and I are brothers in love.” When I got to the station, I was moved spontaneously to say, “Look, if I’ve done anything to offend you, I apologize.” The paddy wagon driver looked at me as if I was totally nuts .

即使发生冲突，我也一样。我逮捕了一个非常愤怒的黑人，他似乎对我怀有强烈的敌意。当我把他押上警车时，他朝我脸上吐了口唾沫——这可真是够狠的——然后还拿着椅子追着我。我们给他戴上手铐，把他塞进警车。在路上，我必须努力让自己摆脱这种情绪，我再次告诉自己：“我和他情同手足。”到了警局，我情不自禁地说：“听着，如果我做了什么冒犯你的事，我道歉。”警车司机看着我，好像我疯了一样。

The next day I had to take him from where he’d been housed overnight to criminal court. When I picked him up, I thought, “Well, if you trust this vision, you’re not going to have to handcuff him.” And I didn’t. We got to a spot in the middle of the corridor which was the place where he’d have jumped me if he had that intention. And he stopped suddenly. So did I. Then he said, “You know, I thought about what you said yesterday, and I want to apologize.” I just felt this deep appreciation .

第二天，我得把他从昨晚的拘留所带到刑事法庭。接他的时候，我心想：“嗯，如果你相信我的预感，就不用给他戴手铐了。” 我确实没戴。我们走到走廊中间，如果他真想袭击我，他早就从这里下手了。他突然停了下来，我也停了下来。然后他说：“你知道吗，我一直在想你昨天说的话，我想向你道歉。” 我当时心里充满了感激。

Turned out on his rap sheet he’d done a lot of time in Michigan and had trouble with guards in jail. I symbolized something. And I saw that turn around, saw a kind of healing, I believe .

结果发现他的犯罪记录显示，他曾在密歇根州服刑很长时间，而且在监狱里和狱警有过冲突。我象征着某种东西。我看到了他的转变，看到了一种治愈，我相信是这样。

So what really happens if you’re going to explore whether or not this vision of our nature really has power? Maybe people will say you’re taking chances. But you’re taking chances without any vision; your vision is your protection. Maybe they’ll say you’re sentimentalizing people. But it’s not about people. It’s about principle and truth. It’s about how the universe is. Maybe they’ll think it’s idealistic; things could never be this way. Well, for me, things are this way already; it’s just up to us to know that more clearly .

那么，如果你要去探索这种关于我们人性的观点是否真的具有力量，究竟会发生什么呢？也许有人会说你是在冒险。但你是在冒险，却没有任何远见；远见才是你的保护伞。也许有人会说你是在过度感伤。但这无关乎人，而是关乎原则和真理，关乎宇宙的本来面目。也许有人会觉得这太理想化，认为事情不可能如此。但对我而言，事情本来就是这样，只是我们需要更清晰地认识到这一点。

I see that my work is to hold to an image of who we all truly are, and to be guided by that. And I have been guided by that. To greater strength and security … within myself and on the street .

我认为我的工作就是坚守我们每个人真实的自我形象，并以此为指引。而我也一直遵循着这个指引，获得了更大的力量和安全感……无论是在内心深处还是在街头巷尾。

~

What follows in the quality of our helping when we begin to know ourselves beyond separateness?

当我们开始超越分离的视角去认识自己时，我们助人的质量会发生怎样的变化？

Perhaps, at the very least, we can be a little less fearful, a little more trusting. When we break through the boundaries of self, we often find that we don’t have to be as defensive as we might have thought or as might have been our habit. Things aren’t inevitably pitted against us. If they appear to be, the possibility of harmony and reconciliation is a little more real. When we’ve had a taste of unity, we’re that much more ready to bring it quickly into any situation, at any given moment, with anybody.

或许，至少我们可以少一些恐惧，多一些信任。当我们突破自我设限时，往往会发现我们不必像想象中或习惯中那样充满防备。事情并非总是与我们作对。即便看似如此，和谐与和解的可能性也更加真实。当我们体验过团结的滋味，就能更随时、更迅速地将这种精神带入任何情境，与任何人相处。

We’ll also be more likely to take initiative and to reach out less self-consciously to those in need. Someone may be a little shy asking for help, and we ourselves may be a little tentative offering it. But we can overcome these boundaries more quickly because we’ve already been working to see that they’re not inevitably so solid. How many times, after all, do we initially hold back with one another, only to laugh when we finally break through the caution and meet openly and freely? How long it takes for this to happen depends entirely upon how much we’re coming into these situations feeling separate. What’s to prevent us from meeting in compassion instantaneously?

我们也会更愿意主动出击，更自在地帮助有需要的人。有些人可能不好意思开口求助，而我们自己也可能在伸出援手时有些犹豫。但我们可以更快地突破这些界限，因为我们已经开始努力认识到它们并非牢不可破。毕竟，我们有多少次最初都对彼此有所保留，最终却在打破戒备、坦诚相待时开怀大笑？这一切发生需要多久，完全取决于我们进入这些情境时有多大的隔阂感。究竟是什么阻碍了我们瞬间以同理心相待呢？

The more we’re able to take such initiative trustingly, the greater sense of range and possibility we’re likely to have in our efforts to help out. We might feel more patience—we’ll work longer and harder with a retarded child or someone in physical therapy—when we have more confidence that there are sources of support beyond ourselves. Something may happen, someone may come along, a moment of insight, a flash of inspiration, a new source of energy. We’re more trusting of the universe because we have experienced nourishment in those moments when we’ve felt at One with it.

我们越能以信任的态度主动采取行动，就越有可能在帮助他人方面拥有更广阔的视野和更大的可能性。当我们更有信心相信自身之外还有其他支持来源时，我们或许会更有耐心——我们会花更多的时间和精力去帮助智障儿童或正在接受物理治疗的人。或许会发生一些事情，或许会有人出现，或许会灵光一闪，或许会迸发出灵感，或许会获得新的能量。当我们感受到与宇宙合一的时刻，并从中汲取滋养时，我们便会更加信任宇宙。

Being less cautious, we’ll be more likely to take risks in the expression of our helping instincts. Perhaps in the midst of a grim situation near a family sickbed, heads shaking, brows all furrowed, we’ll take a chance and say, “This is quite a soap opera we’re all stuck in here.” Now maybe they’ll throw us right out of the room; that’s how much of a soap opera it is. But maybe it’ll be just what’s needed to break the tension. Maybe a few people will be able to come up for a moment’s air, see the horizon beyond the next wave, remember the big picture, then take a deep breath before plunging back in the midst of it all. We’ve succeeded in interrupting the soap opera for a brief public service message. Worth a try anyhow. At the very least, we’re seeing that we can stretch ourselves, go beyond what’s familiar, trust our instincts a little more. All this is possible because we’re not so firmly wed to models of ourselves and how we’re supposed to behave when we’re seeking to help one another. Less afraid that reaching out threatens our own well-being, we’re freer and more venturesome in expressing our caring instincts.

少些谨慎，我们或许更愿意冒险，更乐于表达助人的本能。也许在家人病床旁，气氛凝重，众人摇头叹息，眉头紧锁之时，我们会鼓起勇气说：“这简直就是一场肥皂剧，我们都被困在这里了。” 也许他们会把我们赶出房间；这剧就是这么狗血。但也许，这恰恰是打破僵局所需要的。也许有些人能借此喘口气，看看下一波浪潮之后的地平线，重新审视大局，然后深吸一口气，再重新投入到这一切之中。我们成功地打断了这场肥皂剧，传递了一个简短的公益信息。无论如何，值得一试。至少，我们看到了自己可以拓展视野，超越熟悉的领域，更加相信自己的直觉。这一切之所以成为可能，是因为我们不再那么执着于自我认知模式以及在互助时应该如何表现。我们不再害怕伸出援手会威胁到自身的福祉，因此在表达关爱本能时，我们更加自由、更加大胆。

As we approach other people in this spirit, we’ll also be more likely to communicate what we have in common rather than what divides us. Knocking on someone’s door with a petition protesting utility rates, we won’t have to meet as “righteous activist” and “reluctant housewife.” Maybe we’ll get engrossed in the smell of the soup inside as the door opens. We’ll begin talking recipes, talking grandparents’ recipes, talking grandparents … and then, almost as an afterthought, “Oh, by the way, I had this petition. I don’t know about your utility rates, but ours …” “Oh, yes. Ours too. I don’t usually get involved in this stuff, but sure, right—where do I sign?”

当我们以这种精神与他人交往时，我们更有可能交流彼此的共同点，而不是分歧。当我们带着抗议水电费的请愿书敲开别人家的门时，我们不必以“正义的行动主义者”和“不情愿的家庭主妇”的身份出现。也许门一打开，我们就会被屋里飘来的汤香所吸引。我们会开始聊食谱，聊祖父母的食谱，聊祖父母……然后，几乎像是突然想起什么似的，说道：“哦，对了，我这里有个请愿书。我不知道你们那边的水电费怎么样，但我们这边……”“哦，是的。我们这边也是。我平时不怎么管这些事，不过，好吧——我该在哪儿签名呢？”

As we become less identified with any single aspect of the separate self against another, we’re freer to know which among them all is most appropriate for a given situation. It’s as if we can be anyone to anyone. Resting behind all roles, we can also be, as it were, no one to no one—that is, we can create a space where whoever we’re with has the best chance to come out from behind their self-image. No costumes, no disguises; come as you are.

当我们不再执着于将自我与他人对立起来的某个单一面向时，我们就能更自由地判断在特定情境下，哪个面向才是最合适的。仿佛我们可以成为任何人眼中的任何人。卸下所有角色，我们也可以成为“无我之人”——也就是说，我们可以创造一个空间，让与我们相处的人有机会卸下自我形象的束缚，展现最真实的自我。无需伪装，无需掩饰；做你自己。

The awareness that allows us to rest behind ego, moreover, also gives us a far greater ability to listen to others, to hear what’s really needed. Our intuition can guide our actions. The universe is filled with information. Answers are inherent in questions. The less our mind is busy feeding the ego, the more we can allow our “spiritual radar” to come into play, the more we can tune into One Mind.

此外，这种让我们能够放下自我、安住于其后的觉知，也赋予我们更强的倾听他人、聆听他人真正需求的能力。我们的直觉可以指引我们的行动。宇宙充满信息，答案蕴藏于问题之中。我们的头脑越少被自我所支配，就越能让我们“灵性雷达”发挥作用，越能与万物一体的意识相契合。

Our work to move beyond separateness may also strengthen our sense of abundance. We feel like we need less because we’re coming to see just how much we’ll always have access to. We don’t have to ration our helping acts quite so carefully. We needn’t constantly measure just how much we’ll be able to offer before we get depleted. We don’t have to feel as if we are sacrificing by giving. Beyond separateness, service replenishes. “To forget the Self is to be enlightened by all things.”

我们努力超越分离，或许也能增强我们的富足感。我们感到自己需要的更少，是因为我们逐渐明白，我们永远都能获得如此之多。我们不必再那么小心翼翼地分配助人之举。我们不必总是衡量自己还能付出多少，以免耗尽。我们不必觉得付出是一种牺牲。超越分离，服务本身就能带来滋养。“忘却自我，方能从万物中获得启迪。”

In turn, our helping actions will be less directed by the ego’s personal agenda and need for constant reassurance. We won’t be entering into service so much to gain intimacy, purpose, a sense of usefulness, and so on. We don’t need to go anywhere special to attain these. They’re in us already and available all around, simply as we understand our interrelatedness with all things. Our service, then, is less a function of personal motive and more an expression of spontaneous, appropriate caring.

反过来，我们的助人行为将不再受自我中心的个人目的和对持续肯定的需求所驱使。我们参与服务的目的不再是为了获得亲密感、目标感、价值感等等。我们无需去任何特殊的地方去获得这些。它们早已存在于我们自身，并且触手可及，只要我们理解自身与万物之间的相互关联。因此，我们的服务不再是出于个人动机，而更多地是出于自发的、恰当的关怀。

We’re not so much helping out, then, because it’s “me” needing to tend to “you.” We’re helping out because it’s “Us.” The more we understand and dwell in that truth, the more we serve simply in the way of things. If one of “Us” needs help, if one of Our arms gets caught in a door, naturally we use the other of Our arms to set it free. Helping happens not because it’s been weighed and considered; it happens because the barriers to its lawful and automatic expression have fallen away.

因此，我们并非因为“我”需要照顾“你”而伸出援手，而是因为这是“我们”的本能。我们越理解并深谙此理，就越能自然而然地提供帮助。如果“我们”中的任何一人需要帮助，如果我们的一只手臂被门夹住，我们自然会用另一只手臂将其解救出来。帮助的发生并非出于深思熟虑，而是因为阻碍其自然而然表达的障碍已经消失。

And, finally, what of those moments when we question whether we’ve anything useful for others? What do we really have to offer, what do we really have to give? Everything , it turns out. Everything. If within each of us is that essence of Being which is in all things—call it God, Life, Energy, Consciousness—as open to all that as we are in ourselves, so we have it to share with one another.

最后，当我们质疑自己是否能为他人带来任何价值时，又该如何呢？我们究竟能提供什么，真正能给予什么？答案是：一切。一切。如果我们每个人内在都蕴藏着万物之中的本质——你可以称之为上帝、生命、能量、意识——它像我们自身一样对万物敞开，那么我们便能与他人分享这一切。

What could that mean practically, as more than a lofty abstraction? It could mean that when we’re holding a frightened, battered child … or hearing the grief of a total stranger … or bandaging the wound of an enemy soldier … or sitting with a dying friend … they can feel in who we are the reassurance that they are not simply isolated entities, separate selves, lonely beings, cut off from everything and everyone else. They can feel us in there with them. They can feel the comfort that we are all of us in this together. They have the chance to know, in moments of great pain, that nevertheless we are Not Separate.

这在实际生活中意味着什么？它不仅仅是一个高深的抽象概念。它可能意味着，当我们抱着一个受惊受伤的孩子……或者聆听一个陌生人的悲痛……或者包扎一个敌军士兵的伤口……或者陪伴一个垂死的朋友……他们能从我们身上感受到安慰，让他们知道自己并非孤立的个体，并非与世隔绝的孤独存在。他们能感受到我们与他们同在。他们能感受到我们彼此相连的慰藉。他们有机会在极度痛苦的时刻明白，我们并非彼此分离。

When all else fails, when we’ve done what we can, we still have this essential reassurance to offer one another. It comes as each of us moves beyond attachment to separateness into a greater sense of Unity. “To be enlightened by all things is to remove the barrier between Self and Other.”

当一切都无济于事，当我们竭尽所能之后，我们仍然可以彼此给予这份至关重要的慰藉。它源于我们每个人超越对分离的执着，走向更深层次的合一。“从万物中汲取智慧，便是消除自我与他者之间的隔阂。”

# ↩

3
3
Suffering
受苦

M y idea was pretty simple at the beginning. I started to volunteer in wards with terminally ill children or burn victims—just go in there to cheer them up a little, spread around some giggles. Gradually, it developed that I was going to come in as a clown .

最初我的想法很简单。我开始去病房做义工，照顾那些身患绝症的儿童或烧伤患者——只是进去逗他们开心，带给他们一些欢笑。后来，我的想法逐渐演变成以小丑的身份去那里表演。

First, somebody gave me a red rubber nose, and I put that to work. Then I started doing some elementary makeup. Then I got a yellow, red, and green clown suit. Finally, some nifty, tremendous wing-tip shoes, about two and a half feet long, with green tips and heels, white in the middle. They came from a clown who was retiring and wanted his feet to keep on walking .

首先，有人给了我一个红色橡胶鼻子，我就用上了。然后我开始化一些简单的妆。接着我弄到了一套黄、红、绿三色的小丑服。最后，我又得到了一双非常漂亮、气势磅礴的翼尖鞋，大约两英尺半长，鞋尖和鞋跟是绿色的，鞋面是白色的。这双鞋是一位即将退休的小丑留下的，他想让自己的脚继续“行走”。

It’s a little tricky coming in. Some kids, when they see a clown, they think they’re going to be eaten alive. And kids in hospitals and burn units, of course, are pretty shaky. So it’s always good to lead with some bubbles, just blow some bubbles around the ward. Then I’ll move from bed to bed, just feeling out what’s appropriate: maybe checkers, or blackjack, or go-fish. Or if they’re lying there with tubes coming out of them, I’ll hit the kids with riddles. Riddles are great .

刚开始的时候有点棘手。有些孩子一看到小丑，就觉得会被活活吃掉。当然，在医院和烧伤病房里的孩子通常都很紧张。所以，最好先吹吹泡泡，在病房里到处吹吹泡泡。然后我会挨个病床走，看看什么游戏比较合适：比如下跳棋、玩二十一点或者钓鱼。如果他们身上插着管子躺在那里，我就给他们出谜语。谜语真是个好主意。

Later, if they can manage it, I’ll give them this paper bag that they can fit over their heads. When they put it on and sort of blow their lips together, they can make this crazy sound I call the Funny Mantra. They turn into a living kazoo. I’ll say, “If things get too tough, just take that paper bag from under your pillow and sound off. Maybe that’ll help a little, and it’ll sure surprise the nurses.”

之后，如果他们能做到，我会给他们一个纸袋，套在头上。他们戴上纸袋，抿紧嘴唇，就能发出一种我称之为“滑稽咒语”的怪异声音。他们就像活生生的卡祖笛。我会说：“如果情况太糟糕，就从枕头底下拿出那个纸袋，吹起来。也许会有点用，而且肯定会让护士们大吃一惊。”

Because things do get very tough in there, I’ll tell you. They were very tough for me at the beginning—very. You see some pretty terrible things in these wards. Seeing children dying or mutilated is nothing most of us ever get prepared for. Nobody teaches us to face suffering in this society. We never talk about it until we get hit in the face .

我跟你说，那里的情况真的非常艰难。一开始对我来说尤其如此——非常艰难。你会在那些病房里看到一些非常可怕的事情。亲眼目睹孩子死亡或残疾，是我们大多数人从未预料到的。在这个社会里，没有人教我们如何面对苦难。我们从来不谈论苦难，直到我们自己遭受打击。

Like when I was starting out I was making the rounds one day at a children’s hospital. The shade was pulled on this one room so I couldn’t see, but I peeked in the door. It was a room with badly burned children in it. They had them in chrome crib beds with walls on the side, so they couldn’t crawl out or fall out if it got too terrible in there .

就像我刚入行的时候，有一天我在一家儿童医院巡诊。其中一个房间的窗帘拉上了，我看不见里面，但我还是从门缝里往里看了一眼。房间里躺着几个严重烧伤的孩子。他们睡在带侧墙的铬合金婴儿床上，这样即使情况变得太糟糕，他们也不会爬出来或掉下去。

There was this one little black kid in one of them. He was horribly burned. He looked like burnt toast. Pieces of his face weren’t there. Pieces of his ears were missing. Where was his mouth? You could hardly tell who he was. There was no way of pinning a person to the face, what little there was of it .

其中一具尸体里有个黑人小孩，他被严重烧伤，看起来像烤焦的面包。他的脸部缺了一块，耳朵也缺了一块，嘴巴呢？你几乎认不出他是谁。那张残存的脸根本无法辨认出他是谁。

It was just terrible, just mind-boggling. My jaw dropped, I gasped, and I came completely unglued. I remember flashing back to the antiwar movement. There was a picture of a napalmed kid I used to carry around at demonstrations. Suddenly here was that kid right in front of me. Unbelievably painful to behold .

真是太可怕了，简直难以置信。我目瞪口呆，倒吸一口凉气，彻底崩溃了。我记得当时脑海里闪过反战运动的画面。我以前参加示威游行时，总会带着一张被凝固汽油弹炸伤的孩子的照片。突然间，那个孩子就出现在我眼前。看到这一幕，我感到无比痛苦。

I was overwhelmed. And my mind went off in all sorts of directions. “What’s it going to be like if he lives?” “What if I had a child this happened to?” “What if this happened to me?”

我当时不知所措，思绪纷乱。“如果他活下来会怎样？”“如果我的孩子也遭遇了这种事怎么办？”“如果这种事发生在我身上怎么办？”

So there we were, burnt toast and unglued clown. Quite a sight, I bet. And I’m fighting just to stay there, trying to find a way to get past my horror .

于是，我们就那样待在那里，烤焦的面包和脱胶的小丑。我敢打赌，那景象一定很滑稽。而我却挣扎着想待在那里，努力想办法克服内心的恐惧。

All of a sudden, this other little kid comes whizzing by—I think he was skating along with his IV pole—and he stops, and kinda pushes around me, and looks into the crib at this other kid, and comes out with, “Hey. YOU UGLY!” Just like that. And the burnt kid made this gurgling laugh kind of noise and his face moved around, and all of a sudden I just went for his eyes, and we locked up right there, and everything else just dissolved. It was like going through a tunnel right to his heart. And all the burnt flesh disappeared, and I saw him from another place. We settled right in .

突然，另一个小男孩嗖地一下滑了过来——我猜他是推着输液架滑过来的——他停了下来，绕过我，看着婴儿床里的另一个孩子，然后说：“嘿，你真丑！” 就这么突然。那个烧伤的孩子发出咕噜咕噜的笑声，脸也动了起来，我突然就直直地盯着他的眼睛，我们瞬间凝视着彼此，其他的一切都消失了。就像穿过一条隧道直达他的心脏。所有烧伤的皮肤都消失了，我从另一个角度看到了他。我们就这样安定下来了。

“YOU UGLY!” Right. He ugly. He probably knows how ugly he is more than anyone else. And if he’s gotta deal with people hanging around with saliva coming out of their mouths, it’s gonna be extra horrible. But if somebody just meets him in the eye and says, “Hey, what’s happening? Wanna hear a riddle …?”

“你真丑！”没错，他确实丑。他可能比任何人都清楚自己有多丑。如果他还要应付那些口水直流的人，那就更糟了。但如果有人直视他的眼睛，说：“嘿，最近怎么样？想听个谜语吗……？”

So being able to look You Ugly in the eye … that’s done a lot for me. Because once I do that, I can go on to see what might be done that can ease things up. And you get all kinds of inspiration .

所以，能够直视自己的丑陋……这对我的帮助非常大。因为一旦我这么做了，我就可以继续思考有什么办法能让情况好转。而且你会从中获得各种各样的灵感。

Like, some of us were setting up to show Godzilla in the kids’ leukemia ward. I was making up kids as clowns. One kid was totally bald from chemotherapy, and when I finished doing his face, another kid said, “Go on and do the rest of his head.” The kid loved the idea. And when I was done, his sister said, “Hey, we can show the movie on Billy’s head.” And he really loved that idea. So we set up Godzilla and ran it on Billy’s head, and Billy was pleased as punch, and we were all mighty proud of Billy. It was quite a moment. Especially when the doctors arrived .

当时，我们几个正准备在儿童白血病病房放映《哥斯拉》。我正给孩子们化妆扮成小丑。有个孩子因为化疗秃了个光头，我给他脸上弄好妆后，另一个孩子说：“你再给他头上也弄一下。” 这孩子很喜欢这个主意。等我弄好之后，他妹妹说：“嘿，我们可以把电影放到比利头上放。” 他也特别喜欢这个主意。于是我们把《哥斯拉》放到比利头上放映，比利高兴极了，我们也都为他感到无比自豪。那真是个难忘的时刻。尤其是医生们赶到的时候。

So I don’t know. Burnt skin or bald heads on little kids—what do you do? I guess you just face it—when the kids are really hurting so bad, and so afraid, and probably dying, and everybody’s heart is breaking. Face it, and see what happens after that, see what to do next .

所以，我也不知道。小孩子皮肤烧伤或者秃顶——该怎么办？我想你只能面对现实——当孩子们真的那么痛苦、那么害怕，甚至可能濒临死亡，每个人的心都碎了的时候。面对现实，看看接下来会发生什么，看看下一步该怎么做。

I got the idea of traveling with popcorn. When a kid is crying I dab up the tears with the popcorn and pop it into my mouth or into his or hers. We sit around together and eat the tears .

我想到一个办法，就是带着爆米花旅行。孩子哭的时候，我就用爆米花擦掉他们的眼泪，然后把爆米花塞进自己嘴里或者孩子嘴里。我们围坐在一起，一边吃着爆米花，一边安慰他们。

~

Suffering seems to be a fact of life. How do we face it? Clearly it is a stranger to none of us. Perhaps we’ve not experienced the corrosive pain of illness, persecution, starvation, or violence. We may not have lived with the deterioration and loss of a loved one. Few of us have seen the charred face of a burned child. But each of us has experienced our fair share of not getting what we want or having to deal with what we don’t want. In this, we all know suffering.

苦难似乎是人生的一部分。我们该如何面对它？显然，它对我们每个人来说都不陌生。或许我们从未经历过疾病、迫害、饥饿或暴力的剧痛。我们或许没有经历过亲人病情恶化和离世的痛苦。我们当中很少有人见过被烧伤的孩子焦黑的脸。但我们每个人都经历过无法如愿以偿或不得不面对不愿面对之事的痛苦。在这一点上，我们都懂得苦难。

The way in which we deal with suffering has much to do with the way in which we are able to be of service to others. Of course, not all helping revolves around suffering. Much of what we offer may be in the nature of simple support or guidance: moving a friend’s new furniture, teaching a child to read. But it is the affliction of others that most directly awakens in us the desire to be of care and comfort.

我们应对苦难的方式与我们如何帮助他人息息相关。当然，并非所有的帮助都与苦难有关。我们提供的许多帮助可能只是简单的支持或指导：比如帮朋友搬运新家具，教孩子读书。但正是他人的苦难最能直接地唤起我们关爱和安慰的愿望。

The impulse to do all we can to relieve one another’s pain is the automatic response of our native compassion. But the experience of suffering—in ourselves and in others—triggers off complicated reactions. To investigate these is itself an act of compassion, an essential step toward becoming more effective instruments of mutual support and healing. How then do we respond to the pain we see around us? And, once we have investigated this response, how do we respond to our own afflictions?

我们竭尽所能去减轻彼此的痛苦，这是我们与生俱来的同情心的自然反应。然而，无论是自身还是他人的痛苦经历，都会引发复杂的反应。探究这些反应本身就是一种同情，也是我们成为更有效的互助和疗愈工具的关键一步。那么，我们该如何回应周遭的痛苦？而当我们探究了这种回应之后，又该如何应对自身的苦难呢？

~

At one level, we seem to have an attraction-aversion relationship to human suffering. Sometimes our attraction seems to take a neurotic form. It seems to trigger off an almost morbid fascination. We continually feed ourselves, through newspapers, soap operas, tragedies, and gossip with images of suffering. It’s as if our vicarious involvement with the trials and tribulations of others engages us in the life process in a way that we seem to need but also want to be able to control. We want to watch it, but be able to turn it off at will.

在某种程度上，我们似乎对人类的苦难既趋之若鹜又避之不及。有时，这种趋之若鹜似乎带有某种神经质的意味，仿佛会引发一种近乎病态的迷恋。我们不断地通过报纸、肥皂剧、悲剧和八卦来获取苦难的画面。就好像我们通过间接的方式参与到他人的苦难之中，从而以一种我们既需要又想要掌控的方式融入到人生进程中。我们想观看，却又想随时关掉。

At another and deeper level, however, the suffering of others spontaneously awakens a response of instant empathy.

然而，在另一个更深层次上，他人的痛苦会自发地唤起人们的即时同情心。

You’re right behind a man on the unemployment line. His eyes are red: you can tell he’s been drinking. He finally gets his turn after waiting three hours, only to be told he’s got to come back with the right papers. He’s confused, but he nods; he doesn’t want to make trouble. But as he leaves the line, you can tell he didn’t get it quite right, and he probably won’t make it back next week. He’s heading for a bar and it’s ten-thirty in the morning.

你排在一个领取失业救济金的男人后面。他双眼通红，一看就知道喝过酒。等了三个小时，他终于轮到自己了，却被告知要带齐证件再来。他一脸茫然，但还是点了点头，不想惹麻烦。可当他离开队伍时，你看得出来他没带齐证件，下周恐怕就来不及了。他正往酒吧走去，现在是早上十点半。

Your closest friends, married for twenty years, are fighting bitterly, right there in the restaurant, right there in front of you and their kids. You’ve never seen them act that way before. The marriage is falling apart. One daughter is staring at her soup. The other flashes you a look of panic.

你最亲密的朋友，结婚二十年了，正在餐厅里激烈争吵，就在你和孩子们面前。你从未见过他们这样。他们的婚姻岌岌可危。一个女儿盯着她的汤发呆，另一个女儿惊恐地朝你瞥了一眼。

Your heart goes out to them, goes out to them all. The pain of others gives rise to a desire to help, to comfort, to touch, to say “I’m here, I’m with you, I understand.”

你会对他们感同身受，对他们所有人感同身受。他人的痛苦会激起你想要帮助、安慰、触摸他们的愿望，想要告诉他们“我在这里，我和你在一起，我理解你”。

But it’s one thing to have one’s heart engaged, quite another to have it overwhelmed or broken. Here lies our aversion to suffering. For when it gets too close and too strong—the terrible suffering of a parent, child, lover, best friend—we may experience a pain so excruciating that it can threaten the very fabric of our being, shatter our tenuously held faith, and cast us into deepest despair.

但内心被触动是一回事，被深深震撼或破碎又是另一回事。这正是我们厌恶苦难的原因。因为当苦难来得太近、太强烈时——比如父母、子女、爱人、挚友的惨痛经历——我们可能会感受到一种难以忍受的痛苦，这种痛苦甚至会威胁到我们存在的根基，摧毁我们脆弱的信仰，并将我们推入最深的绝望。

Between the event to which we feel no personal connection and a tragedy that breaks our hearts, there is a vast range of affliction. In this domain we make our choices: Shall I become involved or not, and if so, how deeply? How much human pain to let in, and whose? Because the suffering around us is endless, the choices before us seem limitless. We must weigh them carefully, lest, once we have opened Pandora’s box, pain overwhelm us, and jeopardize our fragile control of the universe around.

从我们毫无个人关联的事件到令我们心碎的悲剧，苦难的范围极其广泛。在这个领域，我们面临着选择：我是否应该介入？如果应该，介入到什么程度？我应该承受多少人间的痛苦？又该承受谁的痛苦？因为我们周围的苦难似乎无穷无尽，摆在我们面前的选择也似乎无穷无尽。我们必须谨慎权衡，否则，一旦打开潘多拉魔盒，痛苦就会将我们淹没，危及我们对周遭世界的脆弱掌控。

This range of choices is recent and perhaps unique to our present culture. Where people live their whole lives in close proximity, there’s very little choice. Suffering involves all. The village’s orphans are everybody’s children.

这种选择范围是近些年才出现的，或许也是我们当今文化所独有的。在人们终生生活在狭小空间里的环境中，选择非常有限。苦难波及所有人。村里的孤儿就是每个人的孩子。

But affluence has bought us privacy, and the apparent power to guard it against the encroachments of other people’s adversity. As individuals and as a society, we set up lines of defense. We isolate poverty, old age, and death so that we need not confront them in our daily lives. The poor are off in ghettos, the elderly in retirement homes, the dying in terminal care wards. We pay to push suffering away.

但富裕为我们带来了隐私，以及抵御他人苦难侵扰的强大力量。作为个人和社会，我们筑起层层防线。我们将贫困、衰老和死亡隔离开来，以免在日常生活中直面它们。穷人被安置在贫民窟，老人被安置在养老院，临终者被安置在临终关怀病房。我们花钱将苦难拒之门外。

But privacy exacts its costs. How quickly, for example, it turns to loneliness and alienation. Our defense against one kind of suffering, ironically, turns out to have invited in another. We may somehow feel safe from the troubles of the world, but we also begin to feel dry, empty, and alone in our insulated havens. Gone is the mutuality and spontaneous support that arise naturally when lives are led in common. With doors closed to the pain of others, we banish that which would release our compassion and engagement with life. We need heart-to-heart resuscitation.

但隐私是有代价的。例如，它很快就会变成孤独和疏离。讽刺的是，我们为了抵御一种痛苦而采取的防御措施，最终却招致了另一种痛苦。我们或许会觉得远离世间的烦恼，但同时也会在与世隔绝的避风港里感到枯燥、空虚和孤独。当人们共同生活时自然而然产生的互助和自发的支持消失了。当我们对别人的痛苦紧闭大门时，我们也扼杀了那些能够释放我们同情心和积极参与生活的力量。我们需要心与心的交流，需要彼此的滋养。

Nor does the privacy actually end up buying us any final protection. Despite it, we’re still interconnected with the peoples of the planet. While our isolation may give us some degree of temporary peace, there’s little security in peace based on exclusion. As America has found out, the insistent goad of the world’s suffering will ultimately force entry even into our well-protected castle. The pain and anger of those who are oppressed shape the challenges of our political life. If their suffering seems abstract, it is nonetheless ever present through networks of communication which extend our knowledge of human affliction to the outermost reaches of the planet. We can push it all away only so far.

隐私最终也无法为我们提供任何最终的保障。尽管如此，我们仍然与地球上的人们息息相关。虽然我们的孤立或许能带来某种程度的暂时和平，但建立在排斥基础上的和平却缺乏真正的安全感。正如美国所经历的那样，世界苦难的持续刺激最终会迫使人们进入我们戒备森严的堡垒。受压迫者的痛苦和愤怒塑造了我们政治生活的挑战。他们的苦难或许看似抽象，但它却通过各种通信网络无处不在，这些网络将我们对人类苦难的认知延伸到地球的最远端。我们只能将这一切推到一定程度。

Because our privacy is finally unfulfilling, and the pain of others ultimately can’t be ignored, we find we must choose how much suffering we can let in, and what to do with it once it’s there.

因为我们的隐私最终无法满足我们的需求，而且我们最终无法忽视他人的痛苦，所以我们发现自己必须选择能够承受多少痛苦，以及一旦痛苦来临该如何处理。

These choices are usually made in the midst of a mighty struggle between the head and the heart.

这些选择通常是在理智与情感激烈斗争中做出的。

The suffering of others spontaneously releases our desire to help out. Our heart begins to open. But then there’s a thought: Is this problem too heavy? Do I have what it takes? If I offer to help, will I ever get away? Set off by fear, the mind is startled into self-defense. The fear, of course, is in part a reaction to the suffering itself. But it is also a response of resistance to the heart’s natural compassion as it reaches out to engage someone’s pain.

他人的苦难会自然而然地激发我们助人的愿望。我们的心开始敞开。但随后一个念头浮现：这个问题会不会太棘手？我能胜任吗？如果我伸出援手，会不会就此脱身？恐惧驱使着我们的大脑进入自我防御状态。当然，这种恐惧部分源于对苦难本身的反应。但它也是对内心自然流露的同情心的一种抗拒，这种同情心驱使我们去体会他人的痛苦。

Fear is the mind’s reaction against the inherent generosity of the heart. Because the heart knows no bounds to its giving, the mind feels called upon to define limits. Under such tension, little wonder our choices of how to respond to the pain of others seem so difficult.

恐惧是头脑对内心固有慷慨的一种反应。因为内心给予没有止境，头脑便会感到需要去设定界限。在这种紧张关系下，我们选择如何回应他人的痛苦似乎如此艰难也就不足为奇了。

Perhaps we seek to resolve this tension without really having to open the door to suffering: a quick call to a sick friend; a charitable contribution slipped through the mail slot; some grain to a third-world country. But do these measures really feed and satisfy the heart, our own and others’? As useful as they may be, they often shortchange our compassion. We know there’s more to helping than this.

或许我们试图在不真正面对苦难的情况下化解这种矛盾：给生病的朋友打个电话；从信箱里塞进一笔捐款；给第三世界国家捐赠一些粮食。但这些举措真的能滋养和满足我们自己和他人的心灵吗？它们或许有用，却往往忽略了我们的同情心。我们知道，助人远不止于此。

Perhaps we open the door partway. We define boundaries of time and space for our involvement: a year off for the Peace Corps; every Tuesday morning at the battered women’s shelter; eight hours a week with AIDS patients. We’ll vote ourselves, but we won’t go out to register others. “I’ll visit Aunt Rosie in the convalescent home, but I won’t bring her back to my house.” Our service takes place in the fifty-minute hour. Careful boundaries assure that suffering won’t spill over into the rest of our lives. These may be necessary; we all have other commitments. As often as not, however, they are artificially contrived to ward off that loss of control which so threatens and frightens the mind.

或许我们会半开大门。我们为自己的参与划定时间和空间的界限：去和平队待一年；每周二上午去受虐妇女庇护所；每周花八小时陪伴艾滋病患者。我们会自己投票，但不会去登记其他人的选民资格。“我会去疗养院探望罗西阿姨，但我不会把她带回家。”我们的奉献仅限于这五十分钟。精心划定的界限确保苦难不会蔓延到我们生活的其他方面。这些界限或许是必要的；我们每个人都有其他的责任。然而，很多时候，这些界限是人为设定的，目的是为了避免那种令人恐惧和不安的失控感。

But frequently these gestures fall short. Our boundaries prove to be Maginot Lines. Suffering presses through. So we retreat to our next line of defense: the mind itself and its array of tactics to protect its security in the face of pain.

但这些姿态往往不足以应对。我们的防线如同马奇诺防线，痛苦如潮水般涌来。于是，我们退守到下一道防线：心灵本身及其一系列在痛苦面前捍卫自身安全的策略。

There is, for example, the early-warning system of denial which often comes into play almost automatically. We blot out the suffering right before our eyes. We walk down the street past beggars and people obviously in pain without even noticing them. An ambulance goes by; it’s just a loud noise, it’ll pass. We hear cries in the night; it’s only a family feud, we turn over and go back to sleep. Potential nuclear annihilation is only twenty minutes away; we can’t handle the thought of it. It’s as if we have an invisible screen that deflects evidence of pain as soon as it gets close enough. How easily we delete it from awareness, without even being aware that we’ve done so.

例如，有一种名为“否认”的早期预警系统，它几乎是自动启动的。我们视而不见眼前的苦难。我们走过街道，路过乞丐和明显痛苦的人，却视而不见。救护车驶过；那只是一声巨响，很快就会过去。夜里听到哭喊声；那不过是家庭纠纷，我们翻个身继续睡。潜在的核毁灭只有二十分钟之遥；我们无法承受这种想法。仿佛我们身上有一层无形的屏障，一旦痛苦的迹象靠近，就会将其阻挡。我们如此轻易地将其从意识中抹去，甚至没有意识到自己已经这样做了。

About suffering they were never wrong,

在苦难这件事上，他们从未犯错。

The Old Masters: how well they understood

古代大师：他们对艺术的理解有多深刻

Its human position; how it takes place

它所处的人类位置；它是如何发生的

While someone else is eating or opening a window or just walking dully along .

当别人在吃饭、开窗或者只是漫不经心地走着的时候。

W. H. AUDEN

W·H·奥登

When this early-warning system fails, the mind must call on other devices in its repertory of response to suffering and the fear of it. One tactic is so simple we usually fail to notice it. We put some concept or idea between ourselves and the suffering. In comes Mary Jones, hurting real bad. As she sits across the desk she suddenly becomes Mary Jones, “schizophrenic.” With a flick of the mind, we’ve turned a person into a problem.

当这种预警系统失效时，大脑就必须调用其他应对痛苦和恐惧的机制。其中一种策略非常简单，我们通常都难以察觉。我们会在自己和痛苦之间设置某种概念或想法。玛丽·琼斯痛苦不堪地走进来。当她坐在桌子对面时，她突然变成了“精神分裂症患者”玛丽·琼斯。仅仅一念之差，我们就把一个人变成了一个问题。

Or we try to stuff suffering into a facile spiritual or philosophical perspective: “It’s just the way of things.” “Suffering is part of the Grand Plan.” “It’s their karma.” “Suffering is grace.” A party line, glib and heartless.

或者我们试图用肤浅的精神或哲学视角来解释苦难：“这就是事物的运行方式。”“苦难是宏伟计划的一部分。”“这是他们的业力。”“苦难是恩典。”这是一种老生常谈，轻率而冷酷无情。

Sometimes we even use the fact of human suffering to justify abstract ideologies. We use it to prove points.

有时我们甚至会利用人类的苦难来为抽象的意识形态辩护。我们用它来证明自己的观点。

~

I broke with a certain circle of antiwar friends, best friends, when dead lives became souvenirs .

当死去的生命变成纪念品时，我与一些反战朋友，甚至是最好的朋友，决裂了。

Some young Americans were invited to Czechoslovakia to meet the representative of the Viet Cong, the NLF. At the end they were given rings of friendship. They were made of steel from shot-down American planes .

一些美国青年受邀前往捷克斯洛伐克，与越共及其盟友——越南南方民族解放阵线（NLF）的代表会面。会面结束时，他们获赠友谊戒指，这些戒指是用被击落的美国飞机残骸的钢材制成的。

Now maybe to some that meant swords into plowshares. But for most, those rings were status symbols, radical macho. They got passed out very selectively. I didn’t hear any talk about the pilots of those planes and their families .

或许对某些人来说，这意味着化剑为犁。但对大多数人而言，那些戒指是身份的象征，是激进男子气概的体现。它们的发放非常谨慎。我没听到任何人谈论那些飞机的飞行员及其家人。

It sounds extreme. But the same thing happened with the slaughter at My Lai and television images of our soldiers burning village huts. Some people were more glad to see those images than they were pained by the death of innocent civilians. You could really see that. Antiwar people, all these .

听起来很极端。但美莱村大屠杀和电视上士兵焚烧村舍的画面也出现了同样的情况。有些人看到这些画面比看到无辜平民的死亡更感到高兴。这一点显而易见。反战人士，所有这些人。

~

“The greatest sin of the age,” wrote the Russian philosopher Nicholas Berdyaev, “is to make the concrete abstract.” That’s what the mind is trying to do through all these devices, and through efforts to explain things away. (Someone falls, and our attention turns quickly from the person to the slippery streets: “They really should do something about that.”) Frequently these devices have the stink of self-righteousness about them—banishing the suffering from our awareness and making us feel good about ourselves at the same time. “If she wasn’t a drunkard, she wouldn’t have ended up that way.” “Well, they always cut school, no wonder they can’t find a job.” “If those people in India didn’t spend so much time meditating, they’d have their economic scene together and there wouldn’t be so much starvation.”

“这个时代最大的罪恶，”俄国哲学家尼古拉斯·别尔嘉耶夫写道，“就是把具体事物抽象化。” 这正是我们的思维试图通过各种手段，以及试图为一切开脱的努力来实现的。（有人摔倒了，我们的注意力迅速从摔倒的人转移到湿滑的路面上：“他们真应该采取措施。”）这些手段常常散发着自以为是的气息——它们试图将痛苦从我们的意识中抹去，同时让我们自我感觉良好。“如果她不是个酒鬼，就不会落得如此下场。”“他们总是逃学，难怪找不到工作。”“如果印度的那些人不把那么多时间花在冥想上，他们的经济状况就会好得多，也不会有那么多饥荒。”

Pity is another way we keep suffering at arm’s length. We may let in a little of someone’s pain, but never enough to threaten our own self-control. We may feel a little moved to respond to the suffering—we’d feel guilty or uncomfortable if we didn’t—but we’d like to get it all over with as soon as possible and get on with our own affairs. Compassion and pity are very different. Whereas compassion reflects the yearning of the heart to merge and take on some of the suffering, pity is a controlled set of thoughts designed to assure separateness. Compassion is the spontaneous response of love; pity, the involuntary reflex of fear.

怜悯是另一种让我们与苦难保持距离的方式。我们或许会感受到他人痛苦的些许，但绝不会多到足以威胁到我们自身的自制力。我们或许会感到一丝触动，想要对苦难做出回应——如果我们不这样做，就会感到内疚或不自在——但我们只想尽快结束这一切，继续忙自己的事情。同情和怜悯截然不同。同情反映了内心渴望融入并分担苦难的愿望，而怜悯则是一种刻意控制的思维模式，旨在确保彼此的疏离。同情是爱的自发反应；怜悯则是恐惧的下意识反射。

~

When you’re blind, you hear very well. The tone of someone’s voice is their face. It never lies. And I’ll hear the difference between someone just caring for me and someone protecting themselves. Like, they want to be concerned. They don’t want to get up and leave. But their mind is elsewhere. And what I hear is their fear and guilt—even in the middle of their concern. It’s such a mixed signal .

当你失明的时候，你的听觉反而异常敏锐。一个人的语气就是他的表情，它从不说谎。我能分辨出别人是真心关心我，还是只是在保护自己。比如，他们表面上关心我，不愿起身离开，但他们的心思却早已飘向远方。我能听出他们内心的恐惧和愧疚——即便是在他们关心我的表象之下。这真是个复杂的信号。

~

Perhaps the strategy for dealing with suffering most familiar in our helping institutions is that of “professional warmth.” Like pity, it’s a stance to keep our distance. Since many professionals even believe that it’s appropriate “not to get involved,” they demonstrate a cool efficiency and impersonal friendliness, at best a façade, at worst plain hypocrisy. They become like their machines: cool green, giving off a competent hum. It’s a way of plasticizing human relationships to keep them sterile, free of contact germs.

或许，在我们这些援助机构中，最常见的应对苦难的策略就是“职业的温暖”。它如同怜悯，是一种保持距离的姿态。由于许多专业人士甚至认为“不介入”才是合适的，他们表现得冷漠高效、不带个人色彩的友善，往好了说是伪装，往坏了说就是彻头彻尾的虚伪。他们变得像机器一样：冷冰冰的，发出一种专业运转的嗡嗡声。这是一种将人际关系塑料化，使其保持无菌状态，避免接触细菌的方式。

Of course it’s understandable how this state of affairs has evolved. The demands on helping professionals to confront so much suffering each day are immense. “Professional warmth” is a survival strategy. But it’s no answer. Our hearts pay the price, helpers and helped alike. Fortunately, awareness of this problem is growing. “The question of suffering and its relation to organic illness has rarely been addressed in the medical literature,” reported the prestigious New England Journal of Medicine in a special article devoted to this issue. But what does it say about our habits that this concern has been such a long time coming?

当然，这种状况的演变是可以理解的。助人专业人士每天都要面对如此多的痛苦，压力巨大。“职业关怀”是一种生存策略，但这并非解决之道。无论是助人者还是受助者，我们的内心都为此付出了代价。幸运的是，人们对这个问题的认识正在不断提高。《新英格兰医学杂志》在一篇专门探讨此问题的特刊中指出：“医学文献中很少提及痛苦及其与器质性疾病的关系。” 但这种关注迟迟未能出现，这又反映了我们怎样的习惯呢？

Frequently, our reactiveness to suffering takes the form of having instantly to do something, do anything. It’s the “we gotta” syndrome: “We gotta” fix this up right away. “We gotta” call this person for advice. It’s tricky, because this impulse may arise from genuine empathy, but the form of action is compulsive. Often what’s happening is that “we gotta” get rid of someone’s pain because it’s hurting us too much. Its true neurotic dimension is most evident when there’s really nothing to do, yet still we must talk to that nurse, question that doctor, call that specialist, rearrange the furniture, change the TV channel, straighten the bed (for the fifth time in the last twenty minutes)—and “Are you sure you’re all right, dear? Really? I mean, really?”

我们对痛苦的反应常常表现为必须立刻做点什么，哪怕是任何事。这就是所谓的“我们必须”综合症：“我们必须”马上解决这个问题。“我们必须”打电话给这个人寻求建议。这很棘手，因为这种冲动可能源于真切的同情，但行动的形式却是强迫性的。通常情况下，发生的情况是“我们必须”消除他人的痛苦，因为这让我们也感到痛苦。当真的无事可做时，这种神经质的一面就表现得最为明显，但我们仍然必须和护士说话，询问医生，打电话给专家，重新布置家具，换电视频道，整理床铺（在过去的二十分钟里已经是第五次了）——然后问：“亲爱的，你确定你没事吗？真的吗？我是说，真的吗？”

Rushing about with this reactive and zealous urgency infects the situation with a toxic tension which is the last kind of mental state anyone who’s suffering needs. This agitation perpetuates itself and compounds suffering. It’s Typhoid Mary disguised as Florence Nightingale. In a helpless lay person, such behavior can be flamboyant. In a helping professional, it’s often more subtle.

这种反应过度、急切的举动会给局面带来一种有害的紧张感，而这正是任何正在遭受痛苦的人最不需要的精神状态。这种焦虑会自我强化，加剧痛苦。这就像是伪装成弗洛伦斯·南丁格尔的伤寒玛丽。在无助的普通人身上，这种行为可能表现得十分张扬；而在专业人士身上，这种行为往往更加隐蔽。

Denial, abstraction, pity, professional warmth, compulsive hyperactivity: these are a few of the ways in which the mind reacts to suffering and attempts to restrict or direct the natural compassion of the heart. This tension between head and heart leaves us tentative and confused. As we reach out, then pull back, love and fear are pitted against one another. As hard as this is for us , what must it be like for those who need our help?

否认、抽象化、怜悯、职业化的热情、强迫性的过度活跃：这些都是头脑应对苦难并试图限制或引导内心自然同情心的方式。这种头脑与心灵之间的张力让我们犹豫不决、困惑迷茫。当我们伸出援手又退缩时，爱与恐惧便开始相互对抗。这对我们来说都如此艰难，那么对于那些需要我们帮助的人来说，又该是怎样的感受呢？

~

Being a long-term patient gives you a unique perspective on the world, and I have to laugh, although sometimes I must say it’s a little bittersweet .

长期住院让我对世界有了独特的视角，我常常笑着说，虽然有时也觉得有点苦乐参半。

Naturally, I’m seen as helpless. They have to lift me, move me, deal with my bowels and all. I don’t look very nice or smell very nice, I suppose. What I often see coming in the room is what you might call Central Casting for “General Hospital.”

当然，我被视为无助之人。他们得抬我、挪动我，还得处理我的排泄等等。我想，我看起来不太好看，闻起来也不太好闻。我经常看到走进房间的，简直就像是从《综合医院》剧组直接挑选出来的演员。

Here comes Miss Aren’t-You-Looking-Better-Today. Which is funny to me, since it’s pretty clear I’m only barely holding my own. Enter stage left we have Nurse Wince. It’s hard for her to look at me. She’s afraid for her own mother, that she’ll end up like me. The doctors stride in; they should play “Pomp and Circumstance” over the PA system regularly. They’re examining my case. They find my case interesting. My visitors … they usually fall into the soap opera too. And so do I, I suppose .

瞧瞧那位“你今天看起来好多了”小姐。我觉得挺搞笑的，因为我明明只是勉强应付而已。温斯护士从舞台左侧登场。她不敢直视我的眼睛。她担心自己的母亲会落得和我一样的下场。医生们大步走了进来；他们应该经常在广播里播放《威风堂堂进行曲》。他们正在检查我的病情。他们觉得我的病情很有意思。我的访客们……他们通常也会被卷入这场肥皂剧。我想，我自己也一样。

On it goes. You’d be surprised at the number of people who talk to you and can’t look you in the eye, even more than we normally can’t look each other in the eye. It’s like a parade of attitudes in here .

这种事还在继续。你会惊讶于有多少人跟你说话却不敢直视你的眼睛，甚至比我们平时彼此不敢直视对方还要多。这里简直就是各种态度的游行。

It’s funny; I laugh. I understand, I really do. I’m not a pretty picture. Their work is hard. But sometimes I just want to cry out, “Hello! Is anybody there? Hello? Hello?”

这真滑稽，我笑了。我明白，真的明白。我长得也不好看。他们的工作很辛苦。但有时候我只想大喊：“喂！有人在吗？喂？喂？”

~

How can we answer back … and in a way that our answers are heard and welcomed? How, in other words, can we engage suffering and stay open to the expression of our natural compassion?

我们如何回应……并且以一种我们的回应能被倾听和接受的方式？换句话说，我们如何面对苦难，并保持开放的心态去表达我们与生俱来的同情心？

First, perhaps, we can start out by just asking these questions of ourselves. They frame the situation in such a way that we can once again open ourselves to new possibilities of response to suffering. They can turn our attention to an examination of the reactions that suffering triggers off in us. Up to now these reactions have been rooted not only in fear but in the denial of fear. Merely to be mindful of this pattern is to be one step closer to our own truth and, in turn, to the truth of someone else’s suffering. Truth is where we will meet. Simply acknowledging our reactiveness to pain, therefore, is itself an initial act of service.

首先，或许我们可以从问自己这些问题开始。这些问题能帮助我们重新审视困境，让我们再次敞开心扉，迎接应对苦难的新可能性。它们能引导我们去审视苦难在我们内心引发的反应。迄今为止，这些反应不仅源于恐惧，更源于对恐惧的否认。仅仅意识到这种模式，就让我们离自身的真相更近了一步，进而也更接近他人苦难的真相。真相是我们相遇之处。因此，仅仅承认我们对痛苦的反应，本身就是一种初步的奉献。

~

As I walk into the sanatorium, I have a little exercise. I know that I’m to be presented with evidence of terrible pain. It’s all right there, right in front of me. And I know that it’s probably going to blow me away the minute I go in, no matter that I’ve worked there six years. So I’ll take note of all that, as if it were a sign on the front door. It gives me a certain amount of sobriety—preparation for entering .

走进疗养院前，我先做个小小的准备。我知道我即将面对的是剧烈的痛苦。一切都摆在那里，就在我眼前。我知道，即便我在那里工作了六年，一进去也可能会被彻底击垮。所以我会把这一切都记下来，就像大门上的告示一样。这让我保持一定的清醒——为进入疗养院做好准备。

In doing that, I find I get a feeling of deep respect for those inside who are suffering from the kinds of pains they’re dealing with. Basic respect for their dignity and their worth. They’re here, they’re equally as human as I am, and their suffering calls my attention to that fact .

这样做之后，我对那些正在遭受痛苦的人们产生了深深的敬意。我对他们的尊严和价值产生了最基本的尊重。他们在这里，他们和我一样都是人，他们的苦难让我意识到这一点。

Sometimes I also find myself honoring them. Not just respect, but honoring them for what they are and what they’re enduring. I’ll try to bring that feeling in the door with me. This gives me strength. And it just starts simply from taking account of what’s going on in me, in the sanatorium, in those inside it .

有时我也会不由自主地对他们表示敬意。不仅仅是尊重，而是敬重他们本身，敬重他们所承受的一切。我会努力把这种感觉带进门来。这给了我力量。而这一切，都源于我认真审视自己、疗养院以及疗养院里每个人的感受。

~

Our tendency when we acknowledge qualities in ourselves like fear of suffering or loss of control may be to judge ourselves. Found selfish, uncaring, impatient, unworthy … we’re embarrassed and uncomfortable at the recognition of our “weakness.” We have not taken to heart the example of the biblical Paul, who said, “My strength is made perfect through weakness.” Yet this often turns out to be the case in our efforts to care for others. Acknowledging our weakness can soften our defensiveness. We’re not so busy protecting ourselves all the time. We’re much more likely to be there for anyone who is wrestling with his or her own sense of weakness, unworthiness, or fear. We’ll hear each other. To acknowledge our humanness, with its mixture of empathy and fear, strengthens our helping hand.

当我们承认自身存在诸如害怕痛苦或失控等特质时，往往会倾向于自我评判。我们会觉得自己自私、冷漠、缺乏耐心、不够好……承认自己的“软弱”会让我们感到尴尬和不自在。我们并没有真正领会圣经中保罗的教诲：“我的能力是在人的软弱上显得完全。”然而，在我们努力关爱他人时，这种情况却常常发生。承认自身的软弱可以软化我们的防御心理。我们不再总是忙于保护自己。我们更有可能去帮助那些正在与自身的软弱、无价值感或恐惧作斗争的人。我们会倾听彼此的心声。承认我们人性中既有同情又有恐惧的复杂情感，会增强我们伸出援手的能力。

But we must do so with compassion for ourselves and a supportive appreciation of our own predicament. Such compassion can come forth more easily when we appreciate that it is the openness of our heart, after all, with which this all began . Our fear is awakened not just by the suffering but by the intensity of our heart’s reaction to it. The ego may have been frightened into all kinds of defense mechanisms to control our innate generosity. But mercy and kindness were our first impulses. Natural compassion was our starting point.

但我们必须以慈悲之心对待自己，并以理解和支持的态度看待自己的困境。当我们意识到这一切的根源在于我们敞开的心扉时，这种慈悲之心便会更容易涌现。我们的恐惧并非仅仅源于苦难本身，更源于我们内心对苦难的强烈反应。或许，为了压制我们与生俱来的慷慨，自我启动了各种防御机制。但怜悯和善意才是我们最初的冲动。自然的慈悲之心才是我们一切的起点。

This compassionate self-acknowledgment may start out with a simple reflection: “I’m really uncomfortable when I visit Uncle Harry because he’s suffering so much. I want so much to help him, but there doesn’t seem to be anything I can do. I see how phony I get when I’m around him. And that’s okay.” But it’s more than okay. This act of acknowledgment begins to go to work for us. The phoniness usually starts to fall away the minute it’s owned up to. Discomfort in the presence of suffering is usually less toxic and infectious when it’s no longer denied. This quality of unjudging awareness not only frees us and others from the consequences of our reactivity; it allows us to enter more consciously into the experience of suffering itself. We’re no longer running away, glancing over our shoulder. We can stop and face what’s right before us. We can look at what is .

这种充满慈悲的自我觉察或许始于简单的反思：“我去看望哈里叔叔时真的感到很不自在，因为他很痛苦。我很想帮助他，但似乎我无能为力。我意识到，在他身边时，我表现得多么虚伪。但这没关系。” 但这远不止于此。这种觉察开始对我们产生积极的影响。一旦承认了虚伪的存在，它通常就会开始消散。当不再否认痛苦带来的不适感时，这种不适感通常不会那么具有毒性，也不会那么具有传染性。这种不加评判的觉察不仅能让我们和他人摆脱因我们的反应而产生的后果，还能让我们更加有意识地进入痛苦本身的体验之中。我们不再逃避，不再回头张望。我们可以停下来，直面眼前的一切。我们可以正视现实。

But we must be quiet to do so, quiet to hear. Yet the first thing we notice when we try is that we’re not quiet at all. We’re a torrent of reactions, and reactions to reactions, one piling in upon the other. Such agitation is hardly the best ground from which to observe the subtleties of any situation. It would be so much easier if we weren’t in the presence of all this suffering. But then again, wasn’t it the suffering and our reactions to it that we set out to observe in the first place?

但我们必须保持安静才能做到这一点，安静才能聆听。然而，当我们尝试这样做时，首先注意到的却是我们根本无法安静下来。我们就像一股洪流，各种反应层出不穷，一个接一个地涌来。如此躁动不安，显然不是观察任何情况微妙之处的最佳状态。如果我们不身处这一切苦难之中，一切都会容易得多。但话说回来，我们最初不正是为了观察苦难以及我们对苦难的反应吗？

So we have to find tranquillity even in the midst of trauma. What’s required is to cultivate a dispassionate Witness within. This Witness, as it grows stronger, can see precisely how we jump the gun in the presence of pain. It notices how our reactions might be perpetuating denial or fear or tension in the situation, the very qualities we’d like to help alleviate. The Witness catches us in the act, but gently, without reproach, so we can simply acknowledge our reactivity and begin to let it fall away, allowing our natural compassion to come more into play. The Witness gives us a little room.

所以，即使身处创伤之中，我们也必须找到内心的平静。这需要我们在内心培养一种冷静的见证者。随着这种见证者的力量增强，它能精准地洞察我们在痛苦面前的冲动反应。它会注意到，我们的反应可能会加剧否认、恐惧或紧张，而这些恰恰是我们想要帮助缓解的。见证者会敏锐地察觉到我们的反应，但语气温和，不带责备，让我们能够坦然承认自己的反应，并开始放下它，从而让与生俱来的同情心更多地发挥作用。见证者会给我们留出一些空间。

Not only does it notice our own reactivity, but it also brings into the light of awareness the actions and reactions of other parties in the situation. Now we can begin, perhaps for the first time, to hear them . Less busy pushing away suffering, less frenzied having to do something about it, we’re able to get a sense of what they’re feeling, of what they feel they need. We may be startled to discover that what they’ve been asking for all along is entirely different from what we’ve been so busy offering: “All I want is for you to sit down here next to me. I don’t care about the nurse; the IV is working fine; the bed is comfortable. Just sit with me.” Quieter now, we can recognize such a need—often without it having to be expressed, perhaps even before it’s consciously felt. We’ll just come into the room and sit down and say “Hello.”

它不仅能觉察到我们自身的反应，还能让我们意识到情境中其他人的行为和反应。现在，我们或许第一次能够开始倾听他们。不再忙于逃避痛苦，不再急于采取行动，我们就能感受到他们的感受，感受到他们的需求。我们可能会惊讶地发现，他们一直以来所寻求的，与我们一直忙于提供的截然不同：“我只想你坐在我旁边。我不在乎护士；输液管运转良好；床也很舒服。就陪我坐一会儿吧。” 现在，我们平静下来，能够识别出这样的需求——通常无需他们表达，甚至可能在他们意识到之前就能察觉。我们只需走进房间，坐下，说声“你好”。

This process of witnessing is dispassionate. It’s not committed to one result or another; it’s open to everything. Because it has, so to speak, no ax to grind, it is more able to see truth. As the Tao Te Ching says, “The truth waits for eyes unclouded by longing.”

这种见证的过程是超然的。它不执着于任何结果，而是对一切持开放态度。因为它没有私心，所以更能看清真相。正如《道德经》所说：“真理等待着不被欲望蒙蔽的双眼。”

The Witness, however, is not passive, complacent, or indifferent. Indeed, while it’s not attached to a particular outcome, its presence turns out to bring about change. As we bring what is into the light of clear awareness, we begin to see that the universe is providing us with abundant clues as to the nature of the suffering before us, what is being asked, what fears have been inhibiting us, and, finally, what might really help . All we have to do is listen—really listen.

然而，见证者并非被动、自满或冷漠。事实上，虽然它并不执着于某种特定的结果，但它的存在却能带来改变。当我们以清晰的觉知审视当下时，我们便开始明白，宇宙正为我们提供丰富的线索，揭示眼前苦难的本质、我们真正需要的是什么、阻碍我们的恐惧是什么，以及最终什么才是真正有效的。我们所要做的，就是倾听——真正地倾听。

Such investigation and inquiry into what is infuses a situation with a quality of freshness and possibility. As we see how reactive we have been, we find ourselves opening to new responses. It was our own reactivity unacknowledged that cut off the spontaneity of our helping heart. Once it is acknowledged, however—and once we begin to work with it—a whole new level of creativity becomes possible.

这种对现状的探究和调查，能为情境注入新鲜感和无限可能。当我们意识到自己过去的反应过度时，便会敞开心扉接受新的回应。正是我们自身未被察觉的反应过度，扼杀了我们助人之心的自发性。然而，一旦我们正视这种反应过度，并开始与之共处，一个全新的创造力层面便会随之而来。

~

I used to have to walk through it automatically. You don’t bother to look. You certainly don’t let much of it in. But it was the children themselves who began to open me up. Once it started, it began to pull me in gradually but steadily. It was very powerful, but you have to take it at your own pace. Because here, in a neonatal intensive care unit, you see incredible beauty and unbearable pain. And you have to figure out how to be with both .

我以前只能机械地走过这一切。你懒得去看，当然也不会让太多东西进入你的内心。但正是孩子们开始打开我的心扉。一旦开始，它便会逐渐而坚定地将我拉入其中。这力量非常强大，但你必须按照自己的节奏来。因为在这里，在新生儿重症监护室里，你会看到令人难以置信的美丽，也会看到难以承受的痛苦。你必须学会如何同时面对这两者。

The children are beautiful because you just get to know them. You can’t nurse them, really nurse them, without knowing them. And you can’t know them, really know them, without seeing their beauty. What can be more beautiful than innocence? And that affects all their features: their tininess, the eyes, the fingers, the sound of their heart—just their breath can move you with its beauty. Part of it seems to come from how fragile they are, how uncertain it is how long they’ll be here—the cliche metaphor of the flower that blooms for a day. It’s like a garden of that in here .

孩子们之所以美丽，是因为你只有真正了解他们。如果你不了解他们，就无法真正地照顾他们。而如果你不欣赏他们的美，就无法真正地了解他们。还有什么比纯真更美呢？纯真体现在他们身上的每一个细节：他们的娇小，他们的眼睛，他们的手指，他们的心跳——甚至他们的呼吸都美得令人动容。这美似乎一部分源于他们的脆弱，源于他们生命短暂的未知——就像那朵只开一天的花，虽然这个比喻略显老套。这里就像一座花园，处处洋溢着这样的美好。

The picture on the surface, though, is also terribly grim. A room full of these little ones, many of whom are right on the edge of life and death, and some of whose faces and movements are pretty distressing. And then their parents: there on the other side of the window, with the most desperate and stricken faces looking in, so helplessly, such pain. It’s something to be inside a picture that’s being looked at with such expressions. But you look back, just to let them know someone’s in here .

然而，表面上的画面也极其凄惨。房间里挤满了孩子，许多都徘徊在生死边缘，有些孩子的表情和动作令人揪心。他们的父母就在窗外，用绝望和痛苦的眼神望着窗外，无助而痛苦。置身于一幅被如此凝视的画面之中，是一种难以言喻的感受。但你还是会回头看看，只是为了让他们知道，这里有人陪伴。

It was the use of machines and extraordinary medical measures that moved several of us to see how much distance we were putting between ourselves and the infants. Even if the machines weren’t there, though, there was that tendency to keep it impersonal, to keep your distance, and you knew that wasn’t any good for the children—for the children least of all .

正是机器的使用和非常规的医疗措施，促使我们中的一些人意识到，我们与婴儿之间拉开了多大的距离。即便没有这些机器，人们仍然倾向于保持冷漠，与婴儿保持距离，而你知道这对孩子没有任何好处——尤其对孩子本身而言。

So a group of us began to talk about it, to open up to our feelings, to decide to be with the children more, and when it got too hard and we’d break down, we’d support each other and talk it over. The more we opened up, it just became natural that we began this new practice of holding infants when the time would come for them to die. It wasn’t a decision as much as something we’d become ready to do. So at the end we’d take them off the monitors and into our arms in a rocker. And we’d sit with them in their final moments .

于是我们几个开始讨论这件事，敞开心扉面对自己的感受，决定多花时间陪伴孩子们。当情绪崩溃、难以自持时，我们会互相扶持，一起倾诉。随着我们越来越坦诚，一种新的习惯也自然而然地出现了：当婴儿的生命走到尽头时，我们会抱着他们。这与其说是一个决定，不如说是我们做好了准备。所以，在生命的最后时刻，我们会把他们从监护仪上抱下来，放在摇椅上，依偎在他们身边，陪伴他们走完人生的最后一程。

It tears you apart, because holding them, sometimes you can feel them go. And the death itself is different. On the machines, it’s monitored as brain death. In your arms, it’s the heart and the breath .

这会让人心碎，因为抱着他们，有时你能感觉到他们的生命正在消逝。而且死亡本身也不同。在机器上，它被监测为脑死亡。在你怀里，那是心脏和呼吸。

It’s so—what’s that word?—poignant. You feel ten dozen things at once. Terrible sadness, because you’d become attached to the child. But glad too, because their suffering is about to end. Maybe anger, at the world, at God, at whatever, for allowing this to happen. And such empathy for the parents. And something like awe and wonder; like there must be some kind of explanation for all this which you don’t yet understand. But patience too, that things become more clear in time. And peace of mind, because you’re doing the best you can. And humble, to be present at such a moment. All of the above, often at once .

这感觉——该怎么形容呢？——真是令人心碎。你会同时感受到无数种情绪。巨大的悲伤，因为你已经对孩子产生了感情。但同时也感到欣慰，因为他们的痛苦即将结束。或许还会感到愤怒，对这个世界，对上帝，对一切，为什么允许这样的事情发生。同时，你也会对孩子的父母感同身受。还有一种敬畏和惊奇的感觉；仿佛这一切背后一定存在某种你尚未理解的解释。但你也拥有耐心，相信随着时间的推移，一切都会明朗起来。内心也感到平静，因为你已经尽力了。同时，你也感到谦卑，能够身处这样的时刻。所有这些情绪，往往同时涌上心头。

You’re sitting with these feelings, as well as sitting there with the child. In fact, you come to see that you’re sitting with all of it on behalf of the child. You’re doing it for yourself, simply to stay cool. But it’s a final act for them as well. You’re offering whatever peace you’ve come to. And it creates such intimacy, impossible to describe, you’re so right with them .

你一边感受着这些情绪，一边陪伴着孩子。事实上，你会意识到，你这样做是为了孩子。你这样做是为了自己，只是为了保持冷静。但这同时也是为了他们，是最后的举动。你把自己内心的平静传递给他们。这创造了一种难以言喻的亲密感，你和他们之间是如此的契合。

It’s unbearable and beautiful at the same time. How do you explain that? It’s just the part of you that’s with them is getting ripped up. But the part of you that’s, like, trying to understand it all … well, that’s beautiful because you see that you can be, we all can be, in the presence of great pain, but still appreciate life, even in its last moments. Especially then .

这感觉既难以承受又无比美好。该如何解释呢？就像你内心与他们同在的那部分被撕裂了一样。但你内心试图理解这一切的那部分……嗯，这很美好，因为你看到，即使身处巨大的痛苦之中，你，我们所有人都可以，依然能够欣赏生命，即便是在生命的最后时刻。尤其是在那种时候。

~

Compassion follows lawfully as we open to the experience of suffering. Simply to observe and to open allows us to hear what is natural, harmonious, and appropriate. Instead of closed minds and mechanical reactions, there is open space and inventiveness. There is the helping of living truth.

当我们敞开心扉体验苦难时，慈悲便会自然而然地产生。仅仅是观察和敞开，就能让我们聆听到自然、和谐与恰当的声音。那时，封闭的心灵和机械的反应被开放的空间和创造力所取代。那时，活生生的真理便会给予帮助。

So the activity of the quiet Witness not only shows us how fearfully reactive we have been to the suffering of others; it also releases within us a yearning to grow in our capacity to care for others. We look anew at how each situation can teach us, how it can help us evolve in our ability to confront and help alleviate suffering. We can be students working on ourselves to become more effective instruments of compassion.

因此，静默见证者的行动不仅让我们看到我们对他人的苦难是多么恐惧和反应过度，也激发了我们内心深处渴望提升关爱他人的能力。我们重新审视每一种境况，思考它如何教导我们，如何帮助我们提升面对和减轻苦难的能力。我们可以成为学生，不断完善自我，成为更有效的慈悲使者。

The collaboration of the Witness and this yearning to grow, born of the inherent mercy of the heart, continues to bring to light patterns of response to suffering we hadn’t noticed before. From situation to situation, we see these reactions repeated again and again. Sometimes they are appropriate. Very often they are unconscious. Instead of being responsive to an actual situation as it is, we come in with our reactions pretaped, just looking for ways to protect them. We may assume people are suffering in ways that they aren’t: “Poor baby.” “This must be awful for you.” “Are you sure you don’t want me to call someone?” “Take something for the pain.” We wince when someone else gets an injection. We project discomfort onto people about their helplessness which doesn’t necessarily exist, or we fail to see the character of the suffering that really is there.

见证者的合作以及这种源于内心固有慈悲的成长渴望，不断揭示出我们之前未曾注意到的应对苦难的模式。在不同的情境中，我们看到这些反应反复出现。有时它们是恰当的，但更多时候是无意识的。我们并非对真实情况做出回应，而是带着预先设定的反应，只想着如何保护自己。我们可能会臆断他人正在遭受他们实际上并未遭受的痛苦：“可怜的孩子。”“这对你来说一定很痛苦。”“你确定不需要我打电话吗？”“吃点止痛药吧。”当别人打针时，我们会感到不适。我们会将他人无助的不安投射到他们身上，而这种无助未必存在；或者，我们看不到真正存在的苦难的本质。

As we begin to notice these tendencies in ourselves, we can look further and see where they come from, how we’ve built them up out of past experience. Certainly some have come from how we’ve dealt previously with the pain of others. But more significant still are our past experiences facing our own suffering. Here is the next critical issue we need to engage—one that any of us who seeks to help another must confront sooner or later.

当我们开始注意到自身存在的这些倾向时，我们可以进一步探究它们的根源，以及我们是如何从过去的经历中逐渐形成的。当然，有些倾向源于我们过去处理他人痛苦的方式。但更重要的是我们过去面对自身痛苦的经历。这正是我们需要探讨的下一个关键问题——任何想要帮助他人的人迟早都必须面对这个问题。

~

My first visit to India included a stop at Benares. In the streets there were hundreds, perhaps thousands, of people with begging bowls who were in the final stages of one illness or another and seemed to be just waiting to die. My heart was deeply pained by the scene. I put lots of change in lots of begging bowls, but even then it didn’t seem like enough. In encounters with these people I usually averted my eyes from meeting theirs. I guess I felt guilty that I had so much and they had so little. Finally I was remaining in the hotel rather than face such massive suffering .

我第一次去印度，其中一站是瓦拉纳西。街上成百上千的人，或许数千人，手捧乞讨的碗，他们都身患绝症，似乎只是在等待死亡。眼前的景象令我心痛不已。我往许多乞讨的碗里放了许多零钱，但即便如此，似乎也远远不够。遇到这些人时，我总是尽量避免与他们目光接触。我想，我大概是感到愧疚，因为我拥有那么多，而他们却如此贫困。最终，我还是选择待在酒店里，而不是去面对如此巨大的苦难。

By the time of my next visit to the city many months later, I had become familiar with the Hindu culture. I now realized that Benares was one of the most sacred cities in India, situated on the banks of the Ganges, the most sacred river. I also had come to know that in this culture, which believed so deeply in reincarnation, the most auspicious place to die was in Benares. To be cremated there on the river bank assured liberation after death. Now as I placed coins in begging bowls I was able to look into the eyes of the people. And to my profound amazement I found in their eyes not the suffering that I had been reticent to face but looks of peace. In fact I even saw in some of their eyes pity for me, lost as I was in illusion. Leprosy, leukemia, blindness, such poverty that they had only a loincloth and begging bowl … and still … peace. How wrong I’d been to assume that they were suffering as I would have been suffering in a similar situation .

几个月后我再次造访这座城市时，我已经对印度教文化有所了解。我意识到贝拿勒斯是印度最神圣的城市之一，坐落在恒河岸边，而恒河是印度最神圣的河流。我也了解到，在这个深信轮回的文化中，贝拿勒斯是最吉祥的死亡之地。在那里的河岸火化可以确保死后获得解脱。现在，当我把硬币放入乞讨的碗里时，我终于能够直视人们的眼睛。令我无比惊讶的是，我在他们的眼中看到的不是我一直试图回避的苦难，而是平静的神情。事实上，我甚至从一些人的眼中看到了对我的怜悯，因为我曾深陷于幻想之中。麻风病、白血病、失明，以及他们只有一块缠腰布和一个乞讨碗的贫困……然而……他们依然拥有平静。我之前以为他们在类似境遇下也会像我一样遭受苦难，这真是大错特错。

~

The link between our reaction to our own pain and the quality of our empathy for that of others needs to be examined carefully. The more we understand it, the deeper, freer, more naturally compassionate our response to the pain we all experience at one time or another.

我们需要仔细审视自身对痛苦的反应与我们对他人的同理心之间的联系。我们越了解这种联系，就越能以更深刻、更自由、更自然的方式回应我们每个人或多或少都会经历的痛苦。

What causes suffering for us in the first place? An unpleasant sensation or situation arises. It could be physical pain, psychological distress, general uncertainty about the future, and so forth. These are potential conditions for suffering. But taken alone, these are not the suffering itself. How we react to them determines how much we will suffer. These reactions can vary.

究竟是什么让我们感到痛苦？首先，某种不愉快的感受或处境出现了。它可能是身体上的疼痛、心理上的痛苦、对未来的不确定感等等。这些都是可能导致痛苦的因素。但就其本身而言，这些并非痛苦的根源。我们如何应对这些因素，决定了我们会承受多少痛苦。而这些应对方式多种多样。

A child and an adult each stub a toe. They both experience pain. The adult has a world view in which such sensation is recognized and incorporated: it’s one of those things, it’ll pass. So the adult experiences the sensation of pain but does not really “suffer” beyond that. Because there is no uncontrolled reactive resistance to speak of, the adult need initiate no action to alleviate the “suffering.”

一个孩子和一个成年人都踢到了脚趾。他们都感到疼痛。成年人的世界观认为这种感觉是可以感知并接受的：这只是小事一桩，过一会儿就好了。因此，成年人体验到了疼痛，但除此之外并没有真正“承受”痛苦。因为不存在任何不受控制的反应性抵抗，成年人无需采取任何措施来缓解这种“痛苦”。

For the child the experience is quite different. Lacking a context that readily allows for stubbed toes, the child identifies with the unpleasant pain and experiences aversion to it. The child puts itself strongly at odds with what is . This resistance to the unpleasant situation is the root of the suffering. Tears may continue after the sensation has subsided. As a reaction, the child runs to the parent for solace.

对孩子来说，这种体验截然不同。由于缺乏容易导致脚趾被撞到的环境，孩子会将这种不适感与自身经历联系起来，并对其产生厌恶。孩子强烈地与现实对抗。这种对不愉快情况的抗拒正是痛苦的根源。即使疼痛感消退后，孩子可能仍然会哭泣。作为一种反应，孩子会跑向父母寻求安慰。

Two people have not eaten in three days. One is a yogi doing a purification fast. Though there are unpleasant sensations in the stomach, there is very little aversion, perhaps even none, hence little or no real suffering. The yogi sits quietly and takes no steps to change the state of affairs.

两个人已经三天没吃东西了。其中一人是正在进行净化斋戒的瑜伽修行者。虽然胃部有些不适，但几乎没有厌恶感，或许根本没有，因此也几乎没有感受到真正的痛苦。这位瑜伽修行者静静地坐着，没有采取任何措施来改变现状。
