Another person, however, lives on the street, has no job, no food stamps, and hasn’t eaten in three days. The unpleasant sensations are painful, and their causes add to them a strong element of suffering: frustration, anger, humiliation. He’s suffering. He goes out begging.

然而，另一个人却流落街头，没有工作，没有食品券，已经三天没吃东西了。这种不适感令人痛苦，而其根源更增添了强烈的痛苦：沮丧、愤怒、屈辱。他饱受折磨。他只能靠乞讨度日。

Two women are in labor. They’re both screaming as a natural response to pain. For one of them the pain represents the heralding of the long-awaited child and is part of the incredible mystery of life. The pain draws her in and fills her not with suffering but with ecstasy. She has never felt so alive and in such deep harmony with her nature. She rejects a pain killer solicitously offered by the midwife.

两个女人正在分娩。她们都因疼痛而发出自然的尖叫。对其中一位来说，这疼痛预示着期盼已久的孩子即将降生，是生命奇妙奥秘的一部分。疼痛将她深深吸引，带给她的不是痛苦，而是狂喜。她从未感到如此鲜活，如此与自己的本性和谐共处。她拒绝了助产士好心递来的止痛药。

For the other woman, the pain of childbirth is what she’s been afraid of since the onset of pregnancy. When it arises, she is unable to push it away. It becomes a source of suffering, not part of an experience of overall joy. She welcomes the pain medication.

对另一位女性来说，分娩的疼痛是她从怀孕之初就一直恐惧的。当疼痛来临时，她无法摆脱。它变成了痛苦的源泉，而不是整体喜悦的一部分。她欣然接受止痛药。

How dramatic, then, the range of potential reactions among us to unpleasant circumstances, whatever their form. Down with a cold? Is it a fearful intimation of mortality or a chance just to let go for a few days? Newly divorced? Do you feel rejected or acknowledge the opportunity to be free of accumulated dependencies? Just fired from work? Are you worthless or free to discover new skills?

那么，面对各种不愉快的境遇，无论其形式如何，我们可能产生的反应是多么丰富多样啊！感冒了？是恐惧地预示着死亡，还是仅仅想借此机会放松几天？刚刚离婚？你会感到被抛弃，还是会意识到这是摆脱长期依赖的良机？刚刚被解雇？你会觉得自己一文不值，还是会借此机会自由地学习新技能？

Obviously, certain circumstances or sensations are more likely to trigger off greater suffering than others. But suffering can exist even without immediate or proximate cause. We experience it frequently in this general, floating form. We simply want things to be other than they are. What we have … isn’t quite enough. Who we are … isn’t quite satisfactory. How we feel … could always be a little better. That which is … just isn’t right.

显然，某些境遇或感受比其他境遇或感受更容易引发更大的痛苦。但即使没有直接或近因，痛苦也可能存在。我们经常以这种普遍的、漂浮的形式体验痛苦。我们只是希望事情不是现在这样。我们拥有的……还不够。我们是谁……还不够令人满意。我们的感受……总可以更好一些。现在的一切……就是不对劲。

In the face of unpleasant circumstance or experience, then, it is often the context, framework, or disposition of mind that determines the extent to which there is suffering.

因此，面对不愉快的境遇或经历，往往是环境、框架或心态决定了痛苦的程度。

We hear stories of great tribulation. A man in great pain with advanced cancer is now denied the strength he always had as a professional carpenter, a supportive husband, and a father of four. A teen-ager is hurt in an automobile crash and has lost the use of both legs. A woman is told she can never have children; she’s become alcoholic; they’ve just fired her from her job. We can easily feel in ourselves the likely reactions such people must experience under such conditions.

我们听闻过无数苦难的故事。一位身患晚期癌症、饱受病痛折磨的男子，失去了他作为专业木匠、贤内助和四个孩子父亲所拥有的力量。一位青少年在车祸中受伤，双腿瘫痪。一位女子被告知她永远无法生育；她开始酗酒；她刚刚被解雇。我们很容易就能体会到这些人身处困境时可能产生的种种反应。

~

~ My God, I can’t believe this is happening to me!

我的天哪，我简直不敢相信这种事会发生在我身上！

~ I’m so totally unprepared .

我完全没有做好准备。

~ I’ll never be the same .

我再也回不到从前了。

~ My life’s a failure .

我的人生一团糟。

~ Everywhere I look now, I only see reason for despair .

~如今我所看到的，只有绝望的理由。

~ I just plain feel sorry for myself, that’s all .

我只是单纯地感到难过，仅此而已。

~ I feel trapped in this useless body .

我感觉自己被困在这具无用的躯壳里。

~ Helpless, utterly helpless …

无助，彻底的无助……

~ I want to scream and I can’t .

我想尖叫，但我尖叫不出来。

~ What did I do to deserve this?

我究竟做错了什么才落得如此下场？

~ I’ll never make it through another day .

我再也熬不过一天了。

~ I don’t want to hear about anybody else’s problems .

我不想听别人的烦恼。

~ Everyone is a stranger. I feel totally alone .

~ 每个人都像陌生人。我感到无比孤独。

~ I keep expecting to wake up and be healed .

我一直期待着醒来后就能痊愈。

~ Why me?

为什么是我？

~

Our hearts go out to these people, not only because of the immediate circumstances but because, intuitively, we recognize the response of mental suffering that we ourselves would experience under such conditions. Their predicament awakens our own fears of pain or loss of control. It’s so easy to empathize with their reactions of resistance.

我们对这些人深表同情，不仅是因为他们身处的困境，更因为我们本能地意识到，如果我们自己身处同样的境地，也会遭受同样的精神痛苦。他们的困境唤起了我们对痛苦或失控的恐惧。我们很容易理解他们那种抗拒的反应。

But it also must be said that other people respond to such trying circumstances differently. While this may happen as a result of remarkable personal growth, forged by the crucible of affliction, we can hear in their responses the possibility that extreme pain need not always be intimately associated with extreme suffering.

但必须指出的是，其他人面对这种困境的反应各不相同。这或许源于苦难淬炼下的个人成长，但我们也能从他们的反应中感受到，极度的痛苦并非总是与极度的苦难紧密相连。

~

It stinks, it’s terrible. But it is what it is, and I’m going to go on living with it for however long I have .

这很糟糕，太可怕了。但事实就是如此，我只能忍受下去，直到我生命的尽头。

~

When your negligence has resulted in someone’s death, I can’t describe the amount of guilt you feel. And then a moment comes when you move from utter humiliation to simple humility. It’s your fault, but also somehow it isn’t. We live lives where such things happen. And in that moment you begin to forgive yourself. You don’t deny what you’ve done. You pass through it, it rips you up, and you come out the other end—with a new possibility that comes from that humility and self-forgiveness .

当你的疏忽导致他人死亡时，那种愧疚感难以言表。然后，你会经历一个从极度羞辱到谦卑的转变。这是你的错，但某种程度上又不是。我们生活在这样的生活中，这样的事情时有发生。在那一刻，你开始原谅自己。你不再否认自己的所作所为。你坦然面对，它撕裂着你的心，但你最终会走出阴霾——带着一种源于谦卑和自我宽恕的全新可能。

~

As long as I was pushing away the pain, it had me nailed to the wall. But then I stopped resisting it. I sort of let it in. It was actually a relief. I felt better in spite of it. No longer at odds with everything .

只要我一直抗拒痛苦，它就如同钉在墙上一样，把我牢牢地钉在原地。但后来我不再抵抗，而是接纳了它。这反而让我感到解脱。尽管如此，我感觉好多了。我不再与一切格格不入。

~

When my daughter was murdered, I felt unbearable anguish. I couldn’t sleep, eat, anything. And then a friend and I prayed together. At one moment I felt God’s mercy. Even though I couldn’t understand this crazy mess, I had a sense that there was something behind it all that made it … meaningful. After that, the hurt didn’t go away, but it was bearable .

女儿遇害时，我感到无比痛苦。我彻夜难眠，食不下咽，什么都做不了。后来，我和一位朋友一起祈祷。那一刻，我感受到了上帝的怜悯。尽管我无法理解这团乱麻，但我隐约觉得这一切背后似乎蕴藏着某种意义。之后，伤痛并没有消失，但却可以承受了。

~

We hear in these testimonies something else with which we can empathize: the possibility of coming up for air even in the midst of the most painful, even agonizing, conditions. Somehow we sense that we could be with pain in some way so as not to be suffering so much. Just as we have known in ourselves the fear and resistance, so we have also had moments when we have experienced pain, yet transcended suffering.

在这些证词中，我们还能听到一些让我们感同身受的东西：即使身处最痛苦、最煎熬的境地，也依然有可能获得喘息之机。我们隐约感觉到，或许我们可以以某种方式与痛苦共处，从而减轻自身的痛苦。正如我们自身也曾体会过恐惧和抗拒，我们也曾经历过痛苦，却最终超越了痛苦本身。

Just the possibility that such pain need not automatically cause continuous suffering is profoundly important. This possibility, in fact, was the foundation stone of the teachings of the Buddha. He saw that if we could break that link between painful conditions and the reactiveness of mind there was hope of liberating ourselves from the continuous experience of suffering. He realized that pain alone is not the enemy; the real enemy is fear and resistance.

仅仅是这种痛苦未必必然导致持续的苦难这一可能性，就意义深远。事实上，这种可能性正是佛陀教义的基石。他认为，如果我们能够切断痛苦境况与心念反应之间的联系，就有望从持续的苦难体验中解脱出来。他意识到，痛苦本身并非敌人；真正的敌人是恐惧和抗拒。

It’s not difficult to recognize how deep are the ways our mind has been conditioned to deal with unpleasant situations by resisting them. Throughout our whole lives we have been encouraged to do anything we can to escape from rather than to explore and investigate unpleasantness. Our society consumes literally tons of aspirin daily. It’s not just physical pain we try to avoid, but all kinds of unpleasant conditions: boredom, restlessness, self-doubt, anger, loneliness, loss, feelings of unworthiness. In our culture we do all we can to push these experiences aside, or keep them at a distance. We choose to be entertained.

不难看出，我们的思维模式早已根深蒂固地被训练成通过抗拒来应对不愉快的情况。我们一生都被鼓励尽一切可能逃避，而不是去探索和探究不愉快的事物。我们的社会每天都消耗大量的阿司匹林。我们试图逃避的不仅仅是身体上的疼痛，还有各种各样的不愉快：无聊、烦躁、自我怀疑、愤怒、孤独、失落、无价值感等等。在我们的文化中，我们竭尽所能地将这些体验抛诸脑后，或者与它们保持距离。我们选择娱乐。

So it gets to the point that the slightest unpleasantness elicits our push against it. We tense in opposition. As the unpleasantness gets stronger, the opposition becomes more formidable. Our hearts are closed down by the fear in our minds—fear of loss of control, of being overwhelmed, ultimately of extinction. Our muscles tighten, our energies become knotted and blocked. And, of course, if suddenly we are hit by enormous affliction and adversity, we’ve no habits except resistance.

于是，哪怕最轻微的不快都会引发我们的抗拒。我们紧绷着身体，做出对抗的姿态。随着不快感的加剧，这种抗拒也愈发强烈。恐惧——害怕失去控制、害怕被压垮、最终害怕消亡——让我们的心扉紧闭。我们的肌肉紧绷，能量阻塞，无法流动。当然，如果突然遭遇巨大的苦难和逆境，我们除了抵抗之外，别无他法。

Under these conditions, to suggest that we turn around and look at what so frightens us—to open a dialogue with the enemy rather than just piling up the sandbags and amassing arsenals—is asking us to go in the face of all our conditioning. It is asking us to walk intentionally to the edge of unexplored territory, to relate to the unknown. No small task. Imagine yourself in a state of pain you particularly fear, really fear, being asked to explore it, investigate it, even somehow make friends with it. Just the thought of it can awaken a dread that reveals the potential enormity of our opposition.

在这种情况下，如果我们被要求转身正视那些令我们如此恐惧的事物——与其只是堆积沙袋、囤积武器，不如与敌人展开对话——那就等于要求我们违背所有根深蒂固的观念。这要求我们主动走向未知的领域边缘，与未知建立联系。这绝非易事。试想一下，你正处于一种你极其恐惧的痛苦之中，却被要求去探索它、研究它，甚至以某种方式与它“交朋友”。仅仅是想到这一点，就足以唤起一种恐惧，这种恐惧揭示了我们所面临的潜在敌人的巨大力量。

Yet many have found that it is possible at least to begin such a process—to face the pain, not defiantly, but gently, with close attention and compassion for ourselves. Perhaps we’ve gone through a divorce and felt the terrible sting of rejection. We’ve lost a partner to death and felt the sudden onslaught of grief. We’ve experienced periods of deep self-doubt or feelings of unworthiness. We’ve just felt deeply depressed by a sense of great separateness from others, cut off, alone, barely touching when we do meet.

然而，许多人发现，至少可以开始这样的过程——面对痛苦，不是以对抗的方式，而是温柔地、细致地关注和关爱自己。或许我们经历过离婚，感受过被拒绝的剧痛；或许我们失去了伴侣，感受过突如其来的悲痛；或许我们经历过深深的自我怀疑或觉得自己一文不值的时期；或许我们只是因为与他人巨大的疏离感而感到深深的沮丧，仿佛被隔绝、孤独，即使见面也鲜有肢体接触。

While we’d just as soon deny our pain because it’s too searing, at a certain point we’ve turned to face it and explore what it is that we are really feeling. This is the beginning of constructive work. We cease resisting and begin to open. In that action we introduce some space into the situation—the space between the pain and our suffering reaction. In that awareness, we see that what we imagined to be unbearable is potentially bearable. There are alternative responses to pain other than resistant reactivity. There are ways to cultivate this space systematically. Certain meditations for opening around pain, whether physical or psychological, assist us in this effort. An example of one of these might help make this process more vivid.

虽然我们宁愿否认痛苦，因为它太过剧烈，但到了某个阶段，我们开始正视它，探索自己真正的感受。这是建设性工作的开始。我们停止抵抗，开始敞开心扉。在这个过程中，我们为这种境况创造了一些空间——痛苦和我们痛苦反应之间的空间。在这种觉察中，我们发现，我们曾经认为无法忍受的痛苦，其实是可以忍受的。除了抵抗性的反应之外，还有其他应对痛苦的方式。我们可以系统地培养这种空间。一些针对痛苦的冥想练习，无论是身体上的还是心理上的，都能帮助我们做到这一点。以下一个例子或许能让这个过程更加生动形象。

OPENING TO PAIN

疼痛的开启

Find a position in which you can remain comfortable and quiet for a few minutes.

找一个能让你保持舒适安静几分钟的姿势。

Bring into your awareness a thought or a bodily sensation that is unpleasant to you. Perhaps it may be an image or memory, a physical pain or ache. Choose only one.

觉察到一个令你不愉快的想法或身体感觉。也许是一幅画面或一段记忆，也可能是身体上的疼痛或酸痛。只需选择其中一种即可。

Let your attention settle around this thought or sensation.

让你的注意力集中在这种想法或感觉上。

Allow yourself to be with the discomfort.

允许自己与不适感共处。

Bring your attention ever more intimately to bear on the thought or sensation.

将你的注意力更加深入地集中到这种想法或感觉上。

Feel the way in which your mind or body tends to push against the unpleasantness, to close it off.

感受一下你的身心是如何抗拒这种不愉快的感觉，并试图将其封闭起来的。

Feel in your mind or in your body both the pain and the resistance against the pain: both present … yet separate from one another.

在你的思想或身体中，感受疼痛和对疼痛的抵抗：两者都存在……但彼此分离。

Notice your tendency to want to identify with the resistance and to deny or isolate or push away the pain.

注意你是否有想要认同这种阻力，并否认、孤立或排斥痛苦的倾向。

But instead of reactively pushing the painful thought or sensation away, stay with it … gently but firmly.

但不要本能地将痛苦的想法或感觉推开，而是要温柔而坚定地陪伴它。

Now start to loosen the ring of resistance that surrounds the painful thought or sensation, loosening its hold in the same way you might allow a fist to open.

现在开始松开围绕着痛苦想法或感觉的阻力圈，就像松开紧握的拳头一样，放松它的束缚。

Consider the possibility that the resistance to the pain may be more painful than the pain itself. Notice how the resistance closes your heart and fills your body and mind with tension and dis-ease.

不妨想想，对疼痛的抗拒或许比疼痛本身更痛苦。注意这种抗拒是如何封闭你的心扉，让你的身心充满紧张和不安的。

Keep relaxing the resistance … the tightness … that have accumulated around the pain.

继续放松疼痛部位周围积聚的阻力……紧绷感……

Notice any fear that has developed around this unpleasant thought or sensation. Allow the fear to melt … to dissolve … along with the resistance … softening … opening … releasing.…

注意围绕这种不愉快想法或感觉而产生的任何恐惧。让恐惧消融……溶解……连同阻力一起……软化……打开……释放……

Let the painful thought or sensation float free … no longer held in the grasp of resistance.

让痛苦的想法或感觉自由飘荡……不再受抵抗的束缚。

Keep letting go of any resistance that tries to smother the experience. Allow the unpleasant thoughts or sensations to come fully into consciousness. No holding … no pushing away … just floating free.…

放下任何试图扼杀这种体验的抗拒。允许那些不愉快的想法或感觉完全进入意识。不要执着……不要抗拒……就让它们自由漂浮……

All grasping relinquished. Just the thought or sensation, and the awareness of it … together … moment to moment.

放下一切执念。只剩下念头或感觉，以及对它们的觉察……两者合一……一刻接一刻。

See that the unpleasant thought is just a thought … the painful sensation is just a sensation … just that … nothing more.…

要知道，不愉快的想法仅仅是一种想法……痛苦的感觉仅仅是一种感觉……仅此而已……仅此而已……

Softening … opening … releasing … allowing … again and again … until there is just thought … just sensation.…

软化……打开……释放……允许……一遍又一遍……直到只剩下思想……只剩下感觉……

And it keeps changing … from moment to moment … it always keeps changing.…

而且它一直在变化……每时每刻都在变化……它总是在变化……

Soft …

柔软的 …

open …

打开 …

gentle …

温和的 …

allowing …

允许……

floating free.…

自由漂浮着……

adapted from Who Dies , STEPHEN LEVINE

改编自斯蒂芬·莱文的《谁死了》

Whether the pain is physical or psychological, the fist that is tightened around it can loosen. As we have been conditioned, so we can be deconditioned, so we can discover the possibility of freedom. As we play the edge of our pain—gently opening, acknowledging, and allowing—the suffering it has caused diminishes. If we further dissolve the boundaries, letting ourselves enter into the pain and the pain enter into us, we can see the possibility of going beyond it to where the heart is freer. We’ve never been so vulnerable, so defenseless, and yet somehow so safe. The surrender we were so frightened of turns out to be not defeat but a kind of victory.

无论痛苦是生理上的还是心理上的，紧握的拳头都可以松开。正如我们曾被某种条件反射所束缚，我们也可以摆脱这种束缚，从而发现自由的可能性。当我们轻轻地触碰痛苦的边缘——温柔地敞开、承认并接纳它——它带来的痛苦就会减轻。如果我们进一步打破界限，让自己进入痛苦，也让痛苦进入我们，我们就能看到超越痛苦、抵达心灵更自由之地的可能性。我们从未如此脆弱、如此无助，却又如此安全。我们曾如此恐惧的臣服，最终并非失败，而是一种胜利。

Or at the very least an opening. We should never underestimate the difficulty of this process, at any time, under any circumstances. It is nothing to hurl at one another—“Open to your pain!”—as if it didn’t require great patience and discipline, a willingness to fail, fall, and try once more. The practice is not heartless, not rooted in any kind of denial of what’s entailed. It is a practice of compassion for ourselves —the very same attentive listening and patient open-heartedness we would eagerly offer another.

或者至少应该提供一个契机。无论何时何地，我们都不应低估这个过程的难度。这绝非一句空话就能说出口的——“敞开心扉面对你的痛苦！”——仿佛它不需要极大的耐心和自律，不需要甘愿失败、跌倒，然后再次尝试。这种做法并非冷酷无情，也并非出于对其中任何环节的否认。它是一种对自己慈悲的修行——正如我们渴望给予他人的那种专注倾听和耐心敞开的心扉。

Opening to our pain, exploring the roots of our suffering, at best with guidance or support, can always increase our opportunity for well-being. But this process also can be of immeasurable value in our efforts to be of service to others. As our understanding of our own suffering deepens, we become available at deeper levels to those we would care for. We are less likely to project suffering that does not exist or deny that which does. We’re much more sensitive and alert to the nuances of human pain.

坦然面对痛苦，探寻苦难的根源，即便在指导或支持下，也能提升我们获得幸福的机会。但这个过程对于我们服务他人也具有不可估量的价值。随着我们对自身痛苦理解的加深，我们也能更深层次地关爱他人。我们更不容易将并不存在的痛苦投射到他人身上，也更不容易否认真实存在的痛苦。我们对人类痛苦的细微差别会更加敏感和警觉。

We do not, however, insist that others go to the edge of their own pain. Under no circumstances do we judge or condemn another’s suffering. We merely continue to work on our own, steadily, continuously, in all areas of our life. Opening to adversity and discovering in it all the places where we are clinging, resisting and denying, we gradually cut the cord between pain and suffering. The pain is there, but we can move beyond the suffering. To the extent that we ourselves are free of suffering, our very being becomes an environment in which others can be free of theirs, if it is in the way of things.

然而，我们并不强迫他人承受痛苦。在任何情况下，我们都不会评判或谴责他人的苦难。我们只是在生活的各个领域，持续不断地、稳步地提升自己。我们敞开心扉面对逆境，从中发现我们所有执着、抗拒和否认的地方，从而逐渐斩断痛苦与苦难之间的纽带。痛苦依然存在，但我们可以超越苦难。当我们自身摆脱了苦难，我们的存在本身就成为了一种环境，让那些身处困境的人也能摆脱苦难。

It is in just this manner that the great spiritual teachers have perennially been of help to humankind. The power of their compassion has been rooted in the fact that they themselves have overcome the entrapment of suffering. They have broken the link between painful circumstance and mental resistance. They have gone beyond it. This doesn’t mean that they have denied the experience of pain. In Gethsemane, on the cross, throughout his life, Christ surely felt and understood the burden of human incarnation. In his humanity, he experienced it. But in his divinity, he transcended it and transformed it into redemption and liberation, a possibility for all. So too the Buddha, having seen what he saw, could look across all the fields of human existence with “the Smile of Unbearable Compassion.” We can feel this same quality of compassion, which combines fully experiencing but also transcending suffering, in the story of the great Tibetan teacher Marpa, who lived on a farm with his family but welcomed many seekers and monks who came to him for instruction and wisdom.

正是通过这种方式，伟大的精神导师们才能长久地帮助人类。他们慈悲的力量源于他们自身已经克服了苦难的束缚。他们打破了痛苦境遇与精神抗拒之间的联系，超越了苦难本身。但这并不意味着他们否认了痛苦的体验。在客西马尼园、十字架上，以及基督的一生中，他无疑都感受到并理解了人类化身的重担。作为人，他体验了这一切。但作为神，他超越了这一切，将其转化为救赎和解脱，成为所有人的可能。同样，佛陀在目睹一切之后，能够以“无比慈悲的微笑”俯瞰人类存在的方方面面。我们也能在伟大的藏传佛教导师玛尔巴的故事中感受到这种慈悲的特质——它既包含对苦难的充分体验，也包含对苦难的超越。玛尔巴与家人居住在农场，但他热情地接待了许多前来寻求教诲和智慧的求道者和僧侣。

~

One day, Marpa’s eldest son was killed. Off by himself, alone with his grief, Marpa wept. One of his students approached him and said, “I don’t understand. You teach that all this is illusion, created by the clinging and desire and resistance. Yet here you are weeping. If all this is illusion, why do you grieve so deeply?”

有一天，玛尔巴的长子被杀了。玛尔巴独自一人，沉浸在悲痛之中，痛哭流涕。他的一位弟子走近他，问道：“我不明白。您教导我们，这一切都是幻象，是由执着、欲望和抗拒所创造的。可您现在却在哭泣。如果这一切都是幻象，您为何如此悲伤？”

Marpa replied, “Yes, everything here is an illusion. And the death of a child is the greatest of these illusions.”

玛尔巴回答说：“是的，这里的一切都是幻象。而孩子的死亡则是这些幻象中最大的一个。”

~

For us, then, investigation of the causes of suffering within is a tool. Here is our work; here is the path. We conduct the journey according to our own individual temperament and intuition. No one can force us to do this. It’s ours to undertake or not, as appropriate. But it can be of equal value in moments when we are helping others and those in which we ourselves are seeking or receiving care. At times we will be able to break the conditioning of mind and let go of the suffering. At other times, until our self-investigative practice is highly developed, we are bound to get lost in resistance to pain.

因此，对我们而言，探究内在痛苦的根源是一种工具。这就是我们的工作；这就是道路。我们根据自身的性情和直觉来踏上这段旅程。没有人可以强迫我们这样做。是否进行，完全取决于我们自己。但无论我们是在帮助他人，还是在寻求或接受关怀，它都同样重要。有时，我们能够打破思维的束缚，放下痛苦。而有时，在我们自我探究的修行尚未高度成熟之前，我们注定会迷失在对痛苦的抗拒之中。

So we work to understand suffering itself—not just the conditions which give rise to it but the nature of our various reactions to it as well. The range turns out to be vast. Some of us become obsessed by our suffering; others try to ignore it. Some curl up in the fetal position and withdraw into themselves; others wander about confused, grabbing at straws in the wind. Some keep businesslike; others childishly irresponsible. Some keep a stiff upper lip; others cry and turn to jelly.

因此，我们努力去理解苦难本身——不仅是造成苦难的种种条件，也包括我们对苦难的各种反应。结果发现，各种反应的范围极其广泛。有些人会沉溺于苦难之中；有些人则会试图忽略它。有些人会蜷缩成胎儿的姿势，把自己封闭起来；有些人则会茫然地四处游荡，徒劳地寻找希望。有些人会保持冷静，有些人则会像孩子一样不负责任。有些人会强忍着痛苦，有些人则会痛哭流涕，崩溃大哭。

Habitual reactions also include the way we respond to help from others. When in pain, we may reach for help swiftly or spurn any aid. We may be embarrassed at discovering our need or assume it is our right to demand help aggressively. We may feel we have been wronged or are being punished by suffering and become angry or play martyr, or we may be softened by pain and receive support graciously.

习惯性反应也包括我们如何回应他人的帮助。当我们感到痛苦时，我们可能会迅速寻求帮助，也可能拒绝任何援助。我们可能羞于发现自己的需要，或者认为我们有权咄咄逼人地要求帮助。我们可能觉得自己受到了不公对待或惩罚，因而变得愤怒或扮演受害者；或者，我们也可能会因痛苦而变得温柔，欣然接受他人的帮助。

For one receiving help, it can be immensely useful to become more conscious of the habitual ways in which we react to our suffering and the help offered to alleviate it. Just seeing these patterns clearly may allow us to discard reactions that cut us off from others at a time when we need them the most.

对于接受帮助的人来说，更加清楚地意识到我们应对痛苦和所获帮助的习惯性反应方式，会非常有益。仅仅是清晰地认识到这些模式，就能让我们摒弃那些在我们最需要帮助的时候，反而将我们与他人隔绝开来的反应。

For one who is seeking to offer help, investigation of our habitual reactions to our own suffering can illuminate the subtle ways in which we may judge others for theirs. Many helpers, when they themselves are suffering, are incapable of accepting support, or at least receiving it easily. Yet they may be impatient with those they’re working with for not accepting aid or counsel readily enough. Chances are, if you can’t accept help, you can’t really give it.

对于想要提供帮助的人来说，审视我们面对自身痛苦的习惯性反应，可以揭示我们可能在哪些微妙之处评判他人的痛苦。许多助人者在自身遭受痛苦时，无法接受帮助，或者至少难以轻易接受。然而，他们却可能因为受助者未能及时接受帮助或建议而感到不耐烦。很有可能，如果你无法接受帮助，你就无法真正给予帮助。

While all of this is an extremely complicated psychodynamic interaction, one thing seems obvious. The more conscious we are in dealing with our own suffering, the more sensitive we will be in treating the pain of others.

虽然这一切都涉及极其复杂的心理动力学互动，但有一点似乎显而易见：我们越能觉察自身的痛苦，就越能体谅他人的痛苦。

~

I have a friend, a chemotherapy nurse in a children’s cancer ward, whose job it is to pry for any available vein in an often emaciated arm to give infusions of chemicals that sometimes last as long as twelve hours and which are often quite discomforting to the child. He is probably the greatest pain giver the children meet in their stay in the hospital. Because he has worked so much with his own pain, his heart is very open. He works with his responsibilities in the hospital as a “laying on of hands with love and acceptance.” There is little in him that causes him to withdraw, that reinforces the painfulness of the experience for the children. He is a warm, open space which encourages them to trust whatever they feel. And it is he whom the children most often ask for at the time they are dying. Although he is the main pain-giver, he is also the main love-giver .

我有个朋友，在儿童癌症病房做化疗护士。他的工作是在孩子们瘦骨嶙峋的手臂上寻找任何可用的血管，给他们输注化疗药物。这些药物有时需要输注长达十二个小时，而且常常让孩子们非常难受。他可能是孩子们在医院里遇到的最痛苦的人。因为他自己也曾饱受病痛折磨，所以他非常宽容。他在医院里尽职尽责，就像“用爱和接纳去抚慰他们”。他很少会退缩，也很少会加剧孩子们的痛苦。他就像一个温暖、开放的空间，鼓励孩子们相信自己的感受。孩子们在临终之际，最常求见的就是他。虽然他是主要的痛苦制造者，但他也是主要的爱的给予者。

~

What objectives can we set, what resources can we call upon then in the great effort to relieve suffering? First we must face it and let it in. Different orders of service and loving kindness follow.

那么，在努力减轻苦难的伟大事业中，我们能设定哪些目标？我们能调动哪些资源？首先，我们必须正视苦难，接纳它。随后，我们才能采取不同形式的服务和慈悲之举。

Our immediate responsibility is to do what we can to alleviate the concrete conditions of human affliction. We work to provide food for the hungry, shelter for the homeless, health care for the sick and feeble, protection for the threatened and vulnerable, schooling for the uneducated, freedom for the oppressed. To this order of service we must always attend first .

我们眼下的责任是尽我们所能减轻人类苦难的实际处境。我们努力为饥饿者提供食物，为无家可归者提供住所，为病弱者提供医疗，为受威胁和弱势群体提供保护，为未受教育者提供教育，为受压迫者争取自由。我们必须始终把这项服务放在首位。

Where we cannot help provide such aid, we may be called on to offer a different kind of support. Perhaps we can help another to reperceive his or her situation so that while it is unpleasant or painful, he or she need suffer less as a reaction to it. This can’t take the form of facile counsel. Such support can come only from the truth of our own being. However much we have been able to break our own reactiveness to pain, however well we have cultivated those qualities of mind and heart that allow us to be open to affliction yet not be reactive to it, we will have that to offer others. The right form, the right words, the right moment, will all follow. At this stage, we do not have help to give , we are help itself.

当我们无法提供此类援助时，或许需要提供另一种支持。或许我们可以帮助他人重新审视自身处境，即便处境令人不快或痛苦，也能减轻其因痛苦而产生的反应。这种支持并非简单的劝告，而是源于我们内心深处的真实感受。无论我们如何克服自身对痛苦的反应，无论我们如何培养心智和心灵的品质，使我们能够坦然面对苦难却不被其左右，我们都能将这些品质给予他人。合适的方式、合适的言辞、合适的时机，自然会随之而来。此时此刻，我们并非拥有可以给予的帮助，我们本身就是帮助。

Even in those situations where another person is completely enmeshed in the web of a suffering mind and is not receptive to help in reperceiving the situation, we can be of comfort. We can offer our own empathy, our own experience, our own understanding of how it feels when we suffer: the resistance, tension, fear, withdrawal, self-pity, doubt, the utter separateness. This compassion will guide our helping hand to appropriate gestures: a simple word of friendship to cut through the isolation; a gentle neck massage to ease the tension; a tender hug or touch to convey love; a meeting of the eyes for a moment beyond it all.

即使在对方完全深陷痛苦的漩涡，难以接受帮助重新审视处境的情况下，我们依然可以给予安慰。我们可以分享自己的同理心、自己的经历，以及我们对痛苦感受的理解：抗拒、紧张、恐惧、退缩、自怜、怀疑，以及彻底的孤立感。这份慈悲将指引我们伸出援手，做出恰当的举动：一句简单的友谊之语，打破彼此的孤寂；一个轻柔的颈部按摩，舒缓紧张；一个温柔的拥抱或抚摸，传递爱意；一次超越一切的眼神交流。

Sometimes we may be able to do all these things at once: nourish the hungry stomach, the famished heart, and the yearning soul. But perhaps there will be nothing we can do . Then we can only be , and be with the person in his or her pain, attending to the quality of our own consciousness. On his or her behalf, we will dwell in whatever truth and understanding we have come to which is beyond suffering. From this, compassion arises. Hearts that have known pain meet in mutual recognition and trust. Such a meeting helps immeasurably.

有时我们或许能够同时做到这一切：满足饥饿的胃、饥渴的心灵和渴望的灵魂。但或许我们无能为力。那时，我们只能存在，与痛苦之人同在，关注自身意识的品质。我们将代表他们，安住于我们已领悟的超越苦难的真理与理解之中。由此，慈悲生起。曾饱受痛苦的心灵相遇，彼此理解，彼此信任。这样的相遇意义非凡。

~

When I left New York harbor for Peru, I instinctively felt I was making a journey that would shape my life. It was 1951; I was robust and eager. I wasn’t even sure what my real mission would be. At that point, there was just an empty lot .

当我离开纽约港前往秘鲁时，我本能地感到自己即将踏上一段塑造我一生的旅程。那是1951年，我精力充沛，充满热情。我甚至不确定自己真正的使命是什么。当时，那里只是一片空地。

It was thirteen thousand five hundred feet high, very cold and demanding. As a Maryknoll sister, I was there to teach school. After a while I became principal. I guess you could say I was a figure, just by being in that role. Then the illness happened, quite suddenly, up there. The doctors said it was rheumatoid arthritis. They said it was ultimately a crippling disease. They said there was nothing really to do about it .

那里海拔一万三千五百英尺，非常寒冷，环境也很艰苦。作为一名玛利诺修女，我在那里教书。过了一段时间，我成了校长。我想，仅仅因为我担任了校长这个职位，我就已经算是个人物了。然后，疾病就在那里突然发作了。医生说是类风湿性关节炎。他们说这最终会致残。他们说对此束手无策。

I went to see other doctors elsewhere, like in Panama, because I wanted to stay in South America. I wouldn’t accept what they were telling me, what I was going to have to face. But it gradually became clear I should come back to the States for some treatment .

我去了其他地方看医生，比如巴拿马，因为我想留在南美。我无法接受他们告诉我的，也无法接受我即将面临的一切。但渐渐地，我意识到我应该回美国接受治疗。

I got good care. However, the doctors said that gold injections would be the only help, but it would prevent me from going back to Peru. I didn’t want them. I was going back. I was fighting it, fighting it all—the illness, my own reactions—self-pity, anger, discouragement, doubt. I wouldn’t give in. But every day it seemed I was losing. Finally I felt I had to quit imposing my own will; that was a big step. I went to the doctors, and they said they could give me this medicine, and after a few months they’d see if I could get onto maintenance and go back to Peru. After all my anger and resistance, there seemed to be some kind of chance. But chance for what?

我得到了很好的照顾。然而，医生说注射金针是唯一有效的办法，但这会让我无法返回秘鲁。我不想注射。我一定要回去。我一直在抗争，抗争一切——疾病，抗争我自己的反应——自怜、愤怒、沮丧、怀疑。我绝不放弃。但似乎每一天我都在败下阵来。最终，我感到我必须放弃强加自己的意志；这是一大步。我去看了医生，他们说可以给我开这种药，几个月后再看看我是否能进入维持治疗阶段，然后返回秘鲁。经历了所有的愤怒和抗拒之后，似乎出现了一线希望。但这希望又能带来什么呢？

I had surgery at the Mayo Clinic, and I did a great deal of reflecting and praying in their chapel. There was a beautiful wooden statue of Christ there, with outstretched hands. I think that’s why it had been chosen, to inspire the hands of surgeons and nurses. As it happened I was there to have my own hands operated on. I remember thinking that even though my hands were going to be broken and crooked, they would still be sacred to me. I’d use them to bring something to somebody, I didn’t know what. My hands could be the compassionate hands of Christ as much as the hands of the doctors and nurses .

我在梅奥诊所做了手术，之后在他们的小教堂里进行了长时间的反思和祈祷。那里有一尊美丽的木制基督像，双手张开。我想，选择这尊雕像的原因就在于此，为了激励外科医生和护士们的双手。碰巧的是，我去那里也是为了做手部手术。我记得当时我在想，即使我的双手会骨折变形，它们对我来说依然是神圣的。我会用它们去帮助别人，虽然我不知道会是什么。我的双手可以像医生和护士的双手一样，成为基督充满慈悲的双手。

So I sought to be able to enter into the world of the sick, and to live with the mystery of suffering. I saw that I had to enter into my own experience of pain, and to face up to it, and to allow myself to be changed by it. Without that nothing could be done. I saw that healing comes with owning our wounds as the first step in moving beyond them .

于是，我努力进入病痛的世界，去体验苦难的奥秘。我意识到，我必须直面自己的痛苦，接纳它，并允许它改变自己。否则，一切都无从谈起。我明白，疗愈的第一步，就是正视自己的伤痛，并以此超越伤痛。

I returned to Peru at a lower altitude. Almost everything had changed, especially my attitude toward the people I was working with. I could feel their terrible poverty and pain in a whole new way. In fact it seemed as if I was seeing it for the first time. How often I’d rushed around trying to solve people’s problems without really seeing them—the pain in their faces, the insecure eyes, the nervous hands, all expressions of the hurt inside. It was only when suffering had actually touched me that I began to feel their condition .

我回到秘鲁，来到了海拔较低的地区。几乎一切都变了，尤其是我对那些与我共事的人们的态度。我以一种全新的方式感受到了他们可怕的贫困和痛苦。事实上，这仿佛是我第一次亲眼目睹这一切。我曾经多么频繁地忙前忙后地试图解决人们的问题，却从未真正关注过他们——他们脸上的痛苦、不安的眼神、紧张的双手，所有这些都是内心伤痛的流露。只有当苦难真正触动我时，我才开始感同身受他们的处境。

The affirmation I got from them was so important: “You’re the same person you were before. And even if you can’t teach or do anything, we’d like you to stay.” Just to see me get up and try to do something seemed to mean a great deal to them. We were meeting on a level where we all suffer. That became our ground .

他们的肯定对我意义非凡：“你还是以前的你。即使你不能教书，不能做任何事，我们也希望你留下来。” 看到我重新振作起来，努力做点什么，对他们来说似乎意义重大。我们相遇在一个共同经历苦难的层面。这成了我们彼此的立足点。

And so my ministry changed. It became the ministry of walking together. Some of us with physical disabilities joined together to share our experiences. We were just being together, trying to understand what was possible for us, share what we could, examples of creativity. Our pain and weakness and deformity proved to be teachers of a great mystery, a small introduction into the kind of dying from which new spirit is born .

于是我的事工发生了改变，变成了携手同行的事工。我们这些身有残疾的人聚在一起，分享彼此的经历。我们只是待在一起，努力理解我们能做到什么，分享我们所能分享的一切，分享创造力的例子。我们的痛苦、虚弱和残疾，最终都成了揭示伟大奥秘的导师，让我们得以窥见那种从死亡中诞生的新生。

We found we had become more sensitive to others, more touched, more able to listen, moved more by feelings than by intellectual concepts. We discovered that the more we opened to the pain of others, the more we found ourselves in their service. Having been brought low, it was just a matter of standing humbly before others, and presenting a visible sign of hope by some silent testimony .

我们发现自己变得更加体贴他人，更容易被触动，更善于倾听，也更容易被情感而非理性概念所打动。我们发现，越是敞开心扉去感受他人的痛苦，就越能感受到自己在为他们服务。即便身处逆境，我们也能谦卑地站在他人面前，用无声的见证传递希望的讯息。

So we would simply walk about, as best we could. Many of the Peruvians we ran into with handicaps were deeply ashamed and hid. We would come to see them, and they would hide, in their own homes. But as we moved about, they would gradually come forth more .

所以我们就只能尽力四处走走。我们遇到的许多秘鲁残疾人士都深感羞愧，躲了起来。我们去看望他们，他们却躲在家里。但随着我们走动，他们也逐渐开始敞开心扉。

I think of Juan, a polio victim at three, who had been hidden by his family in their small mud-brick house until we discovered him at the age of eight. His brother, Julio, took us home one day. There was Juan, his twisted legs underneath him, scooting around the small dirt patio on a circular piece of rubber. His mother was suspicious and didn’t want us to stay. A handicapped child meant she was being punished for something. She was ashamed .

我想起了胡安，他三岁时患上了小儿麻痹症，家人一直把他藏在他们那间简陋的泥砖房里，直到八岁那年我们才发现他。有一天，他的哥哥胡里奥带我们回家。我们看到胡安，他那扭曲的双腿蜷缩在身下，正用一块圆形的橡胶垫在泥土小院子里挪动。他的母亲起了疑心，不想让我们留下。在她看来，一个残疾的孩子意味着她因为什么事受到了惩罚。她感到羞愧。

We returned on several occasions to visit Juan. One time we found him all alone. His family, with the rest of the town, had gone to a religious procession. Of course, he’d never seen one. So we borrowed a bicycle, put Juan on it, and joined in the procession itself. It was his first time outside the house, the first time he’d looked at people from a level higher than the ground, his first procession .

我们后来又去了几次胡安家。有一次，我们发现他独自一人待在那里。他的家人和镇上的其他人一样，都去参加宗教游行了。当然，他以前从未见过这种游行。于是我们借了一辆自行车，让胡安骑上去，也加入了游行队伍。这是他第一次走出家门，第一次从高处俯瞰人群，也是他第一次参加游行。

His parents were momentarily annoyed, but their attitude changed gradually. When we thought it was right to raise the idea, we asked at the next town meeting if we could raise money to send Juan to Lima for physical rehabilitation. Everyone liked the idea and Juan went off to the big city .

他的父母起初有些恼火，但态度逐渐转变。我们觉得时机成熟后，在下次镇民大会上提议筹款送胡安去利马进行康复治疗。大家都赞同这个主意，胡安也去了大城市。

He had a long, hard struggle, with much pain and effort. But one day he returned to the village. He was using braces and a cane. It was very hard for him. But as he began to walk down the streets to his home, people came out of their own homes. They appeared from all over. They were cheering and clapping and they followed him all the way home. It was so wonderful. It was Juan’s second procession .

他经历了漫长而艰辛的斗争，承受了巨大的痛苦和努力。但有一天，他终于回到了村子。他拄着拐杖，戴着支架，走路非常吃力。当他开始沿着街道往家走时，人们纷纷从家中走出来。他们从四面八方涌来，欢呼鼓掌，一路护送他回家。那场面真是太美好了。这是胡安第二次参加游行。

It’s difficult. I have had many ups and downs. That’s the thing about a progressive crippling disease: more and more pain and disability; it keeps on pushing you, making more demands, forcing you to greater discipline .

这很艰难。我经历了很多起起伏伏。这就是渐进性致残疾病的特点：疼痛和残疾与日俱增；它不断地鞭策你，提出更高的要求，迫使你更加自律。

But I have seen much service born of suffering. And I see that our little suffering is not for ourselves. It can have impact throughout the world, that’s how much our lives can mean, that’s how much is possible. And I have been with people who would just cry over that message, cry and cry. And I have cried too .

但我见过许多因苦难而生的奉献。我也明白，我们所承受的些许苦难并非为了我们自身。它能对世界产生深远的影响，这就是我们生命的意义所在，这就是我们所能做到的。我曾亲眼目睹人们听到这番话后痛哭流涕，泪流不止。我也曾如此。

# ↩

4
The Listening Mind

4 聆听的思维

M uch of our capacity to help another person depends upon our state of mind. Sometimes our minds are so scattered, confused, depressed, or agitated, we can hardly get out of bed. At other times we’re clear, alert, and receptive; we feel ready, even eager, to respond generously to the needs of others. Most of the time it’s really not one extreme or the other. Our minds are … well … they’re just our minds. Like old cars, typewriters, or appliances, we put up with their idiosyncrasies with a shrug. What can we do about it anyway?

我们帮助他人的能力很大程度上取决于我们的精神状态。有时，我们心绪纷乱、迷茫、沮丧或焦虑，甚至难以起床。而有时，我们头脑清醒、精神抖擞、乐于倾听；我们感到随时准备好，甚至渴望慷慨地回应他人的需求。大多数时候，我们的状态并非非此即彼。我们的大脑……嗯……它就是我们的大脑。就像老旧的汽车、打字机或家用电器一样，我们耸耸肩，默默忍受着它们的种种怪癖。反正我们又能怎么办呢？

Perhaps we settle for too little. Our mind, after all, is our most potentially powerful tool. With it we have harnessed fire, devised technology, extended our ability to grow and process food, developed ways to protect ourselves from the elements, discovered means to cure illness and extend our life span.

或许我们满足得太少了。毕竟，我们的思想是我们最具潜力的工具。凭借它，我们驾驭了火，发明了技术，拓展了种植和加工食物的能力，发展了抵御自然灾害的方法，发现了治愈疾病和延长寿命的途径。

Our mind is not only the source of ideas, a tool for gathering data, an instrument of training and technique, or a repository of experience and memory. Because the mind’s capacity to think is so brilliant, we tend to be dazzled by it and fail to notice other attributes and functions. There is more to the mind than reason alone. There is awareness itself and what we sometimes think of as the deeper qualities of mind. Most of us know how supportive it is merely to be in the presence of a mind that is open, quiet, playful, receptive, or reflective. These attributes are themselves helpful. Moreover, there is something we frequently experience—perhaps we can call it intuitive awareness—that links us most intimately to the universe and, in allegiance with the heart, binds us together in generosity and compassion. Often it leaps to vision and knowledge instantaneously. “My understanding of the fundamental laws of the universe,” said Albert Einstein, “did not come out of my rational mind.”

我们的心智不仅是思想的源泉、收集数据的工具、训练和技巧的手段，也是经验和记忆的宝库。由于心智的思考能力如此卓越，我们往往被它所折服，而忽略了它的其他属性和功能。心智远不止理性那么简单。它包含着觉知本身，以及我们有时称之为心智更深层次的特质。我们大多数人都知道，仅仅是置身于一个开放、宁静、充满活力、善于接纳或反思的心智之中，就足以令人受益匪浅。这些特质本身就极具价值。此外，我们经常体验到一种东西——或许我们可以称之为直觉觉知——它将我们与宇宙最紧密地联系在一起，并与我们内心深处的情感相契合，将我们凝聚在慷慨和慈悲之中。它常常瞬间转化为洞察力和知识。“我对宇宙基本法则的理解，”阿尔伯特·爱因斯坦曾说，“并非源于我的理性思维。”

This resource of awareness can give us access to deeper power, power to help and heal.

这种觉察力可以赋予我们更深层次的力量，帮助和治愈的力量。

~

I had been meditating for a number of years. My progress, in terms of increased concentration and a more peaceful, quiet quality in my mind, was noticeable, though not dramatic. In the ancient texts I’d read accounts of monks who through meditation had gained great powers, and I kept wondering if the stories were true .

我冥想已有数年。我的进步显而易见，专注力有所提高，内心也更加平和宁静，虽然并非突飞猛进。我曾在古代典籍中读到过一些僧侣通过冥想获得强大力量的记载，我不禁好奇这些故事是否属实。

Then, I visited the wife of the former American ambassador in Thailand, and she told me about a monk who had built a monastery in which heroin and opium addicts were cured in ten days … for fifteen dollars. These kinds of statistics are unheard of in the West. Possibly this was one of those monks with the meditation powers. I prevailed on her to take me to meet him .

后来，我拜访了美国前驻泰国大使的夫人，她告诉我一位僧人建了一座寺院，据说只需十五美元，十天就能治愈海洛因和鸦片成瘾者。这种事在西方简直闻所未闻。或许这位僧人就是拥有这种冥想能力的僧人之一。我恳求她带我去见他。

The monk had previously been a Thai “narc” … something like our federal drug enforcement agency. He had an aunt who I was told was a Buddhist saint, whatever that means. One day she apparently said to him, while he was still a narc, “What are you doing? If you don’t watch out you’re going to end up killing people in this job. Why don’t you help these people instead of hurting them?” He said that he didn’t know how. She apparently told him to clean up his act and she’d show him .

这位僧人以前是泰国的缉毒警……类似于我们联邦缉毒机构的那种。他有个姑姑，据说是一位佛教圣人，我也不知道这是什么意思。有一天，在他还是个缉毒警的时候，她对他说：“你在干什么？你要是不注意，这份工作迟早会害死人的。你为什么不帮助这些人，反而要伤害他们呢？” 他说他不知道该怎么做。她显然是让他改过自新，然后她会好好教训他。

So he left government service and became a monk. Now the Buddhist monks in Thailand are part of the Theravadin tradition which requires very severe renunciation in order to purify your mind so that you can do deep meditation. There are some two hundred and eighteen prohibitions, all of which he adopted. Then he even added ten more on his own, such as never driving in automobiles. This meant that when he had business in Bangkok, about a hundred and fifty miles away, he’d just pick up his walking stick and start walking .

于是他辞去了政府职务，出家为僧。泰国的佛教僧侣属于上座部佛教，这个教派要求僧侣进行极其严格的苦行，以净化心灵，从而进行深度冥想。上座部佛教有两百一十八条戒律，他全部遵守。之后，他又自行增添了十条，例如绝不驾驶汽车。这意味着，当他在一百五十英里外的曼谷有事要办时，他只需拄着拐杖步行即可。

This rigorous training prepared him to do very intensive meditation practice which allowed him to tune to the deeper and more powerful parts of his mind. When his aunt felt he was ready, she instructed him in the preparation of an herbal diuretic which she instructed him to give to the addicts, and he started his monastery .

这种严格的训练使他能够进行非常密集的冥想练习，从而与自己内心深处更强大的力量连接。当他的姑姑觉得他准备好了，便指导他配制一种草药利尿剂，并嘱咐他把这种药剂给瘾君子服用，之后他便开始建立自己的寺院。

When we met him, my most immediate reaction was that I was shaking hands with an oak tree. His presence was immensely powerful and solid. He had us shown through the monastery where some three hundred addicts were undergoing treatment .

我们见到他时，我的第一反应是感觉自己像是在和一棵橡树握手。他的气场强大而沉稳。他带我们参观了修道院，那里大约有三百名瘾君子正在接受治疗。

You could really see who was which. The first-day arrivals all looked like strung-out junkies. They were in one room. Then, further on, by the time they had been there for four days you could really see a change. And by eight days they seemed cheerful, were bumming cigarettes from me, and seemed really friendly—not particularly like addicts at all. And then after ten days they were gone. And their statistics showed seventy percent remained free of addiction afterwards. Amazing .

你真的能一眼看出谁是瘾君子。第一天来的那些人看起来都像吸毒成瘾的瘾君子，他们都挤在一个房间里。后来，过了四天，你就能明显感觉到他们的变化。到了第八天，他们看起来都很开心，还向我要烟，而且非常友好——完全不像瘾君子了。十天后，他们就都离开了。统计数据显示，之后有70%的人成功戒掉了毒瘾。真是不可思议。

When I interviewed the monk, I asked him, “How do you do it?” He said, “Well, it’s simple. I tell them that they can only come for ten days and they may never come again, and that the cure will work.” I asked him if a lot of religious indoctrination was included in the ten-day program. “No,” he said, “none of that. These people aren’t suitable for that.”

我采访那位僧人时问他：“您是怎么做到的？” 他说：“很简单。我告诉他们，他们只能来十天，以后可能再也不会来了，但这样就能治好他们的病。” 我问他，这十天的疗程里是否包含很多宗教灌输。“不，”他说，“完全没有。这些人不适合接受那种东西。”

I had heard that many drug experts, media people, and even some congressmen had come from the West, but that none of them could figure out why what he did worked. The herbal brew clearly wasn’t the whole ballgame. As I hung out with him longer I began to realize that his mind was so centered and one-pointed that his being was stronger than their addiction. Somehow he conveyed to those addicts a sense of their non-addiction that was stronger than their addiction. And I saw that his commitment was so total, that he wasn’t just someone using a skill. He had died into his work. He was the cure .

我听说许多毒品专家、媒体人士，甚至一些国会议员都从西方赶来，但他们都无法弄明白他的方法为何有效。显然，草药汤剂并非全部。随着我与他相处的时间越来越长，我开始意识到，他的精神如此专注，如此一心一意，以至于他的存在本身就比他们的毒瘾更强大。他以某种方式让那些瘾君子感受到一种超越毒瘾的解脱感。我看到他全身心的投入，他不仅仅是在运用某种技巧。他已将生命融入到工作中。他就是解药本身。

This was the example I had been looking for. Just being with him I could feel the extraordinary quality of his mind. Meeting him reassured me that the ancient stories were probably true. I returned to meditation with renewed vigor .

这就是我一直在寻找的例子。仅仅是和他在一起，我就能感受到他非凡的智慧。与他相遇让我更加确信那些古老的故事很可能是真的。我重新焕发活力，继续冥想。

~

Most of us are not really ready to become renunciates in order to develop the concentration and quality of awareness necessary to help others at such an extraordinary level. But if we are prepared to investigate our minds even a little bit, we start a process that can improve our effectiveness in life, and therefore in helping as well. If we are willing to examine the agitation of our own minds and look just beyond it, we quite readily find entry into rooms that hold surprising possibilities: a greater inner calm, sharper concentration, deeper intuitive understanding, and an enhanced ability to hear one another’s heart. Such an inquiry turns out to be critical in the work of helping others.

我们大多数人其实并没有做好遁世修行的准备，去培养帮助他人所需的专注力和觉察力。但如果我们愿意哪怕稍微审视一下自己的内心，就能开启一个提升生活效率，进而提升助人能力的进程。如果我们愿意审视自己内心的躁动，并超越它去探寻更深层次的东西，就能轻易地找到通往充满无限可能的境界：更深层的内心平静、更敏锐的专注力、更深刻的直觉理解，以及更强的倾听他人心声的能力。这样的探索对于助人至关重要。

The phone rings. We turn from the checkbook we were balancing to answer. It’s someone seeking counsel. Even as the person begins to speak, our minds are conflicted. We don’t quite want to leave that column of figures un-added, and yet we know that we have to let go of our bookkeeping to listen carefully to the problem.

电话铃响了。我们放下正在核对的账簿，接起电话。是有人来咨询。对方开口说话时，我们内心却很矛盾。我们不想让那一栏数字漏算，但又知道必须放下账目，认真听对方的问题。

The voice on the other end tries to find words to describe suffering: “I’m just feeling so … it’s like I … I really don’t know, but.…” Painstaking work. But sometimes even as it starts, our mind may begin to wander. “This is going to be a tough one.… Am I up to this?… What about dinner?… I’d better circle that place where I think the bank screwed up.”

电话那头的声音努力寻找合适的词语来描述痛苦：“我感觉……就像……我真的不知道，但是……” 这是一项艰巨的任务。但有时，即使任务刚刚开始，我们的思绪也会开始游离。“这将会是一场硬仗……我能应付得了吗？……晚饭怎么办？……我最好绕着那个我认为银行搞砸的地方转一圈。”

At a certain stage, personal judgments may start competing for attention. “He’s really romanticizing it a lot.… He ought to be done with this one by now.… He’s not hearing what I mean.” We may get a little lost in evaluating—“Is it working? Am I helping?” Or we could as easily turn the evaluation on ourselves, “I don’t care that much. I really don’t like him.”

到了某个阶段，个人评判可能会开始争夺注意力。“他真的把这段感情浪漫化了……他现在应该已经结束这段感情了……他根本没听懂我的意思。”我们可能会陷入评估的漩涡——“这样做有效吗？我帮上忙了吗？”或者，我们也可能轻易地将评估转向自己，“我没那么在意。我其实不喜欢他。”

Sometimes we catch ourselves in distraction and rejoin the person on the other end of the phone. Now it’s better. Something’s beginning to happen. Then we take an intentionally audible in-breath—we’ve got something helpful to say—but the signal goes by; he keeps right on talking. Off goes the mind to utterly unrelated topics: “Call Dad.… That picture on the wall is crooked.… I’m tired.… I have to feed the cat.”

有时我们会突然走神，然后重新集中注意力听电话那头的人说话。现在情况好多了，好像有什么进展了。这时我们会故意吸一口气——我们想说点有用的东西——但对方没反应，继续说个不停。于是我们的思绪又飘到了完全不相干的话题上：“给爸爸打电话……墙上的那幅画歪了……我好累……我得喂猫了。”

This mental chatter goes on and off. Sometimes we really get lost, and by the time we’re back, we realize we’ve missed a key point, and it’s too late to ask for it to be repeated. At other times we can take quick note of our reactions and still stay with it. Perhaps we just let it all run off; it’s not something we even notice—it fades into the background like film-score music we’re hardly aware is there.

这种内心的喋喋不休时断时续。有时我们真的会迷失其中，等回过神来时，才发现自己错过了关键点，而此时再要求重复也为时已晚。有时我们能迅速留意自己的反应，并继续跟进。或许我们干脆任由思绪飘散；我们甚至没有察觉——它就像电影配乐一样，渐渐融入背景，我们几乎意识不到它的存在。

Then the call is over. The voice on the other end says “Thank you.” We reply “You’re welcome.” But how welcome was he? How much room did the mind give him? How much did we really hear? How much did he feel heard? Maybe we sit back in the chair and reflect on that for a moment. Or perhaps we get up, walk to the kitchen, and savor the “thank you” along with a sandwich. Perhaps we simply turn back to the checkbook.

通话结束了。电话那头传来一声“谢谢”。我们回答“不客气”。但我们真的感到被欢迎了吗？我们给了他多少空间？我们真正听到了多少？他又觉得自己被理解了吗？或许我们会靠在椅背上，思考片刻。又或许我们会起身，走到厨房，一边享用三明治，一边细细品味这句“谢谢”。或许我们只是转过身，继续翻看支票簿。

Reckoning, judging, evaluating, leaping in, taking it personally, being bored—the helping act has any number of invitations to reactiveness and distraction. Partly we are agitated because we so intensely want to help. After all, someone’s in pain. We care. So part of the time we are listening, but we may also be using our minds to try to solve the problem. There’s a pull to be efficient, to look for some kind of resolution. We reach for certain familiar models or approaches. In order to be helpful, our analytic mind must stay on top of it all.

权衡、评判、评估、贸然介入、过度解读、感到无聊——助人行为本身就充满了各种诱因，容易导致我们做出过激反应或分心。部分原因是，我们太想帮忙了，所以才会如此焦躁不安。毕竟，有人正在承受痛苦。我们关心他们。因此，我们有时会倾听，但有时也会试图用自己的思维去解决问题。我们渴望高效，渴望找到某种解决方案。我们会不自觉地采用一些熟悉的模式或方法。为了真正帮到别人，我们的分析思维必须始终保持清醒的头脑。

So we jump between listening and judging. But in our zeal to help, we may increase the distance between the person and our own consciousness. We find ourselves primarily in our own thoughts, not with another person. Not only are we listening less, but the concepts our mind is coming up with start to act as a screen that preselects information. One thought rules out another.

于是，我们一会儿倾听，一会儿评判。但出于帮助他人的热情，我们反而可能拉大自己与对方的距离。我们发现自己主要沉浸在自己的思绪中，而不是与对方同在。我们不仅听得少了，而且脑海中浮现的概念也开始像一道屏障，预先筛选信息。一个想法会排除另一个想法。

One of the results of all this mental activity is that there’s less room to meet, less room for a new truth to emerge, less room to let things simply be revealed in “their own good time.” The mind tries to do too many things at once. It’s difficult to know which mental vectors are useful and which are distractions, static on the line, bad connections.

所有这些思维活动导致的结果之一是，彼此交流的空间变小了，新真理涌现的空间变小了，让事物“顺其自然”展现的空间也变小了。人的思维试图同时处理太多事情。我们很难分辨哪些思维活动是有益的，哪些是干扰、干扰信号或不良连接。

This agitation and reactiveness should be no surprise to most of us. We have come to expect and accept this state except in rare situations. Yet it need not be that way.

这种焦虑和反应过度对我们大多数人来说并不意外。除了极少数特殊情况外，我们已经习以为常并接受了这种状态。然而，情况并非必须如此。

~

A big, tough samurai once went to see a little monk. “Monk,” he said, in a voice accustomed to instant obedience, “teach me about heaven and hell!”

从前，一个身材魁梧、作风强悍的武士去拜访一位小和尚。“和尚，”他用一种习惯于立刻服从的语气说道，“请教我天堂和地狱吧！”

The monk looked up at this mighty warrior and replied with utter disdain, “Teach you about heaven and hell? I couldn’t teach you about anything. You’re dirty. You smell. Your blade is rusty. You’re a disgrace, an embarrassment to the samurai class. Get out of my sight. I can’t stand you.”

僧人抬头望着这位威武的武士，满脸不屑地说道：“教你天堂地狱？我什么都教不了你。你肮脏不堪，浑身散发着臭味，刀刃也生锈了。你简直是武士阶层的耻辱，丢尽了武士的脸。滚出我的视线，我受不了你。”

The samurai was furious. He shook, got all red in the face, was speechless with rage. He pulled out his sword and raised it above him, preparing to slay the monk .

武士怒不可遏，浑身颤抖，面色涨红，气得说不出话来。他拔出剑，高高举过头顶，准备斩杀和尚。

“That’s hell,” said the monk softly .

“那是地狱，”僧人轻声说道。

The samurai was overwhelmed. The compassion and surrender of this little man who had offered his life to give this teaching to show him hell! He slowly put down his sword, filled with gratitude, and suddenly peaceful .

武士被深深震撼了。这个小个子男人竟然甘愿牺牲生命，只为让他见识地狱的威严，而他身上却蕴藏着如此的怜悯和臣服！他缓缓放下手中的剑，心中充满感激，顿时感到无比平静。

“And that’s heaven,” said the monk softly .

“那就是天堂，”僧人轻声说道。

~

If we continue to observe our mind over some time, we notice that it’s not always distracted and busy. For all of us, there are times when our minds become concentrated, sharp and clear. Perhaps we are doing a crossword puzzle, playing a video game, reading a mystery story, cleaning house or cooking. For some, it’s the simple tasks that engage us in ways that allow our mind to be composed and focused; for others, it’s complex problem solving.

如果我们持续观察一段时间，就会发现它并非总是心不在焉、忙碌不堪。对我们所有人来说，总会有一些时候，我们的思维会变得专注、敏锐、清晰。也许我们正在做填字游戏、玩电子游戏、阅读悬疑小说、打扫房间或做饭。对一些人来说，正是这些简单的任务让我们全身心投入，从而保持头脑清醒和专注；而对另一些人来说，则是解决复杂的问题。

Many times, however, the needs of others are what bring us to a state of sharp concentration. Whether it’s because we feel very secure with those we’re with or because we are functioning under conditions of extreme crisis, we find that in this state of intense concentration helpful insights arise on their own, as a function of our one-pointedness. In these experiences we meet a resource of remarkable potential. While we may be frustrated in not having access to it all the time, these experiences lead us to inquire whether there might be something we could do more regularly and formally to quiet the mind, strengthen its concentration, make available the deeper insights that often result, and bring them into closer attunement with the empathy and compassion of our heart. How immeasurably this might enhance our ability to help others.

然而，很多时候，正是他人的需求让我们进入高度专注的状态。无论是因为我们与身边的人相处感到安心，还是因为我们身处极端危机之中，我们都会发现，在这种高度专注的状态下，一些有益的洞见会自然而然地涌现，这源于我们全神贯注。在这些经历中，我们邂逅了一种蕴藏着巨大潜能的资源。虽然我们可能因为无法时时运用它而感到沮丧，但这些经历促使我们思考，是否可以更规律、更系统地做一些事情，来平静思绪，增强专注力，从而更容易获得那些常常随之而来的深刻洞见，并使其与我们内心深处的同理心和慈悲心更加契合。这将会极大地提升我们帮助他人的能力。

Traditionally, one such way to begin this investigation is through meditation, systematically observing the mind itself and becoming more familiar with the ways in which we are denied the experience of full concentration. When we do this, with even a simple exercise like focusing our attention on our breath or on a candle flame, we begin to see that there is a continuous stream of thoughts going on all the time. Meditation may be frustrating if we think we can stop this process right away. We can’t. But by penetrating and observing it, we can free ourselves from being carried away by our thoughts.

传统上，探索这种自我意识的方法之一是通过冥想，系统地观察心念本身，并逐渐熟悉我们是如何被剥夺了全然专注的体验。当我们这样做时，即使是像将注意力集中在呼吸或烛火这样简单的练习，我们也会开始意识到，思绪始终在不停地涌动。如果我们认为自己可以立即停止这个过程，冥想可能会令人沮丧。我们做不到。但是，通过深入观察和觉察，我们可以让自己摆脱被思绪牵引的困境。

Our thoughts are always happening. Much like leaves floating down a stream or clouds crossing the sky, they just keep on coming. They arise in the form of sensations, feelings, memories, anticipations, and speculations. And they are all constantly calling for attention: “Think of me.” “Notice me.” “Attend to me.” As each thought passes, either we attend to it or we don’t. While we can’t stop the thoughts themselves, we can stop our awareness from being snared by each one. If you are standing by a river and a leaf floats by, you have your choice of following the leaf with your eye or keeping your attention fixed in front of you. The leaf floats out of your line of vision. Another leaf enters … and floats by.

我们的思绪无时无刻不在发生。就像溪流中飘落的落叶，或是天空中飘过的云朵，它们源源不断地涌现。它们以感觉、情绪、记忆、期待和推测的形式出现，并且不断地呼唤着我们的注意力：“想想我。”“注意我。”“关注我。”每当一个念头掠过，我们要么关注它，要么不关注。虽然我们无法阻止念头本身，但我们可以阻止自己的意识被每一个念头所束缚。如果你站在河边，一片落叶飘过，你可以选择用目光追随它，也可以将注意力集中在眼前。落叶飘出了你的视线。另一片落叶飘了进来……然后又飘走了。

But as we stand on the bank of the river and the leaves float by, there is no confusion as to whether or not we are the leaves. Similarly, it turns out that there is a place in our minds from which we can watch our own mental images go by. We aren’t our thoughts any more than we are the leaves.

但当我们站在河岸边，看着落叶飘过，我们不会再纠结自己是否就是那些落叶。同样地，我们的内心深处也存在着一个可以让我们观察自身心理意象流逝的地方。我们并非我们的思想，正如我们并非落叶一样。

If we imagine that our mind is like the blue sky, and that across it pass thoughts as clouds, we can get a feel for that part of it which is other than our thoughts. The sky is always present; it contains the clouds and yet is not contained by them. So with our awareness. It is present and encompasses all our thoughts, feelings, and sensations; yet it is not the same as them. To recognize and acknowledge this awareness, with its spacious, peaceful quality, is to find a very useful resource within. We see that we need not identify with each thought just because it happens to occur. We can remain quiet and choose which thought we wish to attend to. And we can remain aware behind all these thoughts, in a state that offers an entirely new level of openness and insight.

如果我们想象自己的心智如同蔚蓝的天空，而念头如同云朵般飘过其上，我们就能感受到它与念头之外的那部分。天空始终存在；它包含云朵，却又不被云朵所包含。我们的觉知亦是如此。它存在并包容我们所有的念头、感受和感觉；但它与它们并不相同。认识并接纳这种觉知，以及它那广阔而平和的特质，便能发现内在的宝贵资源。我们明白，我们不必因为念头的出现就认同它。我们可以保持安静，选择我们想要关注的念头。我们可以始终觉知所有这些念头背后的状态，这种状态会带来一种全新的开放性和洞察力。

There are systematic exercises that can help to establish us in the skylike awareness that encompasses thought. One of these meditation exercises is called “Letting Go.” It very quickly can show us through direct personal experience that our awareness is separate from our thoughts. You may want to read it through until you understand it, and then, if you choose, try it.

有一些系统的练习可以帮助我们建立起一种超越思维的、如同天空般的觉知状态。其中一种冥想练习叫做“放下”。它能让我们通过直接的个人体验迅速明白，我们的觉知与我们的思维是分离的。你可以先通读一遍，直到理解为止，然后再根据自己的意愿尝试。

LETTING GO

放手

Find a position in which you can comfortably remain for ten minutes with your back straight but not rigid. This time, instead of picking an object of focus such as the breath, just observe thought itself. Simply let things happen as they do. Just watch. Be aware, as thoughts arise, that the thoughts are there, without getting involved in the content of the thoughts. Let all images, thoughts, and sensations arise and pass away without being bothered, without reacting, without judging, without clinging, without identifying with them. Just keep letting go of one thing after another.

找到一个舒适的姿势，保持背部挺直但不僵硬，可以舒适地停留十分钟。这一次，不要像以往那样选择一个专注的对象，比如呼吸，而是观察念头本身。顺其自然，让一切发生。只是观察。当念头升起时，觉察到它们的存在，但不要执着于念头的内容。让所有的意象、念头和感受生起又消逝，不要在意，不要反应，不要评判，不要执着，不要认同它们。就这样，一个接一个地放下。

The thoughts that arise are not obstacles or hindrances. They are just the objects of our observation. Keep the mind sharply aware, moment to moment, of what is happening, what the mind is attending to. If you feel tense from trying to watch your mind, relax. The sky doesn’t get all tense trying to see the clouds. Everything is just as it is.

升起的念头并非障碍或阻碍，它们只是我们观察的对象。时刻保持觉察，觉察正在发生的一切，觉察你的心念所关注的事物。如果你因为试图观察自己的念头而感到紧张，那就放松。天空不会因为试图观察云朵而变得紧张。一切都如其所是。

Keep in mind the idea of letting go. As thoughts or sensations, images, memories, whatever, rise into your awareness, notice them, witness them, and then let them go. Keep letting go again and again. And of course, once you are really comfortable and at home in pure awareness, then you can let go of the thought of letting go as well.

记住“放下”这个概念。当念头、感觉、画面、记忆等等浮现到你的意识中时，觉察它们，观察它们，然后放下它们。一遍又一遍地放下。当然，一旦你真正感到舒适自在，完全沉浸在纯粹的觉知之中，那么你也可以放下“放下”这个念头了。

For one who has not examined the mind and has always identified completely with passing thoughts, the possibility of being able to rest in awareness free of thought may be a bit disconcerting. It’s a little like the caterpillar pointing up at the butterfly and saying, “You’ll never get me up in one of those things.”

对于从未审视过心灵、一直以来都完全认同于转瞬即逝的念头的人来说，能够安住于无念的觉知之中，或许会让他们感到有些不安。这有点像毛毛虫指着蝴蝶说：“你永远也别想让我变成蝴蝶。”

While we rarely are able to maintain this kind of awareness all the time, we have all experienced it at one time or another.

虽然我们很少能一直保持这种意识，但我们都或多或少有过这种体验。

You’re waiting tables, say, at a busy restaurant, setting one and clearing another, swinging through the kitchen door with an order and a funny remark for the cooks, then coming back out with a trayful and noticing what else needs to be done. The group of eight is eager to order, but they just sat down. The couple in the corner is stretching out their coffee while other folks are on line. It seems right to stop by and say, “Anything else?”

比如说，你在一家繁忙的餐厅当服务员，刚摆好一张桌子，收拾完另一张桌子，就拿着订单和几句玩笑话冲进厨房，然后端着满满一托盘菜出来，注意到还有什么需要做的。那桌八个人急着点餐，但他们才刚坐下。角落里的那对夫妇正悠闲地喝着咖啡，而其他人还在排队等着。这时，你似乎应该走过去问问：“还有什么需要吗？”

Or you’re teaching in a nursery school. You’ve got your eye on the whole room. The boys are hogging the blocks from a couple of girls, as usual. Three kids over there are struggling a little over who’s going to use the two easels. Janet hasn’t played with anyone this morning, but she’s better off working it out herself. Marc looks a little blue … you’d best spend time with him right now.

或者你在幼儿园教书。你环顾着整个教室。几个男孩像往常一样霸占着几个女孩的积木。那边三个孩子正为了谁来用那两张画架而争执不休。珍妮特今天上午还没跟任何人玩过，不过她最好还是自己想办法。马克看起来有点儿情绪低落……你最好现在就陪陪他。

We’re doing it all, attending to obvious needs, but we’re also behind it. The consciousness we have access to is greater than the particular thoughts we’re having or skills we’ve mastered. We have all these. But we have perspective as well—all within our spacious awareness. What’s crucial is that this awareness allows us to hear, along with everything else, whatever it is that’s going on inside us. Our own mental reactions are equally objects to be observed as anything else in our field of awareness . So you notice that perhaps you pushed the couple with the coffee just a little too much. You can see they’re talking over something important. As you pass by, then, you say quietly, “Take a few more minutes; it’s okay.” Or you recognize, as you decide where to put your energies in the classroom, that you’re really quite fascinated by Marc; that’s why you want to work with him. And you’re not all that crazy about Janet. You reconsider where to spend your time.

我们忙于各种事情，满足显而易见的需求，但我们也身处其后。我们所拥有的意识远大于我们正在思考的具体想法或已经掌握的技能。我们拥有所有这些。但我们也拥有视角——这一切都存在于我们广阔的觉知之中。关键在于，这种觉知使我们能够聆听到一切，包括我们内心正在发生的一切。我们自身的心理反应与我们觉知领域中的任何其他事物一样，都是值得观察的对象。所以你注意到，也许你刚才催促那对拿着咖啡的夫妇有点太过了。你看到他们在讨论什么重要的事情。于是，当你走过他们身边时，你轻声说：“再待一会儿吧，没关系。”或者，当你决定在课堂上把精力放在哪里时，你意识到你真的很喜欢马克；这就是你想和他一起工作的原因。而你对珍妮特并没有那么喜欢。于是你重新考虑如何分配你的时间。

In skillful helping action, when our awareness remains quiet and clear, there’s breadth to our perspective. It’s aerial, wide-screen, panoramic, and yet able to focus quickly. With all of this, we are not only thinker-participants but observers of our thinking and participation as well. It’s as if our mind is playing among various focal lengths. We’re watching a TV show and we pull back; it becomes a show within a show, a picture of a picture, both on simultaneously. Of course, that’s true of who we are too. We’re not only a person, say, walking down a city street at night; we’re also, as it were, already home in bed watching the TV show of us walking the street.

在巧妙的助人行动中，当我们的觉察保持平静清明时，我们的视角便会变得开阔。它如同翱翔的天空，宽广无垠，全景式的视野，却又能迅速聚焦。如此一来，我们不仅是思考的参与者，也是我们自身思考和参与的观察者。这就像我们的思维在不同的焦距间游走。我们观看电视节目，然后拉远镜头；它变成了节目中的节目，画面中的画面，两者同时呈现。当然，这同样适用于我们自身。我们不仅仅是一个人，比如说，在夜晚的城市街道上行走；我们也仿佛已经回到家中，躺在床上，观看着我们行走在街上的“电视节目”。

So the quiet mind makes possible an overall awareness of the total situation, including ourselves. It’s sometimes called an awareness of the Gestalt—in which separate elements of consciousness are so integrated that they function as a unity.

因此，平静的心灵使人能够对整体情况（包括我们自身）有全面的觉察。这有时被称为格式塔觉察——在这种觉察中，意识的各个组成部分如此紧密地融合在一起，以至于它们作为一个整体发挥作用。

~

There’s a guy up on the roof, right at the edge, with his infant son in his arms; he’s threatening to throw him off and then jump himself. Homicide-suicide—happens a lot with children. He’s been having trouble with his wife—mother interfering, they lock him out, he’s sleeping in the hallway, and it’s gone to the edge. That’s where he is, and I’m up there with him. I’m the final guy in the hostage recovery system we set up in New York City, which I’ve been working in for eight years and heading up for the last two. We haven’t lost anybody in all that time .

有个男人在屋顶边缘，怀里抱着他年幼的儿子；他威胁要把儿子扔下去，然后自己也跳下去。杀人后自杀——这种事在有孩子的家庭中很常见。他和妻子关系不好——他母亲从中作梗，他们把他锁在门外，他只能睡在走廊里，现在情况已经到了崩溃的边缘。他就在那里，而我和他一起在屋顶上。我是纽约市人质救援系统中的最后一名成员，我参与这个项目已经八年了，最近两年担任负责人。这么多年来，我们没有失去过任何人。

Now, if you’re not able to see the whole picture—how he’s reacting, where and who your backup forces are, what’s on the street, how long it’s been going on, your own past experience, the chance that this is a new kind, and certainly what’s going on inside you from moment to moment—if you can’t hold on to all of that and still be there listening to this guy in a way he can feel … chances are he’s gonna go over the edge. Someone is going to be killed. We’ve learned that .

如果你无法掌握全局——他的反应、你的支援力量在哪里、有哪些人、街上的情况、冲突持续了多久、你过去的经验、这是否是一种新型冲突，当然还有你内心每时每刻的感受——如果你无法同时兼顾所有这些信息，并且还能以一种他能感受到的方式倾听他的心声……那么他很可能会情绪失控。有人会丧命。我们已经吸取了教训。

And he’s in this very intense, complex public situation. Several of us are up there—a net in the street below, a lot going on all around. To say nothing of what’s going on in him: this lack of self-esteem and manliness, feeling pushed around by his family, no work. But I also can recognize this overriding love he has for his child, who he’s convinced would be better off dead than with those two. Sounds crazy, but it was real to him. So there’s a lot for all of us to take in .

他身处一个非常紧张、复杂的公众境地。我们几个人都在上面——下面街道上架着一张网，周围一片混乱。更别提他内心的挣扎了：缺乏自尊和男子气概，感觉被家人摆布，没有工作。但我也能感受到他对孩子的那份深沉的爱，他坚信孩子死了都比跟那两个人在一起好。听起来很疯狂，但对他来说却是真切的。所以，我们所有人都需要好好消化这一切。

So I’m helping him get a sense, an awareness of everything that’s happening, just so he has the picture of it all. And the more he does, the more he is opening up to me. Turns out what concerns him most is that there be a hearing at family court to work out fair custody. He wants a hearing. But he won’t accept a promise from me, or a signed note. He tells us we got to get a lawyer and have it on legal paper—which we send out a car and find a local lawyer and get for him. When he feels he’s got support from the system, he hands us the child. At that point we have to jump him, because we know that’s the crucial moment to prevent the suicide. He gets pissed at me, because we were talking together and now this. And I have to give him this look of “That’s how it all is, kid.” Some part of him understands .

所以我一直在帮他了解情况，让他意识到正在发生的一切，让他对整个事件有个大致的认识。他了解得越多，就越愿意跟我敞开心扉。结果发现，他最关心的是家庭法庭要开庭审理，以确定公平的监护权。他想要开庭。但他不接受我的任何承诺，也不接受我签字的纸条。他告诉我们必须找律师，而且要有正式的法律文件——于是我们派车去找当地的律师，帮他办好了手续。当他觉得得到了法律的支持后，他就把孩子交给了我们。这时我们必须上前阻止他，因为我们知道这是阻止他自杀的关键时刻。他冲我发火，因为我们之前还在好好谈，现在却变成这样。我只能用那种“事情就是这样，孩子”的眼神看着他。他心里多少明白了一些。

Other times, you’re called into very tight situations which you have to loosen up. I was called into a classic family fight scene. A nine-by-twelve room with an eight-by-ten bed, on which is sitting a two-hundred-pound construction worker with a knife in one hand and the hair of his wife, who’s half-naked on the floor, in the other. He’s yelling about her infidelity, and he’s already nicked her. Not much room to move around in. So in talking to him I’m trying to expand the situation. I try to get him to talk about how he got to this point, recognize he still has choices, and think about the future. It’s like I’m making the room bigger, making more room for this guy. And I have to stay very steady to do that, because there is part of me which is saying, “Man, you got a lot of balls accusing your wife of something at a moment like this.” But as soon as I could get him to pull back and look at it all, which is what I’m doing too, you understand, then there’s a chance to see exactly what move will break through the pressure. That’s how this one got resolved .

有时候，你会遇到一些棘手的情况，需要想办法缓和气氛。我曾经被叫去处理一个典型的家庭争吵场景。房间只有九乘十二英尺，一张八乘十英尺的床，床上坐着一个两百磅重的建筑工人，一手拿着刀，一手抓着半裸躺在地板上的妻子的头发。他大声指责妻子不忠，而且已经划伤了她。房间里几乎没有回旋的余地。所以，在和他交谈时，我试图拓展局面。我努力让他说说自己是如何走到这一步的，让他意识到自己仍然有选择，并思考未来。这就像我在扩大房间，为他创造更多空间。我必须保持冷静才能做到这一点，因为我内心深处有个声音在说：“老兄，你居然在这种时候指责你妻子，真是胆子太大了。”但只要我能让他冷静下来，好好审视一下局面——这也是我正在做的，你明白的——就有机会看清究竟哪一步才能突破他的防线。这场比赛就是这样解决的。

Funny thing is, I can’t remember much of what I’ve been saying to people at the end of these episodes. I’m running very much on intuition from moment to moment. I’ve had special training, of course, but that becomes a part of you, and it’s only a part of what you’re calling on .

有趣的是，我几乎记不清在这些节目结尾我跟人们说了些什么。我很大程度上是凭直觉行事。当然，我接受过专门的训练，但这会成为你的一部分，而只是你所运用能力的一部分。

You have to be steady and quiet inside. You have to have a foundation of belief in the absolute value and beauty of life. You can’t get too caught up in it all. You step back, get as much of the picture as possible, and you play it moment to moment. That’s what I’ve learned from hundreds of these situations .

你必须内心保持平静和沉稳。你必须坚信生命的绝对价值和美好。你不能被这一切牵着鼻子走。你要退后一步，尽可能全面地了解情况，然后一步一步地应对。这是我从数百次类似经历中学到的。

~

In the clarity of a quiet mind, there is room for all that is actually happening and whatever else might also be possible. Though we may be mindful of myriad details, our attention never wavers from the specific situation or person in need. The intimacy of our attention becomes a heart-to-heart lifeline made firm and fast; no one need fall from the edge. The quiet appreciation of the total situation and its inherent possibilities steadily moves things toward resolution; we find ways to step back. In a spirit of compassion and reverence for life, these various skills flourish and combine appropriately.

在宁静的心灵深处，一切正在发生的事情以及所有可能发生的事情都得以容纳。尽管我们可能注意到无数细节，但我们的注意力始终不会从具体的处境或需要帮助的人身上转移。我们专注的目光如同心与心的纽带，牢固而可靠；没有人会因此而坠入深渊。对整体情况及其内在可能性的平静欣赏，稳步推动事情走向解决；我们找到了退后一步的方法。在对生命的慈悲和敬畏之心下，这些不同的能力得以蓬勃发展，并恰当地融合在一起。

Such feats might seem to be the result of crisis. Many of us have experienced rising to the occasion under such conditions. The intensity of the situation keeps the mind from wandering. For most of us, fortunately or unfortunately, our helping work doesn’t entail the intensity that brings forth these heightened faculties. But whatever the circumstances, and however extensive the training and experience, it’s important to recognize that the faculties of awareness being called into play are exactly those we have been cultivating and discovering in the practice of meditation and the investigation of awareness. General laws are operating under particular circumstances.

这样的壮举看似危机之下的产物。我们许多人都曾在这样的情境下挺身而出。危机的紧迫性使我们的思绪无法游离。对我们大多数人而言，无论幸运与否，我们的助人工作并不涉及那种足以激发我们超凡能力的紧迫性。但无论境遇如何，无论训练和经验多么丰富，重要的是要认识到，我们所运用的觉知能力，正是我们在冥想练习和觉知探索中不断培养和发现的。普遍规律在特定情境下发挥作用。

Why, for example, if one was tightly attentive to a single object—a man on the edge of a roof—wouldn’t everything else disappear from awareness? Because, as we’ve discovered, it is possible to notice a single thought, sensation, or situation arise, but not get totally lost in identifying with it. We observe the cloud but remain focused on the sky, see the leaf but hold in vision the river. We are that which is aware of the totality. And our skills develop with practice. First, we have to appreciate the value of such qualities of mind and desire to develop them. Next, we have to have faith in the possibility that we can indeed make progress. Finally, we have to explore and practice appropriate techniques. Twenty minutes a day of such practice can lead to results and the incentive to go deeper still. Continuous practice brings about great transformation of mind and leads to a new quality of service.

例如，如果一个人全神贯注于一个物体——比如屋顶边缘的人——为什么其他一切事物不会从意识中消失呢？因为正如我们所发现的，我们可以觉察到某个念头、感觉或情境的出现，却不会完全沉浸其中。我们观察云朵，但依然专注于天空；我们看见树叶，但依然将目光聚焦于河流。我们觉察的是整体。而我们的技能会随着练习而提升。首先，我们必须认识到这种心智品质的价值，并渴望发展它们。其次，我们必须相信自己确实能够取得进步。最后，我们必须探索并练习合适的技巧。每天进行二十分钟的练习就能带来成效，并激励我们进一步深入探索。持续的练习会带来心智的巨大转变，并最终带来一种全新的服务品质。

When we function from this place of spacious awareness rather than from our analytic mind, we are often surprised to find solutions to problems without our having “figured them out.” It’s as if out of the reservoir of our minds which contains everything we know and everything we are sensing at the moment, all that could be useful rises to the surface and presents itself for appropriate action. Sudden flashes of memory, past experience, or understanding seem to get expressed: “I can’t explain it.” “It just came to me.” “It all suddenly became clear.” “I forgot I even knew that.”

当我们从这种开阔的觉知层面而非分析思维出发时，我们常常会惊讶地发现，无需“琢磨”，问题的解决方案就已存在。仿佛从我们心灵的宝库——包含着我们所知的一切以及此刻所感知的一切——中，所有有用的东西都会浮现出来，供我们采取相应的行动。记忆、过往经验或领悟的瞬间闪现，仿佛被表达出来：“我无法解释。”“我突然想到了。”“一切都豁然开朗了。”“我都忘了我曾经知道这些。”

We often call this quality of mind “intuition” but often we don’t trust or honor it. Unlike our thinking mind, which arrives at solutions through a linear process of analysis which we can follow, the intuitive mind seems to leap to a solution. Perhaps the process is going on outside the range of our consciousness; perhaps we are delving into regions of the mind where thinking, in the conventional sense, is not necessary. Whatever, it is still an important resource of our minds and worthy of more than incidental attention.

我们通常称这种思维特质为“直觉”，但我们往往并不信任或重视它。与我们通过线性分析过程得出解决方案的思维方式不同，直觉似乎能直接跳到解决方案。或许这个过程发生在我们的意识之外；或许我们正在探索思维的某个领域，在那里，传统意义上的思考并非必要。无论如何，它仍然是我们思维的重要资源，值得我们给予足够的重视。

~

My father was dying; my mother was panicking. They were three thousand miles away from me. I had a family and a job. And all the familiar questions of these experiences: when to be with them, when to be at home and at work; when to call, when to wait to be called; medical decisions; hospital or home; and simply what to say, how to be .

父亲病危，母亲惊慌失措。他们远在三千英里之外。我有家庭，有工作。所有那些熟悉的困境都涌上心头：何时陪伴他们，何时待在家中，何时工作；何时打电话，何时等待他们的来电；医疗方面的决定；医院还是家；以及，该说什么，该如何面对。

I’d think and think about all this, but I would reach a point where I’d see I had to stop. My mind would go “tilt.” So I would go out and take a walk, or watch the river change tides and empty into the Atlantic. I’d watch kids at the playground. I’d see how the tree line had changed shape at the top of a mountain meadow I’d known for years. Things like that .

我会反复思考这一切，但最终我会意识到我必须停下来。我的思绪会“飘忽不定”。于是我会出去散步，或者看看河流潮起潮落，最终汇入大西洋。我会看看游乐场里的孩子们。我会观察我熟悉多年的山顶草甸上，树木的轮廓发生了怎样的变化。诸如此类的事情。

And sometimes I’d hear: “Right. It’s time to be out there. I’ll leave in two weeks and stay ten days.” Or, “Not so much advice giving.” Or “God is with them.” The right thought. Something that would ring true. These seemed to come out of the blue, but I felt trust in them, and peaceful as a result .

有时我会听到这样的话：“对，是时候出去走走了。我两周后出发，待十天。”或者，“别给我提什么建议。”又或者，“上帝与他们同在。” 都是些正确的想法，一些听起来很真实的话。这些话似乎来得莫名其妙，但我却从中感受到信任，也因此感到平静。

It was very reliable and very inspiring, working that way. All through his illness and all the wild, anxious phone calls, I’d feel answers coming. It was very reassuring. I experienced it as grace. And at the end I was able to be with them at home and have his hand in mine as he died and my arm around my mother .

这种方式非常可靠，也非常鼓舞人心。在他生病期间，尽管我接到了很多焦虑不安的电话，但我总能感觉到答案即将到来。这让我感到非常安心。我把它视为一种恩典。最后，我能够陪伴他们待在家里，在他离世时握着他的手，搂着我的母亲。

~

Ultimately, this kind of listening to the intuitive mind is a kind of surrender based on trust. It’s playing it by ear, listening for the voice within. We trust that it’s possible to hear into a greater totality which offers insight and guidance. Ultimately, but really ultimately, we trust that when we are fully quiet, aware, and attentive, boundaries created by the mind simply blur and dissolve, and we begin to merge into All That Is. And All That Is, by definition, includes answers as well as questions, solutions as well as dilemmas.

归根结底，这种聆听直觉的方式是一种基于信任的臣服。它是一种随机应变、倾听内心声音的方式。我们相信，我们可以聆听到更广阔的整体，从中获得洞见和指引。最终，也是真正意义上的最终，我们相信，当我们完全安静、觉知和专注时，头脑所设定的界限就会模糊消融，我们开始融入万物一体。而万物一体，顾名思义，既包含答案，也包含问题；既包含解决方案，也包含困境。

When we have been used to knowing where we stand at every moment, the experience of resting in awareness without any specific thoughts to hold onto and trusting our intuition, turns out to be a refreshing and exciting adventure. In this choiceless spacious awareness, we don’t necessarily know from moment to moment how everything is going to come out. Nor do we have a clear idea of what is expected of us. Our stance is just one of listening … of fine tuning … trusting that all will become apparent at the proper time.

当我们习惯于时刻掌控自己的处境时，体验到不执着于任何特定念头、全然信赖直觉的觉知，竟会成为一场令人耳目一新、激动人心的冒险。在这种无选择的广阔觉知中，我们未必能预知每时每刻的走向，也未必清楚自己该如何应对。我们所要做的，仅仅是聆听……微调……并相信一切终将在恰当的时机显现。

To rest in awareness also means to stand free of the prejudices of mind that come from identifying with cherished attitudes and opinions. We can listen without being busy planning, analyzing, theorizing … and especially judging. We can open into the moment fully in order to hear it all.

安住于觉知之中，也意味着摆脱因认同于珍视的态度和观点而产生的思维偏见。我们可以聆听，而不忙于计划、分析、理论化……尤其是评判。我们可以全然敞开于当下，聆听一切。

As we learn to listen with a quiet mind, there is so much we hear. Inside ourselves we can begin to hear that “still small voice within,” as the Quakers call it, the voice of our intuitive heart which has so long been drowned out by the noisy thinking mind. We hear our skills and needs, our subtle intentionalities, our limits, our innate generosity.

当我们学会用平静的心灵聆听时，我们会听到许多声音。在我们内心深处，我们开始听到那“内在的微小声音”，正如贵格会教徒所说的那样，那是我们直觉之心的声音，它长期以来都被喧嚣的思维所淹没。我们听到自己的能力和需求，我们微妙的意图，我们的局限，以及我们与生俱来的慷慨。

In other people we hear what help they really require, what license they are actually giving us to help, what potential there is for change. We can hear their strengths and their pain. We hear what support is available, what obstacles must be reckoned with.

从他人身上，我们能感受到他们真正需要的帮助，他们愿意给予我们怎样的帮助，以及他们身上蕴藏着怎样的改变潜力。我们能感受到他们的力量和痛苦。我们能了解到有哪些支持可以利用，以及必须克服哪些障碍。

~

But he learned more from the river than Vasudeva could teach him. He learned from it continually. Above all, he learned from it how to listen with a still heart, with a waiting open soul, without passion, without desire, without judgment, without opinions .

但他从河流中学到的，比瓦苏德瓦能教给他的还要多。他不断地从河流中学习。最重要的是，他从河流中学会了如何用一颗平静的心，用一颗敞开的灵魂去聆听，不带任何激情、欲望、评判或成见。

Siddhartha , H ERMANN H ESSE

悉达多，赫尔曼·黑塞

~

The more deeply we listen, the more we attune ourselves to the roots of suffering and the means to help alleviate it. It is through listening that wisdom, skill, and opportunity find form in an act that truly helps. But more than all these, the very act of listening can dissolve distance between us and others as well.

我们越是深入聆听，就越能体会到痛苦的根源以及减轻痛苦的方法。正是通过聆听，智慧、技能和机遇才能化为行动，真正发挥作用。但更重要的是，聆听本身也能消除我们与他人之间的隔阂。

~

Heard … If they only understood how important it is that we be heard! I can take being in a nursing home. It’s really all right, with a positive attitude. My daughter has her hands full, three kids and a job. She visits regularly. I understand .

听到了……他们要是能明白我们被倾听有多重要就好了！我可以接受住在养老院。只要保持积极的心态，一切都还好。我女儿很忙，要照顾三个孩子，还要工作。她经常来看我。我理解。

But most people here … they just want to tell their story. That’s what they have to give, don’t you see? And it’s a precious thing to them. It’s their life they want to give. You’d think people would understand what it means to us … to give our lives in a story .

但这里的大多数人……他们只是想讲述自己的故事。这就是他们所能给予的，你不明白吗？这对他们来说弥足珍贵。他们想奉献的是自己的人生。你会觉得人们应该能理解，对我们来说，用故事来讲述自己的人生意味着什么。

So we listen to each other. Most of what goes on here is people listening to each other’s stories. People who work here consider that to be … filling time. If they only knew. If they’d just take a minute to listen!

所以我们互相倾听。这里的大部分时间都是大家互相讲述彼此的故事。在这里工作的人却认为这只是……打发时间。他们要是知道就好了。他们要是能花点时间听听就好了！

~

There are so many ways in which we listen to one another. “I hear you,” we say to one another. Such a message would be welcome indeed if, for example, it came in the words of a trapped coal miner or a deaf person who had just undergone corrective ear surgery. In most helping situations, however, “I hear you” reflects a much deeper message: “I understand. I’m with you.” Such a message can be immensely reassuring for a person who has felt isolated or alone in their pain and suffering. The reassurance does not come from the words themselves, of course, but from what the words represent. It comes if the person indeed feels heard.

我们倾听彼此的方式有很多种。“我听到了，”我们彼此说道。如果这句话出自一位被困煤矿的矿工或一位刚刚接受过耳部矫正手术的聋人之口，那无疑会令人倍感欣慰。然而，在大多数需要帮助的情境中，“我听到了”传递着更深层次的信息：“我理解你。我与你同在。”对于那些在痛苦和磨难中感到孤立无援的人来说，这样的信息能带来莫大的安慰。当然，这种安慰并非来自话语本身，而是来自话语所代表的意义。它源于对方真正感受到被倾听。

It may not be that a particular story from one’s life is so important. But sharing it is a way of being together—heart to heart. In those moments we are no longer alone with our fear; we are reminded that we are not forgotten.

或许，人生中的某个特定故事本身并不重要。但分享故事却是一种彼此陪伴的方式——心与心的交流。在那一刻，我们不再独自承受恐惧；我们被提醒，我们并没有被遗忘。

When two people are at one
in their inmost hearts ,
They shatter even the strength of
iron or of bronze .
And when two people understand each other
in their inmost hearts ,
Their words are sweet and strong ,
like the fragrance of orchids .

当两个人心意相通时，他们甚至能粉碎铁或铜的坚韧。当两个人心意相通时，他们的话语甜美而有力，如同兰花的芬芳。

I Ching

易经

To reach its full potential, however, this hearing from the heart requires that we remain alert to entrapments of the mind. Seeking to help others, we may start out open and receptive, but after a short time being with them seems to bring us down rather than lift them up. Somehow their suffering, self-pity, despair, fear, or neediness begins to get to us. It’s a little like trying to pull someone out of quicksand and feeling ourself suddenly starting to sink. As reassuring as it may be for one depressed person to be heard by another depressed person, the relationship doesn’t really open the door to escape from depression. Empathy is not enough.
