然而，要充分发挥这种用心聆听的潜力，我们需要时刻警惕思维的陷阱。当我们想要帮助他人时，或许一开始会敞开心扉、乐于接受，但与他们相处一段时间后，我们却发现这种相处非但没有帮助他们，反而让我们自己也感到沮丧。不知何故，他们的痛苦、自怜、绝望、恐惧或依赖开始影响到我们。这就像试图把人从流沙中拉出来，却发现自己也开始下沉。虽然对于一个抑郁的人来说，被另一个抑郁的人倾听或许会感到安慰，但这种关系并不能真正打开摆脱抑郁的大门。仅仅有同理心是不够的。

Here, once again, our ability to remain alert to our own thoughts as they come and go serves us in our relations with others. We hear into their pain … they feel heard … we meet together inside the confusion. And yet we ourselves are able to note, perhaps even to anticipate , that moment when another’s entrapment of mind might be starting to suck us in. We are as alert to what is happening within us as we are to what is happening in them .

在这里，我们再次意识到，能够觉察自身念头的来来去去，对我们与他人的关系大有裨益。我们倾听他们的痛苦……他们感到被理解……我们在迷茫中相遇。同时，我们自己也能察觉到，甚至预感到，他人的思维困境可能正将我们卷入其中。我们对自身内心的变化和对他人的内心变化一样保持警觉。

The ability to avoid being entrapped by one another’s mind is one of the great gifts we can offer each other. With this compassionate and spacious awareness, and the listening it makes possible, we can offer those we are with a standing invitation to come out from wherever they are caught, if they are ready and wish to do so. It is as if we are in the room of experience with them, but also standing in the doorway, offering our hand, ready to walk out together.

避免被彼此的思维所束缚，是我们能够给予彼此的珍贵礼物之一。怀着这份慈悲而宽广的觉知，以及由此而生的倾听，我们可以向身边的人发出持续的邀请，邀请他们从困境中走出来——如果他们已经准备好，并且愿意这样做的话。这就像我们与他们一同置身于体验的房间，同时也站在门口，伸出手，准备与他们携手走出困境。

~

A woman came to see me who was suffering greatly because of her daughter. She told me her daughter was real bad trouble. “She’s run away to live with my other daughter down in Tennessee, and now she’s forged a check with her sister’s name on it, and she’s gotten pregnant and she’s only sixteen. I’ve been a seamstress all my life, supporting the kids and myself since my husband ran out when the youngest was still in the womb. Now she’s run away, and you can’t imagine what it’s like.…”

一位女士来找我，她因为女儿的事痛苦不堪。她告诉我，她女儿真是个麻烦精。“她离家出走，去田纳西州和我另一个女儿住在一起，现在她伪造了一张冒用她姐姐名字的支票，而且她才十六岁就怀孕了。我这辈子都是个裁缝，从我丈夫在我最小的孩子还在我肚子里的时候就跑了之后，就一直靠我养活自己和孩子们。现在她跑了，你根本无法想象我现在的处境……”

I’m shortening the story. It actually took about fifteen minutes to run it all down. I just listened as openly as I could. I could feel her pain and discouragement and felt my heart hurt at the hard life she had had. At the same moment I felt very quiet inside, figuring maybe all I had to offer was to be with her. A little bit I felt she was wearing the albatross of this story, like the Ancient Mariner, and I was just another in a long line of people who had heard it. So when she finished I said, “Right.”

我把故事简化了一下。其实整个过程大概花了十五分钟。我只是尽可能地敞开心扉地倾听。我能感受到她的痛苦和沮丧，也为她坎坷的人生经历感到心痛。与此同时，我的内心却一片平静，心想或许我能做的只有陪伴她。我感觉她背负着这个故事的沉重包袱，就像古舟子咏唱的航海家一样，而我只是众多听过这个故事的人之一。所以，当她说完后，我说：“好吧。”

She sensed I wasn’t getting caught, and her immediate reaction was “No, you don’t understand.” And she recited the whole thing one more time, fifteen more minutes. And when she’d finished the second time, I said again, “Right.”

她察觉到我没被识破，立刻说道：“不，你不明白。”然后她又把整件事重复了一遍，又过了十五分钟。等她第二次说完后，我又说了一遍：“好的。”

This time she stopped for a moment. She’d heard me. She paused, and then said with a kind of wry smile, “You know, I was kind of a hellion when I was a kid, too.” She just let it go .

这次她停顿了一下。她听到了我的话。她顿了顿，然后带着一丝苦笑说：“你知道吗，我小时候也是个小淘气。”说完，她就没再说什么了。

~

For someone deeply trapped in a prison of thought, how good it can feel to meet a mind that hears, a heart that reassures. It’s as if a listening mind is, in and of itself, an invitation to another mind to listen too. How much it can mean when we accept the invitation and hear the world anew.

对于一个深陷思想牢笼的人来说，遇到一个能够倾听的心灵、一颗能够给予安慰的心，是多么美好。仿佛一个倾听的心灵本身，就是一种邀请，邀请另一个心灵也来倾听。当我们接受这份邀请，以全新的视角聆听世界时，意义又是多么重大。

~

When she first came to see me, this woman hadn’t been speaking for three months. But she was silent in many different ways. Resentful silence: “You do it for me.” Agitated silence: “I’m scared.” Bored silence: “I have nothing.” A kind of interested silence too—but not knowing how to start. After several months she began to speak .

她第一次来见我时，已经三个月没说话了。但她的沉默有很多种。怨恨的沉默：“你这样做是为了我。”焦躁的沉默：“我很害怕。”无聊的沉默：“我一无所有。”还有一种好奇的沉默——却不知如何开口。几个月后，她开始说话了。

Now, after a number of years, she spends a great deal of time talking, and she’s afraid of silence, scared of being quiet. There are things, she says, that she doesn’t want to know. Any movement into silence, from outside or within, is really frightening .

多年之后，她现在大部分时间都在说话，她害怕沉默，害怕保持安静。她说，有些事她不想知道。任何形式的沉默，无论是来自外界还是内心，都让她感到恐惧。

One day there was a noise outside. She paused and said, “What’s that?” I said, “Let’s listen.” She listened for a moment and asked again, “What is it?” I said again, “Let’s listen.” And then she exclaimed, with total delight, “It’s a bird! I haven’t heard a bird in years. It’s beautiful!” I saw it all go by: the noise; the not knowing (imagine the condition of one who doesn’t know the sound of a bird!); her wish to hear; the listening; the sound recognized; the bird .

有一天，外面传来一阵响动。她停下脚步，问道：“那是什么？”我说：“我们来听听。”她听了一会儿，又问：“是什么？”我再次说道：“我们来听听。”然后，她欣喜若狂地喊道：“是鸟！我已经好几年没听到鸟叫了。真好听！”我目睹了这一切：响动；她一无所知（想象一下，一个不认识鸟叫的人会是什么感受！）；她渴望聆听；她倾听；她认出了鸟叫；她看到了那只鸟。

There was another long silence. Then she said, “That’s just so beautiful.”

又是一阵漫长的沉默。然后她开口说道：“真是太美了。”

~

The sage helps the ten thousand things find their own nature .

圣人帮助万物找到自身的本性。

Tao Te Ching

《道德经》

~

Much, then, can be accomplished in the work of compassion by exploring the activity of the mind. Through concentration, we are able to establish a more intimate contact with one another. Through spacious awareness we can sense the totality of situations and allow insight to come into play. More and more we are a vehicle for service. All of this may seem as if we are acquiring something new, but that is not so. Rather, we are clearing away obstacles that have prevented us from using our natural abilities. We regain what Suzuki Roshi, a Zen master, called “beginner’s mind”—one that is open to the freshness of many possibilities.

因此，在慈悲的实践中，探索心智的活动能带来诸多益处。通过专注，我们能够与他人建立更亲密的联系。通过广阔的觉知，我们能够感知到所有情境，并让洞察力发挥作用。我们越来越成为服务的载体。这一切看似我们在获得某种新的东西，但事实并非如此。相反，我们正在清除那些阻碍我们运用自身天赋的障碍。我们重新获得了禅宗大师铃木俊隆所说的“初学者之心”——一种对各种可能性都持开放态度的心。

To dissolve agitations and attachments of the mind is to remove the veils from our heart. It allows us to meet one another in the purity of love.

消除心中的烦躁和执念，就是揭开我们心灵的面纱。它使我们能够在纯粹的爱中相遇。

~

On the bulletin board in the front hall of the hospital where I work, there appeared an announcement. “Yeshi Dhonden,” it read, “will make rounds at six o’clock on the morning of June 10.” The particulars were then given, followed by a notation: “Yeshi Dhonden is Personal Physician to the Dalai Lama.” I am not so leathery a skeptic that I would knowingly ignore an emissary from the gods. Not only might such sangfroid be inimical to one’s earthly well-being, it could take care of eternity as well. Thus, on the morning of June 10, I join the clutch of whitecoats waiting in the small conference room adjacent to the ward selected for the rounds. The air in the room is heavy with ill-concealed dubiety and suspicion of bamboozlement. At precisely six o’clock he materializes, a short, golden, barrelly man dressed in a sleeveless robe of saffron and maroon. His scalp is shaven, and the only visible hair is a scanty black line above each hooded eye .

在我工作的医院前厅的公告栏上，贴着一张告示：“益西·顿登将于6月10日早上六点查房。” 随后列出了具体信息，并附注：“益西·顿登是达赖喇嘛的私人医生。” 我并非那种顽固的怀疑论者，不会故意忽略神明的使者。这种冷漠不仅可能不利于今世的安宁，甚至可能关乎永恒。于是，6月10日早上，我加入了一群身穿白大褂的医生，在查房病房旁边的小会议室里等候。房间里弥漫着难以掩饰的疑虑和欺骗的气氛。六点整，他出现了，一个身材矮胖、皮肤金黄的男人，身穿一件藏红花色和栗色相间的无袖长袍。他的头发剃光了，唯一可见的头发是每只下垂的眼睛上方稀疏的一条黑线。

He bows in greeting while his young interpreter makes the introduction. Yeshi Dhonden, we are told, will examine a patient selected by a member of the staff. The diagnosis is unknown to Yeshi Dhonden as it is to us. The examination of the patient will take place in our presence, after which we will reconvene in the conference room, where Yeshi Dhonden will discuss the case. We are further informed that for the past two hours Yeshi Dhonden has purified himself by bathing, fasting, and prayer. I, having breakfasted well, performed only the most desultory of ablutions, and given no thought at all to my soul, glance furtively at my fellows. Suddenly we seem a soiled, uncouth lot .

他鞠躬致意，年轻的翻译做了介绍。我们被告知，耶西·顿登将为一位工作人员挑选的病人进行检查。诊断结果我们和耶西·顿登一样一无所知。检查将在我们面前进行，之后我们将回到会议室，耶西·顿登将在那里讨论病情。我们还得知，在过去的两个小时里，耶西·顿登通过沐浴、斋戒和祈祷净化了自己。我早餐吃得饱，只是敷衍地洗漱了一下，完全没有考虑过自己的灵魂，偷偷地瞥了一眼同伴们。突然间，我们觉得自己就像一群肮脏、粗鲁的人。

The patient had been awakened early and told that she was to be examined by a foreign doctor, and had been asked to produce a fresh specimen of urine, so when we enter her room, the woman shows no surprise. She has long ago taken on that mixture of compliance and resignation that is the facies of chronic illness. This was to be but another in an endless series of tests and examinations. Yeshi Dhonden steps to the bedside while the rest stand apart, watching. For a long time he gazes at the woman, favoring no part of her body with his eyes, but seeming to fix his glance at a place just above her supine form. I, too, study her. No physical sign or obvious symptom gives a clue to the nature of her disease .

病人一大早就被叫醒，被告知要接受一位外国医生的检查，并被要求提供新鲜的尿样。因此，当我们走进她的病房时，她脸上并没有丝毫惊讶。她早已摆出一副顺从与听天由命的表情，那是慢性病患者特有的神情。这不过是没完没了的检查和检验中的又一次而已。耶西·顿登走到床边，其他人则站在一旁观察。他凝视着病人良久，目光没有落在她身体的任何部位，而是似乎一直停留在她仰卧身体上方的某个地方。我也仔细观察着她。没有任何体征或明显的症状能揭示她患的是什么病。

At last he takes her hand, raising it in both of his own. Now he bends over the bed in a kind of crouching stance, his head drawn down into the collar of his robe. His eyes are closed as he feels for her pulse. In a moment he has found the spot, and for the next half-hour he remains thus, suspended above the patient like some exotic golden bird with folded wings, holding the pulse of the woman beneath his fingers, cradling her hand in his. All the power of the man seems to have been drawn down into this one purpose. It is palpation of the pulse raised to the state of ritual. From the foot of the bed, where I stand, it is as though he and the patient have entered a special place of isolation, of apartness, about which a vacancy hovers, and across which no violation is possible. After a moment the woman rests back upon her pillow. From time to time she raises her head to look at the strange figure above her, then sinks back once more. I cannot see their hands joined in a correspondence that is exclusive, intimate, his fingertips receiving the voice of her sick body through the rhythm and throb she offers at her wrist. All at once I am envious—not of him, not of Yeshi Dhonden for his gift of beauty and holiness, but of her. I want to be held like that, touched so, received. And I know that I, who have palpated a hundred thousand pulses, have not felt a single one .

他终于握住了她的手，双手捧起。他俯身俯身，呈蹲伏状，头埋进长袍领口。他闭着眼睛，探查着她的脉搏。片刻后，他找到了脉搏的位置，接下来的半个小时里，他一直保持着这个姿势，像一只收拢双翼的异域金鸟般悬在病人上方，指尖轻抚着女人的脉搏，双手温柔地捧着她的手。他似乎将全部的力量都倾注于此。这是一种仪式化的脉搏触诊。站在床尾的我，感觉他和病人仿佛进入了一个特殊的、与世隔绝的境地，周围弥漫着一种空旷感，任何事物都无法侵犯。过了一会儿，女人重新躺回枕头上。她不时抬起头，望向头顶上方那个陌生的身影，然后又再次沉了下去。我无法看到他们双手交握，进行着一种专属而亲密的交流，他的指尖透过她手腕的脉搏和跳动，接收着她病弱身体的声音。我突然感到嫉妒——不是嫉妒他，也不是嫉妒耶喜敦登所拥有的美丽与圣洁，而是嫉妒她。我渴望被那样拥抱，那样触摸，那样接纳。而我知道，我，一个摸过十万次脉搏的人，却从未真正感受到过一次。

At last Yeshi Dhonden straightens, gently places the woman’s hand upon the bed, and steps back. The interpreter produces a small wooden bowl and two sticks. Yeshi Dhonden pours a portion of the urine specimen into the bowl and proceeds to whip the liquid with two sticks. This he does for several minutes until a foam is raised. Then, bowing above the bowl, he inhales the odor three times. He sets down the bowl and turns to leave. All this while, he has not uttered a single word .

最后，耶西·顿登直起身子，轻轻地将女人的手放在床上，然后后退一步。翻译拿出一个小木碗和两根棍子。耶西·顿登将一部分尿液样本倒入碗中，然后用两根棍子搅动液体。他这样做了几分钟，直到产生泡沫。接着，他俯身靠近碗，深深地吸了三口气。他放下碗，转身离开。整个过程中，他一言不发。

As he nears the door, the woman raises her head and calls out to him in a voice at once urgent and serene. “Thank you, doctor,” she says, and touches with her other hand the place he had held on her wrist, as though to recapture something that had visited there. Yeshi Dhonden turns back for a moment to gaze at her, then steps into the corridor. Rounds are at an end .

他走到门口时，那女人抬起头，用一种既急切又平静的声音叫他：“谢谢你，医生。”她说着，用另一只手轻轻抚摸着他刚才按压过的手腕，仿佛要找回曾经在那里停留过的某种东西。耶西·顿登转过身，凝视了她片刻，然后走进了走廊。查房结束了。

We are seated once more in the conference room. Yeshi Dhonden speaks now for the first time, in soft Tibetan sounds that I have never heard before. He has barely begun when the young interpreter begins to translate, the two voices continuing in tandem—a bilingual fugue, the one chasing the other. It is like the chanting of monks. He speaks of winds coursing through the body of the woman, currents that break against barriers, eddying. These vortices are in her blood, he says. The last spendings of an imperfect heart. Between the chambers of the heart, long, long before she was born, a wind had come and blown open a deep gate that must never be opened. Through it charge the full waters of her river, as the mountain stream cascades in the springtime, battering, knocking loose the land, and flooding her breath. Thus he speaks, and now he is silent .

我们再次落座于会议室。耶喜顿登开口说话了，他用我从未听过的柔和藏语嗓音说道。他刚开口，年轻的翻译就开始翻译，两人的声音交相呼应——宛如一首双语赋格曲，一曲追逐着另一曲。这如同僧侣的诵经。他讲述着风在女人体内奔涌，水流冲破屏障，翻腾旋转。他说，这些漩涡在她血液里，是她不完美之心最后的流逝。在她出生很久很久以前，在她心脏的两室之间，一阵风吹来，打开了一扇永远不应开启的深邃之门。让她体内奔腾的河水，如同春日山涧奔腾而下，冲击着大地，冲刷着，淹没着她的呼吸。他如此讲述，此刻却沉默不语。

“May we now have the diagnosis?” a professor asks .

“现在可以给出诊断结果了吗？”一位教授问道。

The host of these rounds, the man who knows, answers .

这场回合的主持人，那位知情人士，给出了答案。

“Congenital heart disease,” he says. “Interventricular septal defect, with resultant heart failure.”

“先天性心脏病，”他说。“室间隔缺损，导致心力衰竭。”

A gateway in the heart, I think. That must not be opened. Through it charge the full waters that flood her breath. So! Here then is the doctor listening to the sounds of the body to which the rest of us are deaf. He is more than doctor. He is priest .

我想，那是心中的一个门户。它绝不能打开。让充盈她呼吸的泉水从中涌出。所以！这位医生正在聆听我们其他人听不见的身体之声。他不仅仅是医生，他还是祭司。

I know … I know … the doctor to the gods is pure knowledge, pure healing. The doctor to man stumbles, must often wound; his patient must die, as must he .

我知道……我知道……神明的医生拥有纯粹的知识和纯粹的医术。而凡人的医生则会跌倒，常常会伤人；他的病人终将死去，他自己也一样。

Now and then it happens, as I make my own rounds, that I hear the sounds of his voice, like an ancient Buddhist prayer, its meaning long since forgotten, only the music remaining. Then a jubilation possesses me, and I feel myself touched by something divine .

有时，当我巡视时，会听到他的声音，如同古老的佛教祈祷，其含义早已被遗忘，只剩下旋律。那时，我心中涌起一阵喜悦，感觉自己被某种神圣的力量所触动。

~

# ↩

5
5
Helping Prison
帮助监狱

S o many times each day we support each other informally without ever becoming “helper” or “helped.” Perhaps we’re finding an article of clothing for a partner, cutting bread for one of the children, collecting the mail for the person at the next desk, holding a coat for someone at a restaurant. But a situation defined is a situation confined. The moment the act requires a definition of the roles involved, we risk entrapment.

我们每天都会无数次地以非正式的方式互相帮助，却从未真正成为“帮助者”或“被帮助者”。也许我们帮伴侣找件衣服，帮孩子切面包，帮隔壁桌的人取邮件，或者在餐厅帮人拿着外套。但一旦情境被定义，它就变得局限。一旦某个行为需要界定其中的角色，我们就可能陷入困境。

~

I’ll give you a day in the life .

我来给你描述一下我的一天。

I work in this program with juvenile offenders, ex-drug addicts mostly. And I’m with this very tough, smart kid who tells me, “I got no time for programs, man. I seen programs.” And I feel like saying, “Me neither. I’m not so crazy about programs myself.” But here they are and there we were .

我在这个项目里工作，对象是青少年罪犯，大部分是戒毒者。我遇到一个非常坚强、聪明的孩子，他跟我说：“我没空搞这些项目，伙计。我见过太多项目了。” 我真想说：“我也是。我自己对项目也没什么兴趣。” 但项目就在那里，我们就在那里。

“Whadda you know?” he says. “You’re just a social worker. Social workers are nowhere. Social workers don’t understand shit.” And he’s saying that a little angry and provocative. But it’s a little wry, too. He was playing. And I was liking him at that moment, liking his style .

“你懂什么？”他说，“你不过是个社工。社工一无是处。社工什么都不懂。”他这话带着几分愤怒和挑衅，但也略带讽刺。他是在开玩笑。而那一刻，我挺喜欢他，喜欢他的风格。

So I go, “Yeah, all right. But that’s all you think I am, a social worker? You don’t see anybody here but a social worker?” I was up for playing too .

于是我说：“好吧，行。但你以为我仅仅是个社工吗？你在这里除了社工就看不到其他人吗？”我也想参与其中。

“Well, you got a degree, right? They teach you about other people’s troubles, right? That’s how you got this job. You the Fixer, right?”

“嗯，你拿到学位了，对吧？他们教你如何解决别人的问题，对吧？你就是靠这个找到这份工作的。你是‘问题解决者’，对吧？”

“Sure I got a diploma. I got a wife too. And I got a TV. And I’m into the Boston Celtics. If I’m just a social worker, maybe you’re just an ex-junkie. Is that all that’s happening here?”

“没错，我拿到了文凭。我还有老婆。我还有电视。而且我是波士顿凯尔特人的球迷。如果我只是个社工，那你可能只是个戒毒成功的人。难道这就是全部吗？”

Well, he sort of paused, and he heard it. And there was this moment where I felt something was about to get off the ground, like we were going to get past all this. It sort of hung there, one of those moments when you can feel possibility; maybe we can make it after all. And then … it was like we just missed. You could feel it get close and then pass by. And I swear he sensed that too .

他停顿了一下，听到了。那一刻，我感觉好像有什么事要发生了，好像我们就要渡过难关了。那种感觉就那样悬在那里，那种充满希望的时刻；也许我们最终真的能成功。然后……就像我们擦肩而过。你能感觉到它靠近，然后又擦肩而过。我发誓他也感觉到了。

He said, “You got no idea where I am, man.” And I said, “Well, you got no idea where I am.” He was being straight. I was being straight. Maybe we’d make it another time. Maybe we needed that honesty. But it was frustrating, because it got so close. I really liked this kid. Like, if we could have talked basketball …

他说：“你根本不知道我在哪儿，伙计。”我说：“是啊，你也不知道我在哪儿。”他说的都是实话。我也说的都是实话。也许我们下次还有机会。也许我们需要这种坦诚。但这很令人沮丧，因为我们本来就差一点就能成功。我真的很喜欢这孩子。要是我们能聊聊篮球就好了……

So … bad day, or at least a frustrating one. Anyhow, I come home, lay back, and my wife comes in and tells me she’s thinking about quitting her job at the hospital. I sort of half groan and half laugh. I’d been hoping she’d be the one who’d have it together that evening. We take turns being the one who has it together .

唉……真是糟糕的一天，或者至少是令人沮丧的一天。总之，我回到家，躺下休息，妻子进来告诉我她正在考虑辞掉医院的工作。我半是叹了口气，半是苦笑。我原本希望她能撑到晚上。我们俩轮流撑着呢。

“Okay, what’s the matter?”

“好吧，出什么事了？”

“It’s like prison in there. You’ve either got an ID badge and a stethoscope or you’re flat on your back helpless. It’s Us and Them, the sick and the healthy. The patients get bugged, we get bugged, everybody gets bugged. I can’t stand the roles and the distances. It’s not a hospital—it’s a prison!” And she’s laughing a little, but it’s a strong feeling. And then she gives me this classic, exasperated line, again laughing, “I don’t want to be a nurse, I just want to help!”

“那里简直像监狱。要么你戴着工作证和听诊器，要么你就只能躺在地上无助地躺着。那里分明是‘我们’和‘他们’，病人和健康人。病人被骚扰，我们也被骚扰，每个人都被骚扰。我受不了这种角色分明和人与人之间的距离。那根本不是医院——那是监狱！”她笑着，但语气却很强烈。然后她又笑着，用一种经典的、无奈的语气对我说：“我不想当护士，我只是想帮忙！”

So I say, “Poor kid …” and give her a hug, because it’s obviously been one of those days. And I say something like, “Well, I don’t want to be a social worker either. Social workers don’t understand shit. But what are we going to do? Who’s going to feed the cat? How do we get out of jail?”

所以我就说：“可怜的孩子……”然后抱了抱她，因为很明显，今天对她来说又是糟糕的一天。然后我说：“唉，我也不想当社工。社工什么都不懂。可是我们该怎么办？谁来喂猫？我们怎么才能出狱？”

And we laughed, and had chicken, and talked, and made love. And afterwards she said, “I’m still a little bit at the hospital.” And I said, “I know, I’m still a little bit with that kid.”

我们说说笑笑，吃了炸鸡，聊了聊天，还做了爱。事后她说：“我好像还在医院里待着呢。”我说：“我知道，我好像还在陪着那个孩子呢。”

~

Obviously, it’s often appropriate and harmless to meet in roles in which one is helping and another is being helped. People get sick, nurses nurse. Sinks get stopped up, plumbers plumb. These are voluntary contracts between those with immediate needs and others with relevant skills. Were these to remain simply forms we enter into as needed and then let go of lightly, all would be well. It’s the excess baggage we carry into these functional relationships that may end up confining us. “Helper” and “helped” become states of mind and ways to behave that go way beyond function. Entrapment in these alienates us from one another: a social worker and a juvenile offender just miss; a nurse and a patient seem worlds apart; a priest and a parishioner, so distant, so formal. What otherwise could be a profound and intimate relationship becomes ships passing in the night. In the effort to express compassion, we end up feeling estranged. It’s distressing and puzzling.

显然，在互助关系中，一方帮助另一方通常是恰当且无害的。有人生病，护士就护理病人；水槽堵塞，水管工就疏通管道。这些都是有紧急需求的人和拥有相关技能的人之间自愿达成的协议。如果这些关系仅仅停留在需要时建立、用完后轻松结束的层面，一切都会很顺利。然而，正是我们带入这些功能性关系中的额外负担，最终可能会束缚我们。“帮助者”和“被帮助者”变成了一种心态和行为模式，远远超出了功能本身。深陷其中会让我们彼此疏远：社工和青少年罪犯之间似乎擦肩而过；护士和病人之间仿佛隔着两个世界；牧师和教友之间，如此遥远，如此拘谨。原本可以建立的深刻而亲密的关系，最终却变成了擦肩而过的船只。在努力表达同情的过程中，我们最终却感到疏离。这令人痛苦，也令人困惑。

If it’s prison we’re in, we righteous helpers, what are we charged with? Breaking and entering with the intention of doing good? Felonious assumption of personal responsibility? Selling water by the river? And what is our defense? Early conditioning? “They made me read Helper Rabbit every night until I was eight, Your Honor. In my house, the cry ‘Help!’ was an order, not a plea.” Or later training? “I offer as Exhibit A, Your Honor, this diploma”:

如果我们这些正义的助人者身陷囹圄，我们究竟被控犯了什么罪？非法闯入，意图行善？擅自承担个人责任？在河边卖水？我们的辩护理由又是什么？是早期的教育？“法官大人，他们逼我每晚读《兔子帮手》直到八岁。在我的家里，‘救命！’是命令，不是求救。”还是后来的训练？“法官大人，我呈上这份毕业证书作为证据A”：

[ Your name ] has finally proved himself adequate in the eyes of the undersigned responsible parties, if not in his own . [ Your name ] is now okay . [ Your name ] has mastered certain rules for helping and promises to abide by them . [ Your name ] knows something others don’t know . [ Your name ] has been trained in the use of a number of skills and had them licensed by the state . [ Your name ] will use them to make others whole . [ Your name ] is entitled henceforth to call himself a D.C.P. ( Doctor of Certain Powers ). [ Your name ] may not immediately appreciate the predicament this will put him in or the constraints it may impose upon all. Best not to divulge too much, too soon. Which is why all this has been written in Latin .

[你的名字] 终于在以下署名负责人眼中证明了自己的能力，即便他自己可能并不这么认为。[你的名字] 现在一切安好。[你的名字] 已掌握了一些助人之道，并承诺遵守。[你的名字] 知道一些别人不知道的事情。[你的名字] 接受过多种技能的培训，并获得了州政府颁发的执照。[你的名字] 将运用这些技能帮助他人恢复健康。[你的名字] 从此以后有权称自己为“拥有特定能力的医生”（D.C.P.）。[你的名字] 可能不会立即意识到这会让他陷入怎样的困境，以及这会给所有人带来怎样的限制。最好不要过早透露太多。这就是为什么这一切都是用拉丁文写的。

~

All of us can recognize some truth to the plea of conditioning—first by our parents, then by our teachers. From earliest childhood many of us are told, “Be good and help.” Helpfulness gets encouraged, often rewarded, because it makes the household function more efficiently. “Help out” becomes a euphemism for obedience or compliance.

我们都能体会到这种条件反射式教育的真谛——先是来自父母，后是来自老师。从孩提时代起，许多人就被教导“要乖，要帮忙”。乐于助人会受到鼓励，甚至常常得到奖励，因为它能让家庭运转得更高效。“帮忙”成了服从或顺从的委婉说法。

Once we come to associate it with rewards, we start to use helping in the service of a wide range of personal motives other than the expression of natural compassion. We might empty the trash in order to get the use of the family car, or go to the store to fetch ingredients so that Mother will make our favorite cookies. We might be seeking to compensate for a lack of self-esteem, for feelings of unworthiness or incompleteness. Need praise? Help out. Or perhaps we’re looking for a form of atonement: there’s guilt to assuage. For many, the ability to aid others can provide a needed sense of power or respectability. Maybe some of us help out as a way of compensating for a deeper sense of helplessness; we don’t have to face our own quite so much when we’re busy treating someone else’s. Or maybe we’re just plain lonely. Intimacy is what we’re looking for, and it’s often there to be found in a helping relationship.

一旦我们将助人与奖励联系起来，我们就会开始出于各种各样的个人动机去帮助他人，而不仅仅是出于自然的同情心。我们可能会为了能用家里的车而倒垃圾，或者去商店买食材，好让妈妈做我们最爱吃的饼干。我们或许是在试图弥补自卑、弥补自我价值感的缺失或不完整感。需要赞扬吗？那就去帮忙。或许我们是在寻求某种形式的赎罪：想要减轻内心的愧疚感。对许多人来说，帮助他人的能力可以带来一种必要的力量感或尊严感。也许我们中的一些人帮助他人是为了弥补内心深处的无助感；当我们忙于帮助别人时，就不必过多地面对自己的无助。又或许，我们只是单纯地感到孤独。我们渴望的是亲密感，而这种亲密感往往可以在助人关系中找到。

Rare indeed is the individual for whom the helping act does not arise in part out of some personal motive. To the extent that it does, however, what we are looking for is a role that meets a need … our need. We’re looking to be helpers, not simply to be helpful. A personal agenda leads us to invest in the position, not simply the function. And we invest in others’ reactions to it as well.

确实，很少有人助人的行为完全不带任何个人动机。然而，即便如此，我们所寻求的也是一种满足自身需求的角色……我们自己的需求。我们渴望成为助人者，而不仅仅是乐于助人。个人目的驱使我们投入到这个职位，而不仅仅是它的功能。我们也会关注他人对此的反应。

~

I walk down the street, I’m nobody. Run for a bus, get in line at the store, punch in at work … who are you? Nobody special. And that’s okay. Everybody’s nobody most of the time .

我走在街上，我只是个普通人。追赶公交车，在商店排队，上班打卡……你又是谁？没什么特别的。但这也没什么不好。大多数时候，每个人都只是个普通人。

But walk into that senior center—let me tell you, I’m somebody. “Hello, Mrs. Luchese. How ya been? They’ve been asking for you. Can you go see Mrs. Whoever; she had a fight with her daughter, that louse.” I’m somebody. They say prayers for me, these people. My birthday … some lady—sure, she’s a little screwy—she wants to make it a national holiday. I say, “That’s a great idea. Me and George Washington.” But I like that feeling. I need that feeling—that “somebody.”

但走进那家老年中心——我跟你说，我可是个人物。“你好，卢切斯太太。您好吗？他们一直在找您。您能去看看那位什么太太吗？她跟她女儿吵架了，那个讨厌鬼。”我可是个人物。这些人会为我祈祷。我的生日……有个女人——没错，她有点儿古怪——想把生日定为全国假日。我说：“这主意不错。我和乔治·华盛顿一起过生日。”但我喜欢这种感觉。我需要这种感觉——这种“被人重视”的感觉。

~

Often getting a few perks from our acts seems fine. But most of us can recognize moments when we get a little lost in such personal needs. In any relationship—marriage, friendship, work—there’s that place in us which enjoys being the wise and compassionate one. We understand someone a little too quickly; or volunteer advice just too soon. Sometimes we have to be shown that all of us are better off when we’re free of attachment to being helpers.

从自己的行为中获得一些好处似乎没什么不好。但我们大多数人都能意识到，有时我们会过于沉溺于这种个人需求。在任何关系中——婚姻、友谊、工作——我们内心深处都渴望扮演睿智和富有同情心的角色。我们可能过早地理解他人，或者过早地主动提供建议。有时，我们需要被引导去明白，当我们不再执着于扮演“助人者”的角色时，我们所有人都会过得更好。

~

I happened to have been on a mountaintop in a state of great bliss when a stranger suddenly appeared next to me, sat down, and immediately started to describe this problem he was going through. By the time I’d pulled myself out of the Higher Realms, he’d already detailed the whole drama, the cast of characters, and the decisions he was facing. I hadn’t gotten a bit of it. Nothing. Nobody. Moreover, it was much too late to ask him to run it all down once more. He would have felt very uncomfortable, justifiably .

我当时恰巧在山顶上，沉浸在无比的幸福之中，这时一个陌生人突然出现在我身边，坐了下来，立刻开始讲述他遇到的难题。等我从恍惚中回过神来，他已经把整个事件、人物关系以及他面临的抉择都详细地描述出来了。我一点儿都没听进去。真的，一点儿都没听进去。而且，现在再让他把事情再说一遍也太晚了。他肯定会觉得很不自在，这完全可以理解。

So there I was, intimate confidant to a deep problem, without the slightest idea of who was who and who had done what to whom. My first reaction was to laugh hysterically. It was one of those great Human Condition moments. But this guy was obviously in distress and looking for a kindly pair of ears, so I picked up as best I could .

当时的我，成了他深陷困境的知己，却对谁是谁、谁对谁做了什么一无所知。我的第一反应是歇斯底里地大笑。这真是人生百态的经典时刻之一。但这个人显然很痛苦，渴望有人倾听，所以我尽我所能地理解他。

To my continued amazement, none of the details became any clearer as we walked down the mountain. I kept hoping I’d find out who “she” really was, and what “he” had actually done. No such luck. And I wasn’t about to ask a question that would reveal my total ignorance, make him feel terrible, or lead me to hysterical laughter .

令我更加惊讶的是，下山的路上，所有细节依然没有变得清晰。我一直希望能弄清楚“她”到底是谁，“他”到底做了什么。可惜事与愿违。我也不想问出什么问题，以免暴露我的无知，让他难堪，或者让我自己捧腹大笑。

So we just quietly walked on down. And from time to time I would punctuate the conversation with what seemed like appropriate remarks: “That must have been hard.” “What did you feel then?” “Oh, yes, I’ve been through that one before.” “Boy, things sure do get confused in life.” Great insights like that. And he would nod appreciatively, continue, and I’d contain my sense of this wonderful human absurdity. Meanwhile, I was growing increasingly fond of this guy. And feeling great empathy for his problem—whatever it was .

于是我们就静静地往下走。我不时会插几句自认为合适的话：“那一定很难熬吧。”“你当时是什么感觉？”“哦，是啊，我以前也经历过这种事。”“哎，人生真是充满了各种混乱。”诸如此类的感悟。他会点头表示赞同，继续说下去，而我则努力压抑住内心对这种奇妙人性荒诞的感受。与此同时，我越来越喜欢这个人，也越来越能理解他的困境——不管那是什么。

When we reached the bottom of the hill, he stopped for a moment and then suddenly embraced me. “I just want you to know how incredibly helpful you’ve been,” he said. “You’re one of the most understanding, compassionate people I’ve ever met. Do you think we could have another conversation like this again?” I was dumbfounded. It was one of the great moments in my life. “Sure,” I said. “I’d love to.” And he walked off to join some other people—a number of whom kept coming to me during the day saying, “What did you tell Eddie? He’s just so grateful to you. He says you’re wonderful.”

当我们走到山脚下时，他停顿了一下，然后突然拥抱了我。“我只是想让你知道你帮了我多大的忙，”他说，“你是我见过的最善解人意、最有同情心的人之一。你觉得我们以后还能像这样再聊聊吗？”我当时简直惊呆了。那是我人生中最美好的时刻之一。“当然可以，”我说，“我很乐意。”然后他走开了，和其他人会合——那天，他们中的一些人不停地来找我，问我：“你跟埃迪说了什么？他太感谢你了。他说你真是太好了。”

~

The attachment to the role of helper is frequently reinforced by training that often contributes to a confusion between role and skill. Medical students in grand rounds, for example, get not only a direct view of pathology in patients but an equally intimate view of their teachers as role models. At the conclusion of a residency, a young doctor not only has mastered a complex body of knowledge but has learned how to play doctor as well. This medicine-man persona, while perhaps lending an aura that contributes to healing, also isolates the doctor from those around him.

对助人角色的执着往往通过培训得到强化，而这种培训常常导致角色与技能之间的混淆。例如，医学生在大查房中不仅能直接观察患者的病理，还能近距离观察作为榜样的老师。住院医师培训结束后，年轻医生不仅掌握了复杂的知识体系，也学会了如何扮演医生的角色。这种“医者”的形象，虽然可能赋予医生一种有助于治愈疾病的光环，但也使医生与周围的人产生了隔阂。

But there is another dilemma of the diploma: help becomes know-how. Obviously training is valuable. We want our lawyers, counselors, and teachers to know what they’re doing. Yet to identify them only with their know-how is to shortchange all and turn our relationship into a transaction between one who knows and one who doesn’t. Patterns of behavior get frozen. The aura of know-how in the helper can undermine our confidence as the helped in defining issues for ourselves. We’re a little unsure of the ground, don’t know the technical language, generally uncomfortable. It must be our fault. Best we lie back and take what’s given agreeably … and end up feeling still more helpless.

但文凭还存在另一个困境：帮助变成了专业知识。培训固然重要。我们希望律师、咨询师和教师都具备相应的专业知识。然而，如果仅仅用专业知识来衡量他们，那就等于低估了他们的价值，并将我们之间的关系变成了一种“懂”与“不懂”之间的交易。行为模式因此固化。帮助者身上散发出的专业知识光环会削弱我们作为被帮助者自主解决问题的信心。我们感到有些不确定，不懂专业术语，总之会感到不自在。这一定是我们的错。我们最好还是默默接受，欣然接受……结果却只会感到更加无助。

Identification of service with know-how has considerable occupational hazard for the helper as well. We begin to see people in categories. A psychiatrist treats “paranoid schizophrenics”; a lawyer meets with “litigious parties”; a politician woos “constituents”; a teacher works with “gifted” or “exceptional” children. To apply such discriminative models to people can be functional; to limit people to these does violence to their beings. Indeed, to view the world only in terms of concepts strips it of its mysterious beauty, its power to refresh.

将服务与技能划等号，对服务提供者而言也存在相当大的职业风险。我们开始将人归类。精神科医生治疗“偏执型精神分裂症患者”；律师会见“诉讼当事人”；政治家争取“选民”支持；教师教导“天才”或“特殊”儿童。将这种区分性的模式应用于人或许有其功能性；但将人局限于这些类别，则是对他们的本质的一种伤害。的确，仅仅用概念来看待世界，会剥夺它神秘的美感和焕发活力的力量。

So we are called upon to take what is valuable from our training, but not let it constrict the helping relationship itself. We need to enlist the service of the intellect, but not let it block the intuitive compassion of the heart. Not easy, this task. For the temptation to identify ourselves as What We Know is especially formidable when it comes to helping. We’re moved by the desire to be of service in our lives. When useful know-how comes along that can help us satisfy that desire, it’s not surprising that we embrace it, identify with it, feed it, go to conferences, read books about service (and write them!).

因此，我们需要从训练中汲取宝贵的知识，但又不能让它束缚助人关系本身。我们需要运用理性，但又不能让它阻碍内心深处的直觉和同情。这并非易事。因为在助人这件事上，我们尤其容易受到诱惑，将自己等同于“我们所知的一切”。我们渴望在生活中服务他人。当一些有用的知识能够帮助我们满足这种渴望时，我们欣然接受、认同、滋养它，参加各种会议，阅读（甚至撰写）关于服务的书籍，也就不足为奇了。

Once we have acquired all this knowledge, it’s hard to keep it in perspective. It may dazzle us and make us forget the bedrock of wisdom to which all are privy. It gives us one kind of power but cuts us off from our birthright, the wisdom that comes directly from our common humanity and divinity.

一旦我们掌握了所有这些知识，就很难保持正确的视角。它可能会让我们眼花缭乱，忘记人人皆可拥有的智慧基石。它赋予我们一种力量，却也使我们与生俱来的权利——源自我们共同的人性和神性的智慧——失之交臂。

Finally, when we identify with our special knowledge, we may develop a vested interest in being “right.” In family life we need to prove our theories of child rearing. In professions we defend schools of thought. Helping often slips through the cracks.

最后，当我们认同自己所掌握的专业知识时，我们可能会产生一种强烈的“正确”执念。在家庭生活中，我们需要证明自己的育儿理论；在专业领域，我们捍卫自己的思想流派。而真正需要帮助的人，往往却被忽略了。

~

I believe the real estate industry in this town is unwilling to provide affordable, adequate housing. And I think there are reasons why: property, profit motive, how capitalism works, and so on. I don’t push this analysis at folks. But working as a tenant organizer, I’m looking for ways to get these points across to a large audience. It can get complicated .

我认为这个镇上的房地产行业不愿意提供价格合理、条件良好的住房。我认为这其中有原因：房产价值、逐利动机、资本主义运作方式等等。我不会强迫别人接受这种分析。但作为一名租户组织者，我正在寻找方法，让更多人了解这些观点。这可能会变得很复杂。

I’d been working with a building where conditions were terrible. People there were becoming active—word of mouth in the hallway, some informal meetings, a few natural leaders coming forward—all this even though folks were a little uncertain of themselves and looking to me and my knowledge and experience .

我之前在一栋条件很差的建筑里工作。那里的人们开始活跃起来——走廊里口口相传，举行了一些非正式会议，一些天生的领导者挺身而出——尽管大家都有些缺乏自信，并且把目光投向了我，仰仗我的知识和经验。

Just about the time I was getting some interest from the press, one of the women who was showing some leadership—Carmen, a great lady—realized the time had come where we could push the landlord and get some repairs. He was sufficiently worried to make concessions .

就在我开始引起媒体关注的时候，一位颇具领导力的女性——卡门，一位了不起的女士——意识到时机已到，我们可以向房东施压，要求他进行一些维修。房东也足够重视此事，做出了一些让步。

Problem was, some part of me wanted to hold off. I wanted to wait for a greater confrontation. There was a chance for some publicity, a chance to make a larger point about housing in the city .

问题是，我内心深处其实想拖延时间。我想等待更大的冲突爆发。这样或许能引起公众关注，也能让我有机会就城市住房问题发表更重要的观点。

Carmen made her pitch at a meeting: “Let’s go down there with certain demands, deal with this man, see what we can get. We’re strong, we’re ready.” She ran it down very well. People looked to me: What did I think?

卡门在一次会议上陈述了她的方案：“咱们带着一些要求下去，跟这个人谈谈，看看能争取到什么。我们实力很强，我们已经准备好了。”她把方案说得很清楚。大家都看着我：我的想法是什么？

Now that’s a key moment for an organizer. You’re there to encourage people to move on their own, but you also have a commitment to a larger movement and a set of beliefs about how real change is going to come about. But when they were looking at me, I wasn’t looking at myself .

对组织者来说，这是一个关键时刻。你既要鼓励人们自主行动，也要致力于更大的运动，并坚信真正的变革将如何实现。但当他们看着我的时候，我却没有审视自己。

I manipulated the meeting toward holding off confronting the landlord. I said we shouldn’t sell out too early. I was going for my own agenda. I was persuasive, all the things you learn as an organizer, and I won them over. They’d hold off getting some immediate improvement in their lives .

我巧妙地引导会议，让他们暂缓与房东对抗。我说我们不应该过早出卖自己。我其实是出于自己的目的。我运用了组织者必备的说服技巧，最终赢得了他们的支持。他们愿意暂时搁置一些改善生活的措施。

As the meeting was breaking up, Carmen came up to me. She had this very won’t-leap-to-conclusions-but-won’t-take-any-bullshit look on her face. She said to me, very simply, “Are you being straight?” That’s exactly how she put it. She was right on. She saw it. And she was giving me the chance to see it too. After a moment I said, “No, I’m not.”

会议快结束时，卡门走到我跟前。她脸上带着那种既不妄下结论也不容忍任何胡扯的表情。她很直接地问我：“你没说谎吧？” 她就是这么说的。她说的没错。她看穿了我的心思。而且她也给了我机会去看清这一点。过了一会儿，我说：“不，我没说谎。”

So I got people reassembled and told them I’d realized that I had been pushing my own interests and viewpoint rather than hearing theirs. I pointed out what it was like to be a tenant organizer with a theory of how to make change and build a larger movement. I said I thought they should talk it all over again and I should leave. I’d made what in my work was a bad mistake. They understood. They said, “We still need you,” and I said, “I’ll still be around.” But they started discussing it all again .

于是我把大家重新召集起来，告诉他们我意识到自己一直在强加自己的利益和观点，而没有倾听他们的意见。我指出，作为一名租户组织者，带着一套关于如何变革和建立更大运动的理论，会面临怎样的挑战。我说，我觉得他们应该重新讨论一遍，而我应该离开。我在工作中犯了一个严重的错误。他们理解了。他们说：“我们仍然需要你。”我说：“我还会在这里。”但他们又开始重新讨论这件事。

As I left, Carmen gave me this great look. It was like a look of “Hmmmnnn.…” Curious, respectful, intrigued. It was as if she suddenly saw the whole issue of leadership, right at the moment she was becoming a leader. It was a great moment between us. Very encouraging .

我离开时，卡门给了我一个意味深长的眼神。那眼神仿佛在说：“嗯……”既好奇，又带着敬意，还有些许着迷。就好像她突然领悟了领导力的真谛，就在她即将成为领导者的那一刻。那是我们之间一个非常美好的瞬间，也让我深受鼓舞。

~

Many times we may be alert to the risk of the role. Out of the corner of our eye we catch ourselves acting out our private agendas or see our attachment to certain self-images. But frequently the situation in which we’re working tends to set traps. The dynamics may be subtle. People may need us to play helper. The service organizations so many of us work for have an investment in a collective self-image. Reputations, budgets, relationships in the community, need to be protected and promoted. By building and investing in formal helping institutions we often end up creating distances between who we think we are and those we’d like to serve. There may be some vague awareness of the problem, but in the end we rarely find “Attachment to Being a Helper” on the agendas of most staff meetings. Bring that issue up, the atmosphere in the room might turn a little cool. “Can we get on with business?” So little time, so much help needed.

很多时候，我们或许会意识到自己扮演的角色所带来的风险。我们会不经意间发现自己在为私事奔波，或者执着于某种自我形象。但通常情况下，我们所处的环境本身就会设下陷阱。这种动态变化可能很微妙。人们或许需要我们扮演帮助者的角色。我们许多人所服务的服务机构都致力于维护集体的自我形象。声誉、预算、社区关系都需要维护和提升。通过建立和投资于正式的助人机构，我们最终往往会在我们自认为的自我和我们想要服务的人之间制造隔阂。或许有人隐约意识到这个问题，但最终我们很少在大多数员工会议的议程上看到“执着于助人者”这一项。一旦提出这个问题，会议室里的气氛可能会变得有些冷淡。“我们能开始谈正事了吗？”时间如此紧迫，需要的帮助却如此之多。

Our conditioning, our motives, our training, our attachment to our ideas, the vested interest of organizations … all these, then, can seduce us into believing we’ve got the help, we are the “helpers.” The self-image is very compelling. After all, we like to see ourselves as useful and compassionate. It feels good to be able to offer care to one another. We do have the talents and training to offer. But other factors, other needs are at work as well. We have a personal history to make sense of, a story line we’re trying to write: “This Is Your Life.” We need to present ourselves to others: “What do you do?” “Well, I’m a——” and we’ve got to come up with some kind of answer, at least to ourselves. We’ve got to be somebody, after all. “Helper … yes, I’m a helper.” That’s a worthy identity.

我们的习得、动机、训练、对自身理念的执着、组织的既得利益……所有这些都可能诱使我们相信自己拥有帮助，我们就是“助人者”。自我认知极具说服力。毕竟，我们都喜欢把自己看作有用且富有同情心的人。能够彼此关怀的感觉很好。我们确实拥有可以提供帮助的才能和训练。但其他因素、其他需求也在发挥作用。我们需要理解自身的经历，试图书写自己的人生故事：“这就是你的人生”。我们需要向他人展示自己：“你是做什么的？”“嗯，我是个——”我们必须想出一个答案，至少要对自己说清楚。毕竟，我们必须成为某种存在。“助人者……是的，我是个助人者。”这是一个值得拥有的身份。

Sad, then, that so often it imprisons us, that because of it we find ourselves accomplices to conditions of separateness and division—a world of nurses and patients, social workers and clients, spiritual teachers and seekers, people who know and people who don’t. After all, if some of us are busy being helpers there must be others under continuous pressure to be helped.

令人悲哀的是，它常常禁锢我们，使我们因此成为分离和分裂的帮凶——一个由护士和病人、社工和客户、灵性导师和求道者、知晓者和不知晓者构成的世界。毕竟，如果我们中的一些人忙于助人，就必然有人承受着持续不断的压力，渴望得到帮助。

The condition of helplessness is one that we tend to push away, deny, or stigmatize as a society and as individuals. Our cultural myths neither encourage us to accept a common helplessness nor teach us how to act upon it. When it’s suddenly thrust upon us, we’re unprepared.

作为社会成员和个人，我们往往会回避、否认或污名化无助感。我们的文化迷思既不鼓励我们接受这种普遍存在的无助感，也不教导我们如何应对它。当无助感突然袭来时，我们往往毫无准备。

For example, many of us feel resigned to helplessness as citizens. In a society that so inordinately emphasizes power, many of us feel we have little influence over conditions beyond our most immediate circumstances. We may see injustice and neglect or sense the sterility of mass culture. The quality of education, the organization of work, the anonymity of community life, all may distress us. But we frequently feel impotent to change these conditions. The choices we’re given often seem empty and hollow. Half of us don’t vote for president; even fewer elect local officials. We’re offered thirty brands of blue jeans; everyone knows they’re really the same. The program on television is a bore; we switch channels—some choice. Frustrations accumulate, resignation reigns. “What are we going to do?” we sigh. What’s the point in dwelling upon it? It only makes us feel worse.

例如，我们许多人作为公民都感到无能为力。在一个过度强调权力的社会里，我们许多人觉得自己对自身处境之外的情况几乎无能为力。我们或许目睹不公和忽视，或许感受到大众文化的空洞乏味。教育质量、工作组织、社区生活的匿名性，所有这些都可能令我们感到沮丧。但我们常常感到无力改变现状。我们所拥有的选择往往显得空洞无物。一半的人不投票选举总统；选举地方官员的人就更少了。市面上有三十种牛仔裤品牌；人人都知道它们其实都一样。电视节目枯燥乏味；我们换台——这算什么选择？挫败感不断累积，最终归于无奈。“我们该怎么办？”我们叹息道。纠结于此又有何用？只会让我们感觉更糟。

For those particularly weak and vulnerable, moreover, helplessness becomes a scarlet letter. The jobless steelworker loses self-esteem as well as income. The welfare recipient is at the mercy of bureaucracy and the seeming whim of a worn-out clerk. The senior citizen is haunted as much by the possibility of general helplessness as by any specific infirmity: to spend our last days in a nursing home, neglected and useless …?

对于那些特别弱势和易受伤害的人来说，无助更成了一种耻辱的烙印。失业的钢铁工人不仅失去收入，也失去自尊。领取福利的人只能任由官僚主义摆布，受制于疲惫不堪的办事员的随意决定。老年人不仅要面对具体的疾病，还要面对普遍的无助感：难道要在养老院里度过余生，无人照料，毫无用处吗？

In many societies, however, the state of helplessness is so common that the experience has to be shared. There it is, after all—the poverty, the illness, the homelessness, the hunger, the death. It can’t be denied or pushed to the back of the mind, because it’s simply too prevalent. But as punishing as it can be, people also have a chance to see what strengths can emerge in its face. In the presence of helplessness they can also witness courage, perseverance, patience, acceptance, dignity, and humor.

然而，在许多社会中，无助的状态如此普遍，以至于人们不得不共同经历。毕竟，贫困、疾病、无家可归、饥饿、死亡，这些都真实存在，无法否认，也无法被忽视，因为它们实在太普遍了。尽管无助令人痛苦，但人们也有机会看到在无助面前涌现出的力量。在无助之中，他们也能见证勇气、毅力、耐心、接纳、尊严和幽默。

Here, however, we shun helplessness, and when faced with it, bemoan our fate. We cling to notions of “independence”—it’s the name of our national holiday—as if it were an essential condition of all well-being. The last thing we want is to be robbed of power and placed at the mercy of others. Under any circumstances that’s a challenge. But in our society the most helpless among us are often consigned to a separate class: ghettos, “golden age” communities, hospitals, wards. They’re put or kept somewhere. The rest of us are freer not to face what they represent.

然而，在这里，我们却避讳无助，一旦面对无助，便哀叹自己的命运。我们紧紧抓住“独立”的概念——这是我们国庆节的名称——仿佛它是所有幸福的必要条件。我们最不愿看到的就是被剥夺权力，任人摆布。无论在何种情况下，这都是一个挑战。但在我们的社会里，最无助的人往往被隔离到一个特殊的阶层：贫民窟、“黄金时代”社区、医院、病房。他们被安置或囚禁在某个地方。而我们其他人则更自由地选择不去面对他们所代表的一切。

Then, suddenly, something happens. We’re struck by adversity—and a torrent of reactions. The shock at the loss of power: can’t eat, can’t wash, can’t go to the bathroom alone; just this bell, and how long will it take for them to come this time? The shame: at having been raped and all these strangers know. The guilt: it was just a pleasant drive in the country, and suddenly a little boy is dead. The fear (My God, this is only the beginning!): the first chemotherapy treatment; the first day of torture in prison; the first day the bandages are off, and it’s clear you’re blind. And the helplessness: falling … falling … falling.…

然后，突然间，事情发生了。我们被逆境击垮——随之而来的是一连串的冲击。失去力量的震惊：无法进食，无法洗漱，无法独自上厕所；只有这声铃响，而这次他们又要多久才会来？羞耻：被强奸，而所有这些陌生人都知道。内疚：原本只是一次愉快的乡村兜风，突然间一个小男孩就死了。恐惧（我的天哪，这仅仅是个开始！）：第一次化疗；监狱里遭受酷刑的第一天；绷带拆除的第一天，你才意识到自己失明了。还有无助：坠落……坠落……坠落……

~

It happened in a stroke. It was a stroke. And here I am, in a chair, half-paralyzed. And nobody and nothing prepared me for it, for the mind part of it .

一切都是突如其来的中风。就是中风。现在我坐在椅子上，半身瘫痪。没有任何人、任何事让我做好准备，让我做好应对这一切，尤其是精神上的准备。

Maybe there were chances and I missed them. Times I got sick, friends I might have visited in the hospital. But you do it for them, then you put it all out of your mind. Now I have no choice. I can’t put it out of my mind. I’d do anything to avoid facing it .

或许曾经有过机会，但我错过了。比如我生病的时候，我本可以去医院探望朋友。但你为了他们做了这些事，然后就把一切都抛诸脑后。现在我别无选择。我无法将它们抛诸脑后。我宁愿做任何事来逃避面对它们。

~

Suddenly, the price of our conditioning becomes all too apparent. We’ve clung to models of ourselves as independent, defining ourselves largely in terms of our power to shape our own destiny. There’s been little encouragement to acknowledge and explore our vulnerability. The weak, the afflicted, the vulnerable, the helpless—it’s always been “them.” Now, suddenly, we’re “them.”

突然间，我们习以为常的代价变得无比清晰。我们一直执着于将自己塑造成独立的个体，很大程度上以掌控自身命运的能力来定义自己。我们很少被鼓励去正视和探索自身的脆弱。弱者、受苦者、易受伤害者、无助者——过去总是“他们”。而现在，突然间，我们自己也成了“他们”。

Understandably, our tendency under such circumstances is to look for familiar ways to hold our ground. Behind false facades of courage or self-sufficiency our ego might seek to deny our helplessness. Since others support us in the effort, for a while this strategy keeps us going. But deeper down, there may be something evasive about it. We’re calling upon old strengths, but are we facing the new situation? We’re not quite sure who we are anymore. That’s precisely what’s so traumatic: our ego is adrift. For fear of not recognizing ourselves, we refuse to look into the mirror of the present moment.

在这种情况下，我们自然而然地会倾向于寻找熟悉的方式来站稳脚跟。在虚假的勇气或自给自足的外表下，我们的自我或许会试图否认自身的无助。由于他人的支持，这种策略暂时能让我们坚持下去。但实际上，这其中可能隐藏着某种逃避的成分。我们是在调用旧有的力量，但我们真的面对着新的局面吗？我们甚至开始怀疑自己究竟是谁。这正是创伤所在：我们的自我迷失了方向。因为害怕认不出自己，我们拒绝直面当下的现实。

Because our power is so threatened and our ability to control our environment so curtailed, we may explore ways of using our helplessness to gain power. Perhaps we get others to focus on our predicament. Controlling attention is power. Or perhaps we play on people’s pity, guilt, or sense of duty. Instinctively, we seem to know that we can pull those strings. We remember, after all, how we ourselves used to feel in the presence of someone else’s helplessness.

因为我们的力量受到如此威胁，我们对环境的掌控能力也如此受限，我们可能会想方设法利用自身的无助来获取权力。或许我们会让他人关注我们的困境。掌控注意力就是一种权力。又或许我们会利用人们的怜悯、愧疚或责任感。我们似乎本能地知道自己可以操控这些情绪。毕竟，我们都记得自己曾经在面对他人的无助时是什么感受。

We become so busy trying to find old strengths or new devices to cope with our helplessness that we never really examine the condition itself. We may think we’ll be giving up or giving in. And it’s not surprising that we’re not willing to let go altogether. The challenge is enormous. Not only must we deal with an affliction itself: we’re being asked to confront our helplessness in the face of it. Can we imagine a more difficult task? At some level, we’re being called upon to relinquish every model of ourselves that has kept us going until now—it’s a leap into the void, with no ground to push off from. To enter into and explore our helplessness goes against every learned instinct—like turning a car wheel in the direction of a sudden skid.

我们忙于寻找旧有的力量或新的方法来应对无助，却从未真正审视过这种无助本身。我们或许会认为自己是在放弃或屈服。我们不愿彻底放手，这并不奇怪。挑战巨大。我们不仅要应对疾病本身，还要直面疾病带来的无助。还有比这更难的任务吗？在某种程度上，我们被要求放弃所有支撑我们走到今天的自我认知模式——这就像纵身跃入虚空，没有任何立足之地。进入并探索我们的无助，违背了我们习得的所有本能——就像汽车突然打滑时，我们却要猛打方向盘一样。

Meanwhile, we’re being “helped”—helped, that is, by “helpers.” And so often, as we’ve seen, the character of their work, colored by their own needs for power and self-image, only makes us feel still more alien and diminished. What they seem to want most from us is our compliance. They want us to be “helped.” But that’s not quite the same thing as inviting us, supportively, to explore our helplessness. This could be an obstacle to getting things done quickly and efficiently: “Don’t dwell on such stuff.” It threatens the ego; it’s mysterious; it takes time.

与此同时，我们正在接受“帮助”——确切地说，是被“帮助者”帮助。然而，正如我们所见，他们工作的性质，往往受到自身权力欲和自我形象需求的制约，只会让我们感到更加疏离和渺小。他们似乎最想要的就是我们的顺从。他们想要我们接受“帮助”。但这与引导我们以支持的态度去探索自身的无助截然不同。这可能会成为高效完成任务的障碍：“别纠结于这些事。”这会威胁到自尊；这会让人感到神秘；这会耗费时间。

Perhaps, despite all this, we might have a halting, tentative willingness to examine our helplessness. We might recognize that in the very midst of this upheaval there’s a chance to confront our resistance and go beyond the perimeter of the familiar. With a little support we’d be ready to peer over the edge and look at our worst fears.

或许，即便如此，我们仍会萌生一种犹豫不决、小心翼翼的意愿，去审视自身的无助。我们或许会意识到，正是在这场剧变之中，我们有机会直面内心的抗拒，超越熟悉的界限。只要稍加扶持，我们便能鼓起勇气，窥探边缘，直面内心深处最恐惧的事物。

Still, conditions seem to conspire against it. The weight of circumstance, the accumulation of habits, the entrapment of roles are just too great. Reaching out, trying the best we can, looking for someone who recognizes our little effort, we just don’t get the steady encouragement we need. Maybe there’s one nurse, one friend, one phone call that gives us the courage to pursue this exploration further. But eventually we resign ourselves to joining the ranks of the “helped.” As unhappy as we may be with this role, there seems to be no other option, no adequate support to find a new one.

然而，种种境遇似乎都在阻挠我们。环境的重压、习惯的积累、角色的束缚，这一切都太过沉重。我们竭尽全力，渴望找到一个能认可我们微薄努力的人，却始终得不到所需的持续鼓励。或许一位护士、一位朋友、一通电话能给予我们继续探索的勇气。但最终，我们还是只能无奈地加入“被帮助者”的行列。即便我们并不乐意扮演这样的角色，似乎也别无选择，缺乏足够的帮助去寻找新的出路。

Thus both helper and helped feel constrained. Both may experience the yearning to be free, may make attempts, may at times have small successes. But these often prove to be but short-duration furloughs. We find we’re still doing time. It still feels like Helping Prison.

因此，施助者和受助者都感到束缚。他们都渴望自由，都可能做出尝试，有时也可能取得一些小小的成功。但这些往往只是短暂的喘息。我们发现自己仍然身处牢狱之中，仍然感觉像是在助人监狱里。

The philosopher Gurdjieff pointed out that if we wish to escape from prison, the first thing we must acknowledge is that we are in prison. Without that acknowledgment, no escape is possible. That is, as long as we feel that these roles are inevitable, functional, or the best we can do, it’s unlikely that we’ll be alert to alternatives.

哲学家葛吉夫指出，如果我们想要逃离牢笼，首先必须承认我们身处牢笼之中。若不承认这一点，逃脱便无从谈起。也就是说，只要我们认为这些角色是不可避免的、有效的，或者已经是我们所能做的最好的，我们就不太可能意识到其他的可能性。

Fortunately, many of us do recognize the entrapment of these roles. When we are able to step outside our situations for a moment and recognize the constrictions, we may even be prepared to acknowledge that somehow we ourselves are contributing to this sense of imprisonment.

幸运的是，我们很多人都意识到了这些角色带来的束缚。当我们能够暂时跳出自身处境，意识到这些限制时，我们甚至可能愿意承认，在某种程度上，我们自身也在助长这种囚禁感。

There’s great potential in that recognition alone. It’s the beginning of our escape. Just to be alert to the entrapment can prevent it from taking complete hold without our conscious awareness. We’re more on the lookout for ways to penetrate the walls: a loose brick here, a vent duct there. We find an opportunity and grasp it and suddenly begin to come out from behind the roles.

单凭这种觉察就蕴藏着巨大的潜力。这是我们逃脱的开始。只要对困境保持警觉，就能在不知不觉中避免被彻底困住。我们会更加留意突破困境的方法：这里一块松动的砖头，那里一根通风管道。一旦发现机会，就牢牢抓住，然后突然间，我们便开始从角色扮演中挣脱出来。

With that alertness we are ready to seize opportunities. A doctor comes in to ask how you are feeling, and you notice he’s looking you in the eye; he’s really asking. Now you can tell him how you are feeling … not just what your body is up to. An uncle who’s been deeply depressed drops his guard and tells you just how much he misses his dead wife. The old family constraints fall away. He doesn’t have to be strong, you don’t have to be deferential. You can meet as friends, both of whom have known pain.

有了这份警觉，我们就能抓住机遇。医生进来询问你的感受，你注意到他正看着你的眼睛；他是真心实意地在问。现在你可以告诉他你的感受……而不仅仅是你的身体状况。一位长期深受抑郁折磨的叔叔卸下了防备，向你倾诉他对亡妻的思念。旧有的家庭束缚消失了。他不必坚强，你也不必毕恭毕敬。你们可以像朋友一样相识，彼此都曾经历过痛苦。

What’s interesting when this happens is that we realize that the opportunity to meet behind the roles was present all along. It’s a breakthrough to a state that was there waiting . Everyone breathes a sigh of relief because we feel that we are home again. It’s not so much that we’ve solved a problem through technique, experience, or know-how. We’ve simply remembered who we all really are behind the roles . Of course, there’s more going on than a one-dimensional transaction. After all, we’re human beings here.

当这种情况发生时，有趣的是，我们意识到，其实一直以来，我们都有机会在角色之外相遇。这是一种突破，让我们回归到一种早已存在的境界。每个人都如释重负，因为我们感觉又回到了家。这并非意味着我们通过技巧、经验或知识解决了某个问题，而是我们重新记起了角色之外的自己。当然，这其中蕴含着更深层次的意义。毕竟，我们都是人。

So we don’t need devices or gimmicks to break through the walls of Helping Prison. Nor do we have to deny that we can help or we need help and that there are appropriate forms to give and receive it. What we can do, however, is allow ourselves to open to the fullness of our humanity. We can make room for it all. As we do this, the richness and reciprocity of the helping act itself works to dissolve the barriers created by roles .

所以，我们不需要任何手段或花招来打破“助人牢笼”的壁垒。我们也不必否认自己能够帮助他人或需要帮助，以及给予和接受帮助都有合适的方式。然而，我们真正能做的，是敞开心扉，拥抱我们完整的人性。我们可以为这一切腾出空间。当我们这样做时，助人行为本身所蕴含的丰富性和互惠性，便会消融角色所造成的隔阂。

It’s clear, for example, that as helpers we don’t simply go about dispensing service with nothing in return. We all know how much we get back from caring for others. Nor is it simply material reward, praise, or the feeling of having been useful. Something far more essential can be tapped.

例如，很明显，作为助人者，我们并非无偿付出。我们都知道，关爱他人能给我们带来多少回报。这不仅仅是物质奖励、赞扬或帮助他人的成就感，其中还蕴含着更为深刻的意义。

~

You walk the halls of this place, and what do you see from room to room? Most people peer in and see this retarded child or that one. They focus on this particular mannerism or that deformity. I do it too. It’s very compelling, that picture .

你走在这个地方的走廊里，从一个房间到另一个房间，你看到了什么？大多数人会探头探脑地往里看，看到的是这个智力障碍的孩子，或是那个智力障碍的孩子。他们会关注这个特定的举止或那个缺陷。我也会这样做。这种画面很有冲击力。

But one kid flipped me around on that. We were doing language exercises. And for some godforsaken reason I’d chosen the exchange “How are you?” … “I’m doing fine.” We’d go back and forth. Well, he was having quite a hard time of it, slurring out, “Iy dluee fie” or some such. “Let’s try again, really slowly,” I said. “How … are … you?” And he slurred, “Iy dluee fie.” Then he suddenly burst into this wonderful crazy slurry laugh. It was the nuttiest sound we’d ever heard, either of us. He wasn’t doing fine at all. Neither was I. We were doing terribly. It was absurd. We just began to howl .

但有个孩子让我彻底懵了。当时我们在做语言练习。不知怎么的，我选了“你好吗？”这句对话……“我很好。”我们来回问。结果他磕磕绊绊地说着“Iy dluee fie”之类的。“我们再试一次，慢点说，”我说。“你……好……吗？”他含糊不清地说：“Iy dluee fie。”然后他突然爆发出一阵滑稽的、含糊不清的笑声。那是我们俩都听过最古怪的声音。他一点也不好。我也不好。我们俩都糟透了。太荒唐了。我们俩都开始嚎啕大笑起来。

In the midst of that he suddenly gave me this very clear look—the eyes behind the expression. And I had a sudden thought: “My God, he knows more than I’ll ever know about all this. He sees the whole situation.” At which point he just scrunched up his face like a clown and gave me this wonderful wink .

就在这时，他突然给了我一个意味深长的眼神——透过他表情的背后，我看到了真相。我脑海中闪过一个念头：“我的天，他对这一切的了解比我多得多。他看透了整个局面。”话音刚落，他就像小丑一样皱起脸，朝我眨了眨眼，那表情真是妙极了。

I was just stunned. All I could see was this incredible sense of the humor of things. It was so deep in him. He just had it all in perspective. And he gave that perspective to me .

我当时完全惊呆了。我看到的只有他那令人难以置信的幽默感。这种幽默感深深地根植于他的内心。他对一切都有着清醒的认识，并且把这种认识传递给了我。

When I left him, my head was spinning. I walked down the hall and looked into the other rooms, at kids I’d known, or so I’d thought, for months. It was totally new. I don’t quite know how to describe it. In this room I saw courage. In that room I saw joy. Across the hall, patience. In yet another room, such sweetness: a little boy who was so continuously filled with love, people would just—“die,” I was going to say. “Live,” really .

离开他的时候，我感觉头晕目眩。我沿着走廊走去，环顾其他房间，看着那些我认识了几个月的孩子们——至少我以为我们认识几个月了。一切都那么陌生。我不知道该如何形容。在这个房间里，我看到了勇气。在那个房间里，我看到了快乐。走廊对面，我看到了耐心。在另一个房间里，我看到了如此的甜蜜：一个小男孩，他总是充满爱，人们会——“为之倾倒”，我本想这么说。“真正地，为之活下去”。

I felt so humbled. I swear I had the impulse to go down on my knees. Here I was, going around giving speech therapy, little lessons, little tips. And what was I receiving back in return? Humanity. Basic humanity. The deepest qualities of a person, deeper than you’d see most anywhere .

我感到无比谦卑。我发誓，我当时真想跪下来。我到处给人做语言治疗，教他们一些小技巧，提供一些建议。而我得到的回报是什么呢？是人性。最基本的人性。是人最深层的品质，比你在其他地方看到的都要深刻得多。

What a gift! How much it helped me in my work! In fact it really changed my life. How often can you say that?

真是份珍贵的礼物！它对我的工作帮助太大了！事实上，它真的改变了我的生活。这样的机会，你又有多少呢？

~

When we see that service is not a one-way street, we find that those we are helping give us a continuous stream of clues to help us escape the prison of our self-image. More than simply letting us know what might be working or not, they help us when they question our very models of ourselves. They snap us to; they may even see right through us. And if we can take it, it’s a blessing. We may feel a little foolish, but ultimately, we’re grateful.

当我们意识到服务并非单向付出时，我们会发现，那些被我们帮助的人会不断地提供线索，帮助我们摆脱自我形象的束缚。他们不仅告诉我们哪些方法有效，哪些无效，更重要的是，他们会质疑我们对自身的认知模式。他们让我们幡然醒悟；他们甚至可能一眼看穿我们。如果我们能够接受，那将是一种恩赐。我们或许会觉得自己有点傻，但最终，我们会心怀感激。

The struggles of those we are helping confront us with life at its purest. Their suffering strips away guile and leaves what is real and essential. The deepest human qualities come forth: openness, yearning, patience, courage, forbearance, faith, humor … living truth … living spirit. Moved and touched by these qualities, we’ve no choice but to acknowledge and reaffirm our humanity. Others notice when this happens. We feel them feel it. It’s at these moments that we remember what service is truly all about.

我们所帮助的人们的苦难，让我们直面生命最纯粹的本质。他们的苦难剥去了虚伪的外衣，让我们看到真实而本质的东西。最深层的人性光辉由此展现：坦诚、渴望、耐心、勇气、宽容、信仰、幽默……鲜活的真理……鲜活的精神。被这些品质所感动，我们不得不承认并重申我们的人性。当这一切发生时，其他人会注意到。我们也能感受到他们的感受。正是在这些时刻，我们才真正领悟到服务的真谛。

~

She thanked me for helping. I thanked her for letting me. She said, “You helped me see who I really was.” I said, “You showed me to begin with.”

她感谢我的帮助。我感谢她让我有机会帮助她。她说：“你让我看清了真正的自己。”我说：“是你让我一开始就认识了自己。”

~

Our own experience with helplessness also points the way to escape from the prison of roles.

我们自身对无助的体验也指明了摆脱角色束缚的道路。

~

When I lost my vision, I had been very self-sufficient and together. I was raising five children. I was working. I was volunteering in my community. I was independent enough to be contemplating a divorce from a bad marriage—I’d even given an attorney five hundred dollars. Just before I had to go into the hospital .

失明之前，我一直很独立，生活也很充实。我养育了五个孩子，有工作，还在社区做义工。我经济独立到甚至考虑结束一段糟糕的婚姻——我甚至已经给了律师五百美元。就在我入院之前。

I’d begun to find myself knocking things over and stumbling around. I went to an ophthalmologist, then a neurologist, then a radiologist, then a neurosurgeon. And finally a doctor said, “You have a growth in your brain. If you don’t have surgery it will continue to grow and it will take your life.” Just like that .

我开始发现自己经常碰倒东西，走路也摇摇晃晃。我先去看眼科医生，然后是神经科医生，接着是放射科医生，最后是神经外科医生。最后一位医生说：“你脑子里长了个东西。如果不做手术，它会继续生长，最终会要了你的命。” 就这么简单。

The operation took seven and a half hours. The doctor said he almost lost me twice. He’d removed a tumor the size of a hen’s egg. All I could see was the faintest bit of light .

手术持续了七个半小时。医生说他差点两次失去我。他切除了一个鸡蛋大小的肿瘤。我当时只能看到一丝微弱的光亮。

It didn’t hit me until I got home. I didn’t recognize myself I went into the hospital with long hair; I came out with short. I went in at 145 pounds; I came out at 175, wearing my mother’s dress. I went in and could see; I left and couldn’t. It wasn’t me. And things were bad at home. I couldn’t get a divorce now; I was too dependent. I tried to do things for myself, but it often just created more trouble. My youngest daughter didn’t want to be seen on the street with me. She was ashamed. I felt so bitter. But I kept pushing my feelings away. What had happened? Why me? I just wanted out of there .

直到回到家我才意识到发生了什么。我简直认不出自己了。进医院时我还留着长发，出来时却剪短了。进去时我145磅，出来时却175磅，还穿着我妈妈的裙子。进去时我还能看见，出来时却什么也看不见了。这不是我。家里的情况也很糟糕。我现在没法离婚了，因为我太依赖别人了。我试着自己做事，但往往只会惹出更多麻烦。我的小女儿都不愿意和我一起出门，她感到羞耻。我感到无比痛苦。但我一直努力压抑着自己的感受。到底发生了什么？为什么是我？我只想离开那里。

One nice fall day, I told my husband I was going out. I went down the elevator and out of the house. I got to the corner and just stopped. I stood there, expecting any minute he’d come down and join me. He never came. I just stood there on the corner .

一个秋高气爽的日子，我告诉丈夫我要出门。我乘电梯下楼，走出家门。走到街角，我停了下来。我站在那里，期待着他随时会下来和我一起走。但他始终没有出现。我就那样站在街角。

A lot happened on that corner. I saw my past life. I recalled how lonely and helpless I’d felt as a little girl. And there I was now, just like a child again, only with five of my own. I stayed there a long time. Finally, I said to myself, “Well, here you are and there’s no place to go. It’s time you brought a little help into your life.”

那个街角发生了很多事。我看到了我的过去。我回忆起小时候那种孤独无助的感觉。而现在，我又像个孩子一样，只是多了五个孩子。我在那里待了很久。最后，我对自己说：“好吧，你现在无处可去。是时候给你的生活带来一些帮助了。”

So I went into rehabilitation. And I told them everything I felt. I gave them everything. I gave them my shame and my anger and my fear. I felt it was the truth. And if it was the truth, then how could I be helpless? You don’t suffer from the truth. The truth sets you free .

所以我去了戒毒所。我把我所有的感受都告诉了他们。我把一切都告诉了他们。我把我的羞耻、愤怒和恐惧都告诉了他们。我觉得那就是真相。如果那就是真相，那我又怎么会无助呢？真相不会让你受苦。真相会让你获得自由。

Of course it was hard work, coming to terms with change. But after a while you have nothing left to hide. You want to bring it all out. You want to make room to receive help. And when you’re with a lot of people who are also trying to do that, you get a lot of support. Us blind folks, working together: the more I felt that, the more I found myself beginning to offer help as much as ask for it .

当然，接受改变并非易事。但过了一段时间，你就没什么好隐瞒的了。你想坦诚相待，你想敞开心扉接受帮助。当你身边有很多也在努力做到这一点的人时，你会得到很多支持。我们这些盲人团结互助：我越是感受到这一点，就越发现自己开始主动提供帮助，就像我主动寻求帮助一样。

I met a young man there who was blind from birth. He’d never had a birthday party. So I baked him a cake and organized a party. He blew out the candles he couldn’t see. He was delirious. It was grand. I felt so happy. I had come from that lost blind person on the corner to someone who had seen a need and done something about it .

我在那里遇到一个先天失明的年轻人。他从未过过生日。于是我给他烤了个蛋糕，还组织了一场派对。他吹灭了看不见的蜡烛，兴奋极了。那场面真是太棒了。我感到无比幸福。我从一个在街角迷路的盲人，变成了一个看到需要帮助的人，并为此付出了努力。

I’ve told people something that sounds a little cruel. Everyone should experience temporary blindness, to see how our vision can give us such hangups, how we judge and condemn, and what that does to us all. Like that boy with the birthday cake. There was a blind girl he had fallen for. Then someone said she was unattractive. He stopped seeing her. It brought tears to my eyes. He’d been seeing fine .

我跟人说过一些听起来有点残酷的话。每个人都应该体验一下暂时失明，看看我们的视力会给我们带来怎样的困扰，让我们如何评判和谴责他人，以及这会对我们所有人造成怎样的影响。就像那个男孩爱上了一个盲女。后来有人说她不漂亮，他就再也看不见她了。这让我热泪盈眶。他之前明明看得好好的。

But when you begin to see with that inner eye, that inner eye everyone has, it all changes. Everyone is human, everyone is God’s child. Everyone is helpless, one way or another, and everyone is helpful too. We’re all here for each other … that’s how it is. And we all have something to give, no matter our condition .

但当你开始用那双内在的眼睛去看，那双每个人都拥有的内在的眼睛去看，一切都会改变。每个人都是人，每个人都是上帝的孩子。每个人都会在某些方面感到无助，但每个人也都能帮助别人。我们彼此相伴……就是这样。无论境遇如何，我们每个人都有可以奉献的东西。

There are ups and downs, of course. You start blind and reach out. Sometimes there’s nothing to hold on to, but you still reach. Then you learn to hold on to whatever you get. Then you find someone’s hand and you take it. Then you see you can reach out and hold someone else. Once you start, it all follows. I’ve seen that .

当然，人生总有起伏。你一开始一无所知，只能摸索前行。有时一无所有，但你依然会伸出手。然后你学会珍惜你所拥有的一切。然后你找到一只手，握住它。然后你发现自己也能伸出手去握住别人的手。一旦你开始，一切都会随之而来。我亲眼见证过。

So now, when I work with handicapped people, or anyone really, I find I have a special understanding to share. That’s really all I have to offer. It’s hard to put it into words. It’s just “I understand,” that’s all .

所以现在，当我与残疾人士，或者任何人一起工作时，我发现自己有一种特殊的理解可以分享。这真的是我能提供的全部。很难用语言来表达。就是“我理解”，仅此而已。

And yet, as sure or secure as that may sound, I don’t think you’re ever really secure. What is security? You can lose it in a flash. I know. And I still get shaky. So I have a little prayer: that the Lord will send me someone to help me along the way on my subway journey every day … and that He’ll send someone I can share my faith and strength with too. Both things. That’s how I set off to work. And it usually happens .

然而，尽管这听起来似乎很确定或很稳妥，但我认为你永远无法真正感到安全。安全感是什么？它可能转瞬即逝。我知道。即便如此，我仍然会感到不安。所以我有个小小的祷告：愿上帝每天在我乘坐地铁的路上，派个人来陪伴我……也愿祂派个人来，让我可以与他分享我的信仰和力量。两件事都要。这就是我上班时的祷告。而且通常都会实现。

~

How special that moment when we stop pushing it all away. Here is the moment of truth: the fear, the vulnerability, the doubt, the helplessness—that’s what’s going on, that’s what we’re feeling. We’re alone on a corner. But the moment we accept it, we’re not running anymore. We’ve turned the corner and can finally say, “Now what?”

当我们不再逃避一切的那一刻，是多么特别。真相大白的时刻到了：恐惧、脆弱、怀疑、无助——这就是正在发生的一切，这就是我们正在感受的一切。我们独自站在街角。但当我们接受这一切的那一刻，我们就不再逃避了。我们已经转过街角，终于可以问自己：“接下来该怎么办？”

The minute we accept the place where we may seem helpless, it can cease to be the deepest truth about us. The part of us that’s accepting it isn’t the part of us that’s lost in it. To regain that perspective is the beginning of freedom. Of course there is no assurance that we won’t go under again … and again … and again. But something has changed. There is new buoyancy.

当我们接受自己看似无助的处境时，它便不再是我们内心深处最真实的写照。接受这种处境的我们，并非迷失其中的我们。重拾这种视角，便是自由的开端。当然，我们无法保证自己不会一次又一次地沉沦……但有些东西已经改变。一种新的活力油然而生。

The process is painstaking, and for it to proceed we need great compassion for ourselves—exactly the way we are. And we must allow the universe to be exactly the way it is. Through this process we find that we are no longer pitting ourselves against things. We’re opening to life—first by opening to ourselves, and then gradually expanding outwards.

这个过程十分艰辛，要让它顺利进行，我们需要对自己抱有极大的慈悲——接纳我们本来的样子。我们也必须允许宇宙保持它本来的样子。通过这个过程，我们会发现自己不再与万物对抗。我们敞开心扉拥抱生命——首先是敞开心扉接纳自己，然后逐渐向外扩展。

As we explore our resistances and fears—everything we’d been so busy fighting before—new understanding and resources are revealed. Our old models of ourselves start to dissolve, leaving us open and receptive to the new moment. Now we can begin to work creatively with the unknown. We’re ready to listen and accept guidance and grace, because we’ve made room in ourselves. We may be exhausted, yet at the same moment we feel fresh. Having surrendered into helplessness we can now get on with help.

当我们探索自身的抗拒和恐惧——那些我们过去一直忙于对抗的一切——新的理解和资源便会显现。我们旧有的自我认知开始瓦解，让我们敞开心扉，接纳新的时刻。现在，我们可以开始创造性地与未知共处。我们准备好聆听并接受指引和恩典，因为我们已在内心腾出了空间。我们或许会感到疲惫，但同时又感到神清气爽。当我们坦然接受无助之后，便可以借助帮助继续前行。

But as active participants . Before, we had to be helped. Now, what we are ready for is support , for a process we have set in motion ourselves . So we reach out and receive it eagerly. It’s become part of a dialogue with life, a dialogue in which we have things to say. We want to keep the conversation going. Help has become collaboration.

但我们是积极的参与者。过去，我们需要被帮助。现在，我们渴望的是支持，是支持我们自己启动的进程。所以我们主动寻求并欣然接受。这已成为与生活对话的一部分，一场我们也有话要说的对话。我们希望这场对话能够持续下去。帮助已转变为合作。

In this collaboration we see just how much we ourselves have to offer: our own perseverance, honesty, openness, gratitude, humor. And we may be amazed to find out how hungry people are for these qualities.

在这次合作中，我们看到了自己能贡献多少：我们的毅力、诚实、开放、感恩和幽默感。我们或许会惊讶地发现，人们对这些品质是多么渴望。

~

Sometime after turning the corner of my condition, I began to notice how conscious and thoughtful I was being with everyone around me. I was even a little embarrassed at all this new-found selflessness. But it felt so incredibly real and true and natural .

病情好转后不久，我开始注意到自己对周围的人变得多么体贴周到。我甚至对这种突如其来的无私感到有些不好意思。但这种感觉如此真实、自然，如此真切。

One doctor caught it. “I hear you’ve become the angel of mercy around here,” he said. I said, “It’s true.” He laughed, “I understand.” I said, “You’re familiar with the process, doctor?” He laughed again, and I saw that he was .

一位医生听出了我的心声。“我听说你成了我们这儿的救世主，”他说。我说：“没错。”他笑了，“我明白。”我说：“医生，您熟悉这套流程吗？”他又笑了，我这才明白他的确很熟悉。

“Does it last?” I asked, a little more seriously. And he laughed once more. “No. But it comes back. And you don’t forget. And you appreciate being reminded.”

“它会一直持续下去吗？”我稍微认真地问。他又笑了。“不会。但它会回来的。你不会忘记。而且你会感激有人提醒你。”

~

And so at a certain point “helper” and “helped” simply begin to dissolve. What’s real is the helping —the process in which we’re all blessed, according to our needs and our place at the moment. How much we can get back in giving! How much we can offer in the way we receive! But even “giving” and “receiving” now seem artificial. Where does one begin, the other end? They seem to be happening simultaneously. That’s how it feels, anyway. Isn’t that why everyone’s so pleased?

于是，在某种程度上，“施予者”和“受助者”的概念开始消融。真正重要的是助人本身——在这个过程中，我们每个人都根据自身的需求和当下的处境而得到祝福。我们付出多少，又能收获多少！我们接受多少，又能给予多少！但就连“付出”和“接受”如今也显得虚假。它们的起点和终点在哪里？它们似乎同时发生。至少感觉上是这样。难道这不正是大家如此欣喜的原因吗？

Now at last we’re ready to play the roles—the final twist. Because at one level there is help to be offered and received. At one level there are forms. It’s just that there are other levels as well. As we embrace them all—our helpfulness and our helplessness alike—we find ourselves able to enter into the forms without being entrapped by them. We can accept and thrive in the inevitable ambiguities and paradoxes.

现在，我们终于准备好扮演这些角色——最后的转折点。因为在某种程度上，我们可以提供帮助，也可以接受帮助。在某种程度上，我们可以找到各种形式。只不过，还有其他层面。当我们接纳所有这些层面——无论是我们的助人还是我们的无助——我们就会发现自己能够进入各种形式之中，而不被它们所束缚。我们可以接受并驾驭那些不可避免的模糊性和悖论。

The challenge, then, the opportunity really, is to accept the roles in order to cut through them, and to cut through them in order to be able to participate in them without entrapment . Once we taste the excitement of this process, we begin to recognize its profound implications. It’s a chance to take on form in order to liberate one another from it. This is the true work of a conscious human birth. This is what we’re all here to do.

因此，真正的挑战，或者说机遇，在于接受这些角色，从而超越它们；超越它们，才能不受束缚地参与其中。一旦我们体验到这个过程的兴奋，我们便开始意识到它深远的意义。这是一个让我们获得某种形式，从而将彼此从这种形式中解放出来的机会。这才是人类觉醒的真正意义所在。这才是我们来到这个世界的使命。

So we enter into Helping Prison consciously. Here it is, after all. And it’s fine, it’s fascinating. In fact, Helping Prison is just where we might want to start out if liberation happens to be our goal.

所以，我们是有意识地进入“帮助监狱”这个领域的。毕竟，它就在这里。而且这很好，它引人入胜。事实上，如果我们的目标恰好是获得解放，“帮助监狱”或许正是我们应该着手的地方。

~

You have to go through seven gates to get to where I work: “Solitary,” known here in prison as “Special Housing,” a.k.a. “the Box.” I run education projects, and keep my eyes out for anything else .

要到我工作的地方，你必须穿过七道门：“单独监禁室”，在监狱里被称为“特殊监舍”，又名“盒子”。我负责一些教育项目，并留意其他任何事情。

By the time I’ve passed through the gates, I’ve seen hundreds of people. “Cómo estás?” “Yo, suckah!” “Hey, what’s happening?” And there’s an incredible gallery in here. (That’s what they call cell blocks—galleries.) And a constant game of Who’s Who. I see it at various levels .

等我穿过大门的时候，我已经看到了数百人。“Cómo estás?” “Yo, suckah!” “Hey, what's happen?” 这里面简直像个画廊。（他们把牢房叫做画廊。）而且这里一直上演着一场“谁是谁”的游戏。我从不同的层面看到了这一切。

Inmates are here, for starters, because they’ve either committed or been close to certain crimes. I also see that the system has produced conditions that make it pretty easy for that to happen. But they’ve made decisions too. So you’ve got the one of circumstance and choice weaving back and forth. And, of course, everyone has their story, and all that’s part of it too .

首先，囚犯之所以在这里，是因为他们要么犯了罪，要么差点犯下某些罪行。我也看到，现行体制营造的条件使得这种情况更容易发生。但他们也做出了自己的选择。所以，环境和选择这两个因素交织在一起。当然，每个人都有自己的故事，而这些故事也是其中的一部分。

It’s just as complex with the guards. They’re jailers, but they’re also fellow employees of mine. And they’re stuck in regular routines like the prisoners, stuck having to be “the Man.” But they’re choosing that too. And they’re a little suspicious with me. Are prisoners going to put one over on this guy? That’s okay, but sometimes it’s delicate .

狱警的情况也同样复杂。他们是狱警，但也是我的同事。他们和囚犯一样，被困在固定的作息中，不得不扮演“权威”的角色。但这也是他们自己的选择。他们对我还有些怀疑。囚犯会不会耍我？这没关系，但有时候情况很微妙。

Recently I had two guards around me coming on with “Whadda we gonna do with these Commie teachers?” “I don’t know. I’d like to find them buried under ten feet of snow in the spring.” “You one of these new Commie teachers?” “No, man,” I said. “I’m an anarchist. I got nothing to do with Commies.”

最近，我身边有两个保安走过来问我：“我们该拿这些共产主义老师怎么办？” “我不知道。我希望春天的时候能把他们埋在十英尺厚的雪下面。” “你是这些新来的共产主义老师之一吗？” “不，伙计，”我说。“我是个无政府主义者。我跟共产主义者一点关系都没有。”

It was a hard moment, actually. I saw a real deep hurting kind of suspicion about people like me, brought in here to give inmates education, while they can’t afford to send their sons to college or get them a job in the area, except in this lousy joint .

那真是一段难熬的时刻。我看到他们对像我这样的人怀有一种深深的、痛苦的怀疑，我们被带到这里来给囚犯提供教育，而他们自己却无力送儿子上大学，也无法在当地为他们找到工作，除了在这个破地方。

So it’s pretty complicated. The guards are watching out for anything that’s going to make life difficult. The inmates are looking for whatever’s going to make it easier. These guys are over here, those guys are over there, and I’m coming up the middle. So it’s got to be Something For Everybody. Because you can’t help somebody out if someone else thinks they’re losing because of it .

所以情况相当复杂。狱警们警惕着任何可能让囚犯日子不好过的事情，而囚犯们则想方设法让自己的日子好过一些。这些人在这边，那些人在那边，而我则夹在中间。所以，必须做到人人都有份。因为如果你帮助了别人，却让其他人觉得他们因此吃了亏，那你就帮不了他们了。

So my approach is “Let’s see if we can all shake loose a little and not get too lost in it and see what we can do.” And I’m constantly looking for clues, clues to why we’re all here, clues to what’s possible. My bias generally is for a kind of harmonization, seeing it all like a chord that’s trying to be resolved. I also have to do it because I can’t afford to mess up. Very tense situation, the Box .

所以我的方法是：“看看我们能不能放松一点，别陷得太深，看看我们能做些什么。”我一直在寻找线索，寻找我们为何在此的线索，寻找各种可能性的线索。我通常倾向于某种和谐，把一切都看作一个试图解决的和弦。我也必须这么做，因为我输不起。情况非常紧张，就像身处一个盒子里。

Thirty-two very heavy people—contraband, drugs, violent acts, political prisoners, guys who get raped, guys who rape them. And very close, everybody on the edge, waiting, rapping; everything reverberates .

三十二个沉重的人——走私品、毒品、暴力行为、政治犯、被强奸的人、强奸犯。每个人都靠得很近，徘徊在边缘，等待着，说唱着；一切都在回响。

Meanwhile, here I am, rolling up and down the corridor of the Box on my little office chair, from cell to cell, with books and magazines. Quite a sight, I’m told. And I’ll open up an inmate’s food hatch, peer in, establish contact, and see what kind of program we can get going. I’m on my rolling chair. He’s on his plastic pail, a little puzzled. The guards are glowering, anywhere from suspicious to hostile. I may have a good chair, but I’m afraid .

与此同时，我正坐在我的小办公椅上，在“盒子”监狱的走廊里来回穿梭，从一个牢房走到另一个牢房，手里拿着书和杂志。有人说，这景象相当引人注目。我会打开某个囚犯的送餐口，往里窥视，和他建立联系，看看我们能开展什么样的项目。我坐在我的转椅上。他坐在他的塑料桶上，一脸困惑。狱警们怒目而视，眼神从怀疑到敌意，不一而足。我的椅子或许不错，但我却感到害怕。

But what I seem to be doing here seems to be needed. And what I seem to be doing here is also whatever I must have been curious about to get this job in the first place. It’s a need, I think, simply to explore. What is all of this imprisonment and violence and separation all about, anyway? I’m trying to explore that in myself—the everyday fear and anger in my own life .

但我在这里所做的事情似乎是必要的。而我在这里所做的事情，也正是我当初选择这份工作的原因所在。我想，这是一种探索的需要。这一切的囚禁、暴力和分离究竟意味着什么？我试图在自己身上探索这些——探索我生活中日常的恐惧和愤怒。

That’s my education program in the Box. Are there any answers to this incredible human dilemma? Can we get into some kind of larger, greater conversation where we’re just telling each other, “Look, this is what it feels like to be me going through this, and you tell me what it feels like to be you.” And we’ll try to do that with a certain kind of basic decency and sanity. That seems to me the beginning of freedom—something very much on people’s minds here, everywhere really .

这就是我在“盒子”里提出的教育理念。对于这种令人难以置信的人类困境，是否存在答案？我们能否展开更广泛、更深层次的对话，彼此倾诉：“听着，这就是我经历这一切的感受，你也告诉我你的感受。”我们会努力以基本的体面和理智来进行这样的对话。在我看来，这才是自由的开端——这的确是人们，乃至全世界，都非常关心的问题。

It happens. One day I’m squatting by one of the cells with a kid who is bending my ear off. Angel Cruz. “Hey, mister, thanks for coming by, I gotta list of books, I got me a plan I got to tell you about.” Live wire. He’d been looking at this issue of Solar Age magazine. And he’s no hippie Whole Earth domehead. He’s just into solar cells, not prison cells .

这种事时有发生。有一天，我蹲在一间牢房旁边，一个小孩儿喋喋不休地说个不停。安吉尔·克鲁兹。“嘿，先生，谢谢光临，我这儿有份书单，我还有个计划要跟你说说。”他真是个活宝。他刚才一直在看这期《太阳能时代》杂志。而且他可不是那种嬉皮士，也不是那种只会照搬《地球整体》的傻瓜。他只是对太阳能电池感兴趣，对监狱牢房不感兴趣。

“With one of these, I could move to Alaska, man. Get away from all this shit, grow my own vegetables, cheap electricity, and set up.” And I’m right there with him—the thought of moving to Alaska having occurred to me from time to time .

“有了这玩意儿，我就可以搬去阿拉斯加了，老兄。远离这一切糟心事，自己种菜，用便宜的电，安顿下来。” 我完全同意他的看法——我也时不时地想过搬去阿拉斯加。

“Okay, Angel. Where do you start?”

“好的，安琪儿。你从哪里开始呢？”

“Well, finish up clean here, get me some plans from this other book, do me some more research.…”

“好了，先把这儿收拾干净，再从另一本书里给我找些图纸，再帮我做些研究……”

And we’re really into it, back and forth, when all of a sudden, down the hall, here comes Mayhem. Yelling, screaming, the Goon Squad coming in in special uniforms. Possible riot, chance to spread. But Angel Cruz and I aren’t dropping one stitch in our conversation. Angel Cruz and I are talking Serious Alaska here in the midst of this storm. And there’s some kind of sanctification in it. It’s a place of consecration which we two are keeping going together, both very aware that the stakes of keeping the conversation alive are somehow very high. And we’re doing it .

我们俩聊得正起劲儿来，突然，走廊那边传来一阵骚动。大喊大叫，一群暴徒穿着特制制服冲了进来。暴乱可能爆发，而且会蔓延开来。但我和安吉尔·克鲁兹的谈话丝毫没有中断。在这场风暴中，我和安吉尔·克鲁兹还在认真地讨论着阿拉斯加的严肃话题。这其中似乎蕴含着某种神圣的意义。这是一个神圣的场所，我们俩一起努力维系着它，我们都清楚地意识到，保持对话的重要性不言而喻。而我们正在努力。

I can’t tell you how much that conversation meant. It was so important. Everyone is flipping out. But I’m with Angel at the heart of his dreams, and Angel’s with me at the center of my fear. And we’re out of jail. We’re building a solar hut in Alaska .

我无法形容那次谈话对我意义有多重大。它太重要了。大家都慌了。但我与安吉尔一起，站在他梦想的中心；安吉尔也与我一起，站在我恐惧的中心。我们出狱了。我们正在阿拉斯加建造一座太阳能小屋。

So you might say, “Who’s helping who?” We’re just two guys talking freedom. And yeah, we’ve got these different situations. But we don’t have to get so locked into the Box that we can’t go to Alaska together. And that’s helping relieve me of my biggest burden in life: the feeling that I’m responsible, that I gotta do it. Responsible for this place, and my family, and friends. That’s probably what brought me to the Box in the first place. That’s what I’m doing time for—three counts of taking things personally. Personal responsibility, heavy felony!

所以你可能会问，“到底是谁在帮谁？”我们只是两个男人在谈论自由。没错，我们处境不同。但我们不必被牢牢困住，以至于无法一起去阿拉斯加。这让我卸下了人生最大的重担：那种责任感，那种我必须承担的责任感。对这个地方、我的家人和朋友负责。这大概就是我最初被关进监狱的原因。这就是我服刑的原因——三项“个人责任”，重罪！

So there’s a great deal of to-and-fro in here. I’m telling guys about this, and they’re telling me about that. And they’re giving me advice about my life, and how it all is. Sometimes it’s germane, and sometimes it’s not. But it’s frequently very funny, and I love it. I love moving in and out. I love the whole conversation .

所以这里面有很多来回的对话。我跟他们说这个，他们也跟我说那个。他们会给我一些关于生活和人生的建议。有时候这些建议很中肯，有时候则不然。但通常都很有趣，我喜欢这种互动。我喜欢这种来回交流的感觉。我喜欢整个对话过程。

~

# ↩

6
The Way of Social Action

6社会行动之道

I n the middle of the gentle Indian night, an intruder burst through the bamboo door of the simple adobe hut. He was a government vaccinator, under orders to break resistance against smallpox vaccination. Lakshmi Singh awoke screaming and scrambled to hide herself. Her husband leaped out of bed, grabbed an ax, and chased the intruder into the courtyard .

在印度宁静的夜色中，一个闯入者破开了简陋土坯房的竹门。他是一名政府疫苗接种员，奉命来消除人们对天花疫苗的抵制。拉克什米·辛格尖叫着惊醒，慌忙躲藏起来。她的丈夫从床上跳起来，抓起一把斧头，追着闯入者跑进了院子。

Outside, a squad of doctors and policemen quickly overpowered Mohan Singh. The instant he was pinned to the ground, a second vaccinator jabbed smallpox vaccine into his arm .

外面，一群医生和警察迅速制服了莫汉·辛格。他刚被按倒在地，第二个接种员就将天花疫苗扎进了他的手臂。

Mohan Singh, a wiry 40-year-old leader of the Ho tribe, squirmed away from the needle, causing the vaccination site to bleed. The government team held him until they had injected enough vaccine; then they seized his wife.
