It was a wonderful moment, and the fight stopped, which my mother accepted a little reluctantly. No, I’m joking—she was very pleased. She saw how it all was. Everything after that was just, well, easier—less pressure, less trying, less pushing, happening more by itself. And the visit ended up fine. We just spent time together, and then she went back to her house .

那真是个美好的时刻，争吵停止了，我母亲虽然有点不情愿，但还是接受了。不，我开玩笑的——她非常高兴。她明白了事情的真相。之后的一切都变得轻松多了——压力小了，努力少了，逼迫少了，一切都顺其自然。探望也圆满结束。我们一起度过了一段时光，然后她就回家了。

~

By dispassionately acknowledging our personal needs, we lessen their grip on our actions. More and more we simply observe rather than identify with our motives. It’s not so much that we’re trying to push them away; denial buys us no peace. Rather, we’re loosening our attachment to our motives by stepping behind them. It’s not that they aren’t at play; we’re simply offstage watching. As this happens, our motives seem to lose some of the mischievous, unpredictable power of their shadowy existence. From this vantage point we’re more able to catch sight of some need or expectation as it strives to move a situation to its own gratification, setting us up for potential frustration. We can simply note it, not get lost in it, and continue about our work with greater freedom.

通过冷静地承认自身的需要，我们就能减轻它们对我们行为的控制。我们越来越倾向于观察而非认同自身的动机。这并非是要刻意回避它们——否认并不能带来平静。而是通过退后一步，从动机的角度审视它们，从而放松对它们的执着。并非它们完全消失，而是我们置身事外，以旁观者的视角观察。如此一来，我们的动机似乎便失去了其阴暗存在时那种难以捉摸、难以预测的力量。从这个角度出发，我们更容易察觉到某些需求或期望试图将某种情境转化为满足自身欲望的途径，而这往往会给我们带来潜在的挫败感。我们可以简单地觉察到它们，而不被其所困扰，从而更加自由地继续我们的工作。

By simply witnessing the character and conflict of our reasons for helping out, then, we are making room for an essential change of perspective. Our actions are less hostage to our needs. We can call upon a deeper, more universal source of action, one that is steady, reliable, less likely to burn out. “We love each other. That’s enough.”

因此，仅仅通过觉察我们助人行为背后的动机及其冲突，我们就为一种至关重要的视角转变腾出了空间。我们的行动不再受制于自身需求。我们可以呼唤一种更深层次、更普世的行动源泉，一种稳定可靠、不易耗尽的动力。“我们彼此相爱。这就足够了。”

~

Meanwhile, the work of the Witness continues. Looking further into what we bring to the helping act, we come upon perhaps an even more fundamental cause of burnout: the feeling of personal responsibility; the sense that we are the authors of our actions; our identification of ourselves as the final source of the service . We are the “doer” and we have to keep “doing” or nothing will get “done.”

与此同时，见证者的工作仍在继续。进一步探究我们在助人行为中所投入的，我们或许会发现倦怠的一个更为根本的原因：个人责任感；觉得自己是自身行为的始作俑者；将自己视为服务的最终来源。我们是“行动者”，我们必须不断“行动”，否则一切都将“停滞不前”。

We identify ourselves as the doer in any number of ways. We may take difficulties or failures personally: “Oh God, these kids aren’t learning to read at all. They’ll never make it in society; I’m just not getting through.” Or we may take credit for the accomplishments we seem to have been a part of: “Frankly, I just have to say it was a skillful diagnosis. You can trust these cases to me from now on.” Or we may feel as if we’ve got to set people straight, we’ve got to get them to see: “My wife is so depressed. I really have to take her aside after the kids are asleep and show her what she’s doing to herself.”

我们常常以各种方式将自己定义为行动者。我们可能会把困难或失败归咎于自己：“天哪，这些孩子根本学不会阅读。他们永远也无法融入社会；我就是做不到。”或者，我们可能会把看似自己参与的成就归功于自己：“坦白说，我必须承认，我的诊断非常精准。以后这些病例都可以放心交给我了。”又或者，我们可能觉得必须纠正别人的错误，必须让他们明白：“我妻子非常抑郁。孩子们睡着后，我必须把她拉到一边，让她看看她正在做什么。”

We can see how often we define ourselves as “helpers,” even to the point of buying into an illusion of indispensability. We become so invested in our work that we actually begin to equate who we are with what we do. It becomes a social mannerism, a way we introduce ourselves to one another. “Hello. What do you do?”

我们常常会把自己定义为“助人者”，甚至到了相信自己不可或缺的地步。我们如此投入工作，以至于开始将自我价值与工作内容划上等号。这变成了一种社交习惯，一种自我介绍的方式。“你好，你是做什么的？”

As we watch ourselves going off to work, then, it becomes a little like reading The Little Engine That Could . Up the mountain: “I think I can, I think I can, I think I can.” Coming down: “I thought I could, I thought I could, I thought I could.” Model train, maybe … but always climbing mountains … likely to run down sooner or later.

当我们看着自己出发去上班时，感觉就像在读《小火车头的故事》。上山时：“我想我可以，我想我可以，我想我可以。”下山时：“我以为我可以，我以为我可以，我以为我可以。”也许是模型火车……但总是在爬山……迟早都会掉下来。

But all this can be witnessed. The same observation that made it possible for us to note our reasons for acting can catch us in the process of identifying ourselves as the actor. We recognize how we’re “taking things personally.” We see how our self-esteem is riding on a particular job. It’s clear how invested we are in a project, how each detail must bear our stamp, how we need to check and confirm every step, as if our very sense of identity were at stake. Of course, it can be.

但这一切都是可以观察的。正是这种观察力，让我们能够注意到自己行动的理由，也能在我们认同自己作为演员的过程中捕捉到这一点。我们会意识到自己是如何“把事情看得太重”。我们会发现，我们的自尊心与某个特定的工作息息相关。我们清楚地看到自己对一个项目投入了多少心血，每个细节都必须带有我们的印记，每一步都需要检查和确认，仿佛我们的自我认同感都岌岌可危。当然，这的确可能关乎我们的自我认同感。

But it needn’t be. We’ve performed tasks in other ways than this before. We experience freedom from being the doer in those moments in which we are so at one with our activity (now with this child in the classroom, now with another; now at the bedside of one patient telling jokes, now in the next room hearing someone’s grief) that it simply doesn’t occur to us that we’re “doing” at all. Everything’s just happening. We’re all action.

但其实不必如此。我们以前也用过其他方式完成任务。当我们完全沉浸于自己的活动之中（比如现在在教室里和这个孩子在一起，现在又和另一个孩子在一起；现在在病床边给病人讲笑话，现在又在隔壁房间倾听别人的悲伤）时，我们便体验到了“做事者”的自由，以至于我们根本不会意识到自己是在“做事”。一切都在自然发生。我们本身就是行动。

It’s not always our efforts that burn us out; it’s where the mind is standing in relation to them . The problem is not the work itself but the degree of our identification with it. It’s doers who burn out. But we needn’t always be doers. For as the process of witnessing becomes stronger—as we stay with it despite our reactions to what is being revealed—a subtle shift begins to take place in the direction of perspective and freedom.

并非总是我们的努力让我们精疲力竭，而是我们的心态与努力之间的关系。问题不在于工作本身，而在于我们对工作的认同程度。真正精疲力竭的是那些埋头苦干的人。但我们不必总是埋头苦干。因为随着见证过程的深入——当我们能够超越对所揭示之物的固有反应，坚持见证——一种微妙的转变便会开始发生，朝着更广阔的视角和更自由的方向发展。

If we persevere, our identification with the Witness grows while our attachment to being the doer seems to fall away. Quite remarkably, moreover, we also notice that while our identification as the doer is falling away, much is still being accomplished . We’re still setting about our work, perhaps even more productively. It’s just that we’re not so personally identified with it any more. We see that in this state we’re less likely to be frustrated, to feel rejected, to doubt ourselves, to burn out.

如果我们坚持下去，我们与见证者的认同感会增强，而我们作为行动者的执着似乎会逐渐消退。更令人惊奇的是，我们还会注意到，尽管我们作为行动者的认同感在减弱，但我们仍然取得了许多成就。我们仍在着手工作，甚至可能效率更高。只是我们不再像以前那样与工作本身紧密相连。我们发现，在这种状态下，我们更不容易感到沮丧、被拒绝、自我怀疑或精疲力竭。

~

The sage does nothing, but nothing is left undone .

圣人什么也不做，但却事无巨细，面面俱到。

L AO T SU

老苏

~

As our perspective shifts we see, for example, a certain kind of lawfulness about our work. We see that needs reach for satisfaction, expectations seek confirmation, motives are just asking for it. Taking our initiatives personally means taking their consequences personally too. All these conditions seem inevitably to lead to frustration, fatigue, and burnout. That’s simply how it all works.

随着视角转变，我们发现工作中存在某种规律性。例如，需求渴望得到满足，期望寻求确认，动机本身就是一种必然。将主动行为视为己任，也意味着要承担相应的后果。所有这些似乎都不可避免地导致沮丧、疲惫和职业倦怠。事情就是这样运作的。

In this recognition lies freedom. However much we remain conscious of this process, we’re still in a state of awareness to catch causes of burnout as they seek to take hold. We can note them, and then let go. The process, moreover, is intriguing as well as effective. We can enjoy the Witness’s revelations about the law and order of action even as we participate in the acting. It is as if we are functioning happily on two planes of consciousness at once. As a result, there can be peace where there was once agitation, confidence where there was doubt, trust where there was defensiveness and guilt, and abundant energy where there was burnout.

这种觉察之中蕴藏着自由。无论我们对这个过程保持多么清醒的意识，我们始终处于一种觉察的状态，能够捕捉到倦怠的根源，防止它们悄然滋生。我们可以觉察到它们，然后放下它们。此外，这个过程既引人入胜又卓有成效。即使我们身处行动之中，也能享受到见证者对行动法则和秩序的启示。这仿佛让我们同时在两个意识层面上和谐运作。结果，曾经的躁动可以转化为平静，曾经的怀疑可以转化为自信，曾经的防御和内疚可以转化为信任，曾经的倦怠可以转化为充沛的精力。

Freedom from attachment to our motives and from identification with the doer may seem high goals. Yet simply by holding them in consciousness, and being compassionate with ourselves in the process , we can turn burdensome situations into opportunities for growth.

摆脱对自身动机的执着，以及不认同于行动者本身，看似遥不可及。然而，只要我们觉察到这些动机，并在过程中善待自己，就能将沉重的负担转化为成长的契机。

While it is clear that what we bring into a helping situation may lead to burnout, we ought not underestimate the external pressures. How often we find ourselves in environments or organizations that actually seem to make it harder to help others. What’s natural and spontaneous has now been rigidified by bureaucracy, rules, or standards of accountability. All of this can be incredibly frustrating, because it seems to constrict or thwart the very openness and sense of possibility that those who are suffering most yearn for—and those who wish to help out as well.

虽然我们带入助人情境中的某些因素显然可能导致倦怠，但我们也不应低估外部压力。我们常常发现自己身处的环境或组织中，反而让帮助他人变得更加困难。原本自然而然、自发的举动，如今却被官僚主义、规章制度或问责标准所束缚。所有这些都令人无比沮丧，因为它似乎限制或阻碍了那些最需要帮助的人——以及那些同样渴望伸出援手的人——所渴望的开放心态和无限可能。

~

Here I am in this room with this woman who I know from when we painted the walls together and made beds and worked in the kitchen, where she showed me a thing or two. And I know that those have been the moments when things have passed between us that are really good, really helpful, to both of us .

我此刻就和这位女士待在这个房间里，我们以前一起粉刷墙壁、铺床、在厨房干活，她教了我不少东西。我知道，那些时刻是我们之间交流学习的契机，那些交流对我们彼此都很有益。

But right now, because I’m administering this house for the homeless, suddenly she’s a “deinstitutionalized mental patient,” and I’m having to determine how she’s doing and whether she stays .

但现在，因为我管理着这所收容无家可归者的房子，她突然就成了“非机构化精神病患者”，我不得不决定她的情况如何，以及她是否应该留下来。

And it’s like we’re not alone in the room anymore. I t’s like there are these various ghosts around. There’s the chairman of the advisory board in that corner … the woman from the state agency in that chair … the disgruntled folks on the floor are my volunteers … the fly on the wall is a local reporter … and this nice guy whispering in my ear is the minister of the local church, who’s given us the space. And they’re all talking at once. About this woman. “She’s a potential success story.” “Keep her here until we can document it.” “By any of the regulations she should have been out weeks ago.” “She’s setting a good example for new people.” “She acts like she’s a member of the staff.”

感觉房间里不再只有我们两个人了。好像周围有各种各样的幽灵。角落里坐着顾问委员会主席……椅子上坐着州政府机构的那位女士……地上那些不满的人是我的志愿者……墙上的苍蝇是一位当地记者……还有一位和蔼的男士在我耳边低语，他是当地教堂的牧师，是他给我们提供了场地。他们都在同时议论纷纷，谈论着这位女士。“她很有潜力。”“让她留在这里，直到我们能记录下她的经历。”“按任何规定，她几周前就该离开了。”“她给新来的人树立了好榜样。”“她表现得就像是工作人员一样。”

Now I know from experience that this environment can be mental chaos, probably crazier than the woman herself. That’s pretty terrible, given its power over her life. When you’re stuck in that, forget it. You’re “institutionalized” yourself .

现在我从经验中得知，这种环境会让人精神崩溃，可能比那个女人本身还要疯狂。考虑到它对她生活的影响，这真是太可怕了。一旦身陷其中，就别想了。你也就“被体制化”了。

~

At the very least it makes sense to call upon the Witness to “see how it all is”—to stop judging and reacting and simply take in the total picture. So we see how the administrators have to play it … or the volunteer’s predicament … or the member of the board’s game. As we observe these roles, we’re able to get a sense of what it might be like to have to play any one of them. We appreciate how it all may have evolved, and the delusions that led to it, and the confusions that perpetuate it, and the accommodations that just plain had to be made. We see why it is the way it is, and at as many levels as possible—including the level at which it’s utterly ridiculous and hopeless and how-is-everyone-even-going-to-keep-it-all-marginally-together-let-alone-help-or-be-helped. We’re living in the land of Catch-22 .

至少，呼吁“见证者”去“看清一切”是明智之举——停止评判和反应，而是全然地把握全局。这样，我们就能明白管理者是如何应对的……志愿者的困境……或是董事会成员的博弈。当我们观察这些角色时，就能体会到扮演其中任何一个角色会是怎样的感受。我们能理解这一切是如何演变的，以及导致这一切的种种错觉、持续存在的混乱，以及不得不做出的妥协。我们能明白事情为何如此，并且尽可能地从各个层面去理解——包括那些荒谬至极、令人绝望的层面，以及所有人如何才能勉强维持现状，更遑论互相帮助或互助的困境。我们正生活在《第二十二条军规》的困境之中。

The challenge is to turn it into M*A*S*H . Here we are in the service, with a crazy war going on all around, no idea when it will end, stuck every day with the same fellow idiots. Still we have to find some way to stay conscious. We’d better: Wounded people are coming in from out of the sky and they’re screaming. So what do we do, Hawkeye? Just what a hawkeye is intended to do: hover above and survey the landscape. And then, as so many of us saw, episode after episode, when we’re hard on the job, it’s the one-pointed concentration of the surgeon … and the rest of the time we throw a party. We take in every absurd, contradictory, counterproductive aspect of the war zone and transform it into grist for irony, humor, irreverence, and creative mischief. That’s how we stay nimble inside it. That’s how we keep it from burning us out. Ultimately, that’s how we turn it around.

挑战在于如何把它变成《陆军野战医院》（M*A*S*H）。我们身处战场，周围战火纷飞，不知何时才能结束，每天都和同一群傻瓜战友待在一起。即便如此，我们还是得想办法保持清醒。最好如此：伤员从天而降，发出阵阵惨叫。那么，我们该怎么办，鹰眼？就做鹰眼该做的事：盘旋在空中，观察局势。然后，正如我们许多人在剧中一集又一集看到的那样，当我们全力以赴时，就像外科医生一样全神贯注……而其余时间，我们就开派对。我们把战区里所有荒谬、矛盾、适得其反的方面都吸收进去，并将它们转化为讽刺、幽默、不敬和创造性恶作剧的素材。这就是我们保持敏捷的方式。这就是我们不被它榨干的方式。最终，这就是我们扭转乾坤的方式。

Institutions are formalized mind-sets. These too can be witnessed. To become aware of those sets but see right through them from outside is the most reliable way not to get stuck or burned out by them. We master the rules, but we don’t let them ultimately define us or narrow our field of perception. We encompass the craziness of the situation, so we can be skillful within it or playful when there’s nothing to do but ride through the contradictions. Then we share a sense of the absurd with whoever else is inclined to see it that way. Whoever feels a little lost can find relief in our presence, in our tent, around our desk.

制度是形式化的思维模式。这些模式也是可以观察到的。意识到这些模式的存在，并从外部看穿它们，是避免被它们束缚或精疲力竭的最可靠方法。我们掌握规则，但不会让规则最终定义我们，也不会让规则限制我们的感知范围。我们包容情境中的种种荒谬，因此我们既能巧妙地应对，也能在无计可施时保持轻松愉悦。然后，我们与那些同样倾向于这种视角的人分享这种荒诞感。任何感到迷茫的人都可以在我们的陪伴下，在我们的帐篷里，在我们的办公桌旁找到慰藉。

None of this means that we just suspend judgment forever. We observe … but there is action to be taken too. If we are serious in our criticisms of the practices and habits of helping organizations, however, we’ve got to be light, free, and sufficiently above it all to see where we can untangle the knots and bring about change. Everything is always changing anyway. With the perspective of the Witness, we can see just which pressures, applied with the precision of a judo chop, can move the mass.

这并不意味着我们要永远放弃评判。我们观察……但行动也必不可少。如果我们认真地批评助人机构的实践和习惯，我们就必须保持轻松、自由的心态，并且超脱于一切之外，才能看清问题的症结所在，从而带来改变。反正一切都在不断变化。以见证者的视角，我们就能看清，哪些压力，如同柔道劈砍般精准地施加，才能真正撼动大众。

As frustrating and wearing as these situations can be, part of our service may entail taking some responsibility for them. The institutions we work in are going to reflect the sum total of consciousness invested in them at every moment. So it’s “Our” problem. If it’s “Us” who created it, it’s probably going to have to be “Us” who’ll shake it free.

尽管这些情况令人沮丧和疲惫，但我们服务的一部分可能就包含承担部分责任。我们工作的机构，每时每刻都会反映出投入其中的全部意识。所以，这是“我们”的问题。如果是“我们”造成的，那么很可能也得由“我们”来摆脱它。

Or maybe not. We can never be sure. We’ll watch. Maybe it’s not the right place to be putting our energies now. Maybe the inertia of the system is too great, its effect too strangling. Maybe we just need a break, some breathing space, a walk in the woods for some renewed inspiration. Maybe we’re just tired. It’s always right to be watching for that, always right to care for ourselves when we’re seeking to care for others.

或许并非如此。我们永远无法确定。我们会继续观察。也许现在把精力投入到这里并不合适。也许系统的惯性太大，它的影响太过令人窒息。也许我们只是需要休息一下，喘口气，去树林里散散步，重新找回一些灵感。也许我们只是累了。时刻留意这一点总是没错的，当我们想要照顾他人时，照顾好自己也总是没错的。

So perhaps we quit, not knowing where to go next, but trusting that the right vehicle to express our desire to serve will appear elsewhere, later. Are we going to place limits of circumstance on the expression of compassion?

所以，或许我们会选择放弃，不知何去何从，但我们相信，将来会在别处找到合适的途径来表达我们服务的愿望。难道我们要让环境限制我们表达同情心吗？

Or perhaps we stay. If we do, we try to make sure that we’re as conscious of everyone’s situation as possible, and as alert to how the ground is moving from moment to moment, now obstructing this possibility, now revealing another one.

或许我们会留下。如果留下，我们会尽量确保自己对每个人的处境都了如指掌，并且时刻警惕局势的变化，因为这种变化可能阻碍了我们，也可能带来了另一种可能性。

There may be no single remedy for the frustration and burnout that arise simply from the constricting situations in which we are often required to care for others. What serves us best is the expanded perspective that witnessing makes possible … and what it reveals from moment to moment. You do what you do when you can. And when there’s nothing to do, and burnout tries to rear its ugly head … you M*A*S*H it.

面对因照顾他人而产生的挫败感和倦怠，或许没有单一的灵丹妙药。真正对我们有益的是见证所带来的更广阔的视角……以及它在每个瞬间所揭示的一切。你能做什么就做什么。而当无事可做，倦怠感试图抬头时……那就全力以赴，克服它。

Burnout can arise, as we’ve seen, in what we bring with us into the helping act or what we encounter in the environment in which it’s often conducted. Obviously, frustration and doubt occur too in the course of our work itself, particularly when we try to measure how it’s all going.

正如我们所见，倦怠可能源于我们自身在助人行为中携带的负面情绪，也可能源于我们助人行为所处的环境。当然，在工作过程中，尤其是在我们试图衡量工作进展时，也会出现挫败感和怀疑情绪。

Often, of course, assessment is called for. Sometimes the answer is clear: the wound is healing, the reading skills improving. Or we may want to look beneath these immediate consequences to deeper effects. You’ve established a development program in a small third-world village, but is it leading to self-sufficiency? You’ve comforted a friend, but did you reinforce his self-pity? You’ve exposed neglect in nursing homes, but did you do so in a way which will encourage them to reconsider how they think about society’s elders? All this is a kind of appropriate continuing inquiry into practice, a sharpening of skillful means.

当然，很多时候都需要进行评估。有时答案显而易见：伤口正在愈合，阅读能力正在提高。或者，我们可能需要探究这些直接结果背后的深层影响。你在一个发展中国家的小村庄建立了一个发展项目，但它是否最终实现了自给自足？你安慰了一位朋友，但你是否反而加深了他的自怜？你揭露了养老院的疏忽问题，但你的做法是否能促使他们重新思考对待老年人的方式？所有这些都是对实践的一种恰当的持续探究，是对技巧的精进。

On the other hand, if our habits of self-observation are keen, if the Witness is active, we may note that our efforts to measure our work and ourselves are frequently patterns of insecurity.

另一方面，如果我们有敏锐的自我观察习惯，如果见证者积极参与，我们可能会注意到，我们衡量自己的工作和自身的努力常常是不安全感的体现。

“Did I help?” “Did it work?” “What did he feel?” “Why did she say that?” “What was really going on this morning?” “What if?… what if …?” “Try this … no, try that.” “If only … if only …” And, probably heaviest of all: “Was it really for the best? How do I know? How can I be sure? God, it’s somebody’s life!”

“我帮上忙了吗？”“有用吗？”“他感觉如何？”“她为什么那样说？”“今天早上到底发生了什么？”“如果……如果……？”“试试这个……不，试试那个。”“要是……要是……”或许最沉重的问题是：“这真的是最好的吗？我怎么知道？我怎么才能确定？天哪，这可是人命啊！”

All this is understandable. When suffering is at stake and we’ve offered ourselves to its relief, we naturally have an interest in how situations evolve. But sometimes this compulsive need to know leads us to doubt because we have a hard time coming to terms with the essential ambiguity of helping.

这一切都可以理解。当苦难迫在眉睫，而我们又主动伸出援手时，自然会关心事态的发展。但有时，这种强烈的求知欲反而会让我们产生怀疑，因为我们难以接受助人行为本身固有的模糊性。

Paradoxical and elusive, service is ultimately a journey into the unknown. Did we really help? Help at what level? We often can’t find answers. And we don’t know what to do with that. So we wonder, worry, turn off, give up … or just struggle bravely on, puzzled and burdened, wearing down. See the helper?… He’s the hard-working one over there … the one with the constant frown.

服务既矛盾又难以捉摸，最终是一场未知的旅程。我们真的帮到了别人吗？帮到了什么程度？我们常常找不到答案，也不知道该如何面对。于是，我们开始疑惑、担忧、放弃、麻木……或者只是勇敢地挣扎着，带着困惑和重负，日渐疲惫。看到那位乐于助人的人了吗？……他就是那边那位勤劳的人……那位总是皱着眉头的人。

At some level this challenge is very plain. We can either be frustrated and worn out by uncertainty and doubt or try to find a way to open to the ambiguity, embrace it, work with it, be moved and inspired by it … and thereby come closer to the very heart of service where true freedom is found.

从某种程度上来说，这个挑战非常明确。我们可以选择因不确定性和怀疑而感到沮丧和疲惫，也可以尝试找到一种方法来敞开心扉接受这种模糊性，拥抱它，与它共事，从中汲取灵感和启发……从而更接近服务的真谛，在那里，真正的自由得以体现。

~

The hospital called our hot line service one day, and I was introduced to this man who seemed to be living outside of time, and we went through an experience which I still ponder .

有一天，医院打电话给我们的热线服务，我认识了一位仿佛生活在时间之外的人，我们经历了一段我至今仍在思考的事情。

A woman in her late eighties had just died. Her husband, who was reported to be a hundred and one, was stuck at home and was unable to bury her. So a few of us picked him up in a rented gypsy cab. He came downstairs very slowly, in a long black coat, a snappy hat, a cane, and gold teeth when he smiled—very mysterious looking. Antonio Lopez-Orlano. Quite a gentleman .

一位八十多岁的老妇人刚刚去世。据说她一百零一岁的丈夫被困在家中，无法安葬她。于是我们几个租了一辆黑马车去接他。他缓缓走下楼，身穿黑色长外套，头戴时髦的帽子，拄着拐杖，微笑时露出金牙——显得十分神秘。他叫安东尼奥·洛佩兹-奥拉诺，真是个绅士。

On the way to the funeral he told about Jacquelina. They’d met at a dance, lived together to help out during the Depression, fell in love later. How beautiful she was with her long black hair! When she died, she’d been in the hospital two months. She ran away to see him, but an ambulance caught up with her. They never said good-bye. When we got to the cemetery, he said, “I can ’t look. Open the casket, Raphael—take this photograph, tell me that it’s her.” It was .

在去葬礼的路上，他讲起了杰奎琳娜。他们在一次舞会上相识，为了在大萧条时期互相扶持而住在一起，后来坠入爱河。她长着一头乌黑的长发，多么美丽！她去世时，已经在医院住了两个月。她跑去看他，但救护车追上了她。他们没能好好道别。到了墓地，他说：“我不敢看。拉斐尔，打开棺材——拍张照片，告诉我那是她。” 没错，就是她。

When I took him home, I couldn’t believe my eyes. He was living in an abandoned six-floor building, cold, dirty, garbage, smell of urine. “You live here?” “I do.” “How many others?” “Just one; everyone left.” “How long like this?” “Three years.” I couldn’t believe it. This man, around a century old, living in a freezing, abandoned building, during the coldest winters. I said, “Look, Antonio, I’d like to be your friend, come visit, see if I can help.” He said, “Okay. If you’d like.”

我把他带回家时，简直不敢相信自己的眼睛。他住在一栋废弃的六层楼房里，又冷又脏，到处都是垃圾，还弥漫着尿骚味。“你住这儿？”“是的。”“还有多少人？”“就一个，大家都走了。”“这样多久了？”“三年了。”我简直不敢相信。这位年近百岁的老人，竟然在寒冬腊月里，住在这样一栋冰冷的废弃楼房里。我说：“安东尼奥，我想和你做朋友，你来看看我，看看我能不能帮上什么忙。”他说：“好的，如果你愿意的话。”

Four times a week for over a year I went, sometimes with my twelve-year-old daughter, Monica. And I’ll tell you, it was so confusing, so many mixed signals. I wasn’t sure whether I was coming or going, and to this day I wonder at how complex it was. What did it mean?

一年多以来，我每周去四次，有时会带上我十二岁的女儿莫妮卡。我跟你说，那真是太让人困惑了，各种信号乱七八糟。我甚至都搞不清楚自己是该去还是该走，直到今天，我仍然不明白它到底有多复杂。它到底意味着什么？

I worked to get him social security, food stamps, hot meals, and so on. He accepted them. And then he’d say, sometimes angry, sometimes just a little twinkle, “Stop meddling in my life.” I’d bring people by to verify his eligibility for assistance. “They have to know who you are to help you,” I told him. He hated that. “Who am I then? I know who I am.” Then, when they’d come, he’d be so charming and witty, he had such finesse, and they’d leave amazed and in love with the hundred-and-one-year-old man who was living in this abandoned, freezing building. After they left, he’d look at me. “Before I met you I never had all these problems.” He had me spinning. But I loved him. I truly loved him. He was a beautiful man .

我努力帮他申请社会保障金、食品券、热餐等等。他都接受了。然后他会说，有时生气，有时带着一丝狡黠的笑意：“别管我的生活。” 我会带人来核实他是否符合领取救济的资格。“他们得知道你是谁才能帮你，”我告诉他。他讨厌这样。“那我是谁？我知道我是谁。” 然后，当那些人来的时候，他会变得那么迷人、那么风趣，那么有风度，他们离开时都会惊叹不已，爱上这位住在废弃的、冰冷建筑里的101岁老人。他们走后，他会看着我说：“遇见你之前，我从来没有这些问题。” 他的话让我心神荡漾。但我爱他。我真的爱他。他是一个美好的人。

He had this funny ritual if he thought I was coming on too strong. He’d tighten up his whole body and start heaving these heavy, gasping breaths, like he was being choked or having a fit. It was a great act. Monica and I took to doing it to each other at home. So I’d smile. And he’d say, “You’re not taking me seriously.” And I’d say, “I just can’t figure you out.” And he’d say, “I tell you, Raphael, you’ll be the death of me yet.” Maybe with a twinkle .

如果他觉得我太热情，他就会有个滑稽的习惯。他会绷紧全身，开始剧烈地喘息，就像被人掐住脖子或者癫痫发作一样。这招真绝了。我和莫妮卡在家也经常这么做。所以我会笑着回应。他会说：“你没把我当回事。” 我会说：“我就是搞不懂你。” 他会说：“我跟你说，拉斐尔，你迟早会要了我的命。” 说着，他可能还会眨眨眼。

There were times when I wasn’t sure whether to continue. How can you be sure if you’re really helping someone or if you’re meddling? I’d ask other people—social workers, friends. Who knew? I didn’t. I don’t think he really did. So I would ask for patience, great patience. “Lord, you sure are putting me through some incredible changes. I’m sure there’s a reason behind all this, but I can’t see it.”

有时我甚至不知道该不该继续下去。你怎么能确定自己是在帮助别人，还是在多管闲事呢？我会问其他人——社工、朋友。谁知道呢？我不知道。我想他也不知道。所以我祈求耐心，极大的耐心。“主啊，你让我经历了这么多难以置信的变故。我相信这一切背后一定有原因，但我却看不清。”

It became clear he’d have to move, and I found him a good place. But the day we moved was so painful. He was so angry, leaving his home. I felt so shitty. I arranged the furniture the same way, but it wasn’t the same. Later, we had to give him a bath, which he agreed to but couldn’t do alone. This was a very deep thing, to bathe him. We had to change the water five times. He felt humiliated, ashamed. I thought it was like a new beginning .

很明显他必须搬家，我帮他找到了一处不错的住处。但搬家那天真是太痛苦了。他离开家时非常生气。我感觉糟透了。我把家具摆放得和以前一样，但感觉完全不一样了。后来，我们得给他洗澡，他同意了，但他自己做不了。给他洗澡对他来说意义非凡。我们换了五次水。他感到羞辱和难堪。我觉得这就像是一个新的开始。

Then we noticed his toes, frostbitten terribly, three of them black. It scared him. “We have to go to the hospital, Tonio.” Monica persuaded him. So the first night in his new home he was being set up to go to the hospital. He glared at me. “See.”

然后我们注意到他的脚趾，冻伤得很厉害，其中三个都发黑了。他吓坏了。“我们得去医院，托尼奥。”莫妮卡劝他。于是，在他新家的第一个晚上，我们就安排他去医院。他怒视着我。“瞧。”

They couldn’t believe him there either. But they agreed to let him be treated at home and wait to see about amputation. Several weeks went by, and he started to complain of terrible stomach pains. He had to go back and be admitted. “Ralph, it probably wouldn’t have happened if you hadn’t moved me.” Who knew?

他们当时也不相信他的话。但他们同意让他回家治疗，看看是否需要截肢。几个星期过去了，他开始抱怨剧烈的胃痛。他不得不回去住院。“拉尔夫，要不是你把我转院，这一切可能都不会发生。”谁知道呢？

They said he had advanced cancer. He went down and down. One night they called. “We think you should come.” Monica and I went to him. I read to him from the Bible. Monica oiled his body. I said, “Antonio, you know we love you.” He nodded, and then wanted to sleep. We left, and later he died .

他们说他得了晚期癌症。他的病情每况愈下。一天晚上，他们打电话来说：“我们觉得你应该过来看看。”我和莫妮卡去了他那里。我给他读圣经。莫妮卡给他涂抹了油。我说：“安东尼奥，你知道我们爱你。”他点了点头，然后就想睡觉了。我们离开了，后来他就去世了。

We prepared a funeral, a very nice affair. Many people who had come to love this man attended. There I was at a burial again. I arranged it so that he was buried on top of Jacquelina. Then Monica and I went home .

我们筹办了葬礼，办得非常体面。许多爱戴他的人都来参加了。我又一次参加了葬礼。我安排他葬在杰奎琳娜的墓碑上。之后，我和莫妮卡回家了。

What did it end up meaning? How much did I help, how much did I interfere? I don’t know. How can you know what is the right true story of one man’s time on earth? It’s all a lesson. I did what seemed right in my heart. I tried to be patient. I loved this man .

这一切最终意味着什么？我帮了他多少忙，又干涉了他多少？我不知道。你怎么能知道一个人在世间的真实故事是什么呢？一切都是教训。我做了我内心认为正确的事。我努力保持耐心。我爱这个人。

Whatever else happened—the disruption of his life, the people and the programs, the new apartment, the bath, the hospital, my helping, his dying—I see it a little like that act of his: huffing and puffing and gasping, but playing. We met, who knows why, and we all did the best we could. Add it up, it was wonderful, just wonderful. It still touches me. It’s still alive for me, still going on .

无论后来发生了什么——他生活的变故、那些人和事、新公寓、洗澡、住院、我的帮助、他的离世——我都觉得这一切有点像他当时的举动：气喘吁吁，却依然在玩耍。我们相遇，不知为何，我们都尽了全力。总而言之，那段时光很美好，真的非常美好。它至今仍让我感动。它对我来说依然鲜活，仍在继续。

~

How unfamiliar the ground can be. How elusive the reasons that bring us together, at one moment strangers, at the next partners in the most intimate moments of life, following the impulses of the heart through unexpected turns toward unforeseeable ends. But where does it end? We meet, we help and are helped, then we go our separate ways. The helping act ripples out in time and space and beyond. How to follow its course and all its tributaries? How to measure it as it constantly moves? Who’s to say where it stops … and is one thing … long enough to be named?

这片土地多么陌生。是什么让我们走到一起？前一刻还是陌生人，下一刻就成了生命中最亲密时刻的伴侣，我们顺从内心的冲动，经历意想不到的转折，走向不可预见的终点。但这一切何时才能结束？我们相遇，我们帮助他人，也被他人帮助，然后我们各自离去。助人的行为在时间和空间中不断扩散。如何追踪它的轨迹和所有支流？如何衡量它不断流动的轨迹？谁又能说清它何时停止……而一件事……是否足够长久，可以被命名？

In helping others, we’ll always find ambiguity and paradox. Sometimes these can just rip us apart and lead to self-doubt and self-consciousness, which if allowed to take hold will inevitably burn us out. How else might we deal with this need to know? Perhaps, once more, by remembering that the process of witnessing is focused essentially on what is , not what might be or could be. The Witness does not reach, grasp, or desire. Because it is an instrument of observation, not of need, it merely attends to things.

在帮助他人的过程中，我们总会遇到模棱两可和自相矛盾之处。有时，这些会让我们备受煎熬，导致自我怀疑和自我意识过强，如果任其滋生，最终必将耗尽我们的精力。那么，我们该如何应对这种求知欲呢？或许，我们可以再次记住，见证的过程本质上关注的是“存在”，而非“可能存在”或“或许存在”。见证者不去追求、不去掌控、也不去渴望。因为它是一种观察的工具，而非需求的工具，所以它只是关注事物本身。

When we apply this to moments when our need to know is being frustrated, we experience yet another liberating change of perspective. We begin to allow, and embrace, the full beauty of the helping act because of , not in spite of, its ambiguity and paradox. Its mystery now only testifies to its ability to find its way into places we might never have imagined, to heal in ways we might not have intended.

当我们把这种理念运用到求知欲受挫的时刻，我们会体验到另一种令人解脱的视角转变。我们开始允许并拥抱助人行为的全部美好，正是因为而非尽管它充满暧昧和悖论。它的神秘性如今反而证明了它能够抵达我们可能从未想象过的地方，以我们意想不到的方式带来疗愈。

In those moments when we are not at all sure what our actions have really amounted to, we can simply allow ourselves to be touched by what we have seen. So moving and poignant, the ways of compassion: an old man’s dying body oiled by a young girl he’d only come to know in the last of his hundred and one years. Or perhaps there is no specific outcome to point to at all, only the feeling of having participated in something profound and wonderful. It does not lend itself to words or concepts, yet we know that it has happened. In mystery, we experience revelation.

当我们完全不确定自己的行为究竟产生了什么影响时，我们可以简单地让自己被所见所闻所触动。慈悲之道如此动人，如此深刻：一位老人在弥留之际，由一位他仅在百岁高龄才结识的年轻女孩为他涂抹油膏。或许根本没有具体的结局可言，只有参与了一件意义深远、无比美好的事情的感受。它无法用语言或概念来描述，但我们知道它确实发生过。在神秘之中，我们体验到启示。

With the perspective born of the Witness, then, we’re able to hear when it’s time to let things go and be what they are, as they recede beyond the horizon of our understanding.

因此，凭借见证者的视角，我们能够听出何时应该放手，顺其自然，任由事物发展到我们理解的视野之外。

At this point the need to know begins to fall away—and not simply because we’ve given up or resigned ourselves to ignorance. Quite the contrary: we’ve come into a deeper wisdom, which knows its place and accepts Not Knowing.

此时，求知的欲望开始减弱——这并非因为我们放弃了求知或屈服于无知。恰恰相反：我们获得了一种更深层次的智慧，这种智慧懂得自身的定位，并接受“未知”。

Here, after all, is where so much helping takes place anyway—in the land of Not Knowing. We do our work. We look to see what’s happened, measuring it against past experience, the criteria of our training, the opinions of others, the still, small voice of intuition. We consult all these responsibly. Then we sit, and listen, and let it all fall into place. Sometimes it does, and sometimes it doesn’t. Sometimes we hear how it all is; very often we don’t. Don’t Know . As frequently as this occurs, as much time as we spend Not Knowing, we might as well make ourselves at home there. We’ll be that much less likely to burn ourselves out looking for what’s beyond us. At best we may find pathways into a clearer practice of service.

毕竟，许多助人之事，正是在未知的领域中发生的。我们开展工作，审视已发生之事，并将其与过往经验、训练标准、他人意见以及内心深处那微弱的直觉进行比对。我们负责任地参考所有这些因素。然后，我们静静地坐着，倾听，让一切水落石出。有时，一切水落石出；有时，却并非如此。有时，我们能听清真相；但更多时候，我们却一无所知。我们茫然无知。既然这种情况如此频繁，既然我们花费如此多的时间在“未知”之中，我们不妨就此安顿下来。这样，我们就更不容易因探寻自身之外的事物而精疲力竭。最好的结果是，我们或许能从中找到通往更清晰的服务实践之路。

For example, deep companionship, born of honesty, can often arise when we meet one another in Not Knowing. “What’s the matter?” “I don’t really know.” “Well, I don’t know either, but here I am.” What’s important, potentially even most healing, is that we’re being together in truth , the truth of our present uncertainty. That mutual acknowledgment, and the sense of unity that comes of it, may make possible discoveries we’d never dreamed of in our efforts to figure it all out or pretend we understand. Humility turns out to be the threshold of insight.

例如，当我们彼此都处于“未知”状态时，往往会产生一种源于坦诚的深厚友谊。“怎么了？”“我也不知道。”“嗯，我也不知道，但我在这里。”重要的是，或许也是最具疗愈作用的，我们正坦诚相待，坦诚面对我们当下的不确定性。这种相互的认可，以及由此产生的合一感，或许能让我们发现一些在试图弄明白一切或假装自己理解的过程中从未想过的事情。谦逊，原来是洞察的门槛。

If we can accept Not Knowing, we’ll be less likely to get caught in models or theories, or attached to seeing things work out the way we’d like. More trusting of experience itself, we’re more able to find new insights in new situations. The moments in which we come to the edge of the unfamiliar are less threatening. Our willingness to accept the unknown gives us courage. We can trip, fall, get lost … and still get up again and look around and start out once more. Confusion is now not an enemy; it’s part of our regained innocence.

如果我们能够接受未知，我们就更不容易被各种模型或理论所束缚，也不会执着于事情必须按照我们预想的方向发展。更加信任经验本身，我们就更能在新的情境中找到新的洞见。当我们走到未知的边缘时，恐惧感也会随之减轻。我们愿意接受未知，这赋予了我们勇气。我们可以跌倒、迷失……但依然可以重新站起来，环顾四周，再次出发。困惑不再是敌人，而是我们重获的纯真的一部分。

~

In the beginner’s mind, there are many possibilities. In the expert’s, there are few .

在初学者眼中，可能性很多；在专家眼中，可能性却很少。

SUZUKI ROSHI

铃木郎士

~

If we accept that the ends of our actions often prove unknowable, we’re also freer to be focused on the process of our work as it’s happening. We can be attentive to situations as they occur. What lies before us is it. Helping is right here. Not having to know so badly, not wandering off looking, we’re more able to be present, freer simply to be.

如果我们接受行动的最终结果往往无法预知，我们就能更自由地专注于工作的过程本身。我们可以留意正在发生的情况。眼前的一切就是答案。帮助就在当下。不必执着于探寻，不必四处游荡，我们就能更好地活在当下，更自由地存在。

We needn’t be troubled or worn down, then, by paradox and ambiguity. The mystery of helping can be our ally, our teacher, an environment for wonder and discovery. If we enter into it openly, our actions fall into perspective, a larger pattern we can trust. At rest in the Witness, meanwhile, we greet the outcome of our action with equanimity.

因此，我们不必为悖论和歧义而烦恼或疲惫。助人的奥秘可以成为我们的盟友、导师，一个充满惊奇和发现的环境。如果我们敞开心扉地进入其中，我们的行为便会得到更全面的视角，一个我们可以信赖的更大模式。与此同时，当我们安息于见证者之中时，便能以平静的心态迎接我们行为的结果。

~

A young woman in a small coastal village became pregnant. When questioned about the father, she didn’t want to admit it was a young fisherman. Instead, she pointed to the monastery on the hill and named as the child’s father a particular monk .

一个住在沿海小村庄的年轻女子怀孕了。当被问及孩子的父亲是谁时，她不愿承认是一位年轻的渔夫。相反，她指着山上的寺庙，说出了一位僧人的名字，说孩子的父亲是他。

After the birth, the villagers took the baby up to the monastery and beat on the gate. When the monk came to the door, they said, “This is your child. It is your duty to raise it.”

孩子出生后，村民们把婴儿抱到寺院，敲打寺门。僧人来到门口，他们说：“这是你的孩子，抚养他是你的责任。”

“Ah, so,” said the monk. Then he took the child in his arms and closed the gate .

“啊，原来如此，”僧人说道。然后他抱起孩子，关上了大门。

Nine years later, the same woman became ill and was approaching death. She did not wish to die with this lie on her conscience, so she admitted to the villagers that the young fisherman was the true father. Once again the villagers made their way up the mountain to the monastery and knocked on the gate. When the monk came to the gate, they said, “A great mistake has been made. You are not the father of that child. You need not raise the child any longer. It is our duty to raise it.”

九年后，那位妇人病重垂危。她不愿带着谎言死去，于是向村民们坦白，那个年轻的渔夫才是孩子的亲生父亲。村民们再次来到山上的寺院，敲响了大门。僧人来到门口，村民们说道：“我们犯了一个大错。你不是那个孩子的父亲。你不必再抚养他了，抚养他是我们的责任。”

“Ah, so,” said the monk … and gave back the child .

“啊，原来如此，”僧人说道……然后把孩子还给了别人。

~

Here is a final shift in perspective which can help release us from burnout. We do what we can. Yet we cannot really presume to know the final meaning of our actions. We cannot help but see them against a larger backdrop in which the ultimate significance of a single life may not be clear.

这里还有一种视角上的转变，可以帮助我们摆脱倦怠。我们尽力而为，但我们无法真正预知自己行为的最终意义。我们无法避免地要将它们置于更广阔的背景下看待，而在这个背景下，个体生命的最终意义或许并不清晰。

So, at some level, we care with all our heart … and then we finally let go. We give it all we have … and trust the rest to God, to Nature, to the Universe. We do everything we can to relieve someone’s suffering—our dearest’s, our beloved’s, anyone’s—but we are willing to surrender attachment to how we want things to be, attachment even to the relief of their suffering. Our heart may break … and then we surrender that too.

所以，在某种程度上，我们全心全意地付出……然后最终放手。我们倾尽所有……并将剩余的托付给上帝、自然和宇宙。我们竭尽所能去减轻他人的痛苦——我们最亲近的人、我们挚爱的人，任何人的痛苦——但我们愿意放下对事物发展方向的执着，甚至放下对他们痛苦减轻的执着。我们的心或许会破碎……然后，我们也放下这份伤痛。

This is the final act of service: to acknowledge and honor the integrity of another being as they, like us, pass through the beauty and the pain of a human birth. Its immediate meaning may surpass our understanding. But we are willing to keep the faith—which St. Paul describes as “the evidence of things unseen.” Ultimately, all is well.

这是奉献的最终体现：承认并尊重另一个生命的完整，因为他们和我们一样，经历着人类诞生的美好与痛苦。它的直接意义或许超越了我们的理解。但我们愿意坚守这份信念——圣保罗称之为“未见之事的确据”。最终，一切都会好起来。

We play our part … and act … and burn out … and are helped or help ourselves to stand up again. As we struggle against the challenges and frustrations inherent in service, we will find good counsel, many methods, and much support. The particular approach we have shared is just one, to be called upon, as appropriate, in conjunction with others that ring true to particular needs.

我们尽己所能……积极行动……然后精疲力竭……之后我们会得到帮助，或者依靠自己重新站起来。在与服务中固有的挑战和挫折作斗争的过程中，我们会找到良言、多种方法和诸多支持。我们分享的这种方法只是其中之一，可以根据具体需要，结合其他合适的方法一起使用。

The steps we have sought to emphasize, however, should become something more than corrective medicine, as useful as that is. They should embody health itself. We can do more than simply struggle to stay afloat; we can discover a more reliable source of continuous buoyancy. We can do more than cope. We can see now that burnout need not always be an enemy. If not a best friend, it can at least be a catalyst, even a guide, for the inner work, the work on ourselves, which is the foundation of all true service, and the only way, finally, to maintain energy and inspiration. If we can view the places where we encounter fatigue and doubt as clues and signposts for that inner work, our journey will not only go more lightly but go further, deeper. We will not simply survive. We will grow.

然而，我们所强调的这些步骤，不应仅仅局限于矫正疗法（尽管矫正疗法也很有用）。它们应该体现健康本身。我们不仅可以挣扎求生，还可以找到更可靠的持续动力源泉。我们可以超越应对。我们现在明白，倦怠并非总是敌人。即便它不是最好的朋友，至少也可以成为内在修行的催化剂，甚至是指引。内在修行是所有真正服务的基础，也是最终保持活力和灵感的唯一途径。如果我们能将疲惫和怀疑的时刻视为内在修行的线索和路标，我们的旅程不仅会更加轻松，而且会更加深入、更加远。我们不再只是勉强生存，而是会不断成长。

Meanwhile, it will always serve to stay grounded in humble respect for all that is involved in the work to relieve suffering—a compassion for ourselves which is the source of compassion for all others. Whatever helpful hints for support and freedom we come upon must be tested against daily practice. We will slip and fall again and again. The struggle between heart and mind is fierce and continuous. The need to see suffering relieved is an essential ingredient of our humanity. Inevitably, we will feel the poignance and despair that arise on those occasions when affliction is not eased; indeed, it grows and spreads, cruel and ominous, despite all our efforts. The pain of the world will sear and break our hearts because we can no longer keep them closed. We’ve seen too much now. To some degree or other, we have surrendered into service and are willing to pay the price of compassion.

与此同时，我们始终要谦逊地尊重所有参与减轻苦难的人们——这种对自身的慈悲，正是对他人慈悲的源泉。我们所获得的任何有益的帮助和自由的指引，都必须经受日常实践的检验。我们会一次又一次地跌倒。心与脑之间的斗争激烈而持续。渴望看到苦难得到减轻，是我们人性中不可或缺的组成部分。不可避免地，当苦难无法减轻时，我们会感受到随之而来的痛苦和绝望；事实上，尽管我们竭尽全力，苦难却愈演愈烈，残酷而可怕。世间的苦难会灼伤我们的心，让我们心碎，因为我们再也无法紧闭心扉。我们已经目睹了太多。在某种程度上，我们已经投身于服务，并愿意为慈悲付出代价。

But with it comes the joy of a single, caring act. With it comes the honor of participating in a generous process in which one rises each day and does what one can. With it comes the simple, singular grace of being an instrument of Love, in whatever form, to whatever end.

但随之而来的是一次充满关爱的行动所带来的喜悦。随之而来的是参与慷慨奉献的荣耀，每天起身尽己所能。随之而来的是成为爱的工具的简单而独特的恩典，无论以何种形式，无论最终目的如何。

~

We had just finished a six-week study tour of Kenya’s major game parks, but our American college group had in many ways passed over what was most important to us: the people. So a friend and I set out on our own, feeling our way along the less-traveled roads for the pulse-points—the individual lives and feelings of the Kenyan people. Our trek took us to the small town of Kitale, and while resting our packs near the local market, a man simply walked up to us and introduced himself as Pastor Joseph .

我们刚刚结束了为期六周的肯尼亚主要野生动物保护区考察之旅，但我们这个美国大学团队在很多方面都忽略了对我们来说最重要的东西：人。于是，我和一位朋友决定独自出发，沿着人迹罕至的小路，去探寻肯尼亚的脉搏——感受肯尼亚人民的个人生活和情感。我们的徒步之旅将我们带到了基塔莱小镇，当我们在当地市场附近休息时，一位男士径直走到我们面前，自我介绍说他叫约瑟夫牧师。

Pastor Joseph, we discovered, was a Christian minister working in an area two hundred miles north of Kitale, where a drought had incarcerated the land and its people for three years. Pastor Joseph had collected some five hundred children who were entirely dependent upon him for their sustenance and shelter. We traveled with Joseph up into the drought area, to help him and to learn more about his work. Although we spent five days with him, a few moments tell the story .

我们发现，约瑟夫牧师是一位基督教牧师，在基塔莱以北两百英里处的一个地区工作。那里的土地和人民已经遭受了三年的旱灾。约瑟夫牧师收容了大约五百名儿童，他们的生活和住所完全依赖于他。我们跟随约瑟夫牧师前往旱灾地区，帮助他并更多地了解他的工作。虽然我们和他相处了五天，但几个片段足以说明一切。

We first approached Joseph’s church around noon, after a two-day journey. Except for the children who scurried barefoot beside us on the scorching sand, the feeling surrounding us was of helpless isolation. It was a forgotten place—a vast, almost soundless plain. Thin, brown-skinned inhabitants moved like mirages on the baked white earth of this desert .

经过两天的跋涉，我们大约在中午时分抵达了约瑟的教堂。除了几个赤脚在我们身旁、在滚烫的沙地上奔跑的孩子之外，我们周围弥漫着一种无助的孤寂感。这里仿佛被人遗忘——一片广袤无垠、寂静无声的平原。瘦削的、皮肤黝黑的居民如同海市蜃楼般，在这片炙热的白色沙漠中穿行。

My friend and I were exhausted, but Pastor Joseph beamed as though a two-hundred-mile trek in a crowded, overheating lorry was routine. (It was, I found out later.) He stopped in front of a peeling, green cement-block structure. Squinting, we saw a small wooden cross peeking up above one edge of the warped tin roof. “This is my church!” exclaimed Joseph with irrepressible reverence. His sincerity made us feel ashamed not to see this homely clay form—a structure he found when first coming here—in quite the same way he did .

我和朋友都筋疲力尽，但约瑟夫牧师却容光焕发，仿佛乘坐拥挤闷热的卡车跋涉两百英里是家常便饭。（后来我才知道，的确如此。）他把车停在一座斑驳的绿色水泥砖房前。我们眯起眼睛，看到一个小小的木制十字架从扭曲的铁皮屋顶边缘探出头来。“这是我的教堂！”约瑟夫带着难以抑制的敬畏之情喊道。他的真诚让我们感到惭愧，因为我们没有像他一样，以同样的眼光看待这座简陋的泥土建筑——他初来此地时发现的。

However, the “churchness” of that small, ingenuous structure became more apparent during our stay with Joseph, as did the enormity of his single-handed labor to look after the orphans of a starved, destitute tribe. We watched the sandy, famished faces of the children who stood outside the “church’s” kitchen to receive their daily cups of maize. The same children stood inside it early Sunday morning, singing. Nothing I had ever seen looked less but felt more like a church. Two hundred Turkana tribespeople were packed, naked or half-clothed, on pews made of tattered scraps of wood set on desert stones. Pastor Joseph stood among them, leading the clapping and singing of strong, rhythmical hymns .

然而，在我们与约瑟夫相处的这段时间里，这座简陋小建筑的“教堂”氛围愈发明显，他独自一人照顾一个饥饿贫困部落的孤儿所付出的巨大努力也让我们深感震撼。我们看到孩子们站在“教堂”厨房外，脸上满是沙砾，饥肠辘辘，等待着每天的玉米粥。而到了星期天清晨，同样的孩子们又站在厨房里，唱着歌。我从未见过如此不像教堂，却又如此充满教堂氛围的地方。两百名图尔卡纳部落的村民，有的赤身裸体，有的衣衫褴褛，挤在用破旧木头拼成的长椅上，这些长椅摆放在沙漠的石头上。约瑟夫牧师站在他们中间，带领大家拍手歌唱，唱着铿锵有力、节奏鲜明的赞美诗。

My friend and I, two strangers from across the sea, were welcomed into the church by all. As I reached down to touch the children’s outstretched hands, I found that each child took a finger, then passed it along for a friend to hold. There was no fighting for my two hands, but, rather, a tacit understanding that ten fingers would, in time, be shared by all. We saw this same principle expressed by the children in many ways. For example, as the children were waiting for their cups of maize after the service, the cook brought out a crust of bread for one of the smallest, neediest children. He immediately looked for his friends, then began to break it in fragments to share with them. Seeing these children—experiencing them—I asked Joseph what he wanted most of all to do for them. A great smile lit up his face as he replied, “To give and to give and to give, and to know that is my riches.” He strode out in the desert, explaining his work to me. “I came here three years ago when the drought began.” Pausing, he pulled from his pocket several folded notebook pages of children’s names. “I have collected these children from all parts of Turkanaland. Their parents have died or are too weak to care for them. I walk out in the desert each day to search for children; ten, twenty, or thirty miles in a day. When I find a child who needs my help, I carry him over there.” He motioned to a circular fence made of thorny acacia branches. “The children sleep within the fence when I bring them from the desert. I have Wanted to build the children a shelter for a long while. But I find enough money only for food.”

我和我的朋友，两个来自海外的陌生人，受到了教堂所有人的热情欢迎。当我俯身去触摸孩子们伸出的手时，我发现每个孩子都先伸出一根手指，然后传递给另一个朋友。孩子们并没有争抢我的双手，而是心照不宣地明白，总有一天，十根手指会轮流被大家握住。我们看到孩子们以各种方式表达了同样的理念。例如，礼拜结束后，孩子们在等待玉米粥的时候，厨师拿出一块面包皮，给一个个头最小、最需要帮助的孩子。他立刻找到他的朋友们，然后掰成小块分给他们。看到这些孩子——感受到他们的存在——我问约瑟夫，他最想为他们做什么。他脸上绽放出灿烂的笑容，回答说：“给予，给予，再给予，我知道这就是我的财富。”说完，他大步走到沙漠里，向我解释他的工作。“三年前，旱灾刚开始的时候，我就来到这里了。”他停顿了一下，从口袋里掏出几页折叠好的笔记本，上面写着孩子们的名字。“这些孩子是我从图尔卡纳兰各地收集来的。他们的父母要么去世了，要么虚弱得无力照顾他们。我每天都要到沙漠里走十英里、二十英里甚至三十英里去寻找这些孩子。当我找到需要帮助的孩子时，我就把他带到这里来。”他指着一个用带刺的相思树枝围成的圆形栅栏。“孩子们从沙漠里被我带回来后，就睡在这个栅栏里。我一直想给孩子们建一个住所，但我只能找到足够的钱来买食物。”

I listened to Joseph while drawing the last of my water from a half-gallon pouch. When I offered him a swallow, he smiled but refused. We had been walking under the desert sun for only an hour but already I was feeling weak. He glanced at my friend and me, sensing our condition, then led us to a shade tree as he continued describing his work. “When I go into the desert, I take nothing with me. I know that God is with me. I am going out to find His children, and I know that He comes with me.”

我一边听约瑟讲述，一边从半加仑的水袋里舀出最后一点水。我递给他一口，他笑了笑，却婉拒了。我们在沙漠的烈日下走了才一个小时，我就已经感到虚弱。他看了看我和我的朋友，似乎察觉到了我们的状况，然后领着我们走到一棵树荫下，继续讲述他的工作。“我进沙漠的时候，什么也不带。我知道上帝与我同在。我出去是为了寻找祂的孩子们，我知道祂会与我同行。”

With a simplicity, yet a spiritual toughness which has known and endured great suffering, Joseph told us of several long searches in the desert when he existed for days on edible desert plants and water sucked from their roots. Bowing his head, he added, “These are God’s children I am seeking!”

约瑟以一种朴实无华却又坚韧不拔的精神，讲述了他经历过无数苦难后，在沙漠中多次漫长的寻觅之旅。他曾靠着沙漠中可食用的植物和从根部吸取的水分，连续数日生存。他低下头，说道：“我寻找的，正是上帝的儿女！”

The next day, we sat with Joseph in a corner of his church to do something we all knew was needed: pray. In the background, children sniffled, laughed, and cried—like punctuation marks between our prayers. We rarely spoke. When we lifted our heads and looked into one another’s eyes, it was to affirm a strength growing in us all: the realization that indeed, our prayers were being heard, and that it was natural for them to be heard. We found ourselves in that incredible condition of trusting God, of sensing that there is a higher law to appeal to—and that it was available to all of us .

第二天，我们和约瑟坐在教堂的一个角落里，做一件我们都知道必须做的事：祷告。孩子们在背景里抽泣、欢笑、哭泣——就像我们祷告之间的标点符号。我们很少说话。当我们抬起头，彼此对视时，是为了肯定我们内心正在增长的一种力量：我们意识到，我们的祷告确实被听到了，而且这是理所当然的。我们发现自己处于一种难以置信的状态，那就是信赖上帝，感受到有一种更高的法则可以诉诸——而且这种法则对我们所有人都是适用的。

That afternoon it began to rain. For half an hour, rains poured down on the hard, white earth. The children huddled inside the door of the church and sat silent, watching it. I expected shouts of joy. But, instead, I heard an utter silence—the sound of reverence. Both Joseph and the children were perfectly quiet until the rain stopped. He bowed his head and told me, “This is the hardest rain they have seen in three years. They have seen their parents die because of the drought. What else can they do now but be still and watch?”

那天下午开始下雨。雨水倾盆而下，持续了半个小时，落在坚硬的白色土地上。孩子们挤在教堂门口，静静地坐着，看着雨水落下。我本以为会听到欢呼声，但却听到一片寂静——那是敬畏的声音。约瑟和孩子们都一动不动，直到雨停。他低下头告诉我：“这是他们三年来见过的最大一场雨。他们亲眼目睹父母因旱灾而死。现在除了静静地看着，他们还能做什么呢？”

On our last night in Turkanaland we were served a supper by Joseph’s friends, and told that he would return much later. We had spent the day with children at the church, and watched Joseph disappear at noon, carrying a coughing child across the desert .

在图尔卡纳兰的最后一晚，约瑟的朋友们为我们准备了晚餐，并告诉我们他要很久以后才会回来。那天我们和孩子们在教堂里度过了一天，中午时分，我们眼睁睁地看着约瑟抱着一个咳嗽的孩子穿过沙漠，消失在了夜色中。

One small candle flame flickered across Joseph’s face as he walked into the church late that night, carrying the same child, now asleep in his arms. He gently laid the little one inside the door and came to sit beside us. Closing his eyes, he sat quietly for several moments until his breathing became easier. He looked utterly exhausted. He whispered, “There is no tomorrow here. There is only today and what God asks me to do today.” We listened quietly as his voice grew. “Today I found a child who needed to be taken for special care to a place seven miles away. So I took the child there. But when I arrived, I found that two of the children I had carried there a few days before had died.” His voice maintained its level. “So I will dig their graves tomorrow. And I am grateful to God that I can do that for these people.”

那天深夜，约瑟抱着睡着的孩子走进教堂，一簇小小的烛光掠过他的脸庞。他轻轻地把孩子放在门内，然后走到我们身边坐下。他闭上眼睛，静静地坐了一会儿，直到呼吸渐渐平稳。他看起来筋疲力尽。他低声说道：“这里没有明天，只有今天，以及上帝今天让我做的事。”我们静静地听着，他的声音渐渐高了起来。“今天我发现一个孩子需要被送到七英里外的地方接受特殊照顾。所以我把孩子送到了那里。但是当我到达时，我发现几天前我带去的两个孩子已经去世了。”他的声音依然平静。“所以我明天要挖他们的坟墓。我感谢上帝，让我能为这些人做这件事。”

Joseph’s words hung in silence for a long while. They so overwhelmed me. I couldn’t utter a word. I remember just bowing my head .

约瑟的话语在空气中凝固了许久，让我感到无比震撼。我一句话也说不出来，只记得自己低下了头。

~

8
8
Reprise: Walking
重奏：步行
Each Other Home
彼此回家

W hat is it that so touches us about a single caring act or a life surrendered into service? Perhaps we see our deepest yearnings reflected in others, and this encourages us to believe in our own purity and beauty. These are no longer just ideals to strive for. We can reach them, we can be that way. Images of compassion beckon and encourage us onward.

是什么让我们如此被一个充满关爱的举动或一个奉献一生的行为所深深打动？或许，我们在他人身上看到了自己内心深处的渴望，这鼓励我们相信自身的纯洁和美好。这些不再仅仅是需要努力追求的理想，我们可以达到，我们可以成为那样的人。慈悲的形象召唤着我们，激励着我们继续前行。

~

I went to Nicaragua as a Maryknoll missioner in 1971, before the big earthquake, and before the revolution. I had every expectation and notion about helping people you could imagine. It would bore you to tears to list them—and you’d probably understand every one .

1971年，在尼加拉瓜大地震和革命爆发之前，我以玛利诺会传教士的身份去了那里。我对帮助当地人民充满了各种各样的期望和想法。一一列举出来，恐怕你会觉得无聊透顶——而且你大概也能理解我的每一个想法。

I walked into this barrio, with three hundred people, an old cotton farm, incredibly hot and barren, three trees near an old hacienda, then miles of nothing but small bushes. The idea was to help build it up from there, make room for others. I’d be part of that effort, and part of those people .

我走进这个只有三百人的贫民窟，一个废弃的棉花农场，酷热难耐，寸草不生，一座老庄园附近只有三棵树，再往前就是绵延数英里的矮灌木丛。我的想法是从这里开始建设，为其他人腾出空间。我将成为这项事业的一份子，也将成为这里的一份子。

It wasn’t too long before I realized I was signing up for the course: Life 101. First assignment: the horror of poverty, which until then was something I’d only known about from the eyebrows up. No running water, no electricity, malnutrition, disease. People lived in big one-room houses made from materials we’d throw away in the States. We had to haul water from miles away. Dirty water was kept in a hole in the ground where it could be saved to keep the dust down or wash the patio. It took me a while to tell the difference between a clean dirt floor and a dirty dirt floor .

没过多久，我就意识到自己报名参加了一门课程：人生入门课。第一课：贫困的恐怖，在此之前，我对贫困的了解仅限于皮毛。没有自来水，没有电，营养不良，疾病肆虐。人们住在用我们在美国会扔掉的材料搭建的简陋单间小屋里。我们得从几英里外运水过来。脏水被储存在地上的一个坑里，用来抑制扬尘或冲洗庭院。我花了很长时间才分辨出干净的泥土地面和脏的泥土地面的区别。

But people rarely complained. Not that they were saints and martyrs, but the grumbling was always in a here-we-are-let’s-make-the-best-of-it manner. There was just this moment-to-moment quality to their life. First lesson for me: you do what’s in front of you, you start where you are .

但人们很少抱怨。倒不是说他们是圣人或殉道者，而是他们的抱怨总是带着一种“既然身处此境，那就尽力而为”的态度。他们的生活就是如此，活在当下。我学到的第一课就是：做好眼前的事，从你所在的地方开始。

Second lesson: Who do you think you are, anyway? Because you go in and you’re going to help someone, and then all of a sudden you see they’re a lot stronger than you are in certain very important ways. And how they’re acting has to do with who they are, especially down there. Who they are is all they have—no possessions, no property, very little to protect .

第二课：你到底以为自己是谁？因为你进去是为了帮助别人，结果突然发现他们在某些非常重要的方面比你强大得多。他们的行为方式与他们的身份息息相关，尤其是在那种境地。他们拥有的只有身份——没有财产，没有家产，几乎没有什么需要保护的。

So I go into someone’s hut for the first time, wondering how they could live under such conditions, and I’m embraced by this lovely woman who gives me her only chair and spends three hours talking, and when am I coming back? I cannot believe her liveliness and purity of heart, and she awakens me to my own. So I see that service is beauty .

于是，我第一次走进别人的茅屋，心中疑惑他们如何在这样的条件下生活。一位和蔼可亲的妇人热情地拥抱了我，把她唯一的椅子让给我，和我聊了三个小时，还问我什么时候再来。她的活力和纯洁的心灵让我难以置信，她也唤醒了我内心深处的善良。我这才明白，服务本身就是一种美。

Or a kid comes by and asks to dust our car. We see him later, peering in the window as we’re preparing our main meal. So we invite him in, as payment, and pile his plate high, and he’s eating like there’s no tomorrow. And then he suddenly hears some other kids outside, and he catches himself and takes the food out to them. And I’m blown away. I see that service is remembering .

或者有个孩子过来，问我们能不能帮他擦擦车上的灰尘。后来我们准备正餐的时候，看到他正从窗户往里看。于是我们邀请他进来，算是给他“报酬”，给他盛了满满一盘，他狼吞虎咽地吃着，好像明天就是世界末日似的。突然，他听到外面还有其他孩子，这才意识到自己吃得太饱，赶紧把食物端出去给他们吃。我当时真是感动极了。我这才明白，服务的意义在于记住每一个人。

Or I’d feel uncomfortable about the comfort of our own house; nothing special, but we have beds, not the boards they slept on, and some semblance of privacy, like they’d never known. But they’d come in—“Isn’t this beautiful? Oh, it’s so nice”—without the slightest envy, without anything but appreciation on our behalf. And I see that service is gratitude .

或者我会因为我们家的舒适而感到不自在；虽然没什么特别的，但我们有床，而不是他们睡的木板，而且我们还有一些隐私，这是他们从未体验过的。但他们进来后会说：“这里真漂亮！哦，真好！”——没有一丝嫉妒，只有对我们的感激。我这才明白，服务就是感恩。

Or that service is truth and honesty. Because part of me is romanticizing all this a little. I have to accept that and listen to who I am and be myself all along the way. Because we’re all taking the course, right? But we have different assignments. And so finding common ground helps. Gossip and small talk are important. To sit on a patio in the evening and talk about nothing and say everything. Service is chitchat .

或者说，服务就是真诚和坦率。因为我内心深处有点美化这一切。我必须接受这一点，倾听内心的声音，始终做我自己。因为我们都在经历同样的人生旅程，对吧？但我们的任务各不相同。所以找到共同点很有帮助。闲聊和闲谈也很重要。晚上坐在露台上，漫无目的地闲聊，却又无话不谈。服务就是闲聊。

And service is death, too. You die in service, and you die into service .

服役也意味着死亡。你会在服役中死去，也会为了服役而牺牲。

They told us the insurrection was to begin a day or two beforehand. Someone came by: “The revolution is going to start tomorrow. What are you going to do?” And in our case, we were ready. At that point, if you weren’t for Somoza, you were supporting the Sandinistas. We’d opted for them because from what we’d seen over the years, the signs of the kingdom were more likely to be realized: fraternity, justice, help for the overwhelming majority of the poor. And we’d prepared, and organized civil-defense support, and had the chance to learn how to handle a gun, although I didn’t feel that was being asked of me .

他们提前一两天告诉我们起义就要开始了。有人过来问：“革命明天就要开始了，你们打算怎么办？” 而我们，已经做好了准备。那时候，如果你不支持索摩查，那就只能支持桑地诺民族解放阵线。我们选择了他们，因为这些年来我们所看到的，王国的种种迹象更有可能在他们身上实现：博爱、正义、帮助绝大多数穷人。我们做好了准备，组织了民防支援，还有机会学习如何使用枪支，虽然我觉得没人要求我这么做。

That evening we had to notify the fathers and the sisters, and we buzzed off in our Jeep to see the Franciscans. At about six o’clock, we heard homemade bombs go off, and machine guns, and heavy fire. We hit the floor in this flimsy asbestos house. Here it was .

那天晚上我们得通知神父和修女们，然后就开着吉普车飞奔去见方济各会修士。大约六点钟，我们听到自制炸弹爆炸声、机枪声和猛烈的炮火声。我们赶紧趴在地上，躲进了这间简陋的石棉房里。就是这里。

An hour later, someone from the Sandinistas rushed in: “Come quick, we have a wounded compañero!” It was Armando, shot in the arm—not someone we knew from church, but we knew he was a leader. He was lying there, bleeding in the road. I began to panic. I’d never seen blood before. But my friend, another sister, told me to squat down and hold his arm and she’d go get medicine .

一个小时后，一个桑地诺游击队员冲了进来：“快来，我们有个同志受伤了！”是阿曼多，他手臂中弹了——我们虽然不认识他，但知道他是个领袖。他躺在路边，鲜血直流。我开始慌了。我以前从没见过血。但我的朋友，也是我的姐妹，让我蹲下按住他的胳膊，说她去拿药。

All of a sudden—“There’s a car coming!” National Guard or Sandinista? Everyone else dived behind this pathetic asbestos wall. Armando and I were there in the road, looking at each other. One of those moments: “Okay, here we are. What am I going to do?”

突然——“有车来了！”是国民警卫队还是桑地诺？其他人都躲到了那堵可怜的石棉墙后面。我和阿曼多站在路中间，面面相觑。那一刻，我们茫然地想：“好吧，我们到这儿了。我该怎么办？”

I’m thinking, “How’d I get here?” and “Where’s Julianne?” and “Who the hell is in that car?” and “MOM!” And finally, “Well, if I’m with them and they’re willing to die, I guess it’s all right, and I’ll be willing too. Just don’t tell my mother.” The car drove up. It was friendly. And as he was being bandaged up, Armando and I looked at each other for a quiet second—a kind of acknowledgment—and that was that. He started giving orders again. Then the madness took over .

我当时想着：“我怎么会到这儿来的？”“朱莉安娜在哪儿？”“车里到底是谁？”“妈！”最后，我想：“好吧，如果我和他们在一起，他们也愿意去死，我想这也没什么，我也愿意。只是别告诉我妈。”车开了过来。车里的人很友好。当他被包扎的时候，我和阿曼多静静地对视了一秒——一种心照不宣的默契——然后就没了。他又开始发号施令了。然后，疯狂彻底占据了他的心神。

People came through all night. They brought in kids who died. I’d never seen death before. Their friends would stand around, not knowing what to do. One boy died in my arms. They brought him in all covered with blood. I knew his face but not his name. He was still breathing. But when I lifted him up on a table, he gasped three times and shuddered and gave up the ghost. On the last breath, he really let go. He was so young—soft hands. Nobody knew his name. It was a very sad moment, a still moment. And that was very good for me—very deep, but very, very sad .

整夜都有人来来往往。他们抬着死去的孩子。我以前从未见过死亡。他们的朋友围在一旁，不知所措。一个男孩死在了我的怀里。他们把他抬进来时，他浑身是血。我认得他的脸，却不知道他的名字。他当时还有呼吸。但当我把他抱到桌子上时，他喘了三下气，浑身颤抖，然后就断气了。最后一口气，他彻底地离开了人世。他那么年轻——手很嫩。没有人知道他的名字。那是一个非常悲伤的时刻，一个静谧的时刻。这对我来说意义非凡——非常深刻，但也非常非常悲伤。

Then the fighting started to get heavy again. Everyone went down on the floor. The kids were so frightened, saying prayers and crying. The body was on the floor. But nobody wanted it discovered on their property; it could get them in trouble with the Guard. So he was thrown into a hole, with just a shroud over him. And I thought, “He died of such violence—couldn’t he even get buried?” And I felt all his innocence, and the meaning of his death, and the cost of freedom, and the horror of war. And I thought, “God is supposed to call everyone by his true name. So what’s his name?” And you find yourself saying the Our Father and shaking your fist at the sky at the same moment. And then you’re done with that. And you bandage wounds because there’s nothing else to do. That’s the dying into service .

然后战斗再次变得激烈起来。所有人都倒在了地上。孩子们吓坏了，一边祈祷一边哭泣。尸体躺在地上。但谁也不想让尸体在自家地盘上被发现；这可能会让他们惹上卫兵的麻烦。于是，他被扔进了一个坑里，只盖了一块裹尸布。我想：“他死得如此惨烈——难道连个安葬的地方都没有吗？”我感受到了他的纯真，他死亡的意义，自由的代价，以及战争的恐怖。我想：“上帝应该会用他的真名呼唤每个人。那么，他的名字是什么？”你会发现自己同时念着《天主经》，同时向天空挥舞着拳头。然后，一切都结束了。你只能包扎伤口，因为除此之外别无他事可做。这就是为服务而死。

So what was his name? Who was he? Who were they all? Well, they were people who were allowing me to be there with them. They were sharing life and death and hope with me. And they were sharing faith. And they were sharing that they didn’t know what to do with it all any more than I did. And they were helping bring me an experience of God too, a God who works through people. Because I was seeing “No greater love hath a man than to lay down his life for a friend.” I saw that. I saw that happen .

那么他叫什么名字？他是谁？他们都是谁？嗯，他们是允许我和他们在一起的人。他们与我分享生死和希望。他们分享信仰。他们也坦诚地告诉我，他们和我一样，对这一切也茫然不知所措。他们也帮助我体验到上帝的存在，一位通过人来行事的上帝。因为我看到了“人为朋友舍命，人的爱心没有比这更大的了”。我亲眼目睹了这一切。我亲眼见证了这一切的发生。

So you say you’re going to be with people and you’re going to help. But what does that really mean? It turns out to be an endless series of questions. What do I really hold to be the truth of my life? What do I have to give, and what am I called on to give? How am I a part of human history and great moments of change? Who am I? And where is God in all this?

你说你要陪伴他人，你要帮助他人。但这究竟意味着什么？结果却引出一连串无休止的问题。我真正信奉的人生真谛是什么？我能付出什么？我又被召唤去付出什么？我如何参与人类历史和那些伟大的变革时刻？我是谁？而上帝在这一切中又扮演着怎样的角色？

That’s who he was, that boy; that’s who they all were. They were those questions. Part of me has become those questions. We are questions for one another. And service is exploring them and awakening through them .

那个男孩就是这样，他们所有人都是这样。他们就是那些问题。我的一部分也变成了那些问题。我们彼此都是问题。而服务，就是探索这些问题，并从中觉醒。

How do I measure what it means to have been given all that?

我该如何衡量拥有这一切的意义？

~

So service is “an endless series of questions,” puzzling and insistent. It not only raises questions, it helps to answer them. Service is a curriculum.

所以，服务是“一系列永无止境的问题”，既令人困惑又令人执着。它不仅提出问题，也有助于解答问题。服务本身就是一门课程。

In this curriculum, we encounter our own limitations—a number of which we have met in the course of this book. We have seen, for example, how our ego can lock us into narrow self-images, leaving us tentative and hesitant to reach out. Our resistance to pain can lead us to insulate ourselves from suffering. When our hearts do open in empathy, all too often we close down quickly, frightened by the intensity of our feelings; we substitute denial, pity, or other defense mechanisms for the spontaneous response of the heart. Frequently, we find ourselves so identified with our own needs that we tend to treat others as objects to be manipulated toward our own ends. We see how the restlessness of our minds can hinder our ability to listen; we find ourselves at least one thought away from someone else. And when we try to help through social action, we often so identify an opponent as an enemy that we remain locked in a cycle of recrimination. Meanwhile, as the toxicity of these and other hindrances builds up, we begin to wear down. We burn out. Helping starts to hurt.

在本课程中，我们会遇到自身的局限性——其中一些我们已经在本书中有所提及。例如，我们看到，自我如何将我们禁锢在狭隘的自我认知中，使我们犹豫不决，不敢与人交流。我们对痛苦的抗拒会让我们把自己与苦难隔绝开来。当我们敞开心扉，产生同理心时，我们往往会因为感受的强烈而迅速封闭自己；我们用否认、怜悯或其他防御机制来代替内心的自然反应。我们常常发现自己过于执着于自身的需求，以至于倾向于将他人视为可以操纵以达到自身目的的工具。我们看到，我们躁动不安的思绪会阻碍我们倾听的能力；我们发现自己与他人之间至少隔着一个念头。当我们试图通过社会行动提供帮助时，我们常常将反对者视为敌人，从而陷入相互指责的恶性循环。与此同时，随着这些以及其他障碍的毒性不断累积，我们开始精疲力竭，最终走向崩溃。帮助别人反而会让自己受伤。

But the curriculum of service provides us with information about our strengths as well, and we discover how these contribute to genuinely help-full service. Each time we drop our masks and meet heart-to-heart, reassuring one another simply by the quality of our presence, we experience a profound bond which we intuitively understand is nourishing everyone. Each time we quiet our mind, our listening becomes sharp and clear, deep and perceptive; we realize that we know more than we thought we knew, and can reach out and hear, as if from inside, the heart of someone’s pain. Each time we are able to remain open to suffering, despite our fear and defensiveness, we sense a love in us which becomes increasingly unconditional.

但服务课程也让我们了解自身的优势，并发现这些优势如何促成真正有益的服务。每当我们卸下伪装，敞开心扉地交流，仅仅凭借彼此的存在就给予对方安慰时，我们都会体验到一种深刻的联结，我们凭直觉就能感受到这种联结在滋养着每一个人。每当我们静下心来，我们的聆听就会变得敏锐、清晰、深刻而富有洞察力；我们意识到自己懂得比想象中更多，能够触及他人内心深处的痛苦。每当我们能够克服恐惧和防御，依然敞开心扉去面对苦难时，我们都会感受到一种日益无条件的爱。

As we close our inquiry into service, then, we can see in this mosaic of limitations and strength a still deeper teaching. Common to all those habits which hinder us is a sense of separateness; we are divided within ourselves and cut off from others. Common to all those moments and actions which truly seem to help, however, is the experience of unity; the mind and the heart work in harmony, and barriers between us dissolve.

因此，当我们结束对服务的探究时，我们可以在这幅由局限与力量交织而成的图景中看到更深层次的教诲。所有阻碍我们的习惯都源于一种分离感；我们内心分裂，与他人隔绝。然而，所有真正有益的时刻和行动都源于一种合一的体验；心智与情感和谐运作，彼此间的隔阂消融。

Separateness and unity. How interesting that these root causes, revealed in the experience of helping, turn out to be what most spiritual traditions define as the fundamental issue of life itself. Awakening from our sense of separateness is what we are called to do in all things, not merely in service. Whether these traditions speak of us as being cut off from God, Nature, Original Mind, True Being, the Tao, the Dharma—they call on us, in one voice, to undertake the journey back to unity.

分离与合一。多么奇妙，这些在助人经历中揭示的根本原因，竟与大多数灵性传统所定义的生命本身的根本问题不谋而合。我们被召唤去从分离感中觉醒，这不仅体现在服务他人，更体现在所有方面。无论这些传统如何描述我们与神、自然、本我、真我、道、法的隔绝——它们都以同样的呼唤，召唤我们踏上回归合一的旅程。

Service, from this perspective, is part of that journey. It is no longer an end in itself. It is a vehicle through which we reach a deeper understanding of life. Each step we take, each moment in which we grow toward a greater understanding of unity, steadily transforms us into instruments of that help which truly heals.

从这个角度来看，服务是这段旅程的一部分。它不再是目的本身，而是我们通往更深层次生命理解的途径。我们迈出的每一步，我们朝着更深刻的合一理解不断成长的每一个瞬间，都在稳步地将我们转化为真正疗愈的助人工具。

Service not only reveals a larger vision of life, but steadily moves us along and supports us in our efforts to realize this vision. Each time we seek to respond to appeals for help we are being shown where we must grow in our sense of unity and what inner resources we can call upon to do so. We are constantly given, for example, the chance to experience the inherent generosity of our heart. Each time this happens, our faith in that part of ourselves which is intimately related to the rest of the universe is strengthened. So, too, approaching each act of caring with a desire to grow, we also meet our fears and resistances—but with the opportunity to see them for what they are, and, in so doing, to loosen their hold and ultimately to relinquish them. On the path of service, then, we are constantly given feedback which helps us along the greater journey of awakening .

服务不仅展现了更宏大的人生视野，更稳步地推动我们前进，支持我们实现这一愿景。每当我们回应求助时，我们都在被指引着如何在自我认知中提升，以及我们可以调动哪些内在资源来实现这一目标。例如，我们不断有机会体验到内心固有的慷慨。每一次这样的体验，都会增强我们对自身与宇宙万物紧密相连的那部分力量的信念。同样，当我们怀着成长的渴望去对待每一次关怀时，我们也会直面自身的恐惧和抗拒——但我们有机会看清它们的本质，从而放松它们的束缚，最终放下它们。因此，在服务的道路上，我们不断获得反馈，这些反馈将帮助我们踏上觉醒的伟大旅程。

All the methods we have discussed throughout the book support us in this effort. They are, it turns out, more than helpful hints to improve the quality of service. They are appropriate technology for loosening the hold of separateness and for strengthening our vision of unity.

本书中讨论的所有方法都支持我们实现这一目标。事实证明，它们不仅仅是提升服务质量的实用技巧，更是打破隔阂、强化团结愿景的有效途径。

For example, we may start out to quiet the mind simply to hear the needs of others. To do so we learn to identify less with our own thoughts. Listening more, judging less, then, there is less divisiveness in our awareness. As we loosen our identification with personal motives and models of self, meanwhile, our awareness becomes more panoramic and inclusive; we’re freer to take in more and more. Under these conditions, in turn, all our mental faculties can come into play as needed—memory, training, logic and analysis, intuition, wisdom. Unexpected connections become apparent. We may recognize deeper patterns in the events which are unfolding. As we continue, we may even begin to gain insight into a larger order of lawfulness we cannot understand rationally but which nevertheless resonates within. We come to sense the Way of Things (Tao) of which our actions are but a part. The hold of separateness is thus being broken at its source, in our own mind.

例如，我们最初可能只是为了倾听他人的需求而开始静心。为此，我们学会减少对自身想法的认同。多听少评判，我们的意识中便会减少分裂。随着我们逐渐放下对个人动机和自我模式的认同，我们的意识也变得更加广阔和包容；我们能够更自由地吸收更多。在这种情况下，我们所有的心智能力都能根据需要发挥作用——记忆、训练、逻辑分析、直觉和智慧。意想不到的联系也随之显现。我们或许能够识别出正在发生的事件中更深层次的模式。随着我们不断深入，我们甚至可能开始洞察一种我们无法理性理解却在我们内心产生共鸣的更宏大的法则秩序。我们开始感知万物之道（道），而我们的行为只是其中的一部分。分离的束缚就这样在其源头——我们自身的头脑中——被打破。

These practices open us up to an awareness within ourselves which is itself unitive . Not only do we see and hear more, but our very openness and spaciousness dissolve opposition and discord.

这些练习让我们觉察到自身内在的合一性。我们不仅能看到和听到更多，而且我们自身的开放和包容本身就能消解对立和冲突。

Through these practices, and our efforts to keep our hearts open in the presence of suffering, we find ourselves more available to whoever we are with. Compassion is increasingly an automatic response. We find a deep quality of love infusing our actions with others. The expression of this love, in turn, becomes increasingly our goal, whatever the circumstances. The more unconditionally we share it, the more helpful it is to all.

通过这些修行，以及我们在面对苦难时努力保持内心的开放，我们会发现自己更容易与身边的人相处。慈悲心会逐渐成为一种自然而然的反应。我们会发现，一种深沉的爱会融入我们对待他人的行动中。反过来，无论身处何种境地，表达这份爱都会成为我们越来越追求的目标。我们越是无条件地分享爱，就越能帮助到所有人。

This is the essence of the spiritual path of devotional service. One enters into the helping act not only because there is a need to be met. Service gradually becomes an offering, first to those we are with, but eventually to that greater truth or source of being in which we are all joined in love. Helping becomes an act of reverence, worship, gratitude. It is grace merely to have the chance to serve.

这就是灵性奉献之路的精髓所在。我们参与助人行为，并非仅仅因为有需要需要满足。奉献逐渐演变为一种供养，最初是给予我们身边的人，最终是给予那更伟大的真理或存在的源泉——我们所有人都在爱中与之相连。助人成为一种敬畏、崇拜和感恩的行为。能够有机会服务他人，本身就是一种恩典。

Mother Teresa, for example, bending to hold a dying leper, sees there only “Christ in a distressing disguise.” She’s not “helping a dying leper,” she’s loving God, affirming in whomever she’s with universal qualities of perfection and beauty. One can imagine how it might feel to be held in this spirit during one’s final moments of life.

例如，特蕾莎修女弯腰抱住一位垂死的麻风病人时，看到的只是“披着苦难外衣的基督”。她并非在“帮助垂死的麻风病人”，而是在爱上帝，肯定她所爱之人身上所蕴含的完美与美的普世特质。我们可以想象，在生命的最后时刻，被这种精神所拥抱，会是怎样的感受。

The Hindu deity Hanuman offers a similar example of devotional service. Every act he performs becomes an offering to Rama (God). His service brings him to the very edge of unitive love. How powerful his vision: “When I know who I am, I am you,” he says, kneeling before Rama, “when I don’t know who I am, I serve you.”

印度教神祇哈努曼也展现了类似的虔诚奉献。他所做的每一件事都成为对罗摩（神）的供奉。他的奉献使他达到了与神合一之爱的极致境界。他的愿景多么深刻：“当我明白我是谁时，我就是你，”他跪在罗摩面前说道，“当我迷失自我时，我侍奉你。”

For both of these inspirational figures, and for any of us, the smallest acts of caring—making a sick friend’s bed, filling a bowl on a soup line, welcoming a stranger, comforting a frightened child—can be a means of affirming the greater unity of life in love. As real as this spirit is in us, we have to communicate it to others, in addition to everything else we are doing on their behalf.

对于这两位鼓舞人心的人物，以及我们每个人来说，哪怕是最微小的关怀之举——为生病的朋友铺床、在救济站盛满汤碗、热情地迎接陌生人、安慰受惊的孩子——都能成为彰显生命中爱的伟大统一性的一种方式。这种精神虽然真实存在于我们心中，但除了我们为他人所做的一切之外，我们更应该将它传递给他人。

Placing service in a spiritual perspective in no way diminishes what we have to offer others through training, experience, individuality, special skills, or sense of humor. Quite the reverse. Our particular talents and unique qualities are likely to come forth more reliably when we have a richer and more spacious sense of who we are—the very promise of all spiritual practice.

从灵性的角度看待服务，丝毫不会削弱我们通过训练、经验、个性、特殊技能或幽默感所能给予他人的价值。恰恰相反，当我们对自我有更丰富、更广阔的认知时，我们独特的才能和品质更有可能得到更可靠的展现——这正是所有灵性修行的意义所在。

To the question, “How can I help?” we now see the possibility of a deeper answer than we might once have expected. We can, of course, help through all that we do . But at the deepest level we help through who we are . We help, that is, by appreciating the connection between service and our own progress on the journey of awakening into a fuller sense of unity.

对于“我能如何提供帮助？”这个问题，我们现在看到了一个比我们以往预想的更深刻的答案。当然，我们可以通过我们所做的一切来提供帮助。但在最深层次上，我们通过自身的存在来提供帮助。也就是说，我们通过理解服务与我们自身在觉醒之旅中迈向更完整合一感的过程中所取得的进步之间的联系来提供帮助。

We work on ourselves, then, in order to help others. And we help others as a vehicle for working on ourselves .

因此，我们先提升自我，才能帮助他人；而帮助他人，也是我们提升自我的途径。

In this recognition, we find new freedom and opportunity. External obstacles and old habits—our past experience of service—can now be dealt with in the broader context of our own growth. And each step we take out of the illusion of separateness, we now can see, will inevitably be a blessing to ourselves and all we are with.

在这种认识中，我们找到了新的自由和机遇。外部障碍和旧习——我们过去服务他人的经验——如今都可以放在更广阔的自身成长背景下加以处理。我们现在明白，我们走出分离幻象的每一步，都必然会造福我们自身以及我们所在之处的一切。

In our initial impulse to help out, had we really anticipated so rich a path?

我们最初出于帮助他人的冲动，真的预料到会遇到如此丰厚的回报吗？

As we take to this path, however, we find it neither straight nor smooth. At moments we may become profoundly aware of our oneness with all things. Our sense of possibility expands. Could it be like this more often.… more often than not?

然而，当我们踏上这条道路时，会发现它既不笔直也不平坦。有时，我们会深刻地意识到自己与万物合一。我们对可能性的感知也随之扩展。这样的时刻是否更常出现……更频繁地出现呢？

But then some incident or situation arises and we are thrown back into the pain of separateness once again. At first this must shock us; we thought we were farther along. Yet, after a moment’s pause at the side of the road, a break for a little self-pity and self-recrimination, we have nothing to do but take up the journey once again. Though the road is circuitous, the transformation proceeds inevitably. Gradually we come to sense profound changes in who we are. Our hearts can open and our awareness expand only so far and so often before we must conclude that we are somehow more than we once believed.

然而，总会有一些意外或境况发生，让我们再次陷入分离的痛苦之中。起初，这无疑会让我们感到震惊；我们以为自己已经走得更远了。然而，在路边稍作停留，稍稍自怜自艾、自责一番之后，我们别无选择，只能再次踏上旅程。尽管道路曲折蜿蜒，但转变终究会到来。渐渐地，我们会感受到自身发生的深刻变化。我们的心扉可以敞开，我们的意识可以扩展，但这种扩展终究有限，最终我们不得不承认，我们远比自己曾经认为的更加强大。

How much more? This is for each of us to discover, walking the path at our own pace. The general direction, however, seems clear. Gradually, as our practice continues, the fact of our unity becomes more real and powerful to us than the belief in our separateness .

还有多少？这需要我们每个人自己去发现，按照自己的节奏前行。然而，总体方向似乎很清晰。随着我们不断练习，我们逐渐会发现，我们一体性的事实比我们彼此分离的信念更加真实、更加有力。

We may discover this in the course of ordinary daily work. In a demanding situation we may quietly affirm the fact of unity and suddenly see a breakthrough or insight follow as a result. Or we may come to recognize how our relationship with others has altered; how much more aware we are now of what we have in common than what once seemed to have set us apart.

我们或许会在日常工作中发现这一点。在充满挑战的环境中，我们或许会默默地肯定彼此的团结，并由此突然获得突破或洞见。又或许，我们会意识到自己与他人的关系发生了怎样的变化；我们现在对彼此的共同之处的认识，远比过去那些看似将我们分隔开来的差异要深刻得多。

Or we may experience moments of enlightenment or revelation which defy description. These may be more difficult for us to understand. They may happen instantaneously, and then become less vivid, and fade away. But their impact is such that they are never forgotten, and everything thereafter looks different. In referring to these transcendent moments, some speak of having lost a sense of the individual self altogether, or of having come to see, with undeniable certainty, that who we are is Spirit, beyond form. From such a vantage point, however it is described, separateness is seen to be a creation of mind . All really is One. Such is the testimony, in any case, of what has been “seen.”

或者，我们可能会经历一些难以言喻的顿悟或启示时刻。这些时刻或许更难被我们理解。它们可能瞬间发生，随后变得模糊，最终消逝。但它们的影响如此深远，以至于永难忘怀，此后的一切都变得截然不同。在谈及这些超越的时刻时，有些人说他们完全失去了对个体自我的感知，或者无可辩驳地确信，我们真正的本质是超越形体的灵性。从这样的视角来看，无论如何描述，分离都被视为心智的产物。万物本为一体。无论如何，这就是我们所“看到”的见证。

It is out of these transformative experiences that we find ourselves able to accept a number of seeming paradoxes. We are in the world but not of the world. We are a part of what is formless but we are in form. We exist beyond the polarities of positive and negative, dark and light, good and evil, pleasure and pain, yin and yang; but we function under their cloak as well. Even our perspective on separateness has changed. For while it may indeed be a “delusion of consciousness,” even this delusion seems part of a greater order. It seems to be in the way of things that we develop our initial identification with a separate self and go on to get lost in it. It seems also to be in the way of things that we ultimately come to appreciate this predicament and go on to resolve it. We do so, however, not by returning to an innocence which existed before we felt ourselves to be separate. Rather we grow toward integration, a balance in which we can work within our separateness while resting in the greater unity which lies beyond it.

正是从这些变革性的体验中，我们才能接受许多看似矛盾的事物。我们身处世界，却不属于世界。我们是无形的一部分，却又拥有有形。我们超越了正负、明暗、善恶、苦乐、阴阳等二元对立，却又受其影响。甚至我们对分离的看法也发生了改变。尽管分离或许是一种“意识的错觉”，但即便如此，这种错觉似乎也是更大秩序的一部分。我们最初认同于一个分离的自我，并最终迷失其中，这似乎也是事物发展的必然结果。我们最终领悟到这种困境并找到解决之道，这似乎也是事物发展的必然结果。然而，我们并非回归到感受到自身分离之前的纯真状态，而是走向整合，达到一种平衡，在这种平衡中，我们既能在分离中运作，又能安息于超越分离的更大统一之中。

Separateness is there … to be awakened out of. Service is a perfect vehicle for this awakening.

分离感一直存在……等待着我们去觉醒。服务是实现这种觉醒的完美途径。

We look at our present condition now with great compassion for ourselves and for the work we have taken on. We see the beauty of our humanity in the light of our divinity. From this vision comes a fullness of heart and a profound willingness and eagerness to come to one another’s support.

我们现在以极大的怜悯之心看待自身处境以及我们所承担的工作。我们从神性之光中看到了人性的美好。由此，我们心中充满喜乐，并涌现出彼此扶持的强烈意愿和渴望。

哦，但愿我的祭司袍足够宽大，能将所有受苦的人们都囊括其中。

In this floating world .

在这个浮世绘中。

最终，在这段旅程中，我们自然而然地变得富有同情心，这是我们所见所闻和所理解的自然结果。

Once his brother asked Ryokan to visit his house and speak to his delinquent son. Ryokan came but did not say a word of admonition to the boy. He stayed overnight and prepared to leave the next morning. As the wayward nephew was lacing up Ryokan’s sandals, he felt a drop of warm water. Glancing up, he saw Ryokan looking down at him, his eyes full of tears. Ryokan then returned home, and the nephew changed for the better .

有一次，他的哥哥请良宽去他家，劝劝他那不成器的儿子。良宽来了，却没对那孩子说一句训斥的话。他留宿了一夜，准备第二天早上离开。当那顽劣的侄子正在帮良宽系鞋带时，他感觉到了一滴温水。他抬头一看，只见良宽正低头看着他，眼里噙满了泪水。良宽随后回家了，而那侄子也从此改过自新。

One Rose, One Bowl , J OHN S TEVENS

一朵玫瑰，一个碗，约翰·史蒂文斯

曾经看似工作的事情，现在可以变成一种游戏……一种娱乐……一种快乐地参与生命和形态展开的过程。

I watch these little kindergarten kids, all eager and into their little world, and sometimes they dissolve into little molecules, bounding around, vital and energetic, and the classroom becomes a kind of organism. And it’s so wonderful and comical and so great that, for a moment, I see the whole human condition that way. It’s all like a joyous creation in which the gods and goddesses are taking delight. So why shouldn’t we? And I’ll just plunge into the dance. “Clara, you take the triangle, Margo you have the drum, Stevie has a whistle,” and I pick up the tambourine .

我看着这些幼儿园的小朋友们，个个都兴致勃勃地沉浸在他们的小世界里，有时他们仿佛化作一个个小分子，蹦蹦跳跳，活力四射，整个教室仿佛变成了一个有机体。那景象如此美妙、滑稽、令人惊叹，那一刻，我仿佛看到了整个人类的境况。一切都像是一场充满喜悦的创造，众神都在其中欢欣雀跃。那么，我们为什么不呢？于是，我也要加入这场舞蹈。“克拉拉，你拿三角铁，玛戈，你拿鼓，史蒂维，你拿哨子，”然后我拿起铃鼓。

Sometimes I’ll carry this feeling home with me, and I have it around the house. I feel it at work inside. I’m cleaning up, and calling this friend and that, and dropping in on a person down the hall, and helping them out with whatever. And it’s like the only reason to be here at all is to play. And the fact that this take on things makes me and everyone else feel so good will make me stop for a moment and think, “My God. Maybe it’s true.”

有时候我会把这种感觉带回家，它弥漫在家里的各个角落。在工作中，我也能感受到它的存在。我打扫卫生，给这个朋友打电话，给那个朋友打电话，顺便去走廊尽头拜访一下同事，帮他们做点什么。感觉好像我存在的唯一意义就是享受生活。这种心态让我和周围的人都感觉如此美好，这让我不禁停下来想：“我的天哪，也许这是真的。”
